a.c: A A (named ā in the English, and most commonly ä in other languages). The first letter of the English and of many other alphabets. The capital A of the alphabets of Middle and Western Europe, as also the small letter (a), besides the forms in Italic, black letter, etc., are all descended from the old Latin A, which was borrowed from the Greek Alpha, of the same form; and this was made from the first letter (?) of the Phœnician alphabet, the equivalent of the Hebrew Aleph, and itself from the Egyptian origin. The Aleph was a consonant letter, with a guttural breath sound that was not an element of Greek articulation; and the Greeks took it to represent their vowel Alpha with the ä sound, the Phœnician alphabet having no vowel symbols.

A A (ȧ emph. ā). 1. [Shortened form of an. AS. ān one. See One.] An adjective, commonly called the indefinite article, and signifying one or any, but less emphatically. “At a birth”; “In a word”; “At a blow”. Shak.

A A (ȧ), prep. [Abbreviated form of an (AS. on). See On.] 1. In; on; at; by. [Obs.] “A God's name.” “Torn a pieces.” “Stand a tiptoe.” “A Sundays” Shak. “Wit that men have now a days.” Chaucer. “Set them a work.” Robynson (More's Utopia).
A A. [From AS. of off, from. See Of.] Of. [Obs.] “The name of John a Gaunt.” “What time a day is it?” Shak. “It's six a clock.” B. Jonson.
A A. A barbarous corruption of have, of he, and sometimes of it and of they. “So would I a done” “A brushes his hat.” Shak.
A A. An expletive, void of sense, to fill up the meter

A- A-. A, as a prefix to English words, is derived from various sources. (1) It frequently signifies on or in (from an, a forms of AS. on), denoting a state, as in afoot, on foot, abed, amiss, asleep, aground, aloft, away (AS. onweg), and analogically, ablaze, atremble, etc. (2) AS. of off, from, as in adown (AS. ofdūne off the dun or hill). (3) AS. ā- (Goth. us-, ur-, Ger. er-), usually giving an intensive force, and sometimes the sense of away, on, back, as in arise, abide, ago. (4) Old English y- or i- (corrupted from the AS. inseparable particle ge-, cognate with OHG. ga-, gi-, Goth. ga-), which, as a prefix, made no essential addition to the meaning, as in aware. (5) French à (L. ad to), as in abase, achieve. (6) L. a, ab, abs, from, as in avert. (7) Greek insep. prefix α without, or privative, not, as in abyss, atheist; akin to E. un-.
A 1 A 1 (ā wŭn). A registry mark given by underwriters (as at Lloyd's) to ships in first-class condition. Inferior grades are indicated by A 2 and A 3.
A B C A B C" (ā bē sē"). 1. The first three letters of the alphabet, used for the whole alphabet.

A cappella ‖A cap*pel"la (?). [It. See Chapel.] (Mus.) (a) In church or chapel style; -- said of compositions sung in the old church style, without instrumental accompaniment; as, a mass a capella, i. e., a mass purely vocal. (b) A time indication, equivalent to alla breve.

A cheval ‖A` che*val" (?). [F., lit., on horseback.] Astride; with a part on each side; -- used specif. in designating the position of an army with the wings separated by some line of demarcation, as a river or road.
A F. of L. A. F. of L. (Abbrev.) American Federation of Labor.
A fortiori ‖A for`ti*o"ri (?). [L.] (Logic & Math.) With stronger reason.

A mensa et thoro ‖A men"sa et tho"ro (?). [L., from board and bed.] (Law) A kind of divorce which does not dissolve the marriage bond, but merely authorizes a separate life of the husband and wife. Abbott.

A posteriori ‖A` pos*te`ri*o"ri (?). [L. a (ab) + posterior latter.] 1. (Logic) Characterizing that kind of reasoning which derives propositions from the observation of facts, or by generalizations from facts arrives at principles and definitions, or infers causes from effects. This is the reverse of a priori reasoning.

A priori ‖A` pri*o"ri (?). [L. a (ab) + prior former.] 1. (Logic) Characterizing that kind of reasoning which deduces consequences from definitions formed, or principles assumed, or which infers effects from causes previously known; deductive or deductively. The reverse of a posteriori.

aam.c: Aam ‖Aam (äm or äm), n. [D. aam, fr. LL. ama; cf. L. hama a water bucket, Gr.?] A Dutch and German measure of liquids, varying in different cities, being at Amsterdam about 41 wine gallons, at Antwerp 36½, at Hamburg 38¼. [Written also Aum and Awm.]

aardvark.c: aardvark ‖aard"vark` (ärd"värk`), n. [D., earth-pig.] (Zool.) An edentate mammal, of the genus Orycteropus (Orycteropus afer), somewhat resembling a pig, common in some parts of Southern Africa. It is a nocturnal ungulate, burrows in the ground with its powerful claws, and feeds entirely on ants and termites, which it catches with its long, extensile, slimy tongue. It is the sole extant representative of the order Tubulidentata. [Spelled also Aard-vark.]

aardwolf.c: Aard-wolf ‖Aard"-wolf` (ärd"wŏolf), n. [D, earth-wolf] (Zool.) A carnivorous, striped, quadruped mammal (Proteles cristata, formerly Proteles Lalandii), of South Africa, resembling the fox and hyena. It feeds chiefly on insects. See Proteles.

aaronical.c: Aaronical Aaronic { Aa*ron"ic (a*rŏn"ĭk), Aa*ron"ic*al (-ĭ*kail), } a. Pertaining to Aaron, the first high priest of the Jews.

aarons.c: Aaron's rod Aar"on's rod` (âr"ŭnz rŏd`). [See Exodus vii. 9 and Numbers xvii. 8] 1. (Arch.) A rod with one serpent twined around it, thus differing from the caduceus of Mercury, which has two.

ab.c: Ab- Ab- (ăb). [Latin prep., etymologically the same as E. of, off. See Of.] A prefix in many words of Latin origin. It signifies from, away, separating, or departure, as in abduct, abstract, abscond. See A-(6).
Ab ‖Ab (ăb), n. [Of Syriac origin.] The fifth month of the Jewish year according to the ecclesiastical reckoning, the eleventh by the civil computation, coinciding nearly with August. W. Smith.

abaca.c: Abaca ‖Ab"a*ca (ăb"ȧ*kȧ), n. [The native name.] The Manila-hemp plant (Musa textilis); also, its fiber. See Manila hemp under Manila.

abacinate.c: Abacinate A*bac"i*nate (ȧ*băs"ĭ*nāt), v. t. [LL. abacinatus, p. p. of abacinare; ab off + bacinus a basin.] To blind by a red-hot metal plate held before the eyes. [R.]

abacination.c: Abacination A*bac`i*na"tion (ȧ*băs`ĭ*nā"shŭn), n. The act of abacinating. [R.]

abaciscus.c: Abaciscus ‖Ab`a*cis"cus (ăb`ȧ*sĭs"kŭs), n. [Gr. 'abaki`skos, dim of 'a`bax. See Abacus.] (Arch.) One of the tiles or squares of a tessellated pavement; an abaculus.

abacist.c: Abacist Ab"a*cist (ăb"ȧ*sĭst), n. [LL abacista, fr. abacus.] One who uses an abacus in casting accounts; a calculator.

aback.c: Aback A*back" (ȧ*băk"), adv. [Pref. a- + back; AS. on bæc at, on, or toward the back. See Back.] 1. Toward the back or rear; backward. “Therewith aback she started.” Chaucer.
Aback Ab"ack (ăb"aik), n. An abacus. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

abactinal.c: Abactinal Ab*ac"ti*nal (ăb*ăk"tĭ*nail), a. [L. ab + E. actinal.] (Zool.) Pertaining to the surface or end opposite to the mouth in a radiate animal; -- opposed to actinal. “The aboral or abactinal area.” L. Agassiz.

abaction.c: Abaction Ab*ac"tion (ăb*ăk"shŭn), n. Stealing cattle on a large scale. [Obs.]

abactor.c: Abactor Ab*ac"tor (-tẽr), n. [L., fr. abigere to drive away; ab + agere to drive.] (Law) One who steals and drives away cattle or beasts by herds or droves. [Obs.]

abaculus.c: Abaculus ‖A*bac"u*lus (ȧb*ăk"u*lŭs), n.; pl. Abaculi (-lī). [L., dim. of abacus.] (Arch.) A small tile of glass, marble, or other substance, of various colors, used in making ornamental patterns in mosaic pavements. Fairholt.

abacus.c: Abacus Ab"a*cus (ăb"ȧ*kŭs), n.; E. pl. Abacuses; L. pl. Abaci (-sī). [L. abacus, abax, Gr. 'a`bax] 1. A table or tray strewn with sand, anciently used for drawing, calculating, etc. [Obs.]

abada.c: Abada Ab"a*da (ăb"ȧ*dȧ), n. [Pg., the female rhinoceros.] The rhinoceros. [Obs.] Purchas.

abaddon.c: Abaddon A*bad"don (ȧ*băd"dŭn), n. [Heb. ābaddōn destruction, abyss, fr. ābad to be lost, to perish.] 1. The destroyer, or angel of the bottomless pit; -- the same as Apollyon and Asmodeus.

abaft.c: Abaft A*baft" (ȧ*bȧft"), prep. [Pref. a- on + OE. baft, baften, biaften, AS. beæftan; be by + æftan behind. See After, Aft, By.] (Naut.) Behind; toward the stern from; as, abaft the wheelhouse.
Abaft A*baft", adv. (Naut.) Toward the stern; aft; as, to go abaft.

abaisance.c: Abaisance A*bai"sance (ȧ*bā"sains), n. [For obeisance; confused with F. abaisser, E. abase.] Obeisance. [Obs.] Jonson.

abaiser.c: Abaiser A*bai"ser (ȧ*bā"sẽr), n. Ivory black or animal charcoal. Weale.

abaist.c: Abaist A*baist" (ȧ*bāst"), p. p. Abashed; confounded; discomfited. [Obs.] Chaucer.

abalienate.c: Abalienate Ab*al"ien*ate (ăb*āl"yein*āt; 94, 106), v. t. [L. abalienatus, p. p. of abalienare; ab + alienus foreign, alien. See Alien.] 1. (Civil Law) To transfer the title of from one to another; to alienate.

abalienation.c: Abalienation Ab*al`ien*a"tion (-āl`yein*ā"shŭn), n. [L. abalienatio: cf. F. abaliénation.] The act of abalienating; alienation; estrangement. [Obs.]

abalone.c: Abalone ‖Ab`a*lo"ne (ăb`ȧ*lō"ne), n. (Zool.) A univalve mollusk of the genus Haliotis. The shell is lined with mother-of-pearl, and used for ornamental purposes; the sea-ear. Several large species are found on the coast of California, clinging closely to the rocks.

aband.c: Aband A*band" (ȧ*bănd"), v. t. [Contracted from abandon.] 1. To abandon. [Obs.]

abandon.c: Abandon A*ban"don (ȧ*băn"dŭn), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abandoned (-dŭnd); p. pr. & vb. n. Abandoning.] [OF. abandoner, F. abandonner; a (L. ad) + bandon permission, authority, LL. bandum, bannum, public proclamation, interdiction, bannire to proclaim, summon: of Germanic origin; cf. Goth. bandwjan to show by signs, to designate OHG. ban proclamation. The word meant to proclaim, put under a ban, put under control; hence, as in OE., to compel, subject, or to leave in the control of another, and hence, to give up. See Ban.] 1. To cast or drive out; to banish; to expel; to reject. [Obs.]
Abandon A*ban"don, n. [F. abandon. fr. abandonner. See Abandon, v.] Abandonment; relinquishment. [Obs.]
Abandon ‖A`ban`don" (ȧ`bäN`dôN"), n. [F. See Abandon.] A complete giving up to natural impulses; freedom from artificial constraint; careless freedom or ease.

abandoned.c: Abandoned A*ban"doned (ȧ*băn"dŭnd), a. 1. Forsaken, deserted. “Your abandoned streams.” Thomson.

abandonee.c: Abandonee A*ban`don*ee" (ȧ*băn`dŭn*ē"), n. (Law) One to whom anything is legally abandoned.

abandoner.c: Abandoner A*ban"don*er (ȧ*băn"dŭn*ẽr), n. One who abandons. Beau. & Fl.

abandonment.c: Abandonment A*ban"don*ment (-meint), n. [Cf. F. abandonnement.] 1. The act of abandoning, or the state of being abandoned; total desertion; relinquishment.

abandum.c: Abandum ‖A*ban"dum (ȧ*băn"dŭm), n. [LL. See Abandon.] (Law) Anything forfeited or confiscated.

abanga.c: Abanga ‖A*ban"ga (ȧ*băṉ"gȧ), n. [Name given by the negroes in the island of St. Thomas.] A West Indian palm; also the fruit of this palm, the seeds of which are used as a remedy for diseases of the chest.

abannition.c: Abannition Abannation { Ab`an*na"tion (ăb`ăn*nā"shŭn), Ab`an*nition (ăb`ăn*nĭsh"ŭn), } n. [LL. abannatio; ad + LL. bannire to banish.] (Old Law) Banishment. [Obs.] Bailey.

abarticulation.c: Abarticulation Ab`ar*tic`u*la"tion (ăb`är*tĭk`u*lā"shŭn), n. [L. ab + E. articulation: cf. F. abarticulation. See Article.] (Anat.) Articulation, usually that kind of articulation which admits of free motion in the joint; diarthrosis. Coxe.

abase.c: Abase A*base" (ȧ*bās"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abased (ȧ*bāst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Abasing.] [F. abaisser, LL. abassare, abbassare; ad + bassare, fr. bassus low. See Base, a.]

abasement.c: Abasement A*base"ment (ȧ*bās"meint), n. [Cf. F. abaissement.] The act of abasing, humbling, or bringing low; the state of being abased or humbled; humiliation.

abaser.c: Abaser A*bas"er (ȧ*bās"ẽr), n. He who, or that which, abases.

abash.c: Abash A*bash" (ȧ*băsh"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abashed (ȧ*băsht"); p. pr. & vb. n. Abashing.] [OE. abaissen, abaisshen, abashen, OF. esbahir, F. ébahir, to astonish, fr. L. ex + the interjection bah, expressing astonishment. In OE. somewhat confused with abase. Cf. Finish.] To destroy the self-possession of; to confuse or confound, as by exciting suddenly a consciousness of guilt, mistake, or inferiority; to put to shame; to disconcert; to discomfit.

abashedly.c: Abashedly A*bash"ed*ly (-ĕd*ly̆), adv. In an abashed manner.

abashment.c: Abashment A*bash"ment (-meint), n. [Cf. F. ébahissement.] The state of being abashed; confusion from shame.

abasia.c: Abasia ‖A*ba"si*a (ȧ*bā"zhĭ*ȧ; -zĭ*ȧ), n. [NL.; Gr. 'a- not + ba`sis a step.] (Med.) Inability to coordinate muscular actions properly in walking. AS [archaic] -- A*ba"sic (ȧ*bā"sĭk), a.

abassis.c: Abassis Abassi { ‖A*bas"si (ȧ*băs"sĭ), ‖A*bas"sis (ȧ*băs"sĭs), } n. [Ar. & Per. abāsī, belonging to Abas (a king of Persia).] A silver coin of Persia, worth about twenty cents.

abatable.c: Abatable A*bat"a*ble (ȧ*bāt"ȧ*b'l), a. Capable of being abated; as, an abatable writ or nuisance.

abate.c: Abate A*bate" (ȧ*bāt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abated, p. pr. & vb. n. Abating.] [OF. abatre to beat down, F. abattre, LL. abatere; ab or ad + batere, battere (popular form for L. batuere to beat). Cf. Bate, Batter.] 1. To beat down; to overthrow. [Obs.]
Abate A*bate" (ȧ*bāt"), v. i. [See Abate, v. t.] 1. To decrease, or become less in strength or violence; as, pain abates, a storm abates.
Abate A*bate" (ȧ*bāt"), n. Abatement. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

abatement.c: Abatement A*bate"ment (-meint), n. [OF. abatement, F. abattement.] 1. The act of abating, or the state of being abated; a lessening, diminution, or reduction; removal or putting an end to; as, the abatement of a nuisance is the suppression thereof.

abater.c: Abater A*bat"er (-ẽr), n. One who, or that which, abates.

abattis.c: Abattis Abatis { Ab"a*tis, Aba"t*tis, } (ăb"ȧ*tĭs; French ȧ`bȧ`tē") n. [F. abatis, abattis, mass of things beaten or cut down, fr. abattre. See Abate.] (Fort.) A means of defense formed by felled trees, the ends of whose branches are sharpened and directed outwards, or against the enemy.

abatised.c: Abatised Ab"a*tised (ăb"ȧ*tĭst), a. Provided with an abatis.

abator.c: Abator A*ba"tor (ȧ*bāt"ẽr), n. (Law) (a) One who abates a nuisance. (b) A person who, without right, enters into a freehold on the death of the last possessor, before the heir or devisee. Blackstone.

abattoir.c: Abattoir ‖A`bat`toir" (ȧ`bȧt`twär"), n.; pl. Abattoirs (-twärz"). [F., fr. abattre to beat down. See Abate.] A public slaughterhouse for cattle, sheep, etc.

abature.c: Abature Ab"a*ture (ȧb"ȧ*tur; 135), n. [F. abatture, fr. abattre. See Abate.] Grass and sprigs beaten or trampled down by a stag passing through them. Crabb.

abatvoix.c: Abatvoix ‖A`bat`voix" (ȧ`bȧ`vwä"), n. [F. abattre to beat down + voix voice.] The sounding-board over a pulpit or rostrum.

abawed.c: Abawed Ab*awed" (ăb*äd"), p. p. [Perh. p. p. of a verb fr. OF. abaubir to frighten, disconcert, fr. L. ad + balbus stammering.] Astonished; abashed. [Obs.] Chaucer.

abaxile.c: Abaxile Abaxial { Ab*ax"i*al (ăb*ăks"ĭ*ail), Ab*ax"ile (ăb*ăks"ĭl), } a. [L. ab + axis axle.] (Bot.) Away from the axis or central line; eccentric. Balfour.

abay.c: Abay A*bay" (ȧ*bā"), n. [OF. abay barking.] Barking; baying of dogs upon their prey. See Bay. [Obs.]

abb.c: Abb Abb (ăb), n. [AS. āweb, āb; pref. a- + web. See Web.] Among weavers, yarn for the warp. Hence, abb wool is wool for the abb.
Abb wool Abb" wool (ăb" wŏol). See Abb.

abba.c: Abba Ab"ba (ăb"bȧ), n. [Syriac abbā father. See Abbot.] Father; religious superior; -- in the Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic churches, a title given to the bishops, and by the bishops to the patriarch.

abbacy.c: Abbacy Ab"ba*cy (ăb"bȧ*sy̆), n.; pl. Abbacies (-sĭz). [L. abbatia, fr. abbas, abbatis, abbot. See Abbey.] The dignity, estate, or jurisdiction of an abbot.

abbatial.c: Abbatial Ab*ba"tial (ăb*bā"shail), a. [LL. abbatialis: cf. F. abbatial.] Belonging to an abbey; as, abbatial rights.

abbe.c: Abbe ‖Ab"bé` (ȧb"ba`), n. [F. abbé. See Abbot.] The French word answering to the English abbot, the head of an abbey; but commonly a title of respect given in France to every one vested with the ecclesiastical habit or dress.

abbess.c: Abbess Ab"bess (ăb"bĕs), n. [OF. abaesse, abeesse, F. abbesse, L. abbatissa, fem. of abbas, abbatis, abbot. See Abbot.] A female superior or governess of a nunnery, or convent of nuns, having the same authority over the nuns which the abbots have over the monks. See Abbey.

abbey.c: Abbey Ab"bey (ăb"by̆), n.; pl. Abbeys (-bĭz). [OF. abaïe, abbaïe, F. abbaye, L. abbatia, fr. abbas abbot. See Abbot.] 1. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion and celibacy; also, the monastic building or buildings.

abbot.c: Abbot Ab"bot (ăb"bŭt), n. [AS. abbod, abbad, L. abbas, abbatis, Gr. 'abba^s, fr. Syriac abbā father. Cf. Abba, Abbé.] 1. The superior or head of an abbey.

abbotship.c: Abbotship Ab"bot*ship (ăb"bŭt*shĭp), n. [Abbot + -ship.] The state or office of an abbot.

abbreviate.c: Abbreviate Ab*bre"vi*ate (ăb*brē"vĭ*āt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abbreviated; p. pr. & vb. n. Abbreviating.] [L. abbreviatus, p. p. of abbreviare; ad + breviare to shorten, fr. brevis short. See Abridge.] 1. To make briefer; to shorten; to abridge; to reduce by contraction or omission, especially of words written or spoken.
Abbreviate Ab*bre"vi*ate (ăb*brē"vĭ*at), a. [L. abbreviatus, p. p.] 1. Abbreviated; abridged; shortened. [R.] “The abbreviate form.” Earle.

abbreviated.c: Abbreviated Ab*bre"vi*a`ted (ăb*brē"vĭ*ā`tĕd), a. Shortened; relatively short; abbreviate.

abbreviation.c: Abbreviation Ab*bre`vi*a"tion (?), n. [LL. abbreviatio: cf. F. abbréviation.] 1. The act of shortening, or reducing.

abbreviator.c: Abbreviator Ab*bre"vi*a`tor (?), n. [LL.: cf. F. abbréviateur.] 1. One who abbreviates or shortens.

abbreviatory.c: Abbreviatory Ab*bre"vi*a*to*ry (?), a. Serving or tending to abbreviate; shortening; abridging.

abbreviature.c: Abbreviature Ab*bre"vi*a*ture (?), n. 1. An abbreviation; an abbreviated state or form. [Obs.]

abdal.c: Abdal ‖Ab"dal (?), n. [Ar. badīl, pl. abdāl, a substitute, a good, religious man, saint, fr. badala to change, substitute.] A religious devotee or dervish in Persia.

abderian.c: Abderian Ab*de"ri*an (?), a. [From Abdera, a town in Thrace, of which place Democritus, the Laughing Philosopher, was a native.] Given to laughter; inclined to foolish or incessant merriment.

abderite.c: Abderite Ab*de"rite (?), n. [L. Abderita, Abderites, fr. Gr. 'Abdhri`ths.] An inhabitant of Abdera, in Thrace.

abdest.c: Abdest Ab"dest (?), n. [Per. ābdast; ab water + dast hand.] Purification by washing the hands before prayer; -- a Muslim rite. Heyse.

abdicable.c: Abdicable Ab"di*ca*ble (?), a. Capable of being abdicated.

abdicant.c: Abdicant Ab"di*cant (?), a. [L. abdicans, p. pr. of abdicare.] Abdicating; renouncing; -- followed by of.
Abdicant Ab"di*cant, n. One who abdicates. Smart.

abdicate.c: Abdicate Ab"di*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abdicated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abdicating.] [L. abdicatus, p. p. of abdicare; ab + dicare to proclaim, akin to dicere to say. See Diction.] 1. To surrender or relinquish, as sovereign power; to withdraw definitely from filling or exercising, as a high office, station, dignity; as, to abdicate the throne, the crown, the papacy.
Abdicate Ab"di*cate (?), v. i. To relinquish or renounce a throne, or other high office or dignity.

abdication.c: Abdication Ab`di*ca"tion (?), n. [L. abdicatio: cf. F. abdication.] The act of abdicating; the renunciation of a high office, dignity, or trust, by its holder; commonly the voluntary renunciation of sovereign power; as, abdication of the throne, government, power, authority.

abdicative.c: Abdicative Ab"di*ca*tive (?), a. [L. abdicativus.] Causing, or implying, abdication. [R.] Bailey.

abditive.c: Abditive Ab"di*tive (?), a. [L. abditivus, fr. abdere to hide.] Having the quality of hiding. [R.] Bailey.

abditory.c: Abditory Ab"di*to*ry (?), n. [L. abditorium.] A place for hiding or preserving articles of value. Cowell.

abdomen.c: Abdomen Ab*do"men (?), n. [L. abdomen (a word of uncertain etymol.): cf. F. abdomen.] 1. (Anat.) The belly, or that part of the body between the thorax and the pelvis. Also, the cavity of the belly, which is lined by the peritoneum, and contains the stomach, bowels, and other viscera. In man, often restricted to the part between the diaphragm and the commencement of the pelvis, the remainder being called the pelvic cavity.

abdominal.c: Abdominal Ab*dom"i*nal (?), a. [Cf. F. abdominal.] 1. Of or pertaining to the abdomen; ventral; as, the abdominal regions, muscles, cavity.
Abdominal Ab*dom"i*nal, n.; E. pl. Abdominals, L. pl. Abdominales. A fish of the group Abdominales.

abdominales.c: Abdominales ‖Ab*dom`i*na"les (?), n. pl. [NL., masc. pl.] (Zool.) A group including the greater part of fresh-water fishes, and many marine ones, having the ventral fins under the abdomen behind the pectorals.

abdominalia.c: Abdominalia ‖Ab*dom`i*na"li*a (?), n. pl. [NL., neut. pl.] (Zool.) A group of cirripeds having abdominal appendages.

abdominoscopy.c: abdominoscopy ab*dom`i*nos"co*py (ăb*dŏm`ĭ*nŏs"ko*py̆), n. [L. abdomen + Gr. skopei^n to examine.] (Med.) Examination of the abdomen by means of a laparoscope to detect abdominal diseases.

abdominothoracic.c: Abdominothoracic Ab*dom`i*no*tho*rac"ic (?), a. Relating to the abdomen and the thorax, or chest.

abdominous.c: Abdominous Ab*dom"i*nous (?), a. Having a protuberant belly; pot-bellied.

abduce.c: Abduce Ab*duce" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abduced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abducing.] [L. abducere to lead away; ab + ducere to lead. See Duke, and cf. Abduct.] To draw or conduct away; to withdraw; to draw to a different part. [Obs.]

abduct.c: Abduct Ab*duct" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abducted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abducting.] [L. abductus, p. p. of abducere. See Abduce.] 1. To take away surreptitiously by force; to carry away (a human being) wrongfully and usually by violence; to kidnap.

abduction.c: Abduction Ab*duc"tion (?), n. [L. abductio: cf. F. abduction.] 1. The act of abducing or abducting; a drawing apart; a carrying away. Roget.

abeam.c: Abeam A*beam" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + beam.] (Naut.) On the beam, that is, on a line which forms a right angle with the ship's keel; opposite to the center of the ship's side.

abear.c: Abear A*bear" (?), v. t. [AS. āberan; pref. ā- + beran to bear.] 1. To bear; to behave. [Obs.]

abearing.c: Abearing A*bear"ing, n. Behavior. [Obs.] Sir. T. More.

abecedarian.c: Abecedarian A`be*ce*da"ri*an (?), n. [L. abecedarius. A word from the first four letters of the alphabet.] 1. One who is learning the alphabet; hence, a tyro.

abecedary.c: Abecedary Abecedarian { A`be*ce*da"ri*an, A`be*ce"da*ry (?), } a. Pertaining to, or formed by, the letters of the alphabet; alphabetic; hence, rudimentary.
Abecedary A`be*ce"da*ry (?), n. A primer; the first principle or rudiment of anything. [R.] Fuller.

abed.c: Abed A*bed" (?), adv. [Pref. a- in, on + bed.] 1. In bed, or on the bed.

abele.c: Abele A*bele" (?), n. [D. abeel (abeel-boom), OF. abel, aubel, fr. a dim. of L. albus white.] The white poplar (Populus alba).

abelonian.c: Abelonian Abelite Abelian { A*bel"i*an (?), A"bel*ite (?), A`bel*o"ni*an (?), } n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a sect in Africa (4th century), mentioned by St. Augustine, who states that they married, but lived in continence, after the manner, as they pretended, of Abel.

abelmosk.c: Abelmosk A"bel*mosk` (?), n. [NL. abelmoschus, fr. Ar. abu-l-misk father of musk, i. e., producing musk. See Musk. (or Ar. ḥabb-al-mosk, musk seed RHUD 1.3] (Bot.) An evergreen shrub (Abelmoschus moschatus -- formerly Hibiscus moschatus), of the East and West Indies and Northern Africa, whose musky seeds are used in perfumery and to flavor coffee; -- sometimes called musk mallow. The seeds produce ambrette-seed oil.

aberdevine.c: Aber-de-vine Ab`er-de-vine" (#), n. (Zool.) The European siskin (Carduelis spinus), a small green and yellow finch, related to the goldfinch.

aberr.c: Aberr Ab*err" (?), v. i. [L. aberrare. See Aberrate.] To wander; to stray. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

aberrancy.c: Aberrancy Aberrance { Ab*er"rance (?), Ab*er"ran*cy (?), } n. the state or condition of being aberrant; a wandering from the right way; deviation from truth, rectitude, etc.
aberrancy aberrancy n. 1. an aberrant state or condition.

aberrant.c: Aberrant Ab*er"rant (?), a. [L. aberrans, -rantis, p. pr. of aberrare. See Aberr.] 1. Wandering; straying from the right way.

aberrate.c: Aberrate Ab"er*rate (?), v. i. [L. aberratus, p. pr. of aberrare; ab + errare to wander. See Err.] To go astray; to diverge. [R.]

aberration.c: Aberration Ab`er*ra"tion (?), n. [L. aberratio: cf. F. aberration. See Aberrate.] 1. The act of wandering; deviation, especially from truth or moral rectitude, from the natural state, or from a type. “The aberration of youth.” Hall. “Aberrations from theory.” Burke.

aberuncate.c: Aberuncate Ab`e*run"cate (?), v. t. [L. aberuncare, for aberruncare. See Averruncate.] To weed out. [Obs.] Bailey.

abet.c: Abet A*bet" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abetted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abetting.] [OF. abeter; a (L. ad) + beter to bait (as a bear), fr. Icel. beita to set dogs on, to feed, originally, to cause to bite, fr. Icel. bīta to bite, hence to bait, to incite. See Bait, Bet.] 1. To instigate or encourage by aid or countenance; -- used in a bad sense of persons and acts; as, to abet an ill-doer; to abet one in his wicked courses; to abet vice; to abet an insurrection. “The whole tribe abets the villany.” South.
Abet A*bet" (?), n. [OF. abet, fr. abeter.] Act of abetting; aid. [Obs.] Chaucer.

abetment.c: Abetment A*bet"ment (-meint), n. The act of abetting; as, an abetment of treason, crime, etc.

abettor.c: Abettor Abetter { A*bet"ter, A*bet*tor } (?), n. One who abets; an instigator of an offense or an offender.

abevacuation.c: Abevacuation Ab`e*vac"u*a"tion (?), n. [Pref. ab- + evacuation.] (Med.) A partial evacuation. Mayne. AS

abeyance.c: Abeyance A*bey"ance (?), n. [OF. abeance expectation, longing; a (L. ad) + baer, beer, to gape, to look with open mouth, to expect, F. bayer, LL. badare to gape.] 1. (Law) Expectancy; condition of being undetermined.

abeyant.c: Abeyant A*bey"ant (?), a. Being in a state of abeyance.

abhal.c: Abhal ‖Ab"hal (?), n. The berries of a species of cypress in the East Indies.

abhominal.c: Abhominal Ab*hom`i*nal (?), a. [L. ab away from + homo, hominis, man.] Inhuman. [Obs.] Fuller.

abhor.c: Abhor Ab*hor" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abhorred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abhorring.] [L. abhorrere; ab + horrere to bristle, shiver, shudder: cf. F. abhorrer. See Horrid.] 1. To shrink back with shuddering from; to regard with horror or detestation; to feel excessive repugnance toward; to detest to extremity; to loathe.
Abhor Ab*hor", v. i. To shrink back with horror, disgust, or dislike; to be contrary or averse; -- with from. [Obs.] “To abhor from those vices.” Udall.

abhorrence.c: Abhorrence Ab*hor"rence (?), n. Extreme hatred or detestation; the feeling of utter dislike.

abhorrent.c: Abhorrent Ab*hor"rent (?), a. [L. abhorens, -rentis, p. pr. of abhorrere.] 1. Abhorring; detesting; having or showing abhorrence; loathing; hence, strongly opposed to; as, abhorrent thoughts.

abhorrer.c: Abhorrer Ab*hor"rer (?), n. One who abhors. Hume.

abib.c: Abib ‖A"bib (?), n. [Heb. abīb, lit. an ear of corn. The month was so called from barley being at that time in ear.] The first month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, corresponding nearly to our April. After the Babylonish captivity this month was called Nisan. Kitto.

abidance.c: Abidance A*bid"ance (?), n. The state of abiding; abode; continuance; compliance (with).

abide.c: Abide A*bide" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Abode (?), formerly Abid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abiding (?).] [AS. ābīdan; pref. ā- (cf. Goth. us-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + bīdan to bide. See Bide.] 1. To wait; to pause; to delay. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Abide A*bide", v. t. 1. To wait for; to be prepared for; to await; to watch for; as, I abide my time. “I will abide the coming of my lord.” Tennyson.

abider.c: Abider A*bid"er (?), n. 1. One who abides, or continues. [Obs.] “Speedy goers and strong abiders.” Sidney.

abies.c: Abies ‖A"bi*es (?), n. [L., fir tree.] (Bot.) A genus of coniferous trees, properly called Fir, as the balsam fir and the silver fir. The spruces are sometimes also referred to this genus.

abietene.c: Abietene Ab"i*e*tene (?), n. [L. abies, abietis, a fir tree.] A volatile oil distilled from the resin or balsam of the nut pine (Pinus sabiniana) of California.

abietic.c: Abietic Ab`i*et"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the fir tree or its products; as, abietic acid, called also sylvic acid. Watts.

abietine.c: Abietine Abietin { Ab"i*e*tin, Ab"i*e*tine } (?), n. [See Abietene.] (Chem.) A resinous obtained from Strasburg turpentine or Canada balsam. It is without taste or smell, is insoluble in water, but soluble in alcohol (especially at the boiling point), in strong acetic acid, and in ether. Watts.

abietinic.c: Abietinic Ab`i*e*tin"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to abietin; as, abietinic acid.

abietite.c: Abietite Ab"i*e*tite (?), n. (Chem.) A substance resembling mannite, found in the needles of the common silver fir of Europe (Abies pectinata). Eng. Cyc.

abigail.c: abigail ab"i*gail (?), n. [The proper name used as an appellative.] A lady's waiting-maid. Pepys.

ability.c: Ability A*bil"i*ty (ȧ*bĭl"ĭ*ty̆), n.; pl. Abilities (ȧ*bĭl"ĭ*tĭz). [F. habileté, earlier spelling habilité (with silent h), L. habilitas aptitude, ability, fr. habilis apt. See Able.] The quality or state of being able; power to perform, whether physical, moral, intellectual, conventional, or legal; capacity; skill or competence in doing; sufficiency of strength, skill, resources, etc.; -- in the plural, faculty, talent.

abyme.c: Abyme Abime A*bime" or A*byme" (#), n. [F. abîme. See Abysm.] A abyss. [Obs.]

abiogenesis.c: Abiogenesis Ab`i*o*gen"e*sis (?), n. [Gr. 'a priv. + bi`os life + ge`nesis, origin, birth.] (Biol.) The supposed origination of living organisms from lifeless matter; such genesis as does not involve the action of living parents; spontaneous generation; -- called also abiogeny, and opposed to biogenesis.

abiogenetic.c: Abiogenetic Ab`i*o*ge*net"ic (?), a. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to abiogenesis. Ab`i*o*ge*net"ic*al*ly, adv.

abiogenist.c: Abiogenist Ab`i*og"e*nist (?), n. (Biol.) One who believes that life can be produced independently of antecedent. Huxley.

abiogenous.c: Abiogenous Ab`i*og"e*nous (?), a. (Biol.) Produced by spontaneous generation.

abiological.c: Abiological Ab`i*o*log"ic*al (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. + E. biological.] Pertaining to the study of inanimate things.

abirritant.c: Abirritant Ab*ir"ri*tant (?), n. (Med.) A medicine that diminishes or alleviates irritation.

abirritate.c: Abirritate Ab*ir"ri*tate (?), v. t. [Pref. ab- + irritate.] (Med.) To diminish the sensibility to stimulation of.

abirritation.c: Abirritation Ab*ir`ri*ta"tion (?), n. (Med.) A pathological condition opposite to that of irritation; debility; lack of strength; asthenia. AS

abirritative.c: Abirritative Ab*ir"ri*ta*tive (?), a. (Med.) Characterized by abirritation or debility. AS

abit.c: Abit A*bit" (?),3d sing. pres. of Abide. [Obs.] Chaucer.

abject.c: abject ab"ject (ăb"jĕkt), a. [L. abjectus, p. p. of abjicere to throw away; ab + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.] 1. Cast down; low-lying. [Obs.]
Abject Ab*ject" (ăb*jĕkt"), v. t. [From Abject, a.] To cast off or down; hence, to abase; to degrade; to lower; to debase. [Obs.] Donne.
Abject Ab"ject (ăb"jĕkt), n. A person in the lowest and most despicable condition; a castaway. [Obs.]

abjectedness.c: Abjectedness Ab*ject"ed*ness (ăb*jĕkt"ĕd*nĕs), n. A very abject or low condition; abjectness. [R.] Boyle.

abjection.c: Abjection Ab*jec"tion (ăb*jĕk"shŭn), n. [F. abjection, L. abjectio.] 1. The act of bringing down or humbling. “The abjection of the king and his realm.” Joye.

abjectness.c: Abjectness Ab"ject*ness (ăb"jĕkt*nĕs), n. The state of being abject; abasement; meanness; servility. Grew.

abjudge.c: Abjudge Ab*judge" (ăb*jŭj"), v. t. [Pref. ab- + judge, v. Cf. Abjudicate.] To take away by judicial decision. [R.]

abjudicate.c: Abjudicate Ab*ju"di*cate (?), v. t. [L. abjudicatus, p. p. of abjudicare; ab + judicare. See Judge, and cf. Abjudge.] To reject by judicial sentence; also, to abjudge. [Obs.] Ash.

abjudication.c: Abjudication Ab*ju`di*ca"tion (?), n. Rejection by judicial sentence. [R.] Knowles.

abjugate.c: Abjugate Ab"ju*gate (?), v. t. [L. abjugatus, p. p. of abjugare.] To unyoke. [Obs.] Bailey.

abjunctive.c: Abjunctive Ab*junc"tive (?), a. [L. abjunctus, p. p. of abjungere; ab + jungere to join.] Exceptional. [R.]

abjuration.c: Abjuration Ab`ju*ra"tion (?), n. [L. abjuratio: cf. F. abjuration.] 1. The act of abjuring or forswearing; a renunciation upon oath; as, abjuration of the realm, a sworn banishment, an oath taken to leave the country and never to return.

abjure.c: Abjure Ab*jure" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abjured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abjuring (?).] [L. abjurare to deny upon oath; ab + jurare to swear, fr. jus, juris, right, law; cf. F. abjurer. See Jury.] 1. To renounce upon oath; to forswear; to disavow; as, to abjure allegiance to a prince. To abjure the realm, is to swear to abandon it forever.
Abjure Ab*jure", v. i. To renounce on oath. Bp. Burnet.

ablactate.c: Ablactate Ab*lac"tate (?), v. t. [L. ablactatus, p. p. of ablactare; ab + lactare to suckle, fr. lac milk.] To wean. [R.] Bailey.

ablactation.c: Ablactation Ab`lac*ta"tion (?). n. 1. The weaning of a child from the breast, or of young beasts from their dam. Blount.

ablaqueate.c: Ablaqueate Ab*la"que*ate (?), v. t. [L. ablaqueatus, p. p. of. ablaqueare; fr. ab + laqueus a noose.] To lay bare, as the roots of a tree. [Obs.] Bailey.

ablaqueation.c: Ablaqueation Ab*la`que*a"tion (?), n. [L. ablaqueatio.] The act or process of laying bare the roots of trees to expose them to the air and water. [Obs.] Evelyn.

ablation.c: Ablation Ab*la"tion (?), n. [L. ablatio, fr. ablatus p. p. of auferre to carry away; ab + latus, p. p. of ferre carry: cf. F. ablation. See Tolerate.] 1. A carrying or taking away; removal. Jer. Taylor.

ablatitious.c: Ablatitious Ab`la*ti"tious (?), a. Diminishing; as, an ablatitious force. Sir J. Herschel.

ablative.c: Ablative Ab"la*tive (?), a. [F. ablatif, ablative, L. ablativus fr. ablatus. See Ablation.] 1. Taking away or removing. [Obs.]

ablaut.c: Ablaut ‖Ab"laut (?), n. [Ger., off-sound; ab off + laut sound.] (Philol.) The substitution of one root vowel for another, thus indicating a corresponding modification of use or meaning; vowel permutation; as, get, gat, got; sing, song; hang, hung. Earle.

ablaze.c: Ablaze A*blaze" (?), adv. & a. [Pref. a- + blaze.] 1. On fire; in a blaze, gleaming. Milman.

able.c: Able A"ble (?), a. [comp. Abler (?); superl. Ablest (?).] [OF. habile, L. habilis that may be easily held or managed, apt, skillful, fr. habere to have, hold. Cf. Habile and see Habit.] 1. Fit; adapted; suitable. [Obs.]
Able A"ble, v. t. [See Able, a.] [Obs.] 1. To make able; to enable; to strengthen. Chaucer.

-able -a*ble (-ȧ*b'l). [F. -able, L. -abilis.] An adjective suffix now usually in a passive sense; able to be; fit to be; expressing capacity or worthiness in a passive sense; as, movable, able to be moved; amendable, able to be amended; blamable, fit to be blamed; salable.

ablebodied.c: Able-bodied A`ble-bod"ied (?), a. Having a sound, strong body; physically competent; robust. “Able-bodied vagrant.” Froude. -- A`ble-bod"ied*ness, n..

ablegate.c: Ablegate Ab"le*gate (?), v. t. [L. ablegatus, p. p. of ablegare; ab + legare to send with a commission. See Legate.] To send abroad. [Obs.] Bailey.

Ablegate Ab"le*gate (?), n. (R. C. Ch.) A representative of the pope charged with important commissions in foreign countries, one of his duties being to bring to a newly named cardinal his insignia of office.

ablegation.c: Ablegation Ab`le*ga"tion (?), n. [L. ablegatio.] The act of sending abroad. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

ableminded.c: Able-minded A`ble-mind"ed (#), a. Having much intellectual power. -- A`ble-mind"ed*ness, n.

ableness.c: Ableness A"ble*ness (?), n. Ability of body or mind; force; vigor. [Obs. or R.]

ablepsy.c: Ablepsy Ab"lep*sy (?), n. [Gr.?; 'a priv. +? to see.] Blindness. [R.] Urquhart.

abler.c: Abler A"bler (?), a., comp. of Able. -- A"blest (?), a., superl. of Able.

ablen.c: Ablen Ablet Ab"let (?), Ab"len [F. ablet, ablette, a dim. fr. LL. abula, for albula, dim. of albus white. Cf. Abele.] (Zool.) A small fresh-water fish (Leuciscus alburnus); the bleak.

abligate.c: Abligate Ab"li*gate (?), v. t. [L. ab + ligatus, p. p. of ligare to tie.] To tie up so as to hinder from. [Obs.]

abligurition.c: Abligurition Ab*lig`u*ri"tion (?), n. [L. abligurito, fr. abligurire to spend in luxurious indulgence; ab + ligurire to be lickerish, dainty, fr. lingere to lick.] Prodigal expense for food. [Obs.] Bailey.

ablins.c: Ablins Aiblins ‖Ai"blins, A"blins (?), adv. [See Able.] Perhaps; possibly. [Scotch] Burns.

abloom.c: Abloom A*bloom" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + bloom.] In or into bloom; in a blooming state. Masson.

ablude.c: Ablude Ab*lude" (?), v. t. [L. abludere; ab + ludere to play.] To be unlike; to differ. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

abluent.c: Abluent Ab"lu*ent (?), a. [L. abluens, p. pr. of. abluere to wash away; ab + luere (lavere, lavare). See Lave.] Washing away; carrying off impurities; detergent. -- n. (Med.) A detergent. AS

ablush.c: Ablush A*blush" (?), adv. & a. [Pref. a- + blush.] Blushing; ruddy.

ablution.c: Ablution Ab*lu`tion (?), n. [L. ablutio, fr. abluere: cf. F. ablution. See Abluent.] 1. The act of washing or cleansing; specifically, the washing of the body, or some part of it, as a religious rite.

abluvion.c: Abluvion Ab*lu"vi*on (?), n. [LL. abluvio. See Abluent.] That which is washed off. [R.] Dwight.

ably.c: Ably A"bly (?), adv. In an able manner; with great ability; as, ably done, planned, said.
-ably -a*bly (?). A suffix composed of -able and the adverbial suffix -ly; as, favorably.

abnegate.c: Abnegate Ab"ne*gate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abnegated; p. pr. & vb. n. Abnegating.] [L. abnegatus, p. p. of abnegare; ab + negare to deny. See Deny.] To deny and reject; to abjure. Sir E. Sandys. Farrar.

abnegation.c: Abnegation Ab`ne*ga"tion (?), n. [L. abnegatio: cf. F. abnégation.] a denial; a renunciation.

abnegative.c: Abnegative Ab"ne*ga*tive (?), a. [L. abnegativus.] Denying; renouncing; negative. [R.] Clarke.

abnegator.c: Abnegator Ab"ne*ga`tor (?), n. [L.] One who abnegates, denies, or rejects anything. [R.]

abnet.c: Abnet ‖Ab"net (?), n. [Heb.] The girdle of a Jewish priest or officer.

abnodate.c: Abnodate Ab"no*date (?), v. t. [L. abnodatus, p. p. of abnodare; ab + nodus knot.] To clear (tress) from knots. [R.] Blount.

abnodation.c: Abnodation Ab`no*da"tion (?), n. The act of cutting away the knots of trees. [R.] Crabb.

abnormal.c: Abnormal Ab*nor"mal (?), a. [For earlier anormal, F. anormal, LL. anormalus for anomalus, Gr.?. Confused with L. abnormis. See Anomalous, Abnormous, Anormal.] Not conformed to rule or system; deviating from the type; anomalous; irregular. “That deviating from the type; anomalous; irregular. ” Froude.

abnormality.c: Abnormality Ab`nor*mal"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Abnormalities (?). 1. The state or quality of being abnormal; variation; irregularity. Darwin.

abnormally.c: Abnormally Ab*nor"mal*ly (?), adv. In an abnormal manner; irregularly. Darwin.

abnormity.c: Abnormity Ab*nor"mi*ty (?), n.; pl. Abnormities (?). [LL. abnormitas. See Abnormous.] Departure from the ordinary type; irregularity; monstrosity. “An abnormity... like a calf born with two heads.” Mrs. Whitney.

abnormous.c: Abnormous Ab*nor"mous (?), a. [L. abnormis; ab + norma rule. See Normal.] Abnormal; irregular. Hallam.

aboard.c: Aboard A*board" (?), adv. [Pref. a- on, in + board.] 1. On board; into or within a ship or boat; hence, into or within a railway car.
Aboard A*board", prep. 1. On board of; as, to go aboard a ship.

abodance.c: Abodance A*bod"ance (?), n. [See Bode.] An omen; a portending. [Obs.]

abode.c: Abode A*bode", n. [OE. abad, abood, fr. abiden to abide. See Abide. For the change of vowel, cf. abode, imp. of abide.] 1. Act of waiting; delay. [Obs.] Shak.
Abode A*bode", n. [See Bode, v. t.] An omen. [Obs.]
Abode A*bode", v. t. To bode; to foreshow. [Obs.] Shak.
Abode A*bode", v. i. To be ominous. [Obs.] Dryden.

abodement.c: Abodement A*bode"ment (-meint), n. A foreboding; an omen. [Obs.] “Abodements must not now affright us.” Shak.

abolish.c: Abolish A*bol"ish (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abolished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abolishing.] [F. abolir, L. abolere, aboletum; ab + olere to grow. Cf. Finish.] 1. To do away with wholly; to annul; to make void; -- said of laws, customs, institutions, governments, etc.; as, to abolish slavery, to abolish folly.

abolishable.c: Abolishable A*bol"ish*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. abolissable.] Capable of being abolished.

abolishment.c: Abolishment A*bol"ish*ment (-meint), n. [Cf. F. abolissement.] The act of abolishing; abolition; destruction. Hooker.

abolition.c: Abolition Ab"o*li"tion (?), n. [L. abolitio, fr. abolere: cf. F. abolition. See Abolish.] The act of abolishing, or the state of being abolished; an annulling; abrogation; utter destruction; as, the abolition of slavery or the slave trade; the abolition of laws, decrees, ordinances, customs, taxes, debts, etc.

abolitionism.c: Abolitionism Ab`o*li"tion*ism (?), n. The principles or measures of abolitionists. Wilberforce.

abolitionist.c: Abolitionist Ab`o*li"tion*ist, n. A person who favors the abolition of any institution, especially negro slavery.

abolitionize.c: Abolitionize Ab`o*li`tion*ize (?), v. t. To imbue with the principles of abolitionism. [R.] Bartlett.

aboma.c: Aboma ‖A*bo"ma (?), n. (Zool.) A large South American serpent (Boa aboma).

abomasus.c: Abomasus Abomasum { ‖Ab`o*ma"sum (?), ‖Ab`o*ma"sus (?), } n. [NL., fr. L. ab + omasum (a Celtic word).] (Anat.) The fourth or digestive stomach of a ruminant, which leads from the third stomach omasum. See Ruminantia.

abominable.c: Abominable A*bom"i*na*ble (?), a. [F. abominable. L. abominalis. See Abominate.] 1. Worthy of, or causing, abhorrence, as a thing of evil omen; odious in the utmost degree; very hateful; detestable; loathsome; execrable.

abominableness.c: Abominableness A*bom"i*na*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being abominable; odiousness. Bentley.

abominably.c: Abominably A*bom"i*na*bly (?), adv. In an abominable manner; very odiously; detestably.

abominate.c: Abominate A*bom"i*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abominated; p. pr. & vb. n. Abominating.] [L. abominatus, p. p. or abominari to deprecate as ominous, to abhor, to curse; ab + omen a foreboding. See Omen.] To turn from as ill-omened; to hate in the highest degree, as if with religious dread; loathe; as, to abominate all impiety.

abomination.c: Abomination A*bom`i*na"tion (?), n. [OE. abominacioun, -cion, F. abominatio. See Abominate.] 1. The feeling of extreme disgust and hatred; abhorrence; detestation; loathing; as, he holds tobacco in abomination.

aboon.c: Aboon A*boon" (?), prep. and adv. Above. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]

aboral.c: Aboral Ab*o"ral (?), a. [L. ab. + E. oral.] (Zool.) Situated opposite to, or away from, the mouth.

abord.c: Abord ‖A*bord" (?), n. [F.] Manner of approaching or accosting; address. Chesterfield.
Abord A*bord" (?), v. t. [F. aborder, à (L. ad) + bord rim, brim, or side of a vessel. See Border, Board.] To approach; to accost. [Obs.] Digby.

aboriginal.c: Aboriginal Ab`o*rig"i*nal (?), a. [See Aborigines.] 1. First; original; indigenous; primitive; native; as, the aboriginal tribes of America. “Mantled o'er with aboriginal turf.” Wordsworth.
Aboriginal Ab`o*rig"i*nal, n. 1. An original inhabitant of any land; one of the aborigines.

aboriginality.c: Aboriginality Ab`o*rig`i*nal"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being aboriginal. Westm. Rev.

aborigines.c: Aborigines Ab`o*rig"i*nes (-rĭj"ĭ*nēz), n. pl. [L. Aborigines; ab + origo, especially the first inhabitants of Latium, those who originally (ab origine) inhabited Latium or Italy. See Origin.] 1. The earliest known inhabitants of a country; native races.

aborsement.c: Aborsement A*borse"ment (ȧ*bôrs"meint), n. Abortment; abortion. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

abort.c: Abort A*bort" (ȧ*bôrt"), v. i. [L. abortare, fr. abortus, p. p. of aboriri; ab + oriri to rise, to be born. See Orient.]
Abort A*bort", n. [L. abortus, fr. aboriri.] 1. An untimely birth. [Obs.] Sir H. Wotton.

aborticide.c: Aborticide A*bor"ti*cide (ȧ*bôr"tĭ*sīd), n. [L. abortus + caedere to kill. See Abort.] (Med.) The act of destroying a fetus in the womb; feticide. [archaic] AS

abortifacient.c: Abortifacient A*bor`ti*fa"cient (ȧ*bôr`tĭ*fā"sheint), a. [L. abortus (see Abort, v.) + faciens, p. pr. of facere to make.] Producing miscarriage. -- n. A drug or an agent that causes premature delivery.

abortion.c: Abortion A*bor"tion (ȧ*bôr"shŭn), n. [L. abortio, fr. aboriri. See Abort.] 1. The act of giving premature birth; particularly, the expulsion of the human fetus prematurely, or before it is capable of sustaining life; miscarriage.

abortional.c: Abortional A*bor"tion*al (?), a. Pertaining to abortion; miscarrying; abortive. Carlyle.

abortionist.c: Abortionist A*bor"tion*ist, n. One who performs or procures abortion; among medical personnel, also called an abortion provider.

abortive.c: Abortive A*bor"tive (?), a. [L. abortivus, fr. aboriri. See Abort, v.] 1. Produced by abortion.as, an abortive child. [R.]
Abortive A*bor"tive, n. 1. That which is born or brought forth prematurely; an abortion. [Obs.] Shak.

abortively.c: Abortively A*bor"tive*ly, adv. In an abortive or untimely manner; immaturely; fruitlessly.

abortiveness.c: Abortiveness A*bor"tive*ness, n. The quality of being abortive.

abought.c: Abought A*bought" (?), imp. & p. p. of Aby. [Obs.]

abound.c: Abound A*bound" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Abounded; p. pr. & vb. n. Abounding.] [OE. abounden, F. abonder, fr. L. abundare to overflow, abound; ab + unda wave. Cf. Undulate.] 1. To be in great plenty; to be very prevalent; to be plentiful.

about.c: About A*bout" (?), prep. [OE. aboute, abouten, abuten; AS. ābutan, onbutan; on + butan, which is from be by + utan outward, from ut out. See But, Out.]
About A*bout", adv. 1. On all sides; around.

aboutsledge.c: About-sledge A*bout"-sledge" (?), n. The largest hammer used by smiths. Weale.

above.c: Above A*bove" (?), prep. [OE. above, aboven, abuffe, AS. abufon; an (or on) on + be by + ufan upward; cf. Goth. uf under. √199. See Over.] 1. In or to a higher place; higher than; on or over the upper surface; over; -- opposed to below or beneath.
Above A*bove" (?), adv. 1. In a higher place; overhead; into or from heaven; as, the clouds above.

aboveboard.c: Aboveboard A*bove"board` (?), adv. Above the board or table. Hence: in open sight; without trick, concealment, or deception. “Fair and aboveboard.” Burke.

abovecited.c: Above-cited A*bove"-cit`ed (?), a. Cited before, in the preceding part of a book or writing.

abovedeck.c: Abovedeck A*bove"deck` (?), a. On deck; and hence, like aboveboard, without artifice. Smart.

abovenamed.c: Above-named Above-mentioned A*bove"-men`tioned (?), A*bove"-named` (?), a. Mentioned or named before; aforesaid; mentioned or named earlier in the same text (in written documents).

abovesaid.c: Abovesaid A*bove"said` (?), a. Mentioned or recited before.

abra.c: Abra ‖A"bra (?), n. [Sp., a bay, valley, fissure.] A narrow pass or defile; a break in a mesa; the mouth of a cañon. [Southwestern U. S.]

abracadabra.c: Abracadabra Ab`ra*ca*dab"ra (?), n. [L. Of unknown origin.] A mystical word or collocation of letters written as in the figure. Worn on an amulet it was supposed to ward off fever. At present the word is used chiefly in jest to denote something without meaning; jargon.

abradant.c: Abradant Ab*ra"dant (?), n. A material used for grinding, as emery, sand, powdered glass, etc.

abrade.c: Abrade Ab*rade" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abraded; p. pr. & vb. n. Abrading.] [L. abradere, abrasum, to scrape off; ab + radere to scrape. See Rase, Raze.] To rub or wear off; to waste or wear away by friction; as, to abrade rocks. Lyell.
Abrade A*brade" (?), v. t. Same as Abraid. [Obs.]

abrahamic.c: Abrahamic A`bra*ham"ic (?), a. Pertaining to Abraham, the patriarch; as, the Abrachamic covenant.

abramman.c: Abram-man Abraham-man A"bra*ham-man` (?) or A"bram-man` (?), n. [Possibly in allusion to the parable of the beggar Lazarus in Luke xvi. Murray (New Eng. Dict.).] One of a set of vagabonds who formerly roamed through England, feigning lunacy for the sake of obtaining alms. Nares.

abraid.c: Abraid A*braid" (?), v. t. & i. [OE. abraiden, to awake, draw (a sword), AS. ābredgan to shake, draw; pref. ā- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + bregdan to shake, throw. See Braid.] To awake; to arouse; to stir or start up; also, to shout out. [Obs.] Chaucer.

abranchiata.c: Abranchiata ‖A*bran`chi*a"ta (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr. 'a priv. +?, pl., the gills of fishes.] (Zool.) A group of annelids, so called because the species composing it have no special organs of respiration.

abrase.c: Abrase Ab*rase" (?), a. [L. abrasus, p. p. of abradere. See Abrade.] Rubbed smooth. [Obs.] “An abrase table.” B. Jonson.

abrasion.c: Abrasion Ab*ra"sion (?), n. [L. abrasio, fr. abradere. See Abrade.] 1. The act of abrading, wearing, or rubbing off; the wearing away by friction; as, the abrasion of coins.

abraum.c: Abraum salts Abraum A*braum" or A*braum" salts (?), n. [Ger., fr. abräumen to remove.] A red ocher used to darken mahogany and for making chloride of potassium.

abraxas.c: Abraxas ‖A*brax"as (?), n. [A name adopted by the Egyptian Gnostic Basilides, containing the Greek letters α, β, ρ, α, ξ, α, σ, which, as numerals, amounted to 365. It was used to signify the supreme deity as ruler of the 365 heavens of his system.] A mystical word used as a charm and engraved on gems among the ancients; also, a gem stone thus engraved.

abray.c: Abray A*bray" (?), v. [A false form from the preterit abraid, abrayde.] See Abraid. [Obs.] Spenser.

abreaction.c: Abreaction Ab`re*ac"tion (?), n. [Pref. ab- + reaction, after G. Abreagirung.] (Psychotherapy) the purging of emotional tensions. See Catharsis, below.

abreast.c: Abreast A*breast" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + breast.] 1. Side by side, with breasts in a line; as, “Two men could hardly walk abreast.” Macaulay.

abrenounce.c: Abrenounce Ab`re*nounce" (?), v. t. [L. abrenuntiare; ab + renuntiare. See Renounce.] To renounce. [Obs.] “They abrenounce and cast them off.” Latimer.

abrenunciation.c: Abrenunciation Ab`re*nun`ci*a"tion (?), n. [LL. abrenuntiatio. See Abrenounce.] Absolute renunciation or repudiation. [Obs.]

abreption.c: Abreption Ab*rep"tion (?), n. [L. abreptus, p. p. of abripere to snatch away; ab + rapere to snatch.] A snatching away. [Obs.]

abreuvoir.c: Abreuvoir ‖A`breu`voir" (?), n. [F., a watering place.] (Masonry) The joint or interstice between stones, to be filled with mortar. Gwilt.

abridge.c: Abridge A*bridge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abridged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abridging.] [OE. abregen, OF. abregier, F. abréger, fr. L. abbreviare; ad + brevis short. See Brief and cf. Abbreviate.] 1. To make shorter; to shorten in duration; to lessen; to diminish; to curtail; as, to abridge labor; to abridge power or rights. “The bridegroom... abridged his visit.” Smollett.

abridgment.c: Abridgment A*bridg"ment (-brĭj"meint), n. [OE. abregement. See Abridge.] 1. The act of abridging, or the state of being abridged; diminution; lessening; reduction or deprivation; as, an abridgment of pleasures or of expenses.

abroach.c: Abroach A*broach" (?), v. t. [OE. abrochen, OF. abrochier. See Broach.] To set abroach; to let out, as liquor; to broach; to tap. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Abroach A*broach", adv. [Pref. a- + broach.] 1. Broached; in a condition for letting out or yielding liquor, as a cask which is tapped.

abroad.c: Abroad A*broad" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + broad.] 1. At large; widely; broadly; over a wide space; as, a tree spreads its branches abroad.

abrogable.c: Abrogable Ab"ro*ga*ble (?), a. Capable of being abrogated.

abrogate.c: Abrogate Ab"ro*gate (?), a. [L. abrogatus, p. p.] Abrogated; abolished. [Obs.] Latimer.

Abrogate Ab"ro*gate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abrogated; p. pr. & vb. n. Abrogating.] [L. abrogatus, p. p. of abrogare; ab + rogare to ask, require, propose. See Rogation.] 1. To annul by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or his successor; to repeal; -- applied to the repeal of laws, decrees, ordinances, the abolition of customs, etc.

abrogation.c: Abrogation Ab`ro*ga"tion (?), n. [L. abrogatio, fr. abrogare: cf. F. abrogation.] The act of abrogating; repeal by authority. Hume.

abrogative.c: Abrogative Ab"ro*ga*tive (?), a. Tending or designed to abrogate; as, an abrogative law.

abrogator.c: Abrogator Ab"ro*ga`tor (?), n. One who repeals by authority.

abrood.c: Abrood A*brood" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + brood.] In the act of brooding. [Obs.] Abp. Sancroft.

abrook.c: Abrook A*brook" (?), v. t. [Pref. a- + brook, v.] To brook; to endure. [Obs.] Shak.

abrupt.c: Abrupt Ab*rupt" (?), a. [L. abruptus, p. p. of abrumpere to break off; ab + rumpere to break. See Rupture.] 1. Broken off; very steep, or craggy, as rocks, precipices, banks; precipitous; steep; as, abrupt places. “Tumbling through ricks abrupt,” Thomson.
Abrupt Ab*rupt" (?), n. [L. abruptum.] An abrupt place. [Poetic] “Over the vast abrupt.” Milton.
Abrupt Ab*rupt", v. t. To tear off or asunder. [Obs.] “Till death abrupts them.” Sir T. Browne.

abruption.c: Abruption Ab*rup"tion (?), n. [L. abruptio, fr. abrumpere: cf. F. abruption.] A sudden breaking off; a violent separation of bodies. Woodward.

abruptly.c: Abruptly Ab*rupt"ly, adv. 1. In an abrupt manner; without giving notice, or without the usual forms; suddenly.

abruptlypinnate.c: abruptly-pinnate Abruptly pinnate Abruptly pinnate, abruptly-pinnate adj. 1. (Bot.) pinnate with a pair of leaflets at the apex, i.e. without an odd leaflet, or other appendage, at the end; -- said of a leaf shape

abruptness.c: Abruptness Ab*rupt"ness, n. 1. The state of being abrupt or broken; craggedness; ruggedness; steepness.

abscess.c: Abscess Ab"scess (ăb"sĕs), n.; pl. Abscesses (ăb"sĕs*ĕz). [L. abscessus a going away, gathering of humors, abscess, fr. abscessus, p. p. of absedere to go away; ab, abs + cedere to go off, retire. See Cede.] (Med.) A collection of pus or purulent matter in any tissue or organ of the body caused by infection.

abscession.c: Abscession Ab*sces"sion (?), n. [L. abscessio a separation; fr. absedere. See Abscess.] A separating; removal; also, an abscess. [Obs.] Gauden. Barrough.

abscind.c: Abscind Ab*scind" (?), v. t. [L. absindere; ab + scindere to rend, cut. See Schism.] To cut off. [R.] “Two syllables... abscinded from the rest.” Johnson.

absciss.c: Absciss Ab"sciss (?), n.; pl. Abscisses (?). See Abscissa.

abscissa.c: Abscissa Ab*scis"sa (?), n.; E. pl. Abscissas, L. pl. Abscissæ. [L., fem. of abscissus, p. p. of absindere to cut of. See Abscind.] (Geom.) One of the elements of reference by which a point, as of a curve, is referred to a system of fixed rectilineal coördinate axes.

abscission.c: Abscission Ab*scis"sion (?), n. [L. abscissio. See Abscind.] 1. The act or process of cutting off. “Not to be cured without the abscission of a member.” Jer. Taylor.

abscond.c: Abscond Ab*scond" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Absconded; p. pr. & vb. n. Absconding.] [L. abscondere to hide; ab, abs + condere to lay up; con + dăre (only in comp.) to put. Cf. Do.] 1. To hide, withdraw, or be concealed.
Abscond Ab*scond", v. t. To hide; to conceal. [Obs.] Bentley.

abscondence.c: Abscondence Ab*scond"ence (?), n. Fugitive concealment; secret retirement; hiding. [R.] Phillips.

absence.c: Absence Ab"sence (?), n. [F., fr. L. absentia. See Absent.] 1. A state of being absent or withdrawn from a place or from companionship; -- opposed to presence.

absent.c: Absent Ab"sent (?), a. [F., fr. absens, absentis, p. pr. of abesse to be away from; ab + esse to be. Cf. Sooth.] 1. Being away from a place; withdrawn from a place; not present. “Expecting absent friends.” Shak.

Absent Ab*sent" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Absented; p. pr. & vb. n. Absenting.] [Cf. F. absenter.] 1. To take or withdraw (one's self) to such a distance as to prevent intercourse; -- used with the reflexive pronoun.

absentaneous.c: Absentaneous Ab`sen*ta"ne*ous (?), a. [LL. absentaneus. See absent] Pertaining to absence. [Obs.]

absentation.c: Absentation Ab`sen*ta"tion (?), n. The act of absenting one's self. Sir W. Hamilton.

absentee.c: Absentee Ab`sen*tee" (?), n. One who absents himself from his country, office, post, or duty; especially, a landholder who lives in another country or district than that where his estate is situated; as, an Irish absentee. Macaulay.

absenteeism.c: Absenteeism Ab`sen*tee"ism (?), n. The state or practice of an absentee; esp. the practice of absenting one's self from the country or district where one's estate is situated.

absenter.c: Absenter Ab*sent"er (?), n. One who absents one's self.

absently.c: Absently Ab"sent*ly (?), adv. In an absent or abstracted manner.

absentment.c: Absentment Ab*sent"ment (ăb*sĕnt"meint), n. The state of being absent; withdrawal. [R.] Barrow.

absentminded.c: Absent-minded Ab`sent-mind"ed (?), a. Absent in mind; abstracted; preoccupied. -- Ab`sent-mind"ed*ness, n. -- Ab`sent-mind"ed*ly, adv.

absentness.c: Absentness Ab"sent*ness (?), n. The quality of being absent-minded. H. Miller.

abseybook.c: Absey-book Ab"sey-book` (?), n. An A-B-C book; a primer. [Obs.] Shak.

absinthe.c: Absinthe Absinth { Ab"sinth`, Ab"sinthe` } (ăb"sĭnth`), n. [F. absinthe. See Absinthium.] 1. The plant absinthium or common wormwood.

absinthate.c: Absinthate Ab"sin"thate (ăb*sĭn"that), n. (Chem.) A combination of absinthic acid with a base or positive radical.

absinthial.c: Absinthial Ab*sin"thi*al (ăb*sĭn"thĭ*ail), a. Of or pertaining to wormwood; absinthian.

absinthian.c: Absinthian Ab*sin"thi*an (?), n. Of the nature of wormwood. “Absinthian bitterness.” T. Randolph.

absinthiate.c: Absinthiate Ab"sin"thi*ate (?), v. t. [From L. absinthium: cf. L. absinthiatus, a.] To impregnate with wormwood.

absinthiated.c: Absinthiated Ab*sin"thi*a`ted (?), a. Impregnated with wormwood; as, absinthiated wine.

absinthic.c: Absinthic Ab*sin"thic (?), a. (Chem.) Relating to the common wormwood or to an acid obtained from it.

absinthin.c: Absinthin Ab*sin"thin (?), n. (Chem.) The bitter principle of wormwood (Artemisia absinthium). Watts.

absinthism.c: Absinthism Ab"sin*thism (?), n. The condition of being poisoned by the excessive use of absinth.

absinthium.c: Absinthium Ab*sin"thi*um (?), n. [L., from Gr.?.] (Bot.) The common wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), an intensely bitter plant, used as a tonic and for making the oil of wormwood.

absist.c: Absist Ab*sist" (?), v. i. [L. absistere, p. pr. absistens; ab + sistere to stand, causal of stare.] To stand apart from; top leave off; to desist. [Obs.] Raleigh.

absolute.c: Absolute Ab"so*lute (?), a. [L. absolutus, p. p. of absolvere: cf. F. absolu. See Absolve.] 1. Loosed from any limitation or condition; uncontrolled; unrestricted; unconditional; as, absolute authority, monarchy, sovereignty, an absolute promise or command; absolute power; an absolute monarch.
Absolute Ab"so*lute (?), n. (Geom.) In a plane, the two imaginary circular points at infinity; in space of three dimensions, the imaginary circle at infinity.

absolutely.c: Absolutely Ab"so*lute*ly, adv. In an absolute, independent, or unconditional manner; wholly; positively.

absoluteness.c: Absoluteness Ab"so*lute*ness, n. The quality of being absolute; independence of everything extraneous; unlimitedness; absolute power; independent reality; positiveness.

absolution.c: Absolution Ab`so*lu"tion (?), n. [F. absolution, L. absolutio, fr. absolvere to absolve. See Absolve.] 1. An absolving, or setting free from guilt, sin, or penalty; forgiveness of an offense. “Government... granting absolution to the nation.” Froude.

absolutism.c: Absolutism Ab"so*lu`tism (?), n. 1. The state of being absolute; the system or doctrine of the absolute; the principles or practice of absolute or arbitrary government; despotism.

absolutist.c: Absolutist Ab"so*lu`tist (?), n. 1. One who is in favor of an absolute or autocratic government.
Absolutist Ab"so*lu`tist, a. Of or pertaining to absolutism; arbitrary; despotic; as, absolutist principles.

absolutistic.c: Absolutistic Ab`so*lu*tis"tic (?), a. Pertaining to absolutism; absolutist.

absolutory.c: Absolutory Ab*sol"u*to*ry (?), a. [L. absolutorius, fr. absolvere to absolve.] Serving to absolve; absolving. “An absolutory sentence.” Ayliffe.

absolvable.c: Absolvable Ab*solv"a*ble (?), a. That may be absolved.

absolve.c: Absolve Ab*solve" (#; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Absolved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Absolving.] [L. absolvere to set free, to absolve; ab + solvere to loose. See Assoil, Solve.] 1. To set free, or release, as from some obligation, debt, or responsibility, or from the consequences of guilt or such ties as it would be sin or guilt to violate; to pronounce free; as, to absolve a subject from his allegiance; to absolve an offender, which amounts to an acquittal and remission of his punishment.

absolvent.c: Absolvent Ab*solv"ent (?), a. [L. absolvens, p. pr. of absolvere.] Absolving. [R.] Carlyle.

absolver.c: Absolver Ab*solv"er (?), n. One who absolves. Macaulay.

absonant.c: Absonant Ab"so*nant (?), a. [L. ab + sonans, p. pr. of sonare to sound.] Discordant; contrary; -- opposed to consonant. “Absonant to nature.” Quarles.

absonous.c: Absonous Ab"so*nous (?), a. [L. absonus; ab + sonus sound.] Discordant; inharmonious; incongruous. [Obs.] “Absonous to our reason.” Glanvill.

absorb.c: Absorb Ab*sorb" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Absorbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Absorbing.] [L. absorbere; ab + sorbere to suck in, akin to Gr.?: cf. F. absorber.] 1. To swallow up; to engulf; to overwhelm; to cause to disappear as if by swallowing up; to use up; to include. “Dark oblivion soon absorbs them all.” Cowper.

absorbability.c: Absorbability Ab*sorb`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being absorbable. Graham (Chemistry).

absorbable.c: Absorbable Ab*sorb"a*ble, a. [Cf. F. absorbable.] Capable of being absorbed or swallowed up. Kerr.

absorbedly.c: Absorbedly Ab*sorb"ed*ly, adv. In a manner as if wholly engrossed or engaged.

absorbent.c: absorbent ab*sorb"ent (ăb*sôrb"eint), a. [L. absorbens, p. pr. of absorbere.] Absorbing; swallowing; absorptive.
Absorbent Ab*sorb"ent, n. 1. Anything which absorbs. AS

absorber.c: Absorber Ab*sorb"er (?), n. One who, or that which, absorbs.

absorbing.c: Absorbing Ab*sorb"ing, a. Swallowing, engrossing; as, an absorbing pursuit. -- Ab*sorb"ing, adv.

absorpt.c: Absorpt Ab*sorpt` (?), a. [L. absorptus, p. p.] Absorbed. [Arcahic.] “Absorpt in care.” Pope.

absorption.c: Absorption Ab*sorp"tion (?), n. [L. absorptio, fr. absorbere. See Absorb.] 1. The act or process of absorbing or sucking in anything, or of being absorbed and made to disappear; as, the absorption of bodies in a whirlpool, the absorption of a smaller tribe into a larger.

absorptive.c: Absorptive Ab*sorp"tive (?), a. Having power, capacity, or tendency to absorb or imbibe. E. Darwin.

absorptiveness.c: Absorptiveness Ab*sorp"tive*ness, n. The quality of being absorptive; absorptive power.

absquatulate.c: Absquatulate Ab*squat"u*late (?), v. i. To take one's self off; to decamp. [A jocular word. U. S.]

absque.c: Absque hoc ‖Abs"que hoc (?). [L., without this.] (Law) The technical words of denial used in traversing what has been alleged, and is repeated.

abstain.c: Abstain Ab*stain" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Abstained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abstaining.] [OE. absteynen, abstenen, OF. astenir, abstenir, F. abstenir, fr. L. abstinere, abstentum, v. t. & v. i., to keep from; ab, abs + tenere to hold. See Tenable.] To hold one's self aloof; to forbear or refrain voluntarily, and especially from an indulgence of the passions or appetites; -- with from.
Abstain Ab*stain", v. t. To hinder; to withhold.

abstainer.c: Abstainer Ab*stain"er (?), n. One who abstains; esp., one who abstains from the use of intoxicating liquors.

abstemious.c: Abstemious Ab*ste"mi*ous (?), a. [L. abstemius; ab, abs + root of temetum intoxicating drink.] 1. Abstaining from wine. [Orig. Latin sense.]

abstemiousness.c: Abstemiousness Ab*ste"mi*ous*ness, n. The quality of being abstemious, temperate, or sparing in the use of food and strong drinks. It expresses a greater degree of abstinence than temperance.

abstention.c: Abstention Ab*sten"tion (?), a. [F. See Abstain.] The act of abstaining; a holding aloof. Jer. Taylor.

abstentious.c: Abstentious Ab*sten"tious (?), a. Characterized by abstinence; self-restraining. Farrar.

absterge.c: Absterge Ab*sterge (?), v. t. [L. abstergere, abstersum; ab, abs + tergere to wipe. Cf. F absterger.] To make clean by wiping; to wipe away; to cleanse; hence, to purge. [R.] Quincy.

abstergent.c: Abstergent Ab*ster"gent (?), a. [L. abstergens, p. pr. of abstergere.] Serving to cleanse, detergent.
Abstergent Ab*ster"gent, n. A substance used in cleansing; a detergent; as, soap is an abstergent.

absterse.c: Absterse Ab*sterse" (?), v. t. To absterge; to cleanse; to purge away. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

abstersion.c: Abstersion Ab*ster"sion (?), n. [F. abstersion. See Absterge.] Act of wiping clean; a cleansing; a purging.

abstersive.c: Abstersive Ab*ster"sive (?), a. [Cf. F. abstersif. See Absterge.] Cleansing; purging. Bacon.

abstersiveness.c: Abstersiveness Ab*ster"sive*ness, n. The quality of being abstersive. Fuller.

abstinence.c: Abstinence Ab"sti*nence (?), n. [F. abstinence, L. abstinentia, fr. abstinere. See Abstain.] 1. The act or practice of abstaining; voluntary forbearance of any action, especially the refraining from an indulgence of appetite, or from customary gratifications of animal or sensual propensities. Specifically, the practice of abstaining from intoxicating beverages, -- called also total abstinence.

abstinent.c: Abstinent Ab"sti*nent (?), a. [F. abstinent, L. abstinens, p. pr. of abstinere. See Abstain.] Refraining from indulgence, especially from the indulgence of appetite; abstemious; continent; temperate. Beau. & Fl.

abstorted.c: Abstorted Ab*stort"ed (?), a. [As if fr. abstort, fr. L. ab, abs + tortus, p. p. of torquere to twist.] Wrested away. [Obs.] Bailey.

abstract.c: Abstract Ab"stract` (#; 277), a. [L. abstractus, p. p. of abstrahere to draw from, separate; ab, abs + trahere to draw. See Trace.] 1. Withdraw; separate. [Obs.]
Abstract Ab*stract" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abstracted; p. pr. & vb. n. Abstracting.] [See Abstract, a.]
Abstract Ab*stract", v. t. To perform the process of abstraction. [R.]

Abstract Ab"stract` (?), n. [See Abstract, a.] 1. That which comprises or concentrates in itself the essential qualities of a larger thing or of several things. Specifically: A summary or an epitome, as of a treatise or book, or of a statement; a brief.

abstracted.c: Abstracted Ab*stract"ed (?), a. 1. Separated or disconnected; withdrawn; removed; apart.

abstractedly.c: Abstractedly Ab*stract"ed*ly, adv. In an abstracted manner; separately; with absence of mind.

abstractedness.c: Abstractedness Ab*stract"ed*ness, n. The state of being abstracted; abstract character.

abstracter.c: Abstracter Ab*stract"er (?), n. One who abstracts, or makes an abstract.

abstraction.c: Abstraction Ab*strac"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. abstraction. See Abstract, a.] 1. The act of abstracting, separating, or withdrawing, or the state of being withdrawn; withdrawal.

abstractitious.c: Abstractitious Ab`strac*ti"tious (?), a. Obtained from plants by distillation. [Obs.] Crabb.

abstractive.c: Abstractive Ab*strac"tive (?), a. [Cf. F. abstractif.] Having the power of abstracting; of an abstracting nature. “The abstractive faculty.” I. Taylor.

abstractively.c: Abstractively Ab*strac"tive*ly, adv. In a abstract manner; separately; in or by itself. Feltham.

abstractiveness.c: Abstractiveness Ab*strac"tive*ness, n. The quality of being abstractive; abstractive property.

abstractly.c: Abstractly Ab"stract`ly (#; 277), adv. In an abstract state or manner; separately; absolutely; by itself; as, matter abstractly considered.

abstractness.c: Abstractness Ab"stract`ness, n. The quality of being abstract. “The abstractness of the ideas.” Locke.

abstringe.c: Abstringe Ab*stringe" (?), v. t. [L ab + stringere, strictum, to press together.] To unbind. [Obs.] Bailey.

abstrude.c: Abstrude Ab*strude" (?), v. t. [L. abstrudere. See Abstruse.] To thrust away. [Obs.] Johnson.

abstruse.c: Abstruse Ab*struse" (?), a. [L. abstrusus, p. p. of abstrudere to thrust away, conceal; ab, abs + trudere to thrust; cf. F. abstrus. See Threat.] 1. Concealed or hidden out of the way. [Obs.]

abstrusely.c: Abstrusely Ab*struse"ly, adv. In an abstruse manner.

abstruseness.c: Abstruseness Ab*struse"ness, n. The quality of being abstruse; difficulty of apprehension. Boyle.

abstrusion.c: Abstrusion Ab*stru"sion (?), n. [L. abstrusio. See Abstruse.] The act of thrusting away. [R.] Ogilvie.

abstrusity.c: Abstrusity Ab*stru"si*ty (ăb*strü"sĭ*ty̆), n. Abstruseness; that which is abstruse. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

absume.c: Absume Ab*sume" (ăb*sūm"), v. t. [L. absumere, absumptum; ab + sumere to take.] To consume gradually; to waste away. [Obs.] Boyle.

absumption.c: Absumption Ab*sump"tion (ăb*sŭmp"shŭn; 215), n. [L. absumptio. See Absume.] Act of wasting away; a consuming; extinction. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

absurd.c: Absurd Ab*surd" (ăb*sûrd"), a. [L. absurdus harsh-sounding; ab + (prob) a derivative fr. a root svar to sound; not connected with surd: cf. F. absurde. See Syringe.] Contrary to reason or propriety; obviously and flatly opposed to manifest truth; inconsistent with the plain dictates of common sense; logically contradictory; nonsensical; ridiculous; as, an absurd person, an absurd opinion; an absurd dream.

absurdity.c: Absurdity Ab*surd"i*ty (-ĭ*ty̆), n.; pl. Absurdities (-tĭz). [L. absurditas: cf. F. absurdite.] 1. The quality of being absurd or inconsistent with obvious truth, reason, or sound judgment. “The absurdity of the actual idea of an infinite number.” Locke.

absurdly.c: Absurdly Ab*surd"ly, adv. In an absurd manner.

abuna.c: Abuna ‖A*bu"na (ȧ*bōo"nȧ), n. [Eth. and Ar., our father.] The Patriarch, or head of the Abyssinian Church.

abundance.c: Abundance A*bun"dance (ȧ*bŭn"dains), n. [OE. (h)abundaunce, abundance, F. abondance, L. abundantia, fr. abundare. See Abound.] An overflowing fullness; ample sufficiency; great plenty; profusion; copious supply; superfluity; wealth: -- strictly applicable to quantity only, but sometimes used of number.

abundant.c: Abundant A*bun"dant (?), a. [OE. (h)abundant, aboundant, F. abondant, fr. L. abudans, p. pr. of abundare. See Abound.] Fully sufficient; plentiful; in copious supply; -- followed by in, rarely by with. “Abundant in goodness and truth.” Exod. xxxiv. 6.

abundantly.c: Abundantly A*bun"dant*ly, adv. In a sufficient degree; fully; amply; plentifully; in large measure.

aburst.c: Aburst A*burst" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + burst.] In a bursting condition.

abusable.c: Abusable A*bus"a*ble (?), a. That may be abused.

abuse.c: Abuse A*buse" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Abused (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Abusing.] [F. abuser; L. abusus, p. p. of abuti to abuse, misuse; ab + uti to use. See Use.] 1. To put to a wrong use; to misapply; to misuse; to put to a bad use; to use for a wrong purpose or end; to pervert; as, to abuse inherited gold; to make an excessive use of; as, to abuse one's authority.

Abuse A*buse" (?), n. [F. abus, L. abusus, fr. abuti. See Abuse, v. t.] 1. Improper treatment or use; application to a wrong or bad purpose; misuse; as, an abuse of our natural powers; an abuse of civil rights, or of privileges or advantages; an abuse of language.

abuseful.c: Abuseful A*buse"ful (?), a. Full of abuse; abusive. [R.] “Abuseful names.” Bp. Barlow.

abuser.c: Abuser A*bus"er (?), n. One who abuses [in the various senses of the verb].

abusion.c: Abusion A*bu"sion (?), n. [OE. abusion, abusioun, OF. abusion, fr. L. abusio misuse of words, f. abuti. See Abuse, v. t.] Evil or corrupt usage; abuse; wrong; reproach; deception; cheat. Chaucer.

abusive.c: Abusive A*bu"sive (?), a. [Cf. F. abusif, fr. L. abusivus.] 1. Wrongly used; perverted; misapplied.

abusively.c: Abusively A*bu"sive*ly, adv. In an abusive manner; rudely; with abusive language.

abusiveness.c: Abusiveness A*bu"sive*ness, n. The quality of being abusive; rudeness of language, or violence to the person.

abut.c: Abut A*but" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Abutted; p. pr. & vb. n. Abutting.] [OF. abouter, aboter; cf. F. aboutir, and also abuter; a (L. ad) + OF. boter, buter, to push: cf. F. bout end, and but end, purpose.] To project; to terminate or border; to be contiguous; to meet; -- with on, upon, or against; as, his land abuts on the road.

abutilon.c: Abutilon A*bu"ti*lon (?), n. [Ar. aubūtīlūn.] (Bot.) A genus of malvaceous plants of many species, found in the torrid and temperate zones of both continents; -- called also Indian mallow.

abuttal.c: Abuttal A*but"tal (?), n. The butting or boundary of land, particularly at the end; a headland. Spelman.

abutter.c: Abutter A*but"ter (?), n. One who, or that which, abuts. Specifically, the owner of a contiguous estate; as, the abutters on a street or a river.

abuzz.c: Abuzz A*buzz" (?), a. [Pref. a- + buzz.] In a buzz; buzzing. [Colloq.] Dickens.

abye.c: Abye Aby { A*by", A*bye" } (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Abought (?).] [AS. ābycgan to pay for; pref. ā- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + bycgan to buy. See Buy, and cf. Abide.] 1. To pay for; to suffer for; to atone for; to make amends for; to give satisfaction. [Obs.]

abysm.c: Abysm A*bysm" (?), n. [OF. abisme; F. abime, LL. abyssimus, a superl. of L. abyssus; Gr.?. See Abyss.] An abyss; a gulf. “The abysm of hell.” Shak.

abysmal.c: Abysmal A*bys"mal (?), a. Pertaining to, or resembling, an abyss; bottomless; unending; profound.

abysmally.c: Abysmally A*bys"mal*ly, adv. To a fathomless depth; profoundly. “Abysmally ignorant.” G. Eliot.

abyss.c: Abyss A*byss" (?), n. [L. abyssus a bottomless gulf, fr. Gr.? bottomless; 'a priv. +? depth, bottom.] 1. A bottomless or unfathomed depth, gulf, or chasm; hence, any deep, immeasurable, and, specifically, hell, or the bottomless pit.

abyssal.c: Abyssal A*byss"al (?), a. [Cf. Abysmal.] Belonging to, or resembling, an abyss; unfathomable.

abyssinian.c: Abyssinian Ab`ys*sin"i*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Abyssinia.
Abyssinian Ab`ys*sin"i*an, n. 1. A native of Abyssinia.

acacia.c: Acacia A*ca"ci*a (?), n. (Antiq.) A roll or bag, filled with dust, borne by Byzantine emperors, as a memento of mortality. It is represented on medals.

acacia a*ca"cia (ȧ*kā"shȧ or ȧ*kā"shĭ*ȧ), n.; pl. E. acacias (ȧ*kā"shȧz), L. acaciae (ȧ*kā"shĭ*ē). [L. from Gr. 'akaki`a; orig. the name of a thorny tree found in Egypt; prob. fr. the root ak to be sharp. See Acute.] 1. [capitalized] A genus of leguminous trees and shrubs. Nearly 300 species are Australian or Polynesian, and have terete or vertically compressed leaf stalks, instead of the bipinnate leaves of the much fewer species of America, Africa, etc. Very few are found in temperate climates.

acacine.c: Acacine Acacin Ac"a*cin, Ac"a*cine (?), n. Gum arabic.

academe.c: Academe Ac`a*deme" (?), n. [L. academia. See Academy.] An academy. [Poetic] Shak.

academian.c: Academian Ac`a*de"mi*an (?), n. A member of an academy, university, or college.

academical.c: Academical Academic { Ac`a*dem"ic (?), Ac`a*dem"ic*al (?), } a. [L. academicus: cf. F. académigue. See Academy.] 1. Belonging to the school or philosophy of Plato; as, the Academic sect or philosophy.

academic.c: Academic Ac`a*dem"ic, n. 1. One holding the philosophy of Socrates and Plato; a Platonist. Hume.

academically.c: Academically Ac`a*dem`ic*al*ly, adv. In an academical manner.

academicals.c: Academicals Ac`a*dem"ic*als (?), n. pl. The articles of dress prescribed and worn at some colleges and universities.

academician.c: Academician Ac`a*de*mi"cian (#; 277), n. [F. académicien. See Academy.] 1. A member of an academy, or society for promoting science, art, or literature, as of the French Academy, or the Royal Academy of arts.

academicism.c: Academicism Ac`a*dem"i*cism (?), n. 1. A tenet of the Academic philosophy.

academism.c: Academism A*cad"e*mism (?), n. The doctrines of the Academic philosophy. [Obs.] Baxter.

academist.c: Academist A*cad"e*mist (?), n. [F. academiste.] 1. An Academic philosopher.

academy.c: Academy A*cad"e*my (?), n.; pl. Academies (?). [F. académie, L. academia. Cf. Academe.] 1. A garden or grove near Athens (so named from the hero Academus), where Plato and his followers held their philosophical conferences; hence, the school of philosophy of which Plato was head.

acadian.c: Acadian A*ca"di*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Acadia, or Nova Scotia. “Acadian farmers.” Longfellow. -- n. A native of Acadie.

acajou.c: Acajou ‖Ac"a*jou (?), n. [F. See Cashew.] (Bot.) (a) The cashew tree; also, its fruit. See Cashew. (b) The mahogany tree; also, its timber.

acalephan.c: Acalephan Acaleph { Ac"a*leph (?), Ac`a*le"phan (?) } n.; pl. Acalephs (?), Acalephans (?). [See Acalephæ.] (Zool.) One of the Acalephæ.

acalephae.c: Acalephae ‖Ac`a*le"phæ (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.?, a nettle.] A group of Cœlenterata, including the Medusæ or jellyfishes, and hydroids; -- so called from the stinging power they possess. Sometimes called sea nettles.

acalephoid.c: Acalephoid Ac`ale"phoid (?), a. [Acaleph + -oid.] (Zool.) Belonging to or resembling the Acalephæ or jellyfishes.

acalysinous.c: Acalysinous Acalycine A*cal"y*cine (?), Ac`a*lys`i*nous (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. +? calyx.] (Bot.) Without a calyx, or outer floral envelope.

acantha.c: Acantha ‖A*can"tha (?), n. [Gr.? thorn, fr.? point. See Acute.] 1. (Bot.) A prickle.

acanthaceous.c: Acanthaceous Ac"an*tha"ceous (?), a. 1. Armed with prickles, as a plant.

acanthine.c: Acanthine A*can"thine (?), a. [L. acanthinus, Gr.?, thorny, fr.?. See Acanthus.] Of, pertaining to, or resembling, the plant acanthus.

acanthocarpous.c: Acanthocarpous A*can`tho*car"pous (?), a. [Gr.? thorn +? fruit.] (Bot.) Having the fruit covered with spines.

acanthocephala.c: Acanthocephala ‖A*can`tho*ceph"a*la (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? a spine, thorn +? head.] (Zool.) A group of intestinal worms, having the proboscis armed with recurved spines.

acanthocephalous.c: Acanthocephalous A*can`tho*ceph"a*lous (?), a. (Zool.) Having a spiny head, as one of the Acanthocephala.

acanthophorous.c: Acanthophorous Ac`an*thoph"o*rous (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? spine + fe`rein to bear.] Spine-bearing. Gray.

acanthopodious.c: Acanthopodious A*can`tho*po"di*ous (?), a. [Gr.? thorn +?,?, foot.] (Bot.) Having spinous petioles.

acanthopteri.c: Acanthopteri ‖Ac`an*thop"ter*i (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? thorn +? wing, fin.] (Zool.) A group of teleostean fishes having spiny fins. See Acanthopterygii.
