acanthopterygian.c: Acanthopterygian Ac`an*thop`ter*yg"i*an (?), a. (Zool.) Belonging to the order of fishes having spinose fins, as the perch. -- n. A spiny-finned fish.

acanthopterygii.c: Acanthopterygii ‖Ac`an*thop`ter*yg"i*i (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? thorn +? fin, dim. fr.? wing.] (Zool.) An order of fishes having some of the rays of the dorsal, ventral, and anal fins unarticulated and spinelike, as the perch.

acanthopterygious.c: Acanthopterygious Ac`an*thop`ter*yg"i*ous (?), a. (Zool.) Having fins in which the rays are hard and spinelike; spiny-finned.

acanthus.c: Acanthus A*can"thus (?), n.; pl. E. Acanthuses (?), L. Acanthi (?). [L., from Gr.?. Cf. Acantha.]

acapsular.c: Acapsular A*cap"su*lar (?), a. [Pref. a- not + capsular.] (Bot.) Having no capsule.

acardiac.c: Acardiac A*car"di*ac (?), a. [Gr.?; 'a priv. +? heart.] Without a heart; as, an acardiac fetus.

acaridan.c: Acaridan A*car"i*dan (?), n. [See Acarus.] (Zool.) One of a group of arachnids, including the mites and ticks.

acarina.c: Acarina ‖Ac`a*ri"na (?), prop. n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? a mite.] (Zool.) The order of Arachnida which includes the mites and ticks. Many species are parasitic, and cause diseases like the itch and mange.

acarine.c: acarine ac"a*rine (ăk"ȧ*rĭn), a. (Med.) Of or caused by acari (acarids, or mites); as, acarine diseases.

acaroid.c: Acaroid Ac"a*roid (?), a. [NL., acarus a mite + -oid.] (Zool.) Shaped like or resembling a mite.

acarpelous.c: acarpelous Acarpellous Ac`ar*pel"lous, ac`ar*pel"ous (?), a. [Pref. a- not + carpel.] (Bot.) Having no carpels. Opposite of carpellate.

acarpous.c: Acarpous A*car"pous (?), a. [Gr.?; 'a priv. + karpo`s fruit.] (Bot.) Not producing fruit; unfruitful.

acarus.c: Acarus ‖Ac"a*rus (?), n.; pl. Acari (?). [NL., from Gr.? the cheese mite, tick.] (Zool.) A genus including many species of small mites.

acatalectic.c: Acatalectic A*cat`a*lec"tic (?), a. [L. acatalecticus, Gr.?, not defective at the end; 'a priv. +? to cease.] (Pros.) Not defective; complete; as, an acatalectic verse. -- n. A verse which has the complete number of feet and syllables.

acatalepsy.c: Acatalepsy A*cat"a*lep`sy (?), n. [Gr.?; 'a priv. +? to seize, comprehend.] Incomprehensibility of things; the doctrine held by the ancient Skeptic philosophers, that human knowledge never amounts to certainty, but only to probability.

acataleptic.c: Acataleptic A*cat`a*lep"tic (?), a. [Gr.?.] Incapable of being comprehended; incomprehensible.

acaudate.c: Acaudate A*cau"date (?), a. [Pref. a- not + caudate.] Tailless.

acaulescent.c: Acaulescent Ac`au*les"cent (?), a. [Pref. a- not + caulescent.] (Bot.) Having no stem or caulis, or only a very short one concealed in the ground. Gray.

acauline.c: Acauline A*cau"line (?), a. [Pref. a- not + cauline.] (Bot.) Same as Acaulescent.

acaulous.c: Acaulous Acaulose { A*cau"lose (?), A*cau"lous (?), } a. [Gr.?; 'a priv. +? stalk or L. caulis stalk. See Cole.] (Bot.) Same as Acaulescent.

accadian.c: Accadian Ac*ca"di*an (?), a. [From the city Accad. See Gen. x. 10.] Pertaining to a race supposed to have lived in Babylonia before the Assyrian conquest.

accede.c: Accede Ac*cede" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Acceded; p. pr. & vb. n. Acceding.] [L. accedere to approach, accede; ad + cedere to move, yield: cf. F. accédere. See Cede.]

accedence.c: Accedence Ac*ced"ence (?), n. The act of acceding.

accelerate.c: Accelerate Ac*cel"er*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accelerated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Accelerating.] [L. acceleratus, p. p. of accelerare; ad + celerare to hasten; celer quick. See Celerity.] 1. To cause to move faster; to quicken the motion of; to add to the speed of; -- opposed to retard.

acceleration.c: Acceleration Ac*cel`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. acceleratio: cf. F. accélération.] The act of accelerating, or the state of being accelerated; increase of motion or action; as, a falling body moves toward the earth with an acceleration of velocity; -- opposed to retardation.

accelerative.c: Accelerative Ac*cel"er*a*tive (?), a. Relating to acceleration; adding to velocity; quickening. Reid.

accelerator.c: Accelerator Ac*cel"er*a`tor (?), n. One who, or that which, accelerates. Also as an adj.; as, accelerator nerves.

accelerograph.c: Accelerograph Ac*cel"er*o*graph (?), n. [Accelerate + -graph.] (Mil.) An apparatus for studying the combustion of powder in guns, etc.

accelerometer.c: Accelerometer Ac*cel`er*om"e*ter (?), n. [Accelerate + -meter.] An apparatus for measuring the velocity imparted by gunpowder.

accend.c: Accend Ac*cend" (?), v. t. [L. accendere, accensum, to kindle; ad + candĕre to kindle (only in compounds); rel. to candēre to be white, to gleam. See Candle.] To set on fire; to kindle. [Obs.] Fotherby.

accendibility.c: Accendibility Ac*cend`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. Capacity of being kindled, or of becoming inflamed; inflammability.

accendible.c: Accendible Ac*cend"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being inflamed or kindled; combustible; inflammable. Ure.

accension.c: Accension Ac*cen"sion (?), n. The act of kindling or the state of being kindled; ignition. Locke.

accensor.c: Accensor Ac*cen"sor (?), n. [LL., from p. p. accensus. See Accend.] (R. C. Ch.) One of the functionaries who light and trim the tapers.

accent.c: Accent Ac"cent` (?), n. [F. accent, L. accentus; ad + cantus a singing, canere to sing. See Cant.] 1. A superior force of voice or of articulative effort upon some particular syllable of a word or a phrase, distinguishing it from the others.
Accent Ac*cent" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accented; p. pr. & vb. n. Accenting.] [OF. accenter, F. accentuer.]

accentor.c: Accentor Ac*cen"tor (?), n. [L. ad. + cantor singer, canere to sing.] 1. (Mus.) One who sings the leading part; the director or leader. [Obs.]

accentuable.c: Accentuable Ac*cen"tu*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being accented.

accentual.c: Accentual Ac*cen"tu*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to accent; characterized or formed by accent.

accentuality.c: Accentuality Ac*cen`tu*al"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being accentual.

accentually.c: Accentually Ac*cen"tu*al*ly (?), adv. In an accentual manner; in accordance with accent.

accentuate.c: Accentuate Ac*cen"tu*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accentuated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Accentuating.] [LL. accentuatus, p. p. of accentuare, fr. L. accentus: cf. F. accentuer.] 1. To pronounce with an accent or with accents.

accentuation.c: Accentuation Ac*cen`tu*a"tion (?), n. [LL. accentuatio: cf. F. accentuation.] Act of accentuating; applications of accent. Specifically (Eccles. Mus.), pitch or modulation of the voice in reciting portions of the liturgy.

accept.c: Accept Ac*cept" (ăk*sĕpt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accepted; p. pr. & vb. n. Accepting.] [F. accepter, L. acceptare, freq. of accipere; ad + capere to take; akin to E. heave.]

acceptability.c: Acceptability Ac*cept`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [LL. acceptabilitas.] The quality of being acceptable; acceptableness. “Acceptability of repentance.” Jer. Taylor.

acceptable.c: Acceptable Ac*cept"a*ble (-sĕpt"ȧ*b'l; 277), a. [F. acceptable, L. acceptabilis, fr. acceptare.] Capable, worthy, or sure of being accepted or received with pleasure; pleasing to a receiver; gratifying; agreeable; welcome; as, an acceptable present, one acceptable to us.

acceptableness.c: Acceptableness Ac*cept"a*ble*ness (ăk*sĕpt"ȧ*b'l*nĕs), n. The quality of being acceptable, or suitable to be favorably received; acceptability.

acceptably.c: Acceptably Ac*cept"a*bly, adv. In an acceptable manner; in a manner to please or give satisfaction.

acceptance.c: Acceptance Ac*cept"ance (?), n. 1. The act of accepting; a receiving what is offered, with approbation, satisfaction, or acquiescence; esp., favorable reception; approval; as, the acceptance of a gift, office, doctrine, etc.

acceptation.c: Acceptation Ac`cep*ta"tion (?), n. 1. Acceptance; reception; favorable reception or regard; state of being acceptable. [Obs.]

acceptedly.c: Acceptedly Ac*cept"ed*ly (?), adv. In a accepted manner; admittedly.

accepter.c: Accepter Ac*cept"er (?), n. 1. A person who accepts; a taker.

acceptilation.c: Acceptilation Ac*cep`ti*la"tion (?), n. [L. acceptilatio entry of a debt collected, acquittance, fr. p. p. of accipere (cf. Accept) + latio a carrying, fr. latus, p. p. of ferre to carry: cf. F. acceptilation.] (Civil Law) Gratuitous discharge; a release from debt or obligation without payment; free remission.

acception.c: Acception Ac*cep"tion (?), n. [L. acceptio a receiving, accepting: cf. F. acception.] Acceptation; the received meaning. [Obs.]

acceptor.c: Acceptor Ac*cept"or (#; 277), n. [L.] One who accepts; specifically (Law & Com.), one who accepts an order or a bill of exchange; a drawee after he has accepted.

access.c: Access Ac*cess" (#; 277), n. [F. accès, L. accessus, fr. accedere. See Accede.] 1. A coming to, or near approach; admittance; admission; accessibility; as, to gain access to a prince.

accessarily.c: Accessarily Ac*ces"sa*ri*ly (?), adv. In the manner of an accessary.

accessariness.c: Accessariness Ac*ces"sa*ri*ness, n. The state of being accessary.

accessary.c: Accessary Ac*ces"sa*ry (#; 277), a. Accompanying, as a subordinate; additional; accessory; esp., uniting in, or contributing to, a crime, but not as chief actor. See Accessory.

Accessary Ac*ces"sa*ry (277), n.; pl. Accessaries (?). [Cf. Accessory and LL. accessarius.] (Law) One who, not being present, contributes as an assistant or instigator to the commission of an offense.

accessibility.c: Accessibility Ac*cess`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. accessibilitas: cf. F. accessibilité.] The quality of being accessible, or of admitting approach; receptibility. Langhorne.

accessible.c: Accessible Ac*cess"i*ble (?), a. [L. accessibilis, fr. accedere: cf. F. accessible. See Accede.] 1. Easy of access or approach; approachable; as, an accessible town or mountain, an accessible person.

accessibly.c: Accessibly Ac*cess"i*bly (?), adv. In an accessible manner.

accession.c: Accession Ac*ces"sion (?), n. [L. accessio, fr. accedere: cf. F. accession. See Accede.] 1. A coming to; the act of acceding and becoming joined; as, a king's accession to a confederacy.

accessional.c: Accessional Ac*ces"sion*al (?), a. Pertaining to accession; additional. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

accessorial.c: Accessorial Ac`ces*so"ri*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to an accessory; as, accessorial agency, accessorial guilt.

accessorily.c: Accessorily Ac*ces"so*ri*ly (?), adv. In the manner of an accessory; auxiliary.

accessoriness.c: Accessoriness Ac*ces"so*ri*ness, n. The state of being accessory, or connected subordinately.

accessory.c: Accessory Ac*ces"so*ry (#; 277), a. [L. accessorius. See Access, and cf. Accessary.] Accompanying as a subordinate; aiding in a secondary way; additional; connected as an incident or subordinate to a principal; contributing or contributory; said of persons and things, and, when of persons, usually in a bad sense; as, he was accessory to the riot; accessory sounds in music.

Accessory Ac*ces"so*ry, n.; pl. Accessories (?). 1. That which belongs to something else deemed the principal; something additional and subordinate. “The aspect and accessories of a den of banditti.” Carlyle.

acciaccatura.c: Acciaccatura ‖Ac*ciac`ca*tu"ra (?), n. [It., from acciaccare to crush.] (Mus.) A short grace note, one semitone below the note to which it is prefixed; -- used especially in organ music. Now used as equivalent to the short appoggiatura.

accidence.c: Accidence Ac"ci*dence (?), n. [A corruption of Eng. accidents, pl. of accident. See Accident, 2.] 1. The accidents, of inflections of words; the rudiments of grammar. Milton.

accident.c: Accident Ac"ci*dent (?), n. [F. accident, fr. L. accidens, -dentis, p. pr. of accidere to happen; ad + cadere to fall. See Cadence, Case.] 1. Literally, a befalling; an event that takes place without one's foresight or expectation; an undesigned, sudden, and unexpected event; chance; contingency; often, an undesigned and unforeseen occurrence of an afflictive or unfortunate character; a casualty; a mishap; as, to die by an accident.

accidental.c: Accidental Ac`ci*den"tal (?), a. [Cf. F. accidentel, earlier accidental.] 1. Happening by chance, or unexpectedly; taking place not according to the usual course of things; casual; fortuitous; as, an accidental visit.
Accidental Ac`ci*den"tal (?), n. 1. A property which is not essential; a nonessential; anything happening accidentally.

accidentalism.c: Accidentalism Ac`ci*den"tal*ism (?), n. Accidental character or effect. Ruskin.

accidentality.c: Accidentality Ac`ci*den*tal"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being accidental; accidentalness. [R.] Coleridge.

accidentally.c: Accidentally Ac`ci*den"tal*ly (?), adv. In an accidental manner; unexpectedly; by chance; unintentionally; casually; fortuitously; not essentially.

accidentalness.c: Accidentalness Ac`ci*den"tal*ness, n. The quality of being accidental; casualness.

accidie.c: Accidie Ac"ci*die (?), n. [OF. accide, accidie, LL. accidia, acedia, fr. Gr.?; 'a priv. +? care.] Sloth; torpor. [Obs.] “The sin of accidie.” Chaucer.

accipient.c: Accipient Ac*cip"i*ent (?), n. [L. accipiens, p. pr. of accipere. See Accept.] A receiver. [R.] Bailey

accipiter.c: Accipiter ‖Ac*cip"i*ter (?), n.; pl. E. Accipiters (?). L. Accipitres (?). [L., hawk.] 1. (Zool.) A genus of rapacious birds; one of the Accipitres or Raptores.

accipitral.c: Accipitral Ac*cip"i*tral (?), n. Pertaining to, or of the nature of, a falcon or hawk; hawklike. Lowell.

accipitres.c: Accipitres ‖Ac*cip"i*tres (?), n. pl. [L., hawks.] (Zool.) The order that includes rapacious birds. They have a hooked bill, and sharp, strongly curved talons. There are three families, represented by the vultures, the falcons or hawks, and the owls.

accipitrine.c: Accipitrine Ac*cip"i*trine (#; 277), a. [Cf. F. accipitrin.] (Zool.) Like or belonging to the Accipitres; raptorial; hawklike.

accismus.c: Accismus ‖Ac*cis"mus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?.] (Rhet.) Affected refusal; coyness.

accite.c: Accite Ac*cite" (?), v. t. [L. accitus, p. p. of accire, accere, to call for; ad + ciere to move, call. See Cite.] To cite; to summon. [Obs.]

acclaim.c: Acclaim Ac*claim" (?), v. t. [L. acclamare; ad + clamare to cry out. See Claim, Clamor.] [R.] 1. To applaud. “A glad acclaiming train.” Thomson.
Acclaim Ac*claim", v. i. To shout applause.

acclamation.c: Acclamation Ac`cla*ma"tion (?), n. [L. acclamatio: cf. F. acclamation.] 1. A shout of approbation, favor, or assent; eager expression of approval; loud applause.

acclamatory.c: Acclamatory Ac*clam"a*to*ry (?), a. Pertaining to, or expressing approval by, acclamation.

acclimatable.c: Acclimatable Ac*cli"ma*ta*ble (?), a. Capable of being acclimated.

acclimatation.c: Acclimatation Ac*cli`ma*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. acclimation. See Acclimate.] Acclimatization.

acclimate.c: Acclimate Ac*cli"mate (#; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acclimated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Acclimating.] [F. acclimater; à (l. ad) + climat climate. See Climate.] To habituate to a climate not native; to acclimatize. J. H. Newman.

acclimation.c: Acclimation Ac`cli*ma"tion (?), n. The process of becoming, or the state of being, acclimated, or habituated to a new climate; acclimatization.

acclimatizable.c: Acclimatizable Ac*cli"ma*ti`za*ble (?), a. Capable of being acclimatized.

acclimatization.c: Acclimatization Ac*cli"ma*ti*za"tion (ăk`klī"mȧ*tĭ*zā"shŭn), n. The act of acclimatizing; the process of inuring to a new climate, or the state of being so inured. Darwin.

acclimatize.c: Acclimatize Ac*cli"ma*tize (ăk`klī"mȧ*tīz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acclimatized (ăk`klī"mȧ*tīzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Acclimatizing (ăk`klī"mȧ*tī`zĭng).] To inure or habituate to a climate different from that which is natural; to adapt to the peculiarities of a foreign or strange climate; said of man, the inferior animals, or plants.

acclimature.c: Acclimature Ac*cli"ma*ture (ăk`klī"mȧ*tur; 135), n. The act of acclimating, or the state of being acclimated. [R.] Caldwell.

acclivity.c: Acclivity Ac*cliv"i*ty, n.; pl. Acclivities (?). [L. acclivitas, fr. acclivis, acclivus, ascending; ad + clivus a hill, slope, fr. root kli to lean. See Lean.] A slope or inclination of the earth, as the side of a hill, considered as ascending, in opposition to declivity, or descending; an upward slope; ascent.

acclivous.c: Acclivous Ac*cli"vous (#; 277), a. [L. acclivis and acclivus.] Sloping upward; rising as a hillside; -- opposed to declivous.

accloy.c: Accloy Ac*cloy" (ăk*kloi"), v. t. [OF. encloyer, encloer, F. enclouer, to drive in a nail, fr. L. in + clavus nail.] To fill to satiety; to stuff full; to clog; to overload; to burden. See Cloy. [Obs.] Chaucer.

accoast.c: Accoast Ac*coast" (ăk*kōst"), v. t. & i. [See Accost, Coast.] To lie or sail along the coast or side of; to accost. [Obs.]

accoil.c: Accoil Ac*coil" (ăk*koil"), v. t. [OE. acoillir to receive, F. accueillir; L. ad + colligere to collect. See Coil.] 1. To gather together; to collect. [Obs.] Spenser.

accolade.c: Accolade Ac`co*lade" (ăk`ko*lād" or ăk`ko*lȧd"; 277), n. [F. accolade, It. accolata, fr. accollare to embrace; L. ad + collum neck.] 1. A ceremony formerly used in conferring knighthood, consisting of an embrace, and a slight blow on the shoulders with the flat blade of a sword.

accombination.c: Accombination Ac*com*bi*na"tion (?), n. [L. ad + E. combination.] A combining together. [R.]

accommodable.c: Accommodable Ac*com"mo*da*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. accommodable.] That may be accommodated, fitted, or made to agree. [R.] I. Watts.

accommodableness.c: Accommodableness Ac*com"mo*dable*ness, n. The quality or condition of being accommodable. [R.] Todd.

accommodate.c: Accommodate Ac*com"mo*date (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accommodated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Accommodating (?).] [L. accommodatus, p. p. of accommodare; ad + commodare to make fit, help; con- + modus measure, proportion. See Mode.] 1. To render fit, suitable, or correspondent; to adapt; to conform; as, to accommodate ourselves to circumstances. “They accommodate their counsels to his inclination.” Addison.
Accommodate Ac*com"mo*date, v. i. To adapt one's self; to be conformable or adapted. [R.] Boyle.
Accommodate Ac*com"mo*date (?), a. [L. accommodatus, p. p. of accommodare.] Suitable; fit; adapted; as, means accommodate to end. [Archaic] Tillotson.

accommodating.c: Accommodating Ac*com"mo*da`ting (?), a. Affording, or disposed to afford, accommodation; obliging; as an accommodating man, spirit, arrangement.

accommodation.c: Accommodation Ac*com`mo*da"tion (?), n. [L. accommodatio, fr. accommodare: cf. F. accommodation.]

accommodator.c: Accommodator Ac*com"mo*da`tor (?), n. He who, or that which, accommodates. Warburton.

accompanable.c: Accompanable Ac*com"pa*na*ble (?), a. Sociable. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

accompanier.c: Accompanier Ac*com"pa*ni*er (?), n. He who, or that which, accompanies. Lamb.

accompaniment.c: Accompaniment Ac*com"pa*ni*ment (-meint), n. [F. accompagnement.] That which accompanies; something that attends as a circumstance, or which is added to give greater completeness to the principal thing, or by way of ornament, or for the sake of symmetry. Specifically: (Mus.) A part performed by instruments, accompanying another part or parts performed by voices; the subordinate part, or parts, accompanying the voice or a principal instrument; also, the harmony of a figured bass. P. Cyc.

accompanist.c: Accompanist Ac*com"pa*nist (?), n. The performer in music who takes the accompanying part. Busby.

accompany.c: Accompany Ac*com"pa*ny (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accompanied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Accompanying (?)] [OF. aacompaignier, F. accompagner, to associate with, fr. OF. compaign, compain, companion. See Company.] 1. To go with or attend as a companion or associate; to keep company with; to go along with; -- followed by with or by; as, he accompanied his speech with a bow.
Accompany Ac*com"pa*ny, v. i. 1. To associate in a company; to keep company. [Obs.] Bacon.

accompletive.c: Accompletive Ac*com"ple*tive (?), a. [L. ad + complere, completum, to fill up.] Tending to accomplish. [R.]

accomplice.c: Accomplice Ac*com"plice (?), n. [Ac- (perh. for the article a or for L. ad) + E. complice. See Complice.]

accompliceship.c: Accompliceship Ac*com"plice*ship (?), n. The state of being an accomplice. [R.] Sir H. Taylor.

accomplicity.c: Accomplicity Ac`com*plic"i*ty (?), n. The act or state of being an accomplice. [R.]

accomplish.c: Accomplish Ac*com"plish (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accomplished (?), p. pr. & vb. n. Accomplishing.] [OE. acomplissen, OF. accomplir, F. accomplir; L. ad + complere to fill up, complete. See Complete, Finish.] 1. To complete, as time or distance.

accomplishable.c: Accomplishable Ac*com"plish*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being accomplished; practicable. Carlyle.

accomplished.c: Accomplished Ac*com"plished (?), a. 1. Completed; effected; established; as, an accomplished fact.

accomplishment.c: Accomplishment Ac*com"plish*ment (-meint), n. [F. accomplissement, fr. accomplir.] 1. The act of accomplishing; entire performance; completion; fulfillment; as, the accomplishment of an enterprise, of a prophecy, etc.

accord.c: Accord Ac*cord" (?), n. [OE. acord, accord, OF. acort, acorde, F. accord, fr. OF. acorder, F. accorder. See Accord, v. t.] 1. Agreement or concurrence of opinion, will, or action; harmony of mind; consent; assent.

Accord Ac*cord", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accorded; p. pr. & vb. n. According.] [OE. acorden, accorden, OF. acorder, F. accorder, fr. LL. accordare; L. ad + cor, cordis, heart. Cf. Concord, Discord, and see Heart.] 1. To make to agree or correspond; to suit one thing to another; to adjust; -- followed by to. [R.]
Accord Ac*cord", v. i. 1. To agree; to correspond; to be in harmony; -- followed by with, formerly also by to; as, his disposition accords with his looks.

accordable.c: Accordable Ac*cord"a*ble (?), a. [OF. acordable, F. accordable.] 1. Agreeing. [Obs.] Chaucer.

accordance.c: Accordance Ac*cord"ance (?), n. [OF. acordance.] Agreement; harmony; conformity. “In strict accordance with the law.” Macaulay.

accordant.c: Accordant Ac*cord"ant (?), a. [OF. acordant, F. accordant.] Agreeing; consonant; harmonious; corresponding; conformable; -- followed by with or to.

accordantly.c: Accordantly Ac*cord"ant*ly, adv. In accordance or agreement; agreeably; conformably; -- followed by with or to.

accorder.c: Accorder Ac*cord"er (?), n. One who accords, assents, or concedes. [R.]

according.c: According Ac*cord"ing, p. a. Agreeing; in agreement or harmony; harmonious. “This according voice of national wisdom.” Burke. “Mind and soul according well.” Tennyson.

accordingly.c: Accordingly Ac*cord"ing*ly, adv. 1. Agreeably; correspondingly; suitably; in a manner conformable.

accordion.c: Accordion Ac*cor"di*on (?), n. [See Accord.] (Mus.) A small, portable, keyed wind instrument, whose tones are generated by play of the wind upon free metallic reeds.

accordionist.c: Accordionist Ac*cor"di*on*ist, n. A player on the accordion.

accordment.c: Accordment Ac*cord"ment (ăk*kôrd"meint), n. [OF. acordement. See Accord, v.] Agreement; reconcilement. [Obs.] Gower.

accorporate.c: Accorporate Ac*cor"po*rate (?), v. t. [L. accorporare; ad + corpus, corporis, body.] To unite; to attach; to incorporate. [Obs.] Milton.

accost.c: Accost Ac*cost" (#; 115), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accosted; p. pr. & vb. n. Accosting.] [F. accoster, LL. accostare to bring side by side; L. ad + costa rib, side. See Coast, and cf. Accoast.] 1. To join side to side; to border; hence, to sail along the coast or side of. [Obs.] “So much [of Lapland] as accosts the sea.” Fuller.
Accost Ac*cost", v. i. To adjoin; to lie alongside. [Obs.] “The shores which to the sea accost.” Spenser.
Accost Ac*cost", n. Address; greeting. [R.] J. Morley.

accostable.c: Accostable Ac*cost"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. accostable.] Approachable; affable. [R.] Hawthorne.

accosted.c: Accosted Ac*cost"ed, a. (Her.) Supported on both sides by other charges; also, side by side.

accouchement.c: Accouchement ‖Ac*couche"ment (#; 277), n. [F., fr. accoucher to be delivered of a child, to aid in delivery, OF. acouchier orig. to lay down, put to bed, go to bed; L. ad + collocare to lay, put, place. See Collate.] Delivery in childbed

accoucheur.c: Accoucheur ‖Ac*cou*cheur" (?), n. [F., fr. accoucher. See Accouchement.] A man who assists women in childbirth; a man midwife; an obstetrician.

accoucheuse.c: Accoucheuse ‖Ac*cou*cheuse" (?), n. [F.., fem. of accoucher.] A midwife. [Recent] Dunglison.

account.c: Account Ac*count" (?), n. [OE. acount, account, accompt, OF. acont, fr. aconter. See Account, v. t., Count, n., 1.] 1. A reckoning; computation; calculation; enumeration; a record of some reckoning; as, the Julian account of time.

Account Ac*count" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accounted; p. pr. & vb. n. Accounting.] [OE. acounten, accompten, OF. aconter, à (L. ad) + conter to count. F. conter to tell, compter to count, L. computare. See Count, v. t.]
Account Ac*count", v. i. 1. To render or receive an account or relation of particulars; as, an officer must account with or to the treasurer for money received.
Account book Ac*count" book` (?). A book in which accounts are kept. Swift.

accountability.c: Accountability Ac*count`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state of being accountable; liability to be called on to render an account; the obligation to bear the consequences for failure to perform as expected; accountableness. “The awful idea of accountability.” R. Hall.

accountable.c: Accountable Ac*count"a*ble (?), a. 1. Liable to be called on to render an account; answerable; as, every man is accountable to God for his conduct.
Accountable ness Ac*count"a*ble ness, n. The quality or state of being accountable; accountability.

accountably.c: Accountably Ac*count"a*bly, adv. In an accountable manner.

accountancy.c: Accountancy Ac*count"an*cy (?), n. The art or employment of an accountant.

accountant.c: Accountant Ac*count"ant (?), n. [Cf. F. accomptant, OF. acontant, p. pr.] 1. One who renders account; one accountable.

accountantship.c: Accountantship Ac*count"ant*ship (?), n. [Accountant + -ship.] The office or employment of an accountant.

accouple.c: Accouple Ac*cou"ple (?), v. t. [OF. acopler, F. accoupler. See Couple.] To join; to couple. [R.]

accouplement.c: Accouplement Ac*cou"ple*ment (-kŭp"'l*meint), n. [Cf. F. accouplement.] 1. The act of coupling, or the state of being coupled; union. [R.] Caxton.

accourage.c: Accourage Ac*cour"age (?), v. t. [OF. acoragier; à (L. ad) + corage. See Courage.] To encourage. [Obs.]

accourt.c: Accourt Ac*court" (?), v. t. [Ac-, for L. ad. See Court.] To treat courteously; to court. [Obs.] Spenser.

accoutre.c: Accoutre Accouter { Ac*cou"ter, Ac*cou"tre } (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accoutered or Accoutred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Accoutering or Accoutring.] [F. accouter, OF. accoutrer, accoustrer; à (L. ad) + perh. LL. custor, for custos guardian, sacristan (cf. Custody), or perh. akin to E. guilt.] To furnish with dress, or equipments, esp. those for military service; to equip; to attire; to array.

accoutrements.c: Accoutrements Accouterments { Ac*cou"ter*ments, Ac*cou"tre*ments } (?), n. pl. [F. accoutrement, earlier also accoustrement, earlier also accoustrement. See Accouter.] Dress; trappings; equipment; specifically, the devices and equipments worn by soldiers.

accoy.c: Accoy Ac*coy" (?), v. t. [OF. acoyer; ac-, for L. ad. See Coy.] 1. To render quiet; to soothe. [Obs.] Chaucer.

accredit.c: Accredit Ac*cred"it (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accredited; p. pr. & vb. n. Accrediting.] [F. accréditer; à (L. ad) + crédit credit. See Credit.] 1. To put or bring into credit; to invest with credit or authority; to sanction.

accreditation.c: Accreditation Ac*cred`i*ta"tion (?), n. The act of accrediting; as, letters of accreditation.

accrementition.c: accrementition ac`cre*men*ti"tion (?), n. [See accresce, Increment.] (Physiol.) The process of generation by development of blastema, or fission of cells, in which the new formation is in all respects like the individual from which it proceeds.

accresce.c: accresce ac*cresce" (ăk*krĕs"), v. i. [L. accrescere. See Accrue.] 1. To accrue. [R.]

accrescence.c: accrescence ac*cres"cence (ăk*krĕs"seins), n. [LL. accrescentia.] Continuous growth; an accretion. [R.]

accrescent.c: accrescent ac*cres"cent (ăk*krĕs"seint), a. [L. accrescens, -entis, p. pr. of accrescere; ad + crescere to grow. See Crescent.]

accrete.c: accrete ac*crete" (ăk*krēt"), v. i. [From L. accretus, p. p. of accrescere to increase.] 1. To grow together.
accrete ac*crete", v. t. To make adhere; to add. Earle.
accrete ac*crete", a. 1. Characterized by accretion; made up; as, accrete matter.

accretion.c: accretion ac*cre"tion (ăk*krē"shŭn), n. [L. accretio, fr. accrescere to increase. Cf. Crescent, Increase, Accrue.]

accretive.c: accretive ac*cre"tive (?), a. Relating to accretion; increasing, or adding to, by growth. Glanvill.

accriminate.c: accriminate ac*crim"i*nate (?), v. t. [L. ac- (for ad to) + criminari.] To accuse of a crime. [Obs.] -- Ac*crim`i*na"tion (?), n. [Obs.]

accroach.c: accroach ac*croach" (ăk*krōch"), v. t. [OE. acrochen, accrochen, to obtain, OF. acrochier, F. accrocher; à (L. ad) + croc hook (E. crook).] 1. To hook, or draw to one's self as with a hook. [Obs.]

accroachment.c: Accroachment Ac*croach"ment (ăk*krōch"meint), n. [Cf. F. accrochement.] An encroachment; usurpation. [Obs.] Bailey.

accrue.c: Accrue Ac*crue" (ăk*krü"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Accrued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Accruing.] [See Accrue, n., and cf. Accresce, Accrete.] 1. To increase; to augment.

Accrue Ac*crue", n. [F. accrû, OF. acreü, p. p. of accroitre, OF. acroistre to increase; L. ad + crescere to increase. Cf. Accretion, Crew. See Crescent.] Something that accrues; advantage accruing. [Obs.]

accruer.c: Accruer Ac*cru"er (ăk*krü"ẽr), n. (Law) The act of accruing; accretion; as, title by accruer.

accrument.c: Accrument Ac*cru"ment (ăk*krü"meint), n. The process of accruing, or that which has accrued; increase. Jer. Taylor.

accubation.c: Accubation Ac`cu*ba"tion (ăk*ku*bā"shŭn), n. [L. accubatio, for accubitio, fr. accubare to recline; ad + cubare to lie down. See Accumb.] The act or posture of reclining on a couch, as practiced by the ancients at meals.

accumb.c: Accumb Ac*cumb" (ăk*kŭmb"), v. i. [L. accumbere; ad + cumbere (only in compounds) to lie down.] To recline, as at table. [Obs.] Bailey.

accumbency.c: Accumbency Ac*cum"ben*cy (ăk*kŭm"bein*sy̆), n. The state of being accumbent or reclining. [R.]

accumbent.c: Accumbent Ac*cum"bent (-beint), a. 1. Leaning or reclining, as the ancients did at their meals.
Accumbent Ac*cum"bent, n. One who reclines at table.

accumber.c: Accumber Ac*cum"ber (-bẽr), v. t. To encumber. [Obs.] Chaucer.

accumulate.c: Accumulate Ac*cu"mu*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accumulated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Accumulating.] [L. accumulatus, p. p. of accumulare; ad + cumulare to heap. See Cumulate.] To heap up in a mass; to pile up; to collect or bring together; to amass; as, to accumulate a sum of money.
Accumulate Ac*cu"mu*late (ăk*kū"mu*lāt), v. i. To grow or increase in quantity or number; to increase greatly.
Accumulate Ac*cu"mu*late (-lat), a. [L. accumulatus, p. p. of accumulare.] Collected; accumulated. Bacon.

accumulation.c: Accumulation Ac*cu`mu*la"tion (?), n. [L. accumulatio; cf. F. accumulation.] 1. The act of accumulating, the state of being accumulated, or that which is accumulated; as, an accumulation of earth, of sand, of evils, of wealth, of honors.

accumulative.c: Accumulative Ac*cu"mu*la*tive (?), a. Characterized by accumulation; serving to collect or amass; cumulative; additional. -- Ac*cu"mu*la*tive*ly, adv. -- Ac*cu"mu*la*tive*ness, n.

accumulator.c: Accumulator Ac*cu"mu*la`tor (?), n. [L.] 1. One who, or that which, accumulates, collects, or amasses.

accuracy.c: Accuracy Ac"cu*ra*cy (#; 277), n. [See Accurate.] The state of being accurate; freedom from mistakes, this exemption arising from carefulness; exact conformity to truth, or to a rule or model; precision; exactness; nicety; correctness; as, the value of testimony depends on its accuracy.

accurate.c: Accurate Ac"cu*rate (?), a. [L. accuratus, p. p. and a., fr. accurare to take care of; ad + curare to take care, cura care. See Cure.] 1. In exact or careful conformity to truth, or to some standard of requirement, the result of care or pains; free from failure, error, or defect; exact; as, an accurate calculator; an accurate measure; accurate expression, knowledge, etc.

accurately.c: Accurately Ac"cu*rate*ly, adv. In an accurate manner; exactly; precisely; without error or defect.

accurateness.c: Accurateness Ac"cu*rate*ness, n. The state or quality of being accurate; accuracy; exactness; nicety; precision.

accurse.c: Accurse Ac*curse" (?), v. t. [OE. acursien, acorsien; pref. a + cursien to curse. See Curse.] To devote to destruction; to imprecate misery or evil upon; to curse; to execrate; to anathematize.

accurst.c: Accurst Accursed { Ac*cursed" (?), Ac*curst" (?), } p. p. & a. Doomed to destruction or misery; cursed; hence, bad enough to be under the curse; execrable; detestable; exceedingly hateful; -- as, an accursed deed. Shak. -- Ac*curs"ed*ly, adv. -- Ac*curs"ed*ness, n.

accusable.c: Accusable Ac*cus"a*ble (?), a. [L. accusabilis: cf. F. accusable.] Liable to be accused or censured; chargeable with a crime or fault; blamable; -- with of.

accusant.c: Accusant Ac*cus"ant (?), n. [L. accusans, p. pr. of accusare: cf. F. accusant.] An accuser. Bp. Hall.

accusation.c: Accusation Ac`cu*sa"tion (?), n. [OF. acusation, F. accusation, L. accusatio, fr. accusare. See Accuse.]

accusatival.c: Accusatival Ac*cu`sa*ti"val (?), a. Pertaining to the accusative case.

accusative.c: Accusative Ac*cu"sa*tive (?), a. [F. accusatif, L. accusativus (in sense 2), fr. accusare. See Accuse.]

accusatively.c: Accusatively Ac*cu"sa*tive*ly, adv. 1. In an accusative manner.

accusatory.c: Accusatory Ac*cu"sa*to*ry (?), a. [L. accusatorius, fr. accusare.] Pertaining to, or containing, an accusation; as, an accusatory libel. Grote.

accuse.c: Accuse Ac*cuse", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accused (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Accusing.] [OF. acuser, F. accuser, L. accusare, to call to account, accuse; ad + causa cause, lawsuit. Cf. Cause.] 1. To charge with, or declare to have committed, a crime or offense; (Law) to charge with an offense, judicially or by a public process; -- with of; as, to accuse one of a high crime or misdemeanor.

accused.c: Accused Ac*cused" (?), a. Charged with offense; as, an accused person.

accusement.c: Accusement Ac*cuse"ment (-kūz"meint), n. [OF. acusement. See Accuse.] Accusation. [Obs.] Chaucer.

accuser.c: Accuser Ac*cus"er (?), n. [OE. acuser, accusour; cf. OF. acuseor, fr. L. accusator, fr. accusare.] One who accuses; one who brings a charge of crime or fault.

accusingly.c: Accusingly Ac*cus"ing*ly, adv. In an accusing manner.

accustom.c: Accustom Ac*cus"tom (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Accustomed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Accustoming.] [OF. acostumer, acustumer, F. accoutumer; à (L. ad) + OF. costume, F. coutume, custom. See Custom.] To make familiar by use; to habituate, familiarize, or inure; -- with to.
Accustom Ac*cus"tom, v. i. 1. To be wont. [Obs.] Carew.

accustomable.c: Accustomable Ac*cus"tom*a*ble (?), a. Habitual; customary; wonted. “Accustomable goodness.” Latimer.

accustomably.c: Accustomably Ac*cus"tom*a*bly, adv. According to custom; ordinarily; customarily. Latimer.

accustomance.c: Accustomance Ac*cus"tom*ance (?), n. [OF. accoustumance, F. accoutumance.] Custom; habitual use. [Obs.] Boyle.

accustomed.c: Accustomed Ac*cus"tomed (?), a. 1. Familiar through use; usual; customary. “An accustomed action.” Shak.

ace.c: Ace Ace (ās), n.; pl. Aces (ā"sĕz). [OE. as, F. as, fr. L. as, assis, unity, copper coin, the unit of coinage. Cf. As.]

aceldama.c: Aceldama A*cel"da*ma (?), n. [Gr.?, fr. Syr. ōkēl damō the field of blood.] The potter's field, said to have lain south of Jerusalem, purchased with the bribe which Judas took for betraying his Master, and therefore called the field of blood. Fig.: A field of bloodshed.

acentric.c: Acentric A*cen"tric (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. +? a point, a center.] Not centered; without a center.

acephal.c: Acephal Ac"e*phal (?), n. [Gr.?; 'a priv. +? head: cf. F. acéphale, LL. acephalus.] (Zool.) One of the Acephala.

acephala.c: Acephala ‖A*ceph"a*la (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.?, adj. neut. pl., headless. See Acephal.] (Zool.) That division of the Mollusca which includes the bivalve shells, like the clams and oysters; -- so called because they have no evident head. Formerly the group included the Tunicata, Brachiopoda, and sometimes the Bryozoa. See Mollusca.

acephalan.c: Acephalan A*ceph"a*lan, a. (Zool.) Belonging to the Acephala.

acephali.c: Acephali ‖A*ceph"a*li (?), n. pl. [LL., pl. of acephalus. See Acephal.] 1. A fabulous people reported by ancient writers to have heads.

acephalist.c: Acephalist A*ceph"a*list (?), n. One who acknowledges no head or superior. Dr. Gauden.

acephalocyst.c: Acephalocyst A*ceph"a*lo*cyst (?), n. [Gr. 'ake`falos without a head + ky`stis bladder.] (Zool.) A larval entozoön in the form of a subglobular or oval vesicle, or hydatid, filled with fluid, sometimes found in the tissues of man and the lower animals; -- so called from the absence of a head or visible organs on the vesicle. These cysts are the immature stages of certain tapeworms. Also applied to similar cysts of different origin.

acephalocystic.c: Acephalocystic A*ceph`a*lo*cys"tic (?), a. Pertaining to, or resembling, the acephalocysts.

acequia.c: Acequia A*ce"qui*a (ä*sā"ke*ȧ; Sp. ä*thā"ke*ä), n. [Sp.] A canal or trench for irrigating land. [Sp. Amer.]

acerate.c: Acerate Ac"er*ate (?), n. [See Aceric.] (Chem.) A combination of aceric acid with a salifiable base.

acerb.c: Acerb A*cerb" (?), a. [L. acerbus, fr. acer sharp: cf. F. acerbe. See Acrid.] Sour, bitter, and harsh to the taste, as unripe fruit; sharp and harsh.

acerbate.c: Acerbate A*cerb"ate (?), v. t. [L. acerbatus, p. p. of acerbare, fr. acerbus.] To sour; to imbitter; to irritate.

acerbitude.c: Acerbitude A*cerb"i*tude (?), n. [L. acerbitudo, fr. acerbus.] Sourness and harshness. [Obs.] Bailey.

acerbity.c: Acerbity A*cerb"i*ty (?), n. [F. acerbité, L. acerbitas, fr. acerbus. See Acerb.] 1. Sourness of taste, with bitterness and astringency, like that of unripe fruit.

aceric.c: Aceric A*cer"ic (?), a. [L. acer maple.] Pertaining to, or obtained from, the maple; as, aceric acid. Ure.

acerose.c: Acerose Ac"er*ose` (?), a. [(a) L. acerosus chaffy, fr. acus, gen. aceris, chaff; (b) as if fr. L. acus needle: cf. F. acéreux.] (Bot.) (a) Having the nature of chaff; chaffy. (b) Needle-shaped, having a sharp, rigid point, as the leaf of the pine.

acerous.c: Acerous Ac"er*ous, a. [Gr. α priv. + ke`ras a horn.] (Zool.) (a) Destitute of tentacles, as certain mollusks. (b) Without antennæ, as some insects.

acerval.c: Acerval A*cer"val (?), a. [L. acervalis, fr. acervus heap.] Pertaining to a heap. [Obs.]

acervate.c: Acervate A*cer"vate (?), v. t. [L. acervatus, p. p. of acervare to heap up, fr. acervus heap.] To heap up. [Obs.]
Acervate A*cer"vate (?), a. Heaped, or growing in heaps, or closely compacted clusters.

acervation.c: Acervation Ac`er*va"tion (?), n. [L. acervatio.] A heaping up; accumulation. [R.] Johnson.

acervative.c: Acervative A*cer"va*tive (?), a. Heaped up; tending to heap up.

acervose.c: Acervose A*cer"vose (?), a. Full of heaps. [R.] Bailey.

acescency.c: Acescency Acescence { A*ces"cence (?), A*ces"cen*cy (?), } n. [Cf. F. acescence. See Acescent.] The quality of being acescent; the process of acetous fermentation; a moderate degree of sourness. Johnson.

acescent.c: Acescent A*ces"cent (?), a. [L. acescens, -entis, p. pr. of acescere to turn sour; inchoative of acere to be sour: cf. F. acescent. See Acid.] Turning sour; readily becoming tart or acid; slightly sour. Faraday.
Acescent A*ces"cent, n. A substance liable to become sour.

acetable.c: Acetable Ac"e*ta*ble (?), n. An acetabulum; or about one eighth of a pint. [Obs.] Holland.

acetabulifera.c: Acetabulifera ‖Ac`e*tab`u*lif"e*ra (?), n. pl. [NL. See Acetabuliferous.] (Zool.) The division of Cephalopoda in which the arms are furnished with cup-shaped suckers, as the cuttlefishes, squids, and octopus; the Dibranchiata. See Cephalopoda.

acetabuliferous.c: Acetabuliferous Ac`e*tab`u*lif"er*ous (?), a. [L. acetablum a little cup + -ferous.] Furnished with fleshy cups for adhering to bodies, as cuttlefish, etc.

acetabuliform.c: Acetabuliform Ac`e*tab"u*li*form (?), a. [L. acetabulum + -form.] (Bot.) Shaped like a shallow cup; saucer-shaped; as, an acetabuliform calyx. Gray.

acetabulum.c: Acetabulum ‖Ac`e*tab"u*lum (?), n. [L., a little saucer for vinegar, fr. acetum vinegar, fr. acere to be sour.]

acetal.c: Acetal Ac"e*tal (?), n. [Acetic + alcohol.] (Chem.) A limpid, colorless, inflammable liquid from the slow oxidation of alcohol under the influence of platinum black.

acetaldehyde.c: Acetaldehyde Ac`et*al"de*hyde (?), n. Acetic aldehyde. See Aldehyde.

acetamide.c: Acetamide Ac`et*am"ide (?), n. [Acetyl + amide.] (Chem.) A white crystalline solid, from ammonia by replacement of an equivalent of hydrogen by acetyl.

acetanilide.c: acetanilide ac`et*an"i*lide (ăs`ĕt*ăn"ĭ*lĭd), n. [Acetyl + anilide.] (Med., Chem.) An amide formed from aniline and an acetyl group (C6H5.NH.CO.CH3); it is a white crystalline compound used as an analgesic and also as an antipyretic. It has molecular weight 135.16. [Written also acetanilid] AS

acetarious.c: Acetarious Ac`e*ta"ri*ous (?), a. [L. acetaria, n. pl., salad, fr. acetum vinegar, fr. acere to be sour.] Used in salads; as, acetarious plants.

acetary.c: Acetary Ac"e*ta*ry (ăs"e*ta*ry̆), n. [L. acetaria salad plants.] An acid pulp in certain fruits, as the pear. Grew.

acetate.c: Acetate Ac"e*tate (?), n. [L. acetum vinegar, fr. acere to be sour.] (Chem.) A salt formed by the union of acetic acid with a base or positive radical; as, acetate of lead, acetate of potash.

acetated.c: Acetated Ac"e*ta`ted (?), a. Combined with acetic acid.

acetic.c: Acetic A*ce"tic (#; 277), a. [L. acetum vinegar, fr. acere to be sour.] (Chem.) (a) Of a pertaining to vinegar; producing vinegar; producing vinegar; as, acetic fermentation. (b) Pertaining to, containing, or derived from, acetyl, as acetic ether, acetic acid. The latter is the acid to which the sour taste of vinegar is due.

acetification.c: Acetification A*cet`i*fi*ca"tion (?), n. The act of making acetous or sour; the process of converting, or of becoming converted, into vinegar.

acetifier.c: Acetifier A*cet"i*fi`er (?), n. An apparatus for hastening acetification. Knight.

acetify.c: Acetify A*cet"i*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acetified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Acetifying (?).] [L. acetum vinegar + -fly.] To convert into acid or vinegar.
Acetify A*cet"i*fy, v. i. To turn acid. Encyc. Dom. Econ.

acetimeter.c: Acetimeter Ac`e*tim"e*ter (?), n. [L. acetum vinegar + -meter: cf. F. acétimètre.] An instrument for estimating the amount of acetic acid in vinegar or in any liquid containing acetic acid.

acetimetry.c: Acetimetry Ac`e*tim"e*try (?), n. The act or method of ascertaining the strength of vinegar, or the proportion of acetic acid contained in it. Ure.

acetin.c: Acetin Ac"e*tin (?), n. (Chem.) A combination of acetic acid with glycerin. Brande & C.

acetol.c: acetol ac"e*tol (?), n. [Acetic + -ol as in alcohol.] (Chem.) 1. Methyl ketol; also, any of various homologues of the same.

acetometer.c: Acetometer Ac`e*tom"e*ter (?), n. Same as Acetimeter. Brande & C.

acetonaemia.c: Acetonaemia Acetonemia ‖Ac`e*to*næ"mi*a, Ac`e*to*ne"mi*a (?), n. [NL. See Acetone; Hæma-.] (Med.) A morbid condition characterized by the presence of ketone bodies (including acetone, acetoacetic acid and beta-hydroxybutyric acid) in the blood, as in diabetes.

acetone.c: acetone ac"e*tone (ăs"e*tōn), n. [See Acetic.] (Chem.) A volatile liquid (CH3.CO.CH3); pyroacetic spirit; methyl ketone; -- obtained by fermentation, the distillation of certain acetates, or by the destructive distillation of citric acid, starch, sugar, or gum, with quicklime. It is commonly used as a solvent.

acetonic.c: Acetonic Ac`e*ton"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to acetone; as, acetonic bodies.

acetophenone.c: Acetophenone Ac`e*to*phe"none (-fē"nōn), n. [Acetic + phenyl + one.] (Chem.) A crystalline ketone, CH3.CO.C6H5, which may be obtained by the dry distillation of a mixture of the calcium salts of acetic and benzoic acids. It is used as a hypnotic under the name of hypnone.

acetose.c: Acetose Ac"e*tose` (ăs"e*tōs`), a. Sour like vinegar; acetous.

acetosity.c: Acetosity Ac`e*tos"i*ty (?), n. [LL. acetositas. See Acetous.] The quality of being acetous; sourness.

acetous.c: Acetous A*ce"tous (#; 277), a. [L. acetum vinegar, fr. acere to be sour.] 1. Having a sour taste; sour; acid. “An acetous spirit.” Boyle. “A liquid of an acetous kind.” Bp. Lowth.

acetyl.c: Acetyl Ac"e*tyl (?), n. [L. acetum vinegar + Gr.? substance. See -yl.] (Chem.) A complex, hypothetical radical, composed of two parts of carbon to three of hydrogen and one of oxygen. Its hydroxide is acetic acid.

acetylene.c: Acetylene A*cet"y*lene (?), n. (Chem.) A gaseous compound of carbon and hydrogen, in the proportion of two atoms of the former to two of the latter. It is a colorless gas, with a peculiar, unpleasant odor, and is produced for use as an illuminating gas in a number of ways, but chiefly by the action of water on calcium carbide. Its light is very brilliant. Watts.

ache.c: Ache Ach { Ach, Ache } (?), n. [F. ache, L. apium parsley.] A name given to several species of plants; as, smallage, wild celery, parsley. [Obs.] Holland.
Ache Ache (?), n. [OE. ache, AS. æce, ece, fr. acan to ache. See Ache, v. i.] Continued pain, as distinguished from sudden twinges, or spasmodic pain. “Such an ache in my bones.” Shak.

Ache Ache (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Ached (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Aching (?).] [OE. aken, AS. acan, both strong verbs, AS. acan, imp. ōc, p. p. acen, to ache; perh. orig. to drive, and akin to agent.] To suffer pain; to have, or be in, pain, or in continued pain; to be distressed. “My old bones ache.” Shak.

achaian.c: Achaian Achaean { A*chæ"an (?), A*cha"ian (?) } a. [L. Achaeus, Achaius; Gr.?.] Of or pertaining to Achaia in Greece; also, Grecian. -- n. A native of Achaia; a Greek.

achate.c: Achate A*chate" (?), n. [F. achat purchase. See Cates.]

achatina.c: Achatina ‖Ach`a*ti"na (?), n. [NL., from Gr.? agate.] (Zool.) A genus of land snails, often large, common in the warm parts of America and Africa.

achatour.c: Achatour A*cha*tour" (?), n. [See Cater.] Purveyor; acater. [Obs.] Chaucer.

achean.c: Achean A*che"an (?), a & n. See Achæan, Achaian.

achenium.c: Achenium Achene { A*chene" (?), A*che"ni*um (?) } n. [Gr. 'a priv. +? to gape.] (Bot.) A small, dry, indehiscent fruit, containing a single seed, as in the buttercup; -- called a naked seed by the earlier botanists. [Written also akene and achænium.]

achenial.c: Achenial A*che"ni*al (?), a. Pertaining to an achene.

acheron.c: Acheron Ach"e*ron (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?.] (Myth.) A river in the Nether World or infernal regions; also, the infernal regions themselves. By some of the English poets it was supposed to be a flaming lake or gulf. Shak.

acherontic.c: Acherontic Ach`e*ron"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to Acheron; infernal; hence, dismal, gloomy; moribund.

achievable.c: Achievable A*chiev"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being achieved. Barrow.

achievance.c: Achievance A*chiev"ance (?), n. [Cf. OF. achevance.] Achievement. [Obs.] Sir T. Elyot.

achieve.c: Achieve A*chieve" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Achieved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Achieving (?).] [OE. acheven, OF. achever, achiever, F. achever, to finish; à (L. ad) + OF. chief, F. chef, end, head, fr. L. caput head. See Chief.] 1. To carry on to a final close; to bring out into a perfected state; to accomplish; to perform; -- as, to achieve a feat, an exploit, an enterprise.

achievement.c: Achievement A*chieve"ment (-meint), n. [Cf. F. achèvement, E. Hatchment.] 1. The act of achieving or performing; an obtaining by exertion; successful performance; accomplishment; as, the achievement of his object.

achiever.c: Achiever A*chiev"er (?), n. One who achieves; a winner.

achillean.c: Achillean Ach`il*le"an (?), a. Resembling Achilles, the hero of the Iliad; invincible.

achilles.c: Achilles tendon A*chil"les' ten"don (?), n. [L. Achillis tendo.] (Anat.) The strong tendon formed of the united tendons of the large muscles in the calf of the leg, an inserted into the bone of the heel; -- so called from the mythological account of Achilles being held by the heel when dipped in the River Styx.

achilous.c: Achilous A*chi"lous (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. +? lip.] (Bot.) Without a lip.

aching.c: Aching Ach"ing (?), a. That aches; continuously painful. See Ache. -- Ach"ing*ly, adv.

achiote.c: Achiote ‖A`chi*o"te (?), n. [Sp. achiote, fr. Indian achiotl.] Seeds of the annotto tree; also, the coloring matter, annotto.

achlamydate.c: Achlamydate A*chlam"y*date (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. +?.?. a short cloak.] (Zool.) Not possessing a mantle; -- said of certain gastropods.

achlamydeous.c: Achlamydeous Ach`la*myd"e*ous (?), a. (Bot.) Naked; having no floral envelope, neither calyx nor corolla.

acholia.c: Acholia ‖A*cho"li*a (ȧ*kō"lĭ*ȧ), n. [NL., from Gr. 'acholi`a; 'a priv. + cholh` bile.] (Med.) Deficiency or lack of bile. AS

achromatic.c: Achromatic Ach`ro*mat"ic (?), a. [Gr. 'achrw`matos colorless; 'a priv. + chrw^ma, chrw`matos, color: cf. F. achromatique.] 1. (Opt.) Free from color; transmitting light without decomposing it into its primary colors.

achromatically.c: Achromatically Ach`ro*mat"ic*al*ly (?), adv. In an achromatic manner.

achromatin.c: Achromatin A*chro"ma*tin (?), n. (Biol.) Tissue which is not stained by fluid dyes. W. Flemming.

achromatism.c: Achromatism A*chro"ma*tism (?), n. [Cf. F. achromatisme.] The state or quality of being achromatic; as, the achromatism of a lens; achromaticity. Nichol.

achromatization.c: Achromatization A*chro`ma*ti*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. achromatisation.] The act or process of achromatizing.

achromatize.c: Achromatize A*chro"ma*tize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Achromatized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Achromatizing (?).] [Gr. 'a priv. +? color.] To deprive of color; to make achromatic. [Also spelled achromatise.]

achromatous.c: Achromatous A*chro"ma*tous (?), a. [See Ahromatic.] Lacking, or deficient in, color; as, achromatous blood.

achromatopsy.c: Achromatopsy A*chro"ma*top"sy (?), n. [Gr. 'a priv. +? color +? sight.] Color blindness; inability to distinguish colors; Daltonism.

achromic.c: Achromic A*chro"mic (?), a. [Gr.? colorless;? priv. +? color.] Free from color; colorless; as, in (Physiol. Chem.), the achromic point of a starch solution acted upon by an amylolytic enzyme is the point at which it fails to give any color with iodine.

achroodextrin.c: Achroodextrin Ach`ro*ö*dex"trin (?), n. [Gr.? colorless + E. dextrin.] (Physiol. Chem.) Dextrin not colorable by iodine. See Dextrin.

achroous.c: Achroous Ach"ro*ous (?), a. [Gr.?; 'a priv. +? color.] Colorless; achromatic.

achylous.c: Achylous A*chy"lous (?), a. [Gr.? without juice.] (Physiol.) Without chyle.

achymous.c: Achymous A*chy"mous (?), a. [Gr.? without juice.] (Physiol.) Without chyme.

acicula.c: Acicula ‖A*cic"u*la (?), n.; pl. Aciculæ (?). [L., a small needle, dimin. of acus needle.] (Nat. Hist.) One of the needlelike or bristlelike spines or prickles of some animals and plants; also, a needlelike crystal.

acicular.c: Acicular A*cic"u*lar (?), a. Needle-shaped; slender like a needle or bristle, as some leaves or crystals; also, having sharp points like needles.

aciculated.c: Aciculated Aciculate { A*cic"u*late (?), A*cic"u*la"ted (?) } a. (Nat. Hist.) (a) Furnished with aciculæ. (b) Acicular. (c) Marked with fine irregular streaks as if scratched by a needle. Lindley.

aciculiform.c: Aciculiform A*cic"u*li*form (?), a. [L. acicula needle + -form.] Needle-shaped; acicular.

aciculite.c: Aciculite A*cic"u*lite (?), n. (Min.) Needle ore. Brande & C.

acid.c: Acid Ac"id (?), a. [L. acidus sour, fr. the root ak to be sharp: cf. F. acide. Cf. Acute.] 1. Sour, sharp, or biting to the taste; tart; having the taste of vinegar: as, acid fruits or liquors. Also fig.: Sour-tempered.

Acid process Ac"id proc"ess. (Iron Metal.) That variety of either the Bessemer or the open-hearth process in which the converter or hearth is lined with acid, that is, highly siliceous, material. Opposed to basic process.

acidic.c: Acidic A*cid"ic (?), a. (Min.) 1. Containing a high percentage of silica; -- opposed to basic.

acidiferous.c: Acidiferous Ac`id*if"er*ous (?), a. [L. acidus sour + -ferous.] Containing or yielding an acid.

acidifiable.c: Acidifiable A*cid"i*fi`a*ble (?), a. Capable of being acidified, or converted into an acid.

acidific.c: Acidific Ac`id*if"ic (?), a. Producing acidity; converting into an acid. Dana.

acidification.c: Acidification A*cid`i*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. acidification.] The act or process of acidifying, or changing into an acid.

acidifier.c: Acidifier A*cid"i*fi`er (?), n. (Chem.) A simple or compound principle, whose presence is necessary to produce acidity, as oxygen, chlorine, bromine, iodine, etc.

acidify.c: Acidify A*cid"i*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acidified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Acidifying (?).] [L. acidus sour, acid + -fy: cf. F. acidifier.] 1. To make acid; to convert into an acid; as, to acidify sugar.

acidimeter.c: Acidimeter Ac`id*im"e*ter (?), n. [L. acidus acid + -meter.] (Chem.) An instrument for ascertaining the strength of acids. Ure.

acidimetry.c: Acidimetry Ac`id*im"e*try (?), n. [L. acidus acid + -metry.] (Chem.) The measurement of the strength of acids, especially by a chemical process based on the law of chemical combinations, or the fact that, to produce a complete reaction, a certain definite weight of reagent is required. -- Ac`id*i*met"ric*al (?), a.

acidity.c: Acidity A*cid"i*ty (?), n. [L. acidites, fr. acidus: cf. F. acidité. See Acid.] The quality of being sour; sourness; tartness; sharpness to the taste; as, the acidity of lemon juice.

acidulate.c: Acidulate A*cid"u*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acidulated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Acidulating (?).] [Cf. F. aciduler. See Acidulous.] To make sour or acid in a moderate degree; to sour somewhat. Arbuthnot.

acidulent.c: Acidulent A*cid"u*lent (?), a. Having an acid quality; sour; acidulous. “With anxious, acidulent face.” Carlyle.

acidulous.c: Acidulous A*cid"u*lous (?), a. [L. acidulus, dim. of acidus. See Acid.] Slightly sour; sub-acid; sourish; as, an acidulous tincture. E. Burke.

acierage.c: Acierage Ac`i*er*age (?), n. [F. aciérage, fr. acier steel.] The process of coating the surface of a metal plate (as a stereotype plate) with steellike iron by means of voltaic electricity; steeling.

aciform.c: Aciform Ac"i*form (?), a. [L. acus needle + -form.] Shaped like a needle.

acinaceous.c: Acinaceous Ac"i*na"ceous (?), a. [L. acinus a grape, grapestone.] (Bot.) Containing seeds or stones of grapes, or grains like them.

acinaces.c: Acinaces ‖A*cin"a*ces (?), n. [L., from Gr.?.] (Anc. Hist.) A short sword or saber.

acinaciform.c: Acinaciform Ac`i*nac"i*form (ăs`ĭ*năs"ĭ*fôrm), a. [L. acinaces a short sword + -form: cf. F. acinaciforme.] (Bot.) Scimeter-shaped; as, an acinaciform leaf.

acinetae.c: Acinetae ‖Ac`i*ne"tæ (ăs`ĭ*nē"tē), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'akinhtos immovable.] (Zool.) A group of suctorial Infusoria, which in the adult stage are stationary. See Suctoria.

aciniform.c: Aciniform A*cin"i*form (?), a. [L. acinus a grape, grapestone + -form: cf. F. acinoforme.] 1. Having the form of a cluster of grapes; clustered like grapes.

acinous.c: Acinous Acinose { Ac"i*nose` (?), Ac"i*nous (?) } a. [L. acinosus, fr. acinus grapestone.] Consisting of acini, or minute granular concretions; as, acinose or acinous glands. Kirwan.

acinus.c: Acinus ‖Ac"i*nus (ăs"ĭ*nŭs), n.; pl. Acini (?). [L., grape, grapestone.] 1. (Bot.) (a) One of the small grains or drupelets which make up some kinds of fruit, as the blackberry, raspberry, etc. (b) A grapestone.

acipenser.c: Acipenser ‖Ac`i*pen"ser (?), prop. n. [L., the name of a fish.] (Zool.) A genus of ganoid fishes, including the sturgeons, having the body armed with bony scales, and the mouth on the under side of the head. See Sturgeon.

aciurgy.c: Aciurgy Ac"i*ur`gy (?), n. [Gr.? a point + 'e`rgon work.] Operative surgery.

acknow.c: Acknow Ac*know" (ăk*nō"), v. t. [Pref. a- + know; AS. oncnāwan.] 1. To recognize. [Obs.] “You will not be acknown, sir.” B. Jonson.

acknowledge.c: acknowledge ac*knowl"edge (ăk*nŏl"ĕj), v. t. [imp. & p. p. acknowledged (ăk*nŏl"ĕjd); p. pr. & vb. n. acknowledging (ăk*nŏl"ĕj*ĭng).] [Prob. fr. pref. a- + the verb knowledge. See Knowledge, and cf. Acknow.] 1. To own or admit the knowledge of; to recognize as a fact or truth; to declare one's belief in; as, to acknowledge the being of a God.

acknowledgement.c: Acknowledgement Acknowledgment Ac*knowl"edg*ment, Ac*knowl"edge*ment (ăk*nŏl"ĕj*meint), n. 1. The act of acknowledging; admission; avowal; owning; confession. “An acknowledgment of fault.” Froude.

aclinic.c: Aclinic A*clin"ic (ȧ*klĭn"ĭk), a. [Gr. 'a priv. + kli`nein to incline.] (Physics.) Without inclination or dipping; -- said of the imaginary line near the earth's equator on which the magnetic needle balances itself horizontally, having no dip. The aclinic line is also termed the magnetic equator. Prof. August.

acme.c: acme ac"me (ăk"me), n. [Gr. 'akmh` point, top.] 1. The top or highest point; the culmination.

acne.c: acne ac"ne (ăk"ne), n. [NL., prob. a corruption of Gr. 'akmh`.] (Med.) Inflammation of the sebaceous glands that are associated with hair follicles, leading to visible comedones and pimples, especially on the face, back, and chest.

acnode.c: Acnode Ac"node (?), n. [L. acus needle + E. node.] (Geom.) An isolated point not upon a curve, but whose coördinates satisfy the equation of the curve so that it is considered as belonging to the curve.

acock.c: Acock A*cock" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + cock.] In a cocked or turned up fashion.

acockbill.c: Acockbill A*cock"bill` (?), adv. [Prefix a- + cock + bill: with bills cocked up.] (Naut.) (a) Hanging at the cathead, ready to let go, as an anchor. (b) Topped up; having one yardarm higher than the other.

acold.c: Acold A*cold" (?), a. [Prob. p. p. of OE. acolen to grow cold or cool, AS. ācōlian to grow cold; pref. a- (cf. Goth. er-, orig. meaning out) + cōlian to cool. See Cool.] Cold. [Obs.] “Poor Tom's acold.” Shak.

acology.c: Acology A*col"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? remedy + -logy.] Materia medica; the science of remedies.

acolyctine.c: Acolyctine Ac`o*lyc"tine (?), n. [From the name of the plant.] (Chem.) An organic base, in the form of a white powder, obtained from Aconitum lycoctonum. Eng. Cyc.

acolyte.c: Acolyte Ac`o*lyte (?), n. [LL. acolythus, acoluthus, Gr.? following, attending: cf. F. acolyte.]

acondylous.c: Acondylous Aconddylose { A*cond"dy*lose` (?), A*con"dy*lous (?), } a. [Gr. 'a priv. +? joint.] (Nat. Hist.) Being without joints; jointless.

aconital.c: Aconital Ac`o*ni"tal (?), a. Of the nature of aconite.

aconite.c: Aconite Ac"o*nite (?), n. [L. aconitum, Gr.?: cf. F. aconit.] 1. (Bot.) The herb wolfsbane, or monkshood; -- applied to any plant of the genus Aconitum (tribe Hellebore), all the species of which are poisonous.

aconitic.c: Aconitic Ac`o*nit"ic (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to aconite.

aconitine.c: Aconitine A*con"i*tine (?), n. (Chem.) An intensely poisonous alkaloid, extracted from aconite.

aconitum.c: Aconitum ‖Ac`o*ni"tum (?), n. [L. See Aconite.] The poisonous herb aconite; also, an extract from it.

acontia.c: Acontia ‖A*con"ti*a (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? a little dart.] (Zool.) Threadlike defensive organs, composed largely of nettling cells (cnidæ), thrown out of the mouth or special pores of certain Actiniæ when irritated.

acontias.c: Acontias ‖A*con"ti*as (?), n. [NL., from Gr.?, fr.?, dim.? dart.] (Zool.) Anciently, a snake, called dart snake; now, one of a genus of reptiles closely allied to the lizards.

acopic.c: acopic a*cop"ic (ȧ*kŏp"ĭk), a. [Gr. 'a priv. + ko`pos striking. weariness, ko`ptein to strike.] (Med.) Relieving weariness; restorative. AS

acorn.c: Acorn A"corn (?), n. [AS. æcern, fr. æcer field, acre; akin to D. aker acorn, Ger. ecker, Icel. akarn, Dan. agern, Goth. akran fruit, akrs field; -- orig. fruit of the field. See Acre.] 1. The fruit of the oak, being an oval nut growing in a woody cup or cupule.
Acorn cup A"corn cup (?). The involucre or cup in which the acorn is fixed.

acorned.c: Acorned A"corned (?), a. 1. Furnished or loaded with acorns.

acornshell.c: Acorn-shell A"corn-shell` (?), n. (Zool.) One of the sessile cirripeds; a barnacle of the genus Balanus. See Barnacle.

acosmism.c: Acosmism A*cos"mism (?), n. [Gr. 'a priv. +? world.] A denial of the existence of the universe as distinct from God.

acosmist.c: Acosmist A*cos"mist (?), n. [See Acosmism.] One who denies the existence of the universe, or of a universe as distinct from God. G. H. Lewes.

acotyledon.c: Acotyledon A*cot`y*le"don (#; 277), n. [Gr. 'a priv. +? anything cup-shaped. See Cotyledon.] (Bot.) A plant which has no cotyledons, as the dodder and all flowerless plants.

acotyledonous.c: Acotyledonous A*cot`y*led"on*ous (#; 277), a. Having no seed lobes, as the dodder; also applied to plants which have no true seeds, as ferns, mosses, etc.

acouchy.c: Acouchy A*cou"chy (?), n. [F. acouchi, from the native name Guiana.] (Zool.) A small species of agouti (Dasyprocta acouchy).

acoumeter.c: Acoumeter A*cou"me*ter (?), n. [Gr.? to hear + -meter.] (Physics.) An instrument for measuring the acuteness of the sense of hearing. Itard.

acoumetry.c: Acoumetry A*cou"me*try (?), n. [Gr.? to hear + -metry.] The measuring of the power or extent of hearing.

acoustic.c: Acoustic A*cous"tic (#; 277), a. [F. acoustique, Gr.? relating to hearing, fr.? to hear.] Pertaining to the sense of hearing, the organs of hearing, or the science of sounds; auditory.
Acoustic A*cous"tic, n. A medicine or agent to assist hearing.

acoustical.c: Acoustical A*cous"tic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to acoustics.

acoustically.c: Acoustically A*cous"tic*al*ly (?), adv. In relation to sound or to hearing. Tyndall.

acoustician.c: Acoustician Ac`ous*ti"cian (?), n. One versed in acoustics. Tyndall.

acoustics.c: Acoustics A*cous"tics (#; 277), n. [Names of sciences in -ics, as, acoustics, mathematics, etc., are usually treated as singular. See -ics.] (Physics.) The science of sounds, teaching their nature, phenomena, and laws.

acquaint.c: Acquaint Ac*quaint" (?), a. [OF. acoint. See Acquaint, v. t.] Acquainted. [Obs.]

Acquaint Ac*quaint", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acquainted; p. pr. & vb. n. Acquainting.] [OE. aqueinten, acointen, OF. acointier, LL. adcognitare, fr. L. ad + cognitus, p. p. of cognoscere to know; con- + noscere to know. See Quaint, Know.] 1. To furnish or give experimental knowledge of; to make (one) to know; to make familiar; -- followed by with.

acquaintable.c: Acquaintable Ac*quaint"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. OF. acointable]. Easy to be acquainted with; affable. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

acquaintance.c: Acquaintance Ac*quaint"ance (?), n. [OE. aqueintance, OF. acointance, fr. acointier. See Acquaint.] 1. A state of being acquainted, or of having intimate, or more than slight or superficial, knowledge; personal knowledge gained by intercourse short of that of friendship or intimacy; as, I know the man; but have no acquaintance with him.

acquaintanceship.c: Acquaintanceship Ac*quaint"ance*ship, n. A state of being acquainted; acquaintance. Southey.

acquaintant.c: Acquaintant Ac*quaint"ant (?), n. [Cf. F. acointant, p. pr.] An acquaintance. [R.] Swift.

acquainted.c: Acquainted Ac*quaint"ed, a. Personally known; familiar. See To be acquainted with, under Acquaint, v. t.

acquaintedness.c: Acquaintedness Ac*quaint"ed*ness, n. State of being acquainted; degree of acquaintance. [R.] Boyle.

acquest.c: Acquest Ac*quest" (#), n. [OF. aquest, F. acquêt, fr. LL. acquestum, acquisītum, for L. acquisītum, p. p. (used substantively) of acquirere to acquire. See Acquire.]

acquiesce.c: Acquiesce Ac`qui*esce" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Acquiesced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Acquiescing (?)] [L. acquiescere; ad + quiescere to be quiet, fr. quies rest: cf. F. acquiescer. See Quiet.] 1. To rest satisfied, or apparently satisfied, or to rest without opposition and discontent (usually implying previous opposition or discontent); to accept or consent by silence or by omitting to object; -- followed by in, formerly also by with and to.

acquiescency.c: Acquiescency Ac`qui*es"cen*cy (?), n. The quality of being acquiescent; acquiescence.

acquiescent.c: Acquiescent Ac`qui*es"cent (?), a. [L. acquiescens, -centis; p. pr.] Resting satisfied or submissive; disposed tacitly to submit; assentive; as, an acquiescent policy.

acquiescently.c: Acquiescently Ac`qui*es"cent*ly, adv. In an acquiescent manner.

acquiet.c: Acquiet Ac*qui"et (?), v. t. [LL. acquietare; L. ad + quies rest. See Quiet and cf. Acquit.] To quiet. [Obs.]

acquirability.c: Acquirability Ac*quir"a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being acquirable; attainableness. [R.] Paley.

acquirable.c: Acquirable Ac*quir"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being acquired.

acquire.c: Acquire Ac*quire" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acquired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Acquiring (?).] [L. acquirere, acquisitum; ad + quarere to seek for. In OE. was a verb aqueren, fr. the same, through OF. aquerre. See Quest..] To gain, usually by one's own exertions; to get as one's own; as, to acquire a title, riches, knowledge, skill, good or bad habits.

acquirement.c: Acquirement Ac*quire"ment (-meint), n. The act of acquiring, or that which is acquired; attainment. “Rules for the acquirement of a taste.” Addison.

acquirer.c: Acquirer Ac*quir"er (?), n. A person who acquires.

acquisite.c: Acquisite Ac"qui*site (?), a. [L. acquisitus, p. p. of acquirere. See Acquire.] Acquired. [Obs.] Burton.

acquisition.c: Acquisition Ac`qui*si"tion (?), n. [L. acquisitio, fr. acquirere: cf. F. acquisition. See Acquire.] 1. The act or process of acquiring.

acquisitively.c: Acquisitively Ac*quis"i*tive*ly, adv. In the way of acquisition.

acquisitiveness.c: Acquisitiveness Ac*quis"i*tive*ness, n. 1. The quality of being acquisitive; propensity to acquire property; desire of possession.

acquist.c: Acquist Ac*quist" (?), n. [Cf. Acquest.] Acquisition; gain. Milton.

acquit.c: Acquit Ac*quit" (?), p. p. Acquitted; set free; rid of. [Archaic] Shak.

Acquit Ac*quit", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acquitted; p. pr. & vb. n. Acquitting.] [OE. aquiten, OF. aquiter, F. acquitter;? (L. ad) + OF. quiter, F. quitter, to quit. See Quit, and cf. Acquiet.] 1. To discharge, as a claim or debt; to clear off; to pay off; to requite.

acquitment.c: Acquitment Ac*quit"ment (-meint), n. [Cf. OF. aquitement.] Acquittal. [Obs.] Milton.

acquittal.c: Acquittal Ac*quit"tal (?), n. 1. The act of acquitting; discharge from debt or obligation; acquittance.

acquittance.c: Acquittance Ac*quit"tance (?), n. [OF. aquitance, fr. aquiter. See Acquit.] 1. The clearing off of debt or obligation; a release or discharge from debt or other liability.
Acquittance Ac*quit"tance, v. t. To acquit. [Obs.] Shak.

acquitter.c: Acquitter Ac*quit"ter (?), n. One who acquits or releases.

acrania.c: Acrania ‖A*cra"ni*a (?), n. [NL., from Gr. 'a priv. +? skull.] 1. (Physiol.) Partial or total absence of the skull.

acraze.c: Acraze Acrase { A*crase", A*craze" } (?), v. t. [Pref. a- + crase; or cf. F. écraser to crush. See Crase, Craze.]

acrasy.c: Acrasy Acrasia { ‖A*cra"si*a (?), Ac"ra*sy (?) } n. [Gr. akrasia.] Excess; intemperance. [Obs. except in Med.] Farindon.

acraspeda.c: Acraspeda ‖A*cras"pe*da (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'a priv. +? border.] (Zool.) A group of acalephs, including most of the larger jellyfishes; the Discophora.

acre.c: Acre A"cre (?), n. [OE. aker, AS. æcer; akin to OS. accar, OHG. achar, Ger. acker, Icel. akr, Sw. åker, Dan. ager, Goth. akrs, L. ager, Gr.?, Skr. ajra. √2, 206.] 1. Any field of arable or pasture land. [Obs.]

acreable.c: Acreable A"cre*a*ble (?), a. Of an acre; per acre; as, the acreable produce.

acreage.c: Acreage A"cre*age (?), n. Acres collectively; as, the acreage of a farm or a country.

acred.c: Acred A"cred (?), a. Possessing acres or landed property; -- used in composition; as, large-acred men.

acrid.c: Acrid Ac"rid (?), a. [L. acer sharp; prob. assimilated in form to acid. See Eager.] 1. Sharp and harsh, or bitter and not, to the taste; pungent; as, acrid salts.

acridness.c: Acridness Acridity { A*crid"i*ty (?), Ac"rid*ness (?) } n. The quality of being acrid or pungent; irritant bitterness; extreme bitterness; acrimony; as, the acridity of a plant, of a speech.

acridly.c: Acridly Ac"rid*ly (?), adv. In an acid manner.

acrimonious.c: Acrimonious Ac"ri*mo"ni*ous (?), a. [Cf. LL. acrimonious, F. acrimonieux.] 1. Acrid; corrosive; as, acrimonious gall. [Archaic] Harvey.

acrimoniously.c: Acrimoniously Ac`ri*mo"ni*ous*ly, adv. In an acrimonious manner.

acrimoniousness.c: Acrimoniousness Ac`ri*mo"ni*ous*ness, n. The quality of being acrimonious; asperity; acrimony.

acrimony.c: Acrimony Ac"ri*mo*ny (?), n.; pl. Acrimonies (?). [L. acrimonia, fr. acer, sharp: cf. F. acrimonie.] 1. A quality of bodies which corrodes or destroys others; also, a harsh or biting sharpness; as, the acrimony of the juices of certain plants. [Archaic] Bacon.

acrisy.c: acrisy acrisia { ‖a*cris"i*a (ȧ*krĭs"ĭ*ȧ), ac"ri*sy (ăk"rĭ*sy̆), } n. [LL. acrisia, Gr. 'akrisi`a; 'a priv. + kri`nein to separate, to decide.] 1. Inability to judge.

acrita.c: Acrita ‖Ac"ri*ta (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? indiscernible; 'a priv. +? to distinguish.] (Zool.) The lowest groups of animals, in which no nervous system has been observed.

acritan.c: Acritan Ac"ri*tan (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Acrita. -- n. An individual of the Acrita.

acritical.c: Acritical A*crit"ic*al (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. +? critical.] (Med.) Having no crisis; giving no indications of a crisis; as, acritical symptoms, an acritical abscess. [R.] AS

acritochromacy.c: Acritochromacy Ac`ri*to*chro"ma*cy (?), n. [Gr.? undistinguishable; 'a priv. +? to separate, distinguish +? color.] Color blindness; achromatopsy.

acritude.c: Acritude Ac"ri*tude (?), n. [L. acritudo, from acer sharp.] Acridity; pungency joined with heat. [Obs.]

acrity.c: Acrity Ac"ri*ty (?), n. [L. acritas, fr. acer sharp: cf. F. âcreté.] Sharpness; keenness. [Obs.]

acroamatical.c: Acroamatical Acroamatic { Ac`ro*a*mat"ic (?), Ac`ro*a*mat"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?, fr.? to hear.] Communicated orally; oral; -- applied to the esoteric teachings of Aristotle, those intended for his genuine disciples, in distinction from his exoteric doctrines, which were adapted to outsiders or the public generally. Hence: Abstruse; profound.

acroatic.c: Acroatic Ac`ro*at"ic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? to hear.] Same as Acroamatic.

acrobat.c: Acrobat Ac"ro*bat (?), n. [F. acrobate, fr. Gr.? walking on tiptoe, climbing aloft;? high +? to go.] One who practices rope dancing, high vaulting, or other daring gymnastic feats.

acrobatic.c: Acrobatic Ac`ro*bat"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. acrobatique.] Pertaining to an acrobat.

acrobatism.c: Acrobatism Ac"ro*bat*ism (?), n. Feats of the acrobat; daring gymnastic feats; high vaulting.

acrocarpous.c: Acrocarpous Ac`ro*car"pous (?), a. [Gr.? extreme, highest +? fruit.] (Bot.) (a) Having a terminal fructification; having the fruit at the end of the stalk. (b) Having the fruit stalks at the end of a leafy stem, as in certain mosses.

acrocephalic.c: Acrocephalic Ac`ro*ce*phal"ic (?), a. [Gr.? highest +?. See Cephalic.] Characterized by a high skull.

acroceraunian.c: Acroceraunian Ac`ro*ce*rau"ni*an (?), a. [L. acroceraunius, fr. Gr.? high, n. pl.? heights +? thunderbolt.] Of or pertaining to the high mountain range of “thunder-smitten” peaks (now Kimara), between Epirus and Macedonia. Shelley.

acrodactylum.c: Acrodactylum ‖Ac`ro*dac"tyl*um (?), n. [NL., from Gr.? topmost +? finger.] (Zool.) The upper surface of the toes, individually.

acrodont.c: Acrodont Ac"ro*dont (?), n. [Gr. 'a`kros summit + 'odoy`s, 'odo`ntos, a tooth.] (Zool.) One of a group of lizards having the teeth immovably united to the top of the alveolar ridge. -- a. Of or pertaining to the acrodonts.

acrogen.c: Acrogen Ac"ro*gen (?), n. [Gr. 'a`kros extreme, high + -gen.] (Bot.) A plant of the highest class of cryptogams, including the ferns, etc. See Cryptogamia.

acrogenous.c: Acrogenous Ac*rog"e*nous (?), a. (Bot.) Increasing by growth from the extremity; as, an acrogenous plant.

acrolein.c: Acrolein A*cro"le*in (?), n. [L. acer sharp + olēre to smell.] (Chem.) A limpid, colorless, highly volatile liquid, obtained by the dehydration of glycerin, or the destructive distillation of neutral fats containing glycerin. Its vapors are intensely irritating. Watts.

acrolith.c: Acrolith Ac"ro*lith (?), n. [L. acrolthus, Gr. 'akroli`qos with the ends made of stone; 'a`kros extreme + li`qos stone.] (Arch. & Sculp.) A statue whose extremities are of stone, the trunk being generally of wood. Elmes.

acrolithic.c: Acrolithic Acrolithan { A*crol"i*than (?), Ac`ro*lith"ic (?), } a. Pertaining to, or like, an acrolith.

acromegaly.c: Acromegaly Ac`ro*meg"a*ly (ăk`ro*mĕg"ȧ*ly̆), n. [NL. acromegalia, fr. Gr. 'a`kron point, peak + me`gas, mega`loy, big.] (Med.) Chronic enlargement of many bones of the skeleton, especially bones of hands, feet and face; the condition is due to excessive secretion of growth hormone.

acromial.c: Acromial A*cro"mi*al (?), a. [Cf. F. acromial.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the acromion. Dunglison.

acromion.c: Acromion ‖A*cro"mi*on (?), n. [Gr.?; 'a`kros extreme +? shoulder: cf. F. acromion.] (Anat.) The outer extremity of the shoulder blade.

acromonogrammatic.c: Acromonogrammatic Ac`ro*mon`o*gram*mat"ic (?), a. [Gr. 'a`kros extreme +? alone +? a letter.] Having each verse begin with the same letter as that with which the preceding verse ends.

acronychal.c: Acronychal Acronyc { A*cron"yc (?), A*cron"ych*al (?), } a. [Gr. 'akro`nychos at nightfall; 'a`kros + ny`x night.] (Astron.) Rising at sunset and setting at sunrise, as a star; -- opposed to cosmical.

acronycally.c: Acronycally A*cron"yc*al*ly, adv. In an acronycal manner as rising at the setting of the sun, and vice versa.

acronyctous.c: Acronyctous Ac"ro*nyc"tous (?), a. [Gr. 'akro`nyktos; 'a`kros + ny`x, nykto`s, night.] (Astron.) Acronycal.

acropetal.c: Acropetal A*crop"e*tal (?), a. [Gr. 'a`kros summit + L. petere to seek.] (Bot.) Developing from below towards the apex, or from the circumference towards the center; centripetal; -- said of certain inflorescence.

acrophony.c: Acrophony A*croph"o*ny (?), n. [Gr. 'a`kros extreme +? sound.] The use of a picture symbol of an object to represent phonetically the initial sound of the name of the object.

acropodium.c: Acropodium ‖Ac`ro*po"di*um (?), n. [Gr. 'a`kros topmost + poy`s, podo`s, foot.] (Zool.) The entire upper surface of the foot.

acropolis.c: Acropolis A*crop"o*lis (?), n. [Gr. 'akro`polis; 'a`kros extreme + po`lis city.] The upper part, or the citadel, of a Grecian city; especially, the citadel of Athens.

acropolitan.c: Acropolitan Ac"ro*pol"i*tan (?), a. Pertaining to an acropolis.

acrospire.c: Acrospire Ac"ro*spire (?), n. [Gr.? +? anything twisted.] (Bot.) The sprout at the end of a seed when it begins to germinate; the plumule in germination; -- so called from its spiral form.
Acrospire Ac"ro*spire, v. i. To put forth the first sprout.

acrospore.c: Acrospore Ac"ro*spore (?), n. [Gr.? +? fruit.] (Bot.) A spore borne at the extremity of the cells of fructification in fungi.

across.c: Across A*cross" (#; 115), prep. [Pref. a- + cross: cf. F. en croix. See Cross, n.] From side to side; athwart; crosswise, or in a direction opposed to the length; quite over; as, a bridge laid across a river. Dryden.
Across A*cross", adv. 1. From side to side; crosswise; as, with arms folded across. Shak.

acrostic.c: Acrostic A*cros"tic (?) (?), n. [Gr.?;? extreme +? order, line, verse.] 1. A composition, usually in verse, in which the first or the last letters of the lines, or certain other letters, taken in order, form a name, word, phrase, or motto.

acrostical.c: Acrostical Acrostic { A*cros"tic (?), A*cros"tic*al (?), } n. Pertaining to, or characterized by, acrostics.

acrostically.c: Acrostically A*cros"tic*al*ly, adv. After the manner of an acrostic.

acrotarsium.c: Acrotarsium ‖Ac`ro*tar"si*um (?), n. [NL., from Gr.? topmost +? tarsus.] (Zool.) The instep or front of the tarsus.

acroteleutic.c: Acroteleutic Ac`ro*te*leu"tic (ăk`ro*te*lū"tĭk), n. [Gr. 'a`kros extreme + teley`th end.] (Eccles.) The end of a verse or psalm, or something added thereto, to be sung by the people, by way of a response.

acroter.c: Acroter Ac"ro*ter (ăk`ro*tẽr or ȧ*krō*tẽr), n. [F. acrotère. See Acroterium.] (Arch.) Same as Acroterium.

acroterial.c: Acroterial Ac`ro*te"ri*al (ăk`ro*tē"rĭ*ail), a. Pertaining to an acroterium; as, acroterial ornaments. P. Cyc.

acroterium.c: Acroterium ‖Ac`ro*te`ri*um (-ŭm), n.; pl. Acroteria (?). [L., fr. Gr. 'akrwth`rion summit, fr. 'a`kros topmost.] (Arch.) (a) One of the small pedestals, for statues or other ornaments, placed on the apex and at the basal angles of a pediment. Acroteria are also sometimes placed upon the gables in Gothic architecture. J. H. Parker. (b) One of the pedestals, for vases or statues, forming a part roof balustrade.

acrotic.c: acrotic a*crot"ic (ȧ*krŏt"ĭk), a. [Gr. 'akro`ths an extreme, fr. 'a`kros.] 1. (Med.) Pertaining to or affecting the surface of the body. AS

acrotism.c: acrotism ac"ro*tism (ăk"ro*tĭz'm), n. [Gr. 'a priv. + kro`tos a rattling, beating.] (Med.) Lack or defect of pulsation. AS

acrotomous.c: Acrotomous A*crot"o*mous (?), a. [Gr. 'akro`tomos cut off sharp; 'a`kros extreme + te`mnein to cut.] (Min.) Having a cleavage parallel with the base.

acrylic.c: acrylic a*cryl"ic (ȧ*krĭl"ĭk), a. 1. (Chem.) Of or containing acryl, the hypothetical radical (R.CH:CH.CO-) of which acrolein (H2C:CH.CHO) is the hydride; as, acrylic acid. The characteristic residue in an acrylic compound is the carbonyl group attached directly to an ethylenic carbon.

act.c: Act Act (ăkt), n. [L. actus, fr. agere to drive, do: cf. F. acte. See Agent.] 1. That which is done or doing; the exercise of power, or the effect, of which power exerted is the cause; a performance; a deed.
Act Act, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Acted; p. pr. & vb. n. Acting.] [L. actus, p. p. of agere to drive, lead, do; but influenced by E. act, n.] 1. To move to action; to actuate; to animate. [Obs.]
Act Act, v. i. 1. To exert power; to produce an effect; as, the stomach acts upon food.

actable.c: Actable Act"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being acted. Tennyson.

actinal.c: Actinal Ac"ti*nal (?), a. [Gr.?,?, ray.] (Zool.) Pertaining to the part of a radiate animal which contains the mouth. L. Agassiz.

actinaria.c: Actinaria ‖Ac`ti*na"ri*a (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.?,?, ray.] (Zool.) An order of Anthozoa, including those which have simple tentacles and do not form stony corals. Sometimes, in a wider sense, applied to all the Anthozoa, expert the Alcyonaria, whether forming corals or not.

acting.c: Acting Act"ing (?), a. 1. Operating in any way.

actinia.c: Actinia ‖Ac*tin"i*a (?), n.; pl. L. Actiniæ (?), E. Actinias (?). [Latinized fr. Gr.?,?, ray.] (Zool.) (a) An animal of the class Anthozoa, and family Actinidæ.
