From a resemblance to flowers in form and color, they are often called animal flowers and sea anemones. [See Polyp.]. (b) A genus in the family Actinidæ.

actinic.c: Actinic Ac*tin"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to actinism; as, actinic rays.

actiniform.c: Actiniform Ac*tin"i*form (?), a. [Gr.?,?, ray + -form.] Having a radiated form, like a sea anemone.

actinism.c: Actinism Ac"tin*ism (?), n. [Gr.?,? ray.] The property of radiant energy (found chiefly in solar or electric light) by which chemical changes are produced, as in photography.

actinium.c: Actinium Ac*tin"i*um (?), n. [Gr.?,?, ray.] (Chem.) A supposed metal, said by Phipson to be contained in commercial zinc; -- so called because certain of its compounds are darkened by exposure to light.

actinochemistry.c: Actino-chemistry Ac`ti*no-chem"is*try (?), n. Chemistry in its relations to actinism. Draper.

actinogram.c: Actinogram Ac*tin"o*gram (?), n. [Gr.?,?, ray + -gram.] A record made by the actinograph. [Obsolescent]

actinograph.c: Actinograph Ac*tin"o*graph (?), n. [Gr.?,?, ray + -graph.] An instrument for measuring and recording the variations in the actinic or chemical force of rays of light. Nichol.

actinoid.c: Actinoid Ac"tin*oid (?), a. [Gr.?,?, ray + -oid.] Having the form of rays; radiated, as an actinia.

actinolite.c: Actinolite Ac*tin"o*lite (?), n. [Gr.?,?, ray + -lite.] (Min.) A bright green variety of amphibole occurring usually in fibrous or columnar masses.

actinolitic.c: Actinolitic Ac`tin*o*lit"ic (?), a. (Min.) Of the nature of, or containing, actinolite.

actinology.c: Actinology Ac`ti*nol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.?,?, ray + -logy.] The science which treats of rays of light, especially of the actinic or chemical rays.

actinomere.c: Actinomere Ac*tin"o*mere (?), n. [Gr.?,?, ray +? part.] (Zool.) One of the radial segments composing the body of one of the Cœlenterata.

actinometer.c: Actinometer Ac`ti*nom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.?,?, ray + -meter] (a) An instrument for measuring the direct heating power of the sun's rays. (b) An instrument for measuring the actinic effect of rays of light.

actinometric.c: Actinometric Ac`ti*no*met"ric (?), a. Pertaining to the measurement of the intensity of the solar rays, either (a) heating, or (b) actinic.

actinometry.c: Actinometry Ac`ti*nom"e*try (?), n. 1. The measurement of the force of solar radiation. Maury.

actinomycosis.c: Actinomycosis Ac`ti*no*my*co"sis (ăk`tĭ*no*mī*kō"sĭs), n. [NL.] (Med.) A chronic infectious disease of cattle and man due to infection with actinomycetes, especially by Actinomyces bovis in cattle and by Actinomyces israeli or Arachnia propionica in man. It is characterized by hard swellings usually in the mouth and jaw. In man the disease may also affect the abdomen or thorax. In cattle it is called also lumpy jaw or big jaw.

actinophone.c: Actinophone Ac*tin"o*phone (?), n. [Gr.?,?, ray +? voice.] (Physics) An apparatus for the production of sound by the action of the actinic, or ultraviolet, rays.

actinophonic.c: Actinophonic Ac*tin`o*phon"ic (?), a. (Physics) Pertaining to, or causing the production of, sound by means of the actinic, or ultraviolet, rays; as, actinophonic phenomena.

actinophorous.c: Actinophorous Ac`ti*noph"o*rous (?), a. [Gr.?,?, ray + fe`rein to bear.] Having straight projecting spines.

actinosome.c: Actinosome Ac*tin"o*some (?), n. [Gr.? ray +? body.] (Zool.) The entire body of a cœlenterate.

actinost.c: Actinost Ac"tin*ost (?), n. [Gr.?,?, ray +? bone.] (Anat.) One of the bones at the base of a paired fin of a fish.

actinostome.c: Actinostome Ac*tin"o*stome (?), n. [Gr.?,?, a ray +? mouth.] (Zool.) The mouth or anterior opening of a cœlenterate animal.

actinotrocha.c: Actinotrocha ‖Ac`ti*not"ro*cha (?), n. pl. [NL.; Gr.?,?, a ray +? a ring.] (Zool.) A peculiar larval form of Phoronis, a genus of marine worms, having a circle of ciliated tentacles.

actinozoa.c: Actinozoa ‖Ac"ti*no*zo"a (?), n. pl. [Gr.?,?, ray + zw^,on animal.] (Zool.) A group of Cœlenterata, comprising the Anthozoa and Ctenophora. The sea anemone, or actinia, is a familiar example.

actinozoal.c: Actinozoal Ac`ti*no*zo"al (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Actinozoa.

actinula.c: Actinula ‖Ac*tin"u*la (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.?,?, a ray.] (Zool.) A kind of embryo of certain hydroids (Tubularia), having a stellate form.

action.c: Action Ac"tion (?), n. [OF. action, L. actio, fr. agere to do. See Act.] 1. A process or condition of acting or moving, as opposed to rest; the doing of something; exertion of power or force, as when one body acts on another; the effect of power exerted on one body by another; agency; activity; operation; as, the action of heat; a man of action.

actionable.c: Actionable Ac"tion*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. LL. actionabilis. See Action.] That may be the subject of an action or suit at law; as, to call a man a thief is actionable.

actionably.c: Actionably Ac"tion*a*bly, adv. In an actionable manner.

actionist.c: Actionist Actionary { Ac"tion*a*ry (?), Ac"tion*ist (?), } n. [Cf. F. actionnaire.] (Com.) A shareholder in joint-stock company. [Obs.]

activate.c: Activate Ac"ti*vate (?), v. t. To make active. [Obs.]

activation.c: activation activation n. 1. the process of making active.

active.c: Active Ac"tive (?), a. [F. actif, L. activus, fr. agere to act.] 1. Having the power or quality of acting; causing change; communicating action or motion; acting; -- opposed to passive, that receives; as, certain active principles; the powers of the mind.

actively.c: Actively Ac"tive*ly, adv. 1. In an active manner; nimbly; briskly; energetically; also, by one's own action; voluntarily, not passively.

activeness.c: Activeness Ac"tive*ness, n. The quality of being active; nimbleness; quickness of motion; activity.

activity.c: Activity Ac*tiv"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Activities (?). [Cf. F. activité, LL. activitas.] The state or quality of being active; nimbleness; agility; vigorous action or operation; energy; active force; as, an increasing variety of human activities. “The activity of toil.” Palfrey.

actless.c: Actless Act"less (?), a. Without action or spirit. [R.]

acton.c: Acton Ac"ton (?), n. [OF. aketon, auqueton, F. hoqueton, a quilted jacket, fr. Sp. alcoton, algodon, cotton. Cf. Cotton.] A stuffed jacket worn under the mail, or (later) a jacket plated with mail. [Spelled also hacqueton.] [Obs.] Halliwell. Sir W. Scott.

actor.c: Actor Ac"tor (?), n. [L. actor, fr. agere to act.] 1. One who acts, or takes part in any affair; a doer.

actress.c: Actress Ac`tress (?), n. [Cf. F. actrice.] 1. A female actor or doer. [Obs.] Cockeram.

actual.c: Actual Ac"tu*al (#; 135), a. [OE. actuel, F. actuel, L. actualis, fr. agere to do, act.] 1. Involving or comprising action; active. [Obs.]
Actual Ac"tu*al (?), n. (Finance) Something actually received; real, as distinct from estimated, receipts. [Cant]

actualist.c: Actualist Ac"tu*al*ist, n. One who deals with or considers actually existing facts and conditions, rather than fancies or theories; a realist; -- opposed to idealist. J. Grote.

actuality.c: Actuality Ac`tu*al"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Actualities (?). The state of being actual; reality; as, the actuality of God's nature. South.

actualization.c: Actualization Actualisation Ac`tu*al*i*sa"tion, Ac`tu*al*i*za"tion (?), n. A making actual or really existent; giving the appearance of reality. [R.] Emerson.

actualize.c: Actualize Ac"tu*al*ize (?), v. t. To make actual; to realize in action. [R.] Coleridge.

actually.c: Actually Ac"tu*al*ly, adv. 1. Actively. [Obs.] “Neither actually... nor passively.” Fuller.

actualness.c: Actualness Ac"tu*al*ness, n. Quality of being actual; actuality.

actuarial.c: Actuarial Ac`tu*a"ri*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to actuaries; as, the actuarial value of an annuity.

actuary.c: Actuary Ac"tu*a*ry (?), n.; pl. Actuaries (?). [L. actuarius copyist, clerk, fr. actus, p. p. of agere to do, act.] 1. (Law) A registrar or clerk; -- used originally in courts of civil law jurisdiction, but in Europe used for a clerk or registrar generally.

actuate.c: Actuate Ac"tu*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Actuated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Actuating (?).] [LL. actuatus, p. p. of actuare, fr. L. actus act.] 1. To put into action or motion; to move or incite to action; to influence actively; to move as motives do; -- more commonly used of persons.
Actuate Ac"tu*ate (?), a. [LL. actuatus, p. p. of actuare.] Put in action; actuated. [Obs.] South.

actuation.c: Actuation Ac`tu*a"tion (?), n. [Cf. LL. actuatio.] A bringing into action; movement. Bp. Pearson.

actuator.c: Actuator Ac"tu*a`tor (?), n. One who actuates, or puts into action. [R.] Melville.

actuosity.c: Actuosity Ac`tu*os"i*ty (?), n. Abundant activity. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

acturience.c: Acturience Ac*tu"ri*ence (?), n. [A desid. of L. agere, actum, to act.] Tendency or impulse to act. [R.]

acuate.c: Acuate Ac"u*ate (?), v. t. [L. acus needle.] To sharpen; to make pungent; to quicken. [Obs.] “[To] acuate the blood.” Harvey.

acuition.c: Acuition Ac`u*i"tion (?), n. [L. acutus, as if acuitus, p. p. of acuere to sharpen.] The act of sharpening. [Obs.]

acuity.c: Acuity A*cu"i*ty (?), n. [LL. acuitas: cf. F. acuité.] Sharpness or acuteness, as of a needle, wit, etc.

aculeate.c: Aculeate A*cu"le*ate (?), a. [L. aculeatus, fr. aculeus, dim. of acus needle.] 1. (Zool.) Having a sting; covered with prickles; sharp like a prickle.

aculeated.c: Aculeated A*cu"le*a`ted (?), a. Having a sharp point; armed with prickles; prickly; aculeate.

aculeolate.c: Aculeolate A*cu"le*o*late (?), a. [L. aculeolus little needle.] (Bot.) Having small prickles or sharp points. Gray.

aculeous.c: Aculeous A*cu"le*ous (?), a. Aculeate. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

aculeus.c: Aculeus ‖A*cu"le*us (?), n.; pl. Aculei (?). [L., dim. of acus needle.] 1. (Bot.) A prickle growing on the bark, as in some brambles and roses. Lindley.

acumen.c: Acumen A*cu"men (?), n. [L. acumen, fr. acuere to sharpen. Cf. Acute.] Quickness of perception or discernment; penetration of mind; the faculty of nice discrimination. Selden.

acuminate.c: Acuminate A*cu"mi*nate (?), a. [L. acuminatus, p. p. of acuminare to sharpen, fr. acumen. See Acumen.] Tapering to a point; pointed; as, acuminate leaves, teeth, etc.
Acuminate A*cu"mi*nate (?), v. t. To render sharp or keen. [R.] “To acuminate even despair.” Cowper.
Acuminate A*cu"mi*nate, v. i. To end in, or come to, a sharp point. “Acuminating in a cone of prelacy.” Milton.

acumination.c: Acumination A*cu`mi*na"tion (?), n. A sharpening; termination in a sharp point; a tapering point. Bp. Pearson.

acuminose.c: Acuminose A*cu"mi*nose` (?), a. Terminating in a flat, narrow end. Lindley.

acuminous.c: Acuminous A*cu"mi*nous (?), a. Characterized by acumen; keen. Highmore.

acupressure.c: Acupressure Ac`u*pres"sure (?), n. [L. acus needle + premere, pressum, to press.] (Surg.) A mode of arresting hemorrhage resulting from wounds or surgical operations, by passing under the divided vessel a needle, the ends of which are left exposed externally on the cutaneous surface. Simpson.

acupuncture.c: Acupuncture Ac`u*punc"ture (ăk`u*pŭṉk"tur or ăk"u*pŭṉk`chur), n. [L. acus needle + punctura a pricking, fr. pungere to prick: cf. F. acuponcture.] Pricking with a needle; a needle prick. Specifically (Med.): The insertion of needles into the living tissues for remedial purposes, such as to relieve pain. It was first recorded as being practised in China, and the technique is believed to be over 2,000 years old. AS
Acupuncture Ac`u*punc"ture (?), v. t. To treat with acupuncture.

acute.c: Acute A*cute" (?), a. [L. acutus, p. p. of acuere to sharpen, fr. a root ak to be sharp. Cf. Ague, Cute, Edge.] 1. Sharp at the end; ending in a sharp point; pointed; -- opposed to blunt or obtuse; as, an acute angle; an acute leaf.
Acute A*cute", v. t. To give an acute sound to; as, he acutes his rising inflection too much. [R.] Walker.

acuteangled.c: Acute-angled A*cute"-an`gled (-ăṉ"g'ld), a. Having acute angles; as, an acute-angled triangle, a triangle with every one of its angles less than a right angle.

acutely.c: Acutely A*cute"ly, adv. In an acute manner; sharply; keenly; with nice discrimination.

acuteness.c: Acuteness A*cute"ness, n. 1. The quality of being acute or pointed; sharpness; as, the acuteness of an angle. AS

acutifoliate.c: Acutifoliate A*cu`ti*fo"li*ate (?), a. [L. acutus sharp + folium leaf.] (Bot.) Having sharp-pointed leaves.

acutilobate.c: Acutilobate A*cu`ti*lo"bate (?), a. [L. acutus sharp + E. lobe.] (Bot.) Having acute lobes, as some leaves.

acutorsion.c: Acutorsion Ac`u*tor"sion (?), n. [L. acus needle + torsion.] (Med.) The twisting of an artery with a needle to arrest hemorrhage. [archaic] AS

acyclic.c: Acyclic A*cyc"lic (?), a. [Pref. a- not + cyclic.] Not cyclic; not disposed in cycles or whorls; as: (a) (Bot.) Of a flower, having its parts inserted spirally on the receptacle. (b) (Org. Chem.) Having an open-chain structure; aliphatic.

acyl.c: Acyl Ac"yl (?), n. [Acid + -yl.] (Org. Chem.) An acid radical, as acetyl, malonyl, or benzoyl. An acyl radical can be depicted as R-CO-, where -CO- is the carbonyl group, and R is the group that characterizes the acyl moiety.

ad.c: Ad- ‖Ad- (?). [A Latin preposition, signifying to. See At.] As a prefix ad- assumes the forms ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-, assimilating the d with the first letter of the word to which ad- is prefixed. It remains unchanged before vowels, and before d, h, j, m, v. Examples: adduce, adhere, adjacent, admit, advent, accord, affect, aggregate, allude, annex, appear, etc. It becomes ac- before qu, as in acquiesce.
Ad captandum ‖Ad cap*tan"dum (?). [L., for catching.] A phrase used adjectively sometimes of meretricious attempts to catch or win popular favor.
Ad hominem ‖Ad hom"i*nem (?). [L., to the man.] A phrase applied to an appeal or argument addressed to the principles, interests, or passions of a man.
Ad infinitum ‖Ad in`fi*ni"tum (?). [L., to infinity.] Without limit; endlessly.
Ad libitum ‖Ad lib"i*tum (?). At one's pleasure; as one wishes.

Ad valorem ‖Ad va*lo"rem (?). [L., according to the value.] (Com.) A term used to denote a duty or charge laid upon goods, at a certain rate per cent upon their value, as stated in their invoice, -- in opposition to a specific sum upon a given quantity or number; as, an ad valorem duty of twenty per cent.

adact.c: Adact Ad*act" (?), v. t. [L. adactus, p. p. of adigere.] To compel; to drive. [Obs.] Fotherby.

adactylous.c: Adactylous Adactyl { A*dac"tyl (?), A*dac"tyl*ous (?), } a. [Gr. 'a priv. +? finger.] (Zool.) (a) Without fingers or without toes. (b) Without claws on the feet (of crustaceous animals).

adage.c: Adage Ad"age (?), n. [F. adage, fr. L. adagium; ad + the root of L. aio I say.] An old saying, which has obtained credit by long use; a proverb.

adagial.c: Adagial A*da"gi*al (?), a. Pertaining to an adage; proverbial. “Adagial verse.” Barrow.

adagio.c: Adagio ‖A*da"gio (?), a. & adv. [It. adagio; ad (L. ad) at + agio convenience, leisure, ease. See Agio.] (Mus.) Slow; slowly, leisurely, and gracefully. When repeated, adagio, adagio, it directs the movement to be very slow.
Adagio ‖A*da"gio, n. A piece of music in adagio time; a slow movement; as, an adagio of Haydn.

adam.c: Adam Ad"am (?), n. 1. The name given in the Bible to the first man, the progenitor of the human race.

adamant.c: Adamant Ad"a*mant (ăd"ȧ*mănt), n. [OE. adamaunt, adamant, diamond, magnet, OF. adamant, L. adamas, adamantis, the hardest metal, fr. Gr. 'ada`mas, -antos; 'a priv. + dama^,n to tame, subdue. In OE., from confusion with L. adamare to love, be attached to, the word meant also magnet, as in OF. and LL. See Diamond, Tame.] 1. A stone imagined by some to be of impenetrable hardness; a name given to the diamond and other substances of extreme hardness; but in modern mineralogy it has no technical signification. It is now a rhetorical or poetical name for the embodiment of impenetrable hardness.

adamantean.c: Adamantean Ad`a*man*te"an (?), a. [L. adamantēus.] Of adamant; hard as adamant. Milton.

adamantine.c: Adamantine Ad`a*man"tine (?), a. [L. adamantinus, Gr.?.] 1. Made of adamant, or having the qualities of adamant; incapable of being broken, dissolved, or penetrated; as, adamantine bonds or chains.

adambulacral.c: Adambulacral Ad`am*bu*la"cral (?), a. [L. ad + E. ambulacral.] (Zool.) Next to the ambulacra; as, the adambulacral ossicles of the starfish.

adamical.c: Adamical Adamic { A*dam"ic (?), A*dam"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to Adam, or resembling him.

adamite.c: Adamite Ad"am*ite (?), n. [From Adam.] 1. A descendant of Adam; a human being.

adams.c: Adam's apple Ad"am's ap"ple (?). See under Adam.

adansonia.c: Adansonia ‖Ad`an*so"ni*a (?), n. [From Adanson, a French botanist.] (Bot.) A genus of great trees related to the Bombax. There are two species, Adansonia digitata, the baobab or monkey-bread of Africa and India, and Adansonia Gregorii, the sour gourd or cream-of-tartar tree of Australia. Both have a trunk of moderate height, but of enormous diameter, and a wide-spreading head. The fruit is oblong, and filled with pleasantly acid pulp. The wood is very soft, and the bark is used by the natives for making ropes and cloth. D. C. Eaton.

adapt.c: Adapt A*dapt", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adapted; p. pr. & vb. n. Adapting.] [L. adaptare; ad + aptare to fit; cf. F. adapter. See Apt, Adept.] To make suitable; to fit, or suit; to adjust; to alter so as to fit for a new use; -- sometimes followed by to or for.

adaptableness.c: Adaptableness Adaptability { A*dapt`a*bil"i*ty (?), A*dapt"a*ble*ness (?), } n. The quality of being adaptable; suitableness. “General adaptability for every purpose.” Farrar.

adaptable.c: Adaptable A*dapt"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being adapted.

adaptation.c: Adaptation Ad`ap*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. adaptation, LL. adaptatio.] 1. The act or process of adapting, or fitting; or the state of being adapted or fitted; fitness. “Adaptation of the means to the end.” Erskine.

adaptedness.c: Adaptedness A*dapt"ed*ness (?), n. The state or quality of being adapted; suitableness; special fitness.

adaptive.c: Adaptive A*dapt"ive (?), a. Suited, given, or tending, to adaptation; characterized by adaptation; capable of adapting. Coleridge. -- A*dapt"ive*ly, adv.

adaptiveness.c: Adaptiveness A*dapt"ive*ness, n. The quality of being adaptive; capacity to adapt.

adaptly.c: Adaptly A*dapt"ly, adv. In a suitable manner. [R.] Prior.

adar.c: Adar ‖A"dar (?), n. [Heb. adär.] The twelfth month of the Hebrew ecclesiastical year, and the sixth of the civil. It corresponded nearly with March.

adarce.c: Adarce ‖A*dar"ce (?), n. [L. adarce, adarca, Gr.?.] A saltish concretion on reeds and grass in marshy grounds in Galatia. It is soft and porous, and was formerly used for cleansing the skin from freckles and tetters, and also in leprosy. Dana.

adatis.c: Adatis ‖Ad"a*tis (?), n. A fine cotton cloth of India.

adaunt.c: Adaunt A*daunt" (?), v. t. [OE. adaunten to overpower, OF. adonter; à (L. ad) + donter, F. dompter. See Daunt.] To daunt; to subdue; to mitigate. [Obs.] Skelton.

adaw.c: Adaw A*daw" (?), v. t. [Cf. OE. adawe of dawe, AS. of dagum from days, i. e., from life, out of life.] To subdue; to daunt. [Obs.]
Adaw A*daw", v. t. & i. [OE. adawen to wake; pref. a- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-) + dawen, dagon, to dawn. See Daw.] To awaken; to arouse. [Obs.]

adays.c: Adays A*days" (?), adv. [Pref. a- (for on) + day; the final s was orig. a genitive ending, afterwards forming adverbs.] By day, or every day; in the daytime. [Obs.] Fielding.

add.c: Add Add (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Added; p. pr. & vb. n. Adding.] [L. addere; ad + dare to give, put. Cf. Date, Do.] 1. To give by way of increased possession (to any one); to bestow (on).
Add Add (?), v. i. 1. To make an addition. To add to, to augment; to increase; as, it adds to our anxiety. “I will add to your yoke.” 1 Kings xii. 14.

addax.c: Addax Ad"dax (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) One of the largest African antelopes (Hippotragusnasomaculatus or Oryx nasomaculatus).

addeem.c: Addeem Ad*deem" (?), v. t. [Pref. a- + deem.] To award; to adjudge. [Obs.] “Unto him they did addeem the prise.” Spenser.

addendum.c: Addendum ‖Ad*den"dum (?), n.; pl. Addenda (?). [L., fr. addere to add.] A thing to be added; an appendix or addition.

adder.c: Adder Add"er (?), n. [See Add.] One who, or that which, adds; esp., a machine for adding numbers.

Adder Ad"der, n. [OE. addere, naddere, eddre, AS. nædre, adder, snake; akin to OS. nadra, OHG. natra, natara, Ger. natter, Goth. nadrs, Icel. naðr, masc., naðra, fem.: cf. W. neidr, Gorn. naddyr, Ir. nathair, L. natrix, water snake. An adder is for a nadder.] 1. A serpent. [Obs.] “The eddre seide to the woman.” Wyclif. Gen. iii. 4.)
Adder fly/ Ad"der fly/ (?). A dragon fly.

adderstongue.c: Adder's-tongue Ad"der's-tongue` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) A genus of ferns (Ophioglossum), whose seeds are produced on a spike resembling a serpent's tongue. (b) The yellow dogtooth violet. Gray.

adderwort.c: Adderwort Ad"der*wort` (?), n. (Bot.) The common bistort or snakeweed (Polygonum bistorta).

addibility.c: Addibility Add`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quantity of being addible; capability of addition. Locke.

addible.c: Addible Add"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being added. “Addible numbers.” Locke.

addict.c: Addict Ad*dict", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Addicted; p. pr. & vb. n. Addicting.] [L. addictus, p. p. of addicere to adjudge, devote; ad + dicere to say. See Diction.] 1. To apply habitually; to devote; to habituate; -- with to. “They addict themselves to the civil law.” Evelyn.

addictedness.c: Addictedness Ad*dict"ed*ness, n. The quality or state of being addicted; attachment.

addiction.c: Addiction Ad*dic"tion (?), n. [Cf. L. addictio an adjudging.] The state of being addicted; devotion; inclination. “His addiction was to courses vain.” Shak.

addisons.c: Addison's disease Ad"di*son's dis*ease" (?). [Named from Thomas Addison, M. D., of London, who first described it.] (Med.) A morbid condition causing a peculiar brownish discoloration of the skin, hypotension, and loss of weight; it is due to insufficient secretion of adrenocortical hormones. Untreated disease is usually fatal. Called also chronic adrenocortical insufficiency

additament.c: Additament Ad*dit"a*ment (ăd*dĭt"ȧ*meint), n. [L. additamentum, fr. additus, p. p. of addere to add.] An addition, or a thing added. Fuller.

addition.c: Addition Ad*di"tion (?), n. [F. addition, L. additio, fr. addere to add.] 1. The act of adding two or more things together; -- opposed to subtraction or diminution. “This endless addition or addibility of numbers.” Locke.

additional.c: Additional Ad*di"tion*al (?), a. Added; supplemental; in the way of an addition.

additionally.c: Additionally Ad*di"tion*al*ly, adv. By way of addition.

addititious.c: Addititious Ad`di*ti"tious (?), a. [L. addititius, fr. addere.] Additive. [R.] Sir J. Herschel.

additive.c: Additive Ad"di*tive (?), a. [L. additivus.] (Math.) Proper to be added; positive; -- opposed to subtractive.

additory.c: Additory Ad"di*to*ry (?), a. Tending to add; making some addition. [R.] Arbuthnot.

addle.c: Addle Ad"dle (?), n. [OE. adel, AS. adela, mud.]
Addle Ad"dle, a. Having lost the power of development, and become rotten, as eggs; putrid. Hence: Unfruitful or confused, as brains; muddled. Dryden.
Addle Ad"dle, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Addled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Addling (?).] To make addle; to grow addle; to muddle; as, he addled his brain. “Their eggs were addled.” Cowper.
Addle Ad"dle, v. t. & i. [OE. adlen, adilen, to gain, acquire; prob. fr. Icel. öðlask to acquire property, akin to oðal property. Cf. Allodial.] 1. To earn by labor. [Prov. Eng.] Forby.

addlepate.c: Addle-pate Addle-head Addle-brain { Ad"dle-brain` (?), Ad"dle-head` (?), Ad"dle-pate (?), } n. A foolish or dull-witted fellow. [Colloq.]

addlepated.c: Addle-pated Addle-headed Addle-brained { Ad"dle-brained` (?), Ad"dle-head`ed (?), Ad"dle-pa`ted (?), } a. Dull-witted; stupid. “The addle-brained Oberstein.” Motley.

addlings.c: Addlings Ad"dlings (?), n. pl. [See Addle, to earn.] Earnings. [Prov. Eng.] Wright.

addoom.c: Addoom Ad*doom" (?), v. t. [Pref. a- + doom.] To adjudge. [Obs.] Spenser.

addorsed.c: Addorsed Ad*dorsed" (?), a. [L. ad + dorsum, back: cf. F. adossé.] (Her.) Set or turned back to back.

address.c: Address Ad*dress" (ăd*drĕs"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Addressed (-drĕst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Addressing.] [OE. adressen to raise erect, adorn, OF. adrecier, to straighten, address, F. adresser, fr. à (L. ad) + OF. drecier, F. dresser, to straighten, arrange. See Dress, v.] 1. To aim; to direct. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Address Ad*dress" (ăd*drĕs"), v. i. 1. To prepare one's self. [Obs.] “Let us address to tend on Hector's heels.” Shak.
Address Ad*dress, n. [Cf. F. adresse. See Address, v. t.]

addressee.c: Addressee Ad`dress*ee" (?), n. One to whom anything is addressed.

addression.c: Addression Ad*dres"sion (?), n. The act of addressing or directing one's course. [Rare & Obs.] Chapman.

adduce.c: Adduce Ad*duce" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adduced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adducing (?).] [L. adducere, adductum, to lead or bring to; ad + ducere to lead. See Duke, and cf. Adduct.] To bring forward or offer, as an argument, passage, or consideration which bears on a statement or case; to cite; to allege.

adducent.c: Adducent Ad*du"cent (?), a. [L. addunces, p. pr. of adducere.] (Physiol.) Bringing together or towards a given point; -- a word applied to those muscles of the body which pull one part towards another. Opposed to abducent.

adducible.c: Adducible Ad*du"ci*ble (?), a. Capable of being adduced.

adduct.c: Adduct Ad*duct" (?), v. t. [L. adductus, p. p. of adducere. See Adduce.] (Physiol.) To draw towards a common center or a middle line. Huxley.

adduction.c: Adduction Ad*duc"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. adduction. See Adduce.] 1. The act of adducing or bringing forward.

adductive.c: Adductive Ad*duc"tive (?), a. Adducing, or bringing towards or to something.

adductor.c: Adductor Ad*duc"tor (?), n. [L., fr. adducere.] (Anat.) A muscle which draws a limb or part of the body toward the middle line of the body, or closes extended parts of the body; -- opposed to abductor; as, the adductor of the eye, which turns the eye toward the nose.

addulce.c: Addulce Ad*dulce" (?), v. t. [Like F. adoucir; fr. L. ad. + dulcis sweet.] To sweeten; to soothe. [Obs.] Bacon.

adeem.c: Adeem A*deem" (?), v. t. [L. adimere. See Ademption.] (Law) To revoke, as a legacy, grant, etc., or to satisfy it by some other gift.

adelantadillo.c: Adelantadillo ‖A`de*lan`ta*dil"lo (?), n. [Sp.] A Spanish red wine made of the first ripe grapes.

adelantado.c: Adelantado ‖A`de*lan*ta"do (?), n. [Sp., prop. p. of adelantar to advance, to promote.] A governor of a province; a commander. Prescott.

adelaster.c: Adelaster ‖Ad*e*las"ter (?), n. [Gr.? not manifest +? a star.] (Bot.) A provisional name for a plant which has not had its flowers botanically examined, and therefore has not been referred to its proper genus.

adelocodonic.c: Adelocodonic A*del`o*co*don"ic (?), a. [Gr.? invisible +? a bell.] (Zool.) Applied to sexual zooids of hydroids, that have a saclike form and do not become free; -- opposed to phanerocodonic.

adelopod.c: Adelopod A*del"o*pod (?), n. [Gr.? invisible +?,?, foot.] (Zool.) An animal having feet that are not apparent.

adelphia.c: Adelphia ‖A*del"phi*a (?), n. [Gr. 'adelfo`s brother.] (Bot.) A “brotherhood,” or collection of stamens in a bundle; -- used in composition, as in the class names, Monadelphia, Diadelphia, etc.

adelphous.c: Adelphous A*del"phous (?), a. [Gr. 'adelfo`s brother.] (Bot.) Having coalescent or clustered filaments; -- said of stamens; as, adelphous stamens. Usually in composition; as, monadelphous. Gray.

adempt.c: Adempt A*dempt" (ȧ*dĕmt"; 215), p. p. [L. ademptus, p. p. of adimere to take away.] Taken away. [Obs.]

ademption.c: Ademption A*demp"tion (ȧ*dĕmp"shŭn), n. [L. ademptio, fr. adimere, ademptum, to take away; ad + emere to buy, orig. to take.] (Law) The revocation or taking away of a grant, donation, legacy, or the like. Bouvier.

adeno.c: Adeno- Aden- Aden- or Adeno-. [Gr. 'adh`n, 'ade`nos, gland.] Combining forms of the Greek word for gland; -- used in words relating to the structure, diseases, etc., of the glands.

adenalgy.c: adenalgy adenalgia { ‖ad`e*nal"gi*a (ăd`e*năl"jĭ*ȧ), ad"e*nal`gy (ăd"e*năl`jy̆), } n. [Gr. 'adh`n gland + 'a`lgos pain.] (Med.) Pain in a gland. Called also adenodynia

adeniform.c: adeniform a*den"i*form (ȧ*dĕn"ĭ*fôrm), a. [Aden- + -form.] Shaped like a gland; adenoid. Dunglison.

adenography.c: Adenography Ad`e*nog"ra*phy (?), n. [Adeno- + -graphy.] That part of anatomy which describes the glands.

adenoidal.c: Adenoidal Adenoid { Ad"e*noid (?), Ad`e*noid"al (?) } a. Glandlike; glandular.

adenology.c: Adenology Ad`e*nol"o*gy (?), n. [Adeno- + -logy.] The part of physiology that treats of the glands.

adenoma.c: adenoma ‖ad`e*no"ma (ăd`e*nō"mȧ), n.; L. pl. -mata (#). [NL.; adeno- + -oma.] (Med.) A benign tumor of epithelial tissue with a glandlike structure. -- Ad`e*nom"a*tous (?), a.AS

adenophorous.c: Adenophorous Ad`e*noph"o*rous (?), a. [Adeno- + Gr. foro`s bearing.] (Bot.) Producing glands.

adenophyllous.c: Adenophyllous Ad`e*noph"yl*lous (?), a. [Adeno- + Gr. fy`llon leaf.] (Bot.) Having glands on the leaves.

adenosclerosis.c: Adenosclerosis ‖Ad"e*no*scle*ro"sis (ăd`e*no*skle*rō"sĭs), n. [NL.; adeno- + sclerosis.] (Med.) The hardening of a gland. AS

adenose.c: Adenose Ad"e*nose` (?; 277), a. Like a gland; full of glands; glandulous; adenous.

adenotomy.c: Adenotomy Ad`e*not"o*my (?), n. [Adeno- + Gr.? a cutting,? to cut.] (Anat.) Dissection of, or incision into, a gland or glands.

aden.c: Aden ulcer A"den ul"cer (ä"dein ŭl"sẽr or ā"dein ŭl"sẽr). [So named after Aden, a seaport in Southern Arabia, where it occurs.] (Med.) One of the numerous names of the lesion of Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis. Called also Aleppo boil, Aleppo button, Aleppo evil, Bagdad boil, Biskra boil, Cochin China ulcer, Delhi boil, Jerico boil, Oriental boil, Oriental sore, Persian ulcer, tropical ulcer, etc.

adept.c: Adept A*dept" (?), n. [L. adeptus obtained (sc. artem),?he who has obtained an art, p. p. of adipsci to arrive?at, to obtain; ad + apisci to pursue. See Apt, and cf. Adapt.] One fully skilled or well versed in anything; a proficient; as, adepts in philosophy.
Adept A*dept", a. Well skilled; completely versed; thoroughly proficient.

adeption.c: Adeption A*dep"tion (?), n. [L. adeptio. See Adept, a.] An obtaining; attainment. [Obs.]

adeptness.c: Adeptness A*dept"ness, n. The quality of being adept; skill.

adequacy.c: Adequacy Ad"e*qua*cy (?), n. [See Adequate.] The state or quality of being adequate, proportionate, or sufficient; a sufficiency for a particular purpose; as, the adequacy of supply to the expenditure.

adequate.c: Adequate Ad"e*quate (?), a. [L. adaequatus, p. p. of adaequare to make equal to; ad + aequare to make equal, aequus equal. See Equal.] Equal to some requirement; proportionate, or correspondent; fully sufficient; as, powers adequate to a great work; an adequate definition.
Adequate Ad"e*quate (?), v. t. [See Adequate, a.] 1. To equalize; to make adequate. [R.] Fotherby.

adequately.c: Adequately Ad"e*quate*ly (?), adv. In an adequate manner.

adequateness.c: Adequateness Ad"e*quate*ness, n. The quality of being adequate; suitableness; sufficiency; adequacy.

adequation.c: Adequation Ad`e*qua"tion (?), n. [L. adaequatio.] The act of equalizing; act or result of making adequate; an equivalent. [Obs.] Bp. Barlow.

adesmy.c: Adesmy A*des"my (?), n. [Gr.? unfettered; 'a priv. +? a fetter.] (Bot.) The division or defective coherence of an organ that is usually entire.

adessenarian.c: Adessenarian Ad*es`se*na"ri*an (?), n. [Formed fr. L. adesse to be present; ad + esse to be.] (Eccl. Hist.) One who held the real presence of Christ's body in the eucharist, but not by transubstantiation.

adfected.c: Adfected Ad*fect"ed (?), a. [L. adfectus or affectus. See Affect, v.] (Alg.) See Affected, 5.

adhamant.c: Adhamant Ad*ha"mant (?), a. [From L. adhamare to catch; ad + hamus hook.] Clinging, as by hooks.

adhere.c: Adhere Ad*here" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Adhered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adhering (?).] [L. adhaerere, adhaesum; ad + haerere to stick: cf. F. adhérer. See Aghast.] 1. To stick fast or cleave, as a glutinous substance does; to become joined or united; as, wax to the finger; the lungs sometimes adhere to the pleura.

adherence.c: Adherence Ad*her"ence (?), n. [Cf. F. adhérence, LL. adhaerentia.] 1. The quality or state of adhering.

adherency.c: Adherency Ad*her"en*cy (?), n. 1. The state or quality of being adherent; adherence. [R.]

adherent.c: Adherent Ad*her"ent (?), a. [L. adhaerens, -entis, p. pr.: cf. F. adhérent.] 1. Sticking; clinging; adhering. Pope.
Adherent Ad*her"ent, n. 1. One who adheres; one who adheres; one who follows a leader, party, or profession; a follower, or partisan; a believer in a particular faith or church.

adherently.c: Adherently Ad*her"ent*ly, adv. In an adherent manner.

adherer.c: Adherer Ad*her"er (?), n. One who adheres; an adherent.

adhesion.c: Adhesion Ad*he"sion (?), n. [L. adhaesio, fr. adhaerere: cf. F. adhésion.] 1. The action of sticking; the state of being attached; intimate union; as, the adhesion of glue, or of parts united by growth, cement, or the like.

adhesive.c: Adhesive Ad*he"sive (?), a. [Cf. F. adhésif.] 1. Sticky; tenacious, as glutinous substances.

adhesively.c: Adhesively Ad*he"sive*ly, adv. In an adhesive manner.

adhesiveness.c: Adhesiveness Ad*he"sive*ness, n. 1. The quality of sticking or adhering; stickiness; tenacity of union.

adhibit.c: Adhibit Ad*hib"it (?), v. t. [L. adhibitus, p. p. of adhibere to hold to; ad + habere to have.] 1. To admit, as a person or thing; to take in. Muirhead.

adhibition.c: Adhibition Ad`hi*bi"tion (?), n. [L. adhibitio.] The act of adhibiting; application; use. Whitaker.

adhort.c: Adhort Ad*hort" (?), v. t. [L. adhortari. See Adhortation.] To exhort; to advise. [Obs.] Feltham.

adhortation.c: Adhortation Ad`hor*ta"tion (?), n. [L. adhortatio, fr. adhortari to advise; ad + hortari to exhort.] Advice; exhortation. [Obs.] Peacham.

adhortatory.c: Adhortatory Ad*hor"ta*to*ry (?), a. Containing counsel or warning; hortatory; advisory. [Obs.] Potter.

adiabatic.c: Adiabatic Ad`i*a*bat"ic (?), a. [Gr. 'adia`batos not passable; 'a priv. + dia` through + bai`nein to go.] (Physics) Not giving out or receiving heat. -- Ad`i*a*bat`ic*al*ly, adv.

adiactinic.c: Adiactinic Ad`i*ac*tin"ic (?), a. [Pref. a- not + diactinic.] (Chem.) Not transmitting the actinic rays.

adiantum.c: Adiantum ‖Ad`i*an"tum (?), n. [L., fr. Gr. 'adi`anton, maidenhair; 'a priv. + diai`nein to wet.] (Bot.) A genus of ferns, the leaves of which shed water; maidenhair. Also, the black maidenhair, a species of spleenwort.

adiaphorist.c: Adiaphorist Ad`i*aph"o*rist (ăd`ĭ*ăf"o*rĭst), n. [See Adiaphorous.] (Eccl. Hist.) One of the German Protestants who, with Melanchthon, held some opinions and ceremonies to be indifferent or nonessential, which Luther condemned as sinful or heretical. Murdock.

adiaphoristic.c: Adiaphoristic Ad`i*aph`o*ris"tic (ăd`ĭ*ăf`o*rĭs"tĭk), a. Pertaining to matters indifferent in faith and practice. Shipley.

adiaphorous.c: Adiaphorous Ad`i*aph"o*rous (ăd`ĭ*ăf"o*rŭs), a. [Gr. 'adia`foros; 'a priv. + dia`foros different; dia` through + fe`rein to bear.] 1. Indifferent or neutral. Jer. Taylor. AS

adiathermic.c: Adiathermic Ad`i*a*ther"mic (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. + dia` through +?heat.] Not pervious to heat.

adieu.c: Adieu A*dieu" (?), interj. & adv. [OE. also adew, adewe, adue, F.? dieu, fr. L. ad to + deus God.] Good-by; farewell; an expression of kind wishes at parting.
Adieu A*dieu", n.; pl. Adieus (?). A farewell; commendation to the care of God at parting. Shak.

adight.c: Adight A*dight" (?), v. t. [p. p. Adight.] [Pref. a- (intensive) + OE. dihten. See Dight.] To set in order; to array; to attire; to deck, to dress. [Obs.]

adios.c: Adios ‖A`dios" (ä`dyos"), interj. [Sp., fr. L. ad to + deus god. Cf. Adieu.] Adieu; farewell; good-by; -- chiefly used among Spanish-speaking people; as, adios amigos (good-bye friends).

adipescent.c: Adipescent Ad`i*pes"cent (?), a. [L. adeps, adipis, fat + -escent.] Becoming fatty.

adipic.c: Adipic A*dip"ic (ȧ*dĭp"ĭk), a. [L. adeps, adipis, fat.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or derived from, fatty or oily substances; -- applied to certain acids obtained from fats by the action of nitric acid.

adipocerate.c: Adipocerate Ad`i*poc"er*ate (?), v. t. To convert into adipocere.

adipoceration.c: Adipoceration Ad`i*poc`er*a"tion (?), n. The act or process of changing into adipocere.

adipocere.c: Adipocere Ad"i*po*cere` (?), n. [L. adeps, adipis, fat + cera wax: cf. F. adipocere.] A soft, unctuous, or waxy substance, of a light brown color, into which the fat and muscle tissue of dead bodies sometimes are converted, by long immersion in water or by burial in moist places. It is a result of fatty degeneration.

adipoceriform.c: Adipoceriform Ad`i*po*cer"i*form (?), a. [Adipocere + -form.] Having the form or appearance of adipocere; as, an adipoceriform tumor.

adipogenous.c: adipogenous ad`i*pog"e*nous (ăd`ĭ*pŏj"e*nŭs), a. [See Adipose; -genous.] (Med.) Producing fat. AS

adipolysis.c: adipolysis ‖ad`i*pol"y*sis (ăd`ĭ*pŏl"ĭ*sĭs), n. [NL.; L. adeps, adipis, fat + Gr. ly`sis a loosing.] (Physiol.) The digestion of fats.

adipolytic.c: Adipolytic Ad`i*po*lyt"ic (?), a. [L. adeps, adipis, fat + Gr.? to loose.] (Chem.) Hydrolyzing fats; converting neutral fats into glycerin and free fatty acids, esp. by the action of an enzyme; as, adipolytic action. Contrast saponify, to hydrolyze fat by the action of an alkali.

adipose.c: Adipose Ad"i*pose` (?), n. (Physiol.) The fat present in the cells of adipose tissue, composed mainly of varying mixtures of tripalmitin, tristearin, and triolein. It solidifies after death.
Adipose Ad"i*pose` (?; 277), a. [L. adeps, adipis, fat, grease.] Of or pertaining to animal fat; fatty.

adiposity.c: Adiposity Adiposeness { Ad"i*pose`ness (?), Ad`i*pos"i*ty (?), } n. The state of being fat; fatness.

adipsia.c: Adipsia Adipsy ‖A*dip"si*a, A*dip"sy (ăd"ĭp*sy̆), n. [Gr. 'a`dipsos not thirsty; 'a priv. + di`psa thirst.] (Med.) Absence of thirst.

adipsous.c: Adipsous A*dip"sous (?), a. [Gr. 'a`dipsos; 'a priv. + di`psa, thirst.] Quenching thirst, as certain fruits.

adit.c: adit ad"it (ăd"ĭt), n. [L. aditus, fr. adire, aditum, to go to; ad + ire to go.] 1. An entrance or passage. Specifically: The nearly horizontal opening by which a mine is entered, or by which water and ores are carried away; -- called also drift and tunnel.

adjacency.c: Adjacency Adjacence { Ad"ja"cence (?), Ad*ja"cen*cy (?), } [Cf. LL. adjacentia.] 1. The state or attribute of being adjacent or contiguous; contiguity; the attribute of being so near as to be touching; as, the adjacency of lands or buildings.

adjacent.c: Adjacent Ad*ja"cent (?), a. [L. adjacens, -centis, p. pr. of adjacere to lie near; ad + jacēre to lie: cf. F. adjacent.] Lying near, close, or contiguous; neighboring; bordering on; as, a field adjacent to the highway. “The adjacent forest.” B. Jonson.
Adjacent Ad*ja"cent, n. That which is adjacent. [R.] Locke.

adjacently.c: Adjacently Ad*ja"cent*ly, adv. So as to be adjacent.

adject.c: Adject Ad*ject" (?), v. t. [L. adjectus, p. p. of adjicere to throw to, to add to; ad + jacĕre to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.] To add or annex; to join. Leland.

adjection.c: Adjection Ad*jec"tion (?), n. [L. adjectio, fr. adjicere: cf. F. adjection. See Adject.] The act or mode of adding; also, the thing added. [R.] B. Jonson.

adjectional.c: Adjectional Ad*jec"tion*al (?), a. Pertaining to adjection; that is, or may be, annexed. [R.] Earle.

adjectival.c: Adjectival Ad`jec*ti"val (?), a. Of or relating to the relating to the adjective; of the nature of an adjective; adjective. W. Taylor (1797)

adjectivally.c: Adjectivally Ad`jec*ti"val*ly, adv. As, or in the manner of, an adjective; adjectively.

adjective.c: Adjective Ad"jec*tive, n. [L. adjectivum (sc. nomen), neut. of adjectivus that is added, fr. adjicere: cf. F. adjectif. See Adject.] 1. (Gram.) A word used with a noun, or substantive, to express a quality of the thing named, or something attributed to it, or to limit or define it, or to specify or describe a thing, as distinct from something else. Thus, in phrase, “a wise ruler,” wise is the adjective, expressing a property of ruler.
Adjective Ad"jec*tive, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adjectived (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adjectiving (?).] To make an adjective of; to form or change into an adjective. [R.]

adjectively.c: Adjectively Ad"jec*tive*ly, adv. In the manner of an adjective; as, a word used adjectively.

adjoin.c: Adjoin Ad*join" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adjoined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adjoining.] [OE. ajoinen, OF. ajoindre, F. adjoindre, fr. L. adjungere; ad + jungere to join. See Join, and cf. Adjunct.] To join or unite to; to lie contiguous to; to be in contact with; to attach; to append.
Adjoin Ad*join" (ăd*join"), v. i. 1. To lie or be next, or in contact; to be contiguous; as, the houses adjoin.

adjoining.c: Adjoining Ad*join"ing, a. Joining to; contiguous; adjacent; as, an adjoining room. “The adjoining fane.” Dryden.

adjoint.c: Adjoint Ad"joint (?), n. An adjunct; a helper. [Obs.]

adjourn.c: Adjourn Ad*journ (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adjourned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adjourning (?).] [OE. ajornen, OF. ajoiner, ajurner, F. ajourner; OF. a (L. ad) + jor, jur, jorn, F. jour, day, fr. L. diurnus belonging to the day, fr. dies day. Cf. Journal, Journey.] To put off or defer to another day, or indefinitely; to postpone; to close or suspend for the day; -- commonly said of the meeting, or the action, of convened body; as, to adjourn the meeting; to adjourn a debate.

Adjourn Ad*journ", v. i. To suspend business for a time, as from one day to another, or for a longer period, or indefinitely; usually, to suspend public business, as of legislatures and courts, or other convened bodies; as, congress adjourned at four o'clock; the court adjourned without day.

adjournal.c: Adjournal Ad*journ"al (?), n. Adjournment; postponement. [R.] “An adjournal of the Diet.” Sir W. Scott.

adjournment.c: Adjournment Ad*journ"ment (-meint), n. [Cf. f. adjournement, OF. ajornement. See Adjourn.] 1. The act of adjourning; the putting off till another day or time specified, or without day.

adjudge.c: Adjudge Ad*judge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adjudged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adjudging (?).] [OE. ajugen, OF. ajugier, fr. L. adjudicare; ad + judicare to judge. See Judge, and cf. Adjudicate.] 1. To award judicially in the case of a controverted question; as, the prize was adjudged to the victor.

adjudgment.c: Adjudgment Ad*judg"ment (-meint), n. The act of adjudging; judicial decision; adjudication. Sir W. Temple.

adjudicate.c: Adjudicate Ad*ju"di*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adjudicated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adjudicating (?)] [L. adjudicatus, p. p. of adjudicare. See Adjudge.] To adjudge; to try and determine, as a court; to settle by judicial decree.
Adjudicate Ad*ju"di*cate, v. i. To come to a judicial decision; as, the court adjudicated upon the case.

adjudication.c: Adjudication Ad*ju`di*ca"tion (?), n. [L. adjudicatio: cf. F. adjudication.] 1. The act of adjudicating; the act or process of trying and determining judicially.

adjugate.c: Adjugate Ad"ju*gate (?), v. t. [L. adjugatus, p. p. of adjugare; ad + jugum a yoke.] To yoke to. [Obs.]

adjument.c: Adjument Ad"ju*ment (ăd"ju*meint), n. [L. adjumentum, for adjuvamentum, fr. adjuvare to help; ad + juvare to help.] Help; support; also, a helper. [Obs.] Waterhouse.

adjunct.c: Adjunct Ad"junct` (?), a. [L. adjunctus, p. p. of adjungere. See Adjoin.] Conjoined; attending; consequent.
Adjunct Ad"junct`, n. 1. Something joined or added to another thing, but not essentially a part of it.

adjunction.c: Adjunction Ad*junc"tion (?), n. [L. adjunctio, fr. adjungere: cf. F. adjonction, and see Adjunct.] The act of joining; the thing joined or added.

adjunctive.c: Adjunctive Ad*junc"tive (?), a. [L. adjunctivus, fr. adjungere. See Adjunct.] Joining; having the quality of joining; forming an adjunct.
Adjunctive Ad*junc"tive, n. One who, or that which, is joined.

adjunctively.c: Adjunctively Ad*junc"tive*ly, adv. In an adjunctive manner.

adjunctly.c: Adjunctly Ad*junct"ly (?), adv. By way of addition or adjunct; in connection with.

adjuration.c: Adjuration Ad`ju*ra"tion (?), n. [L. adjuratio, fr. adjurare: cf. F. adjuration. See Adjure.] 1. The act of adjuring; a solemn charging on oath, or under the penalty of a curse; an earnest appeal.

adjuratory.c: Adjuratory Ad*ju"ra*to*ry (?), a. [L. adjuratorius.] Containing an adjuration.

adjure.c: Adjure Ad*jure" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adjured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adjuring (?)]. [L. adjurare, adjurdium, to swear to; later, to adjure: cf. F. adjurer. See Jury.] To charge, bind, or command, solemnly, as if under oath, or under the penalty of a curse; to appeal to in the most solemn or impressive manner; to entreat earnestly.

adjust.c: Adjust Ad*just" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adjusted; p. pr. & vb. n. Adjusting.] [OF. ajuster, ajoster (whence F. ajouter to add), LL. adjuxtare to fit; fr. L. ad + juxta near; confused later with L. ad and justus just, right, whence F. ajuster to adjust. See Just, v. t. and cf. Adjute.] 1. To make exact; to fit; to make correspondent or conformable; to bring into proper relations; as, to adjust a garment to the body, or things to a standard.

adjustable.c: Adjustable Ad*just"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being adjusted.

adjuster.c: Adjuster Ad*just"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, adjusts.

adjusting.c: Adjusting surface Adjusting plane { Adjusting plane, Adjusting surface. } (Aëronautics) A small plane or surface, usually capable of adjustment but not of manipulation, for preserving lateral balance in an aëroplane or flying machine.

adjustment.c: Adjustment Ad*just"ment (-meint), n. [Cf. F. ajustement. See Adjust.] 1. The act of adjusting, or condition of being adjusted; act of bringing into proper relations; regulation.

adjutancy.c: Adjutancy Ad"ju*tan*cy (-tain*sy̆), n. [See Adjutant.] 1. The office of an adjutant.

adjutant.c: Adjutant Ad"ju*tant (?), n. [L. adjutans, p. pr. of adjutare to help. See Aid.] 1. A helper; an assistant.

adjutator.c: Adjutator Ad"ju*ta`tor (?), n. (Eng. Hist.) A corruption of Agitator.

adjute.c: Adjute Ad*jute" (?), v. t. [F. ajouter; confused with L. adjutare.] To add. [Obs.]

adjutor.c: Adjutor Ad*ju"tor (?), n. [L., fr. adjuvare. See Aid.] A helper or assistant. [Archaic] Drayton.

adjutory.c: Adjutory Ad*ju"to*ry (?), a. [L. adjutorius.] Serving to help or assist; helping. [Obs.]

adjutrix.c: Adjutrix Ad*ju"trix (?), n. [L. See Adjutor.] A female helper or assistant. [R.]

adjuvant.c: Adjuvant Ad"ju*vant (?), a. [L. adjuvans, p. pr. of adjuvare to aid: cf. F. adjuvant. See Aid.] Helping; helpful; assisting. [R.] “Adjuvant causes.” Howell.
Adjuvant Ad"ju*vant (ăd"ju*vaint), n. [L. adjuvamentum, fr. adjuvare to help; ad + juvare to help.] 1. An assistant. [R.] Yelverton. AS

adlegation.c: Adlegation Ad`le*ga"tion (?), n. [L. adlegatio, allegatio, a sending away; fr. adlegare, allegare, to send away with a commission; ad in addition + legare to send as ambassador. Cf. Allegation.] A right formerly claimed by the states of the German Empire of joining their own ministers with those of the emperor in public treaties and negotiations to the common interest of the empire. Encyc. Brit.

admarginate.c: Admarginate Ad*mar"gin*ate (?), v. t. [Pref. ad- + margin.] To write in the margin. [R.] Coleridge.

admaxillary.c: Admaxillary Ad*max"il*la*ry (?), a. [Pref. ad- + maxillary.] (Anat.) Near to the maxilla or jawbone.

admeasure.c: Admeasure Ad*meas"ure (?; 135), v. t. [Cf. OF. amesurer, LL. admensurare. See Measure.] 1. To measure.

admensuration.c: Admensuration Ad*men`su*ra"tion (?), n. [LL. admensuratio; L. ad + mensurare to measure. See Mensuration.] Same as Admeasurement.

adminicle.c: Adminicle Ad*min"i*cle (?), n. [L. adminculum support, orig., that on which the hand rests; ad + manus hand + dim. ending -culym.] 1. Help or support; an auxiliary. Grote.

adminicular.c: Adminicular Ad`mi*nic"u*lar (?), a. Supplying help; auxiliary; corroborative; explanatory; as, adminicular evidence. H. Spencer.

administer.c: Administer Ad*min"is*ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Administered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Administering.] [OE. aministren, OF. aministrer, F. administer, fr. L. administrare; ad + ministrare to serve. See Minister.] 1. To manage or conduct, as public affairs; to direct or superintend the execution, application, or conduct of; as, to administer the government or the state.
Administer Ad*min"is*ter, v. i. 1. To contribute; to bring aid or supplies; to conduce; to minister.

administerial.c: Administerial Ad*min`is*te"ri*al (?), a. Pertaining to administration, or to the executive part of government.

administrable.c: Administrable Ad*min"is*tra*ble (?), a. Capable of being administered; as, an administrable law.

administrant.c: Administrant Ad*min"is*trant (?), a. [F., p. pr. of administrer. See Administer.] Executive; acting; managing affairs. -- n. One who administers.

administrate.c: Administrate Ad*min"is*trate (?), v. t. [L. administratus, p. p. of administrare.] To administer. [R.] Milman.

administration.c: Administration Ad*min`is*tra"tion (?; 277), n. [OE. administracioun, L. administratio: cf. F. administration.] 1. The act of administering; government of public affairs; the service rendered, or duties assumed, in conducting affairs; the conducting of any office or employment; direction; management.

administrative.c: Administrative Ad*min"is*tra`tive (ăd*mĭn"ĭs*trā`tĭv), a. [L. administrativus: cf. F. administratif.] Pertaining to administration; administering; executive; as, an administrative body, ability, or energy. -- Ad*min"is*tra`tive*ly, adv.

administrator.c: Administrator Ad*min`is*tra"tor (?), n. [L.] 1. One who administers affairs; one who directs, manages, executes, or dispenses, whether in civil, judicial, political, or ecclesiastical affairs; a manager.

administratorship.c: Administratorship Ad*min`is*tra"tor*ship, n. The position or office of an administrator.

administratrix.c: Administratrix Ad*min`is*tra"trix (?), n. [NL.] A woman who administers; esp., one who administers the estate of an intestate, or to whom letters of administration have been granted; a female administrator.

admirable.c: Admirable Ad"mi*ra*ble (?), a. [L. admirabilis: cf. F. admirable.] 1. Fitted to excite wonder; wonderful; marvelous. [Obs.]

admirableness.c: Admirableness Ad"mi*ra*ble*ness, n. The quality of being admirable; wonderful excellence.

admirably.c: Admirably Ad"mi*ra*bly, adv. In an admirable manner.

admiral.c: Admiral Ad"mi*ral (?), n. [OE. amiral, admiral, OF. amiral, ultimately fr. Ar. amīr-al-bahr commander of the sea; Ar. amīr is commander, al is the Ar. article, and amīr-al, heard in different titles, was taken as one word. Early forms of the word show confusion with L. admirabilis admirable, fr. admirari to admire. It is said to have been introduced into Europe by the Genoese or Venetians, in the 12th or 13th century. Cf. Ameer, Emir.] 1. A naval officer of the highest rank; a naval officer of high rank, of which there are different grades. The chief gradations in rank are admiral, vice admiral, and rear admiral. The admiral is the commander in chief of a fleet or of fleets.

admiralship.c: Admiralship Ad"mi*ral*ship, n. The office or position oaf an admiral; also, the naval skill of an admiral.

admiralty.c: Admiralty Ad"mi*ral*ty (?), n.; pl. Admiralties (?). [F. amirauté, for an older amiralté, office of admiral, fr. LL. admiralitas. See Admiral.] 1. The office or jurisdiction of an admiral. Prescott.

admirance.c: Admirance Ad*mir"ance (?), n. [Cf. OF. admirance.] Admiration. [Obs.] Spenser.

admiration.c: Admiration Ad`mi*ra"tion (?), n. [F., fr. L. admiratio. See Admire.] 1. Wonder; astonishment. [Obs.]

admirative.c: Admirative Ad*mir"a*tive (?), a. Relating to or expressing admiration or wonder. [R.] Earle.

admire.c: Admire Ad*mire" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Admired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Admiring (?).] [F. admirer, fr. L. admirari; ad + mirari to wonder, for smirari, akin to Gr.? to smile, Skr. smi, and E. smile.] 1. To regard with wonder or astonishment; to view with surprise; to marvel at. [Archaic]
Admire Ad*mire", v. i. To wonder; to marvel; to be affected with surprise; -- sometimes with at.

admired.c: Admired Ad*mired" (?), a. 1. Regarded with wonder and delight; highly prized; as, an admired poem.

admirer.c: Admirer Ad*mir"er (?), n. One who admires; one who esteems or loves greatly. Cowper.

admiring.c: Admiring Ad*mir"ing, a. Expressing admiration; as, an admiring glance. -- Ad*mir"ing*ly, adv. Shak.

admissibility.c: Admissibility Ad*mis`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. admissibilité.] The quality of being admissible; admissibleness; as, the admissibility of evidence.

admissible.c: Admissible Ad*mis"si*ble (?), a. [F. admissible, LL. admissibilis. See Admit.] Entitled to be admitted, or worthy of being admitted; that may be allowed or conceded; allowable; as, the supposition is hardly admissible. -- Ad*mis"si*ble*ness, n. -- Ad*mis"si*bly, adv.

admission.c: Admission Ad*mis"sion (?), n. [L. admissio: cf. F. admission. See Admit.] 1. The act or practice of admitting.

admissive.c: Admissive Ad*mis"sive (?), a. Implying an admission; tending to admit. [R.] Lamb.

admit.c: Admit Ad*mit" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Admitted; p. pr. & vb. n. Admitting.] [OE. amitten, L. admittere, admissum; ad + mittere to send: cf. F. admettre, OF. admettre, OF. ametre. See Missile.] 1. To suffer to enter; to grant entrance, whether into a place, or into the mind, or consideration; to receive; to take; as, they were into his house; to admit a serious thought into the mind; to admit evidence in the trial of a cause.

admittable.c: Admittable Ad*mit"ta*ble (?), a. Admissible. Sir T. Browne.

admittance.c: Admittance Ad*mit"tance (?), n. 1. The act of admitting.
Admittance Ad*mit"tance, n. (Elec.) The reciprocal of impedance.

admittatur.c: Admittatur ‖Ad`mit*ta"tur (?), n. [L., let him be admitted.] The certificate of admission given in some American colleges.

admittedly.c: Admittedly Admitted Ad*mit"ted (?), a. Received as true or valid; acknowledged. -- Ad*mit"ted*ly adv. Confessedly.

admix.c: Admix Ad*mix" (?), v. t. [Pref. ad- + mix: cf. L. admixtus, p. p. of admiscere. See Mix.] To mingle with something else; to mix. [R.]

admixtion.c: Admixtion Ad*mix"tion (?; 106), n. [L. admixtio.] A mingling of different things; admixture. Glanvill.

admixture.c: Admixture Ad*mix"ture (?; 135), n. [L. admiscere, admixtum, to admix; ad + miscere to mix. See Mix.]

admonish.c: Admonish Ad*mon"ish (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Admonished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Admonishing.] [OE. amonesten, OF. amonester, F. admonester, fr. a supposed LL. admonesstrare, fr. L. admonere to remind, warn; ad + monere to warn. See Monition.] 1. To warn or notify of a fault; to reprove gently or kindly, but seriously; to exhort. “Admonish him as a brother.” 2 Thess. iii. 15.

admonishment.c: Admonishment Ad*mon"ish*ment (-meint), n. [Cf. OF. amonestement, admonestement.] Admonition. [R.] Shak.

admonition.c: Admonition Ad`mo*ni"tion (?), n. [OE. amonicioun, OF. amonition, F. admonition, fr. L. admonitio, fr. admonere. See Admonish.] Gentle or friendly reproof; counseling against a fault or error; expression of authoritative advice; friendly caution or warning.

admonitive.c: Admonitive Ad*mon"i*tive (?), a. Admonitory. [R.] Barrow. -- Ad*mon"i*tive*ly, adv.

admonitorial.c: Admonitorial Ad*mon`i*to"ri*al (?), a. Admonitory. [R.] “An admonitorial tone.” Dickens.

admonitory.c: Admonitory Ad*mon"i*to*ry (?), a. [LL. admonitorius.] That conveys admonition; warning or reproving; as, an admonitory glance. -- Ad*mon"i*to*ri*ly, (?), adv.

admortization.c: Admortization Ad*mor`ti*za"tion (?), n. [LL. admortizatio. Cf. Amortization.] (Law) The reducing or lands or tenements to mortmain. See Mortmain.

admove.c: Admove Ad*move" (?), v. t. [L. admovere. See Move.] To move or conduct to or toward. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

adnascent.c: Adnascent Ad*nas"cent (?), a. [L. adnascens, p. pr. of adnasci to be born, grow.] Growing to or on something else. “An adnascent plant.” Evelyn.

adnate.c: Adnate Ad"nate (?), a. [L. adnatus, p. p. of adnasci. See Adnascent, and cf. Agnate.] 1. (Physiol.) Grown to congenitally.

adnation.c: Adnation Ad*na"tion (?), n. (Bot.) The adhesion or cohesion of different floral verticils or sets of organs.

adnominal.c: Adnominal Ad*nom"i*nal (?), a. [L. ad + nomen noun.] (Gram.) Pertaining to an adnoun; adjectival; attached to a noun. Gibbs. -- Ad*nom"i*nal*ly, adv.

adnoun.c: Adnoun Ad"noun` (?), n. [Pref. ad- + noun.] (Gram.) An adjective, or attribute. [R.] Coleridge.

adnubilated.c: Adnubilated Ad*nu"bi*la`ted (?), a. [L. adnubilatus, p. p. of adnubilare.] Clouded; obscured. [R.]

ado.c: Ado A*do" (ȧ*dōo"), (1) v. inf., (2) n. [OE. at do, northern form for to do. Cf. Affair.] 1. To do; in doing; as, there is nothing ado. “What is here ado?” J. Newton.

adobe.c: Adobe ‖A*do"be (ȧ*dō"ba), n. [Sp.] 1. An unburnt brick dried in the sun; also used as an adjective, as, an adobe house, in Texas or New Mexico.

adolescence.c: Adolescence Ad`o*les"cence (?), n. [Fr., fr. L. adolescentia.] The state of growing up from childhood to manhood or womanhood; youth, or the period of life between puberty and maturity, generally considered to be, in the male sex, from fourteen to twenty-one. Sometimes used with reference to the lower animals.

adolescency.c: Adolescency Ad`o*les"cen*cy (?), n. The quality of being adolescent; youthfulness.

adolescent.c: Adolescent Ad`o*les"cent (ăd`o*lĕs"seint), a. [L. adolescens, p. pr. of adolescere to grow up to; ad + the inchoative olescere to grow: cf. F. adolescent. See Adult.] Growing; advancing from childhood to maturity.

adonai.c: Adonai ‖Ad`o*na"i (?), n. [Heb. adōnāi, lit., my lord.] A Hebrew name for God, usually translated in the Old Testament by the word “Lord”.

adonean.c: Adonean Ad`o*ne"an (-nē"ain), a. [L. Adonēus.] Pertaining to Adonis; Adonic. “Fair Adonean Venus.” Faber.

adonic.c: Adonic A*don"ic (?), a. [F. adonique: cf. L. Adonius.] Relating to Adonis, famed for his beauty. -- n. An Adonic verse.

adonis.c: Adonis ‖A*do"nis (ȧ*dō"nĭs), n. [L., gr. Gr. 'A`dwnis.] 1. (Gr. Myth.) A youth beloved by Venus for his beauty. He was killed in the chase by a wild boar.

adonist.c: Adonist A*do"nist (ȧ*dō"nĭst), n. [Heb. ădōnāi my Lords.] One who maintains that points of the Hebrew word translated “Jehovah” are really the vowel points of the word “Adonai.” See Jehovist.

adonize.c: Adonize Ad"o*nize (ăd"o*nīz), v. t. [Cf. F. adoniser, fr. Adonis.] To beautify; to dandify.

adoors.c: Adoors Adoor { A*door (?), A*doors (?), } At the door; of the door; as, out adoors. Shak.

adopt.c: Adopt A*dopt" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adopted; p. pr. & vb. n. Adopting.] [L. adoptare; ad + optare to choose, desire: cf. F. adopter. See Option.] 1. To take by choice into relationship, as, child, heir, friend, citizen, etc.; esp. to take voluntarily (a child of other parents) to be in the place of, or as, one's own child.

adoptable.c: Adoptable A*dopt"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being adopted.

adopted.c: Adopted A*dopt"ed (?), a. Taken by adoption; taken up as one's own; as, an adopted son, citizen, country, word. -- A*dopt"ed*ly, adv.

adoption.c: Adoption A*dop"tion (?), n. [L. adoptio, allied to adoptare to adopt: cf. F. adoption.] 1. The act of adopting, or state of being adopted; voluntary acceptance of a child of other parents to be the same as one's own child.

adoptionist.c: Adoptionist A*dop"tion*ist, n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a sect which maintained that Christ was the Son of God not by nature but by adoption.

adoptive.c: Adoptive A*dopt"ive (?), a. [L. adoptivus: cf. F. adoptif.] Pertaining to adoption; made or acquired by adoption; fitted to adopt; as, an adoptive father, an child; an adoptive language. -- A*dopt"ive*ly, adv.

adorable.c: Adorable A*dor"a*ble (?), a. [L. adorabilis, fr. adorare: cf. F. adorable.] 1. Deserving to be adored; worthy of divine honors.

adorableness.c: Adorableness A*dor"a*ble*ness, n. The quality of being adorable, or worthy of adoration. Johnson.

adorably.c: Adorably A*dor"a*bly, adv. In an adorable manner.

adoration.c: Adoration Ad`o*ra"tion (?), n. [L. adoratio, fr. adorare: cf. F. adoration.] 1. The act of playing honor to a divine being; the worship paid to God; the act of addressing as a god.

adore.c: adore a*dore" (ȧ*dōr"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. adored (ȧ*dōrd"); p. pr. & vb. n. adoring (ȧ*dōr"ĭng).] [OE. aouren, anouren, adoren, OF. aorer, adorer, F. adorer, fr. L. adorare; ad + orare to speak, pray, os, oris, mouth. In OE. confused with honor, the French prefix a- being confused with OE. a, an, on. See Oral.] 1. To worship with profound reverence; to pay divine honors to; to honor as a deity or as divine.

adorement.c: Adorement A*dore"ment (ȧ*dōr"meint), n. The act of adoring; adoration. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

adorer.c: Adorer A*dor"er (ȧ*dōr"ẽr), n. One who adores; a worshiper; one who admires or loves greatly; an ardent admirer. “An adorer of truth.” Clarendon.

adorn.c: Adorn A*dorn" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adorned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adorning.] [OE. aournen, anournen, adornen, OF. aorner, fr. L. aaornare; ad + ornare to furnish, embellish. See Adore, Ornate.] To deck or dress with ornaments; to embellish; to set off to advantage; to render pleasing or attractive.

adorner.c: Adorner A*dorn"er (?), n. He who, or that which, adorns; a beautifier.

adornment.c: Adornment A*dorn"ment (-meint), n. [Cf. OF. adornement. See Adorn.] An adorning; an ornament; a decoration.

adosculation.c: Adosculation Ad*os"cu*la"tion (?), n. [L. adosculari, adosculatum, to kiss. See Osculate.] (Biol.) Impregnation by external contact, without intromission.

adown.c: Adown A*down" (?), adv. [OE. adun, adoun, adune. AS. of dūne off the hill. See Down.] From a higher to a lower situation; downward; down, to or on the ground. [Archaic] “Thrice did she sink adown.” Spenser.

adpress.c: Adpress Ad*press" (?), v. t. [L. adpressus, p. p. of adprimere.] See Appressed. -- Ad*pressed", (?), a.

adrad.c: Adrad A*drad" (?), p. a. [P. p. of adread.] Put in dread; afraid. [Obs.] Chaucer.

adragant.c: Adragant Ad"ra*gant (?), n. [F., a corruption of tragacanth.] Gum tragacanth. Brande & C.

adread.c: Adread A*dread" (?), v. t. & i. [AS. andrædan, ondræ; pref. a- (for and against) + dræden to dread. See Dread.] To dread. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

adreamed.c: Adreamed A*dreamed" (?), p. p. Visited by a dream; -- used in the phrase, To be adreamed, to dream. [Obs.]

adrenalin.c: Adrenalin Adrenaline Ad*re"nal*ine (?), n. Also Ad*re"nal*in (?). (Physiol. Chem.) a hormone secreted by the adrenal medulla that acts as a powerful stimulant in reponse to fear or stress; it stimulates autonomic nerve action. It can be obtained as a crystalline substance, C9H13NO3. It is used in medicine as a vasoconstrictor (hemostatic) and cardiac stimulant, also to reduce allergic reactions and to stimulate the heart in cases of cardiac arrest. MI11

adrian.c: Adrian A"dri*an (?), a. [L. Hadrianus.] Pertaining to the Adriatic Sea; as, Adrian billows.

adriatic.c: Adriatic A`dri*at"ic (?), a. [L. Adriaticus, Hadriaticus, fr. Adria or Hadria, a town of the Veneti.] Of or pertaining to a sea so named, the northwestern part of which is known as the Gulf of Venice.

adrift.c: Adrift A*drift" (?), adv. & a. [Pref. a- (for on) + drift.] Floating at random; in a drifting condition; at the mercy of wind and waves. Also fig.

adrip.c: Adrip A*drip" (?), adv. & a. [Pref. a- in + drip.] In a dripping state; as, leaves all adrip. D. G. Mitchell.

adrogate.c: Adrogate Ad"ro*gate (?), v. t. [See Arrogate.] (Rom. Law) To adopt (a person who is his own master).

adrogation.c: Adrogation Ad`ro*ga"tion (?), n. [L. adrogatio, arrogatio, fr. adrogare. See Arrogate.] (Rom. Law) A kind of adoption in ancient Rome. See Arrogation.

adroit.c: Adroit A*droit" (?), a. [F. adroit; à (L. ad) = droit straight, right, fr. L. directus, p. p. of dirigere. See Direct.] Dexterous in the use of the hands or in the exercise of the mental faculties; exhibiting skill and readiness in avoiding danger or escaping difficulty; ready in invention or execution; -- applied to persons and to acts; as, an adroit mechanic, an adroit reply. “Adroit in the application of the telescope and quadrant.” Horsley. “He was adroit in intrigue.” Macaulay.

adroitly.c: Adroitly A*droit"ly, adv. In an adroit manner.

adroitness.c: Adroitness A*droit"ness, n. The quality of being adroit; skill and readiness; dexterity.

adry.c: Adry A*dry" (?), a. [Pref. a- (for on) + dry.] In a dry or thirsty condition. “A man that is adry.” Burton.

adscititious.c: Adscititious Ad`sci*ti"tious (?), a. [L. adscitus, p. p. of adsciscere, asciscere, to take knowingly; ad + sciscere to seek to know, approve, scire to know.] Supplemental; additional; adventitious; ascititious. “Adscititious evidence.” Bowring. -- Ad`sci*ti"tious*ly, adv.

adscript.c: Adscript Ad"script (?), a. [L. adscriptus, p. p. of adscribere to enroll. See Ascribe.] Held to service as attached to the soil; -- said of feudal serfs.
Adscript Ad"script (?), n. One held to service as attached to the glebe or estate; a feudal serf. Bancroft.

adscriptive.c: Adscriptive Ad*scrip"tive (?), a. [L. adscriptivus. See Adscript.] Attached or annexed to the glebe or estate and transferable with it. Brougham.

adsignify.c: Adsignify Ad*sig"ni*fy (?), v. t. [L. adsignificare to show.] To denote additionally. [R.] Tooke.

adstrict.c: Adstrict Ad*strict" (?), v. t. -- Ad*stric"tion, (?) n. See Astrict, and Astriction.

adsuki.c: Adsuki bean Ad*su"ki bean (ăd*sōo"kĭ; ăd*zōo"kĭ). [Jap. adzuki.] A cultivated variety of the Asiatic gram, now introduced into the United States.

adularia.c: Adularia ‖Ad`u*la"ri*a (?), n. [From Adula, a mountain peak in Switzerland, where fine specimens are found.] (Min.) A transparent or translucent variety of common feldspar, or orthoclase, which often shows pearly opalescent reflections; -- called by lapidaries moonstone.

adulate.c: Adulate Ad"u*late (?), v. t. [L. adulatus, p. p. of adulari.] To flatter in a servile way. Byron.

adulation.c: Adulation Ad`u*la"tion (?), n. [F. adulation, fr. L. adulatio, fr. adulari, adulatum, to flatter.] Servile flattery; praise in excess, or beyond what is merited.

adulator.c: Adulator Ad"u*la`tor (?), n. [L., fr. adulari: cf. F. adulateur.] A servile or hypocritical flatterer. Carlyle.

adulatory.c: Adulatory Ad"u*la*to*ry (?), a. [L. adulatorius, fr. adulari: cf. OF. adulatoire.] Containing excessive praise or compliment; servilely praising; flattering; as, an adulatory address.

adulatress.c: Adulatress Ad"u*la`tress (?), n. A woman who flatters with servility.

adult.c: Adult A*dult" (?), a. [L. adultus, p. p. of adolescere, akin to alere to nourish: cf. F. adulte. See Adolescent, Old.] Having arrived at maturity, or to full size and strength; matured; as, an adult person or plant; an adult ape; an adult age.
Adult A*dult", n. A person, animal, or plant grown to full size and strength; one who has reached maturity.

adulter.c: Adulter A*dul"ter (?), v. i. [L. adulterare.] To commit adultery; to pollute. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

adulterant.c: Adulterant A*dul"ter*ant (?), n. [L. adulterans, p. pr. of adulterare.] That which is used to adulterate anything. -- a. Adulterating; as, adulterant agents and processes.

adulterate.c: Adulterate A*dul"ter*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adulterated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adulterating (?).] [L. adulteratus, p. p. of adulterare, fr. adulter adulterer, prob. fr. ad + alter other, properly one who approaches another on account of unlawful love. Cf. Advoutry.]
Adulterate A*dul"ter*ate, v. i. To commit adultery. [Obs.]

adulteration.c: Adulteration A*dul`ter*a"tion (?), n. [L. adulteratio.] 1. The act of adulterating; corruption, or debasement (esp. of food or drink) by foreign mixture.

adulterator.c: Adulterator A*dul"ter*a`tor (?), n. [L.] One who adulterates or corrupts. [R.] Cudworth.

adulterer.c: Adulterer A*dul"ter*er (?), n. [Formed fr. the verb adulter, with the E. ending -er. See Advoutrer.] 1. A man who commits adultery; a married man who has sexual intercourse with a woman not his wife.

adulteress.c: Adulteress A*dul"ter*ess (?), n. [Fem. from L. adulter. Cf. Advoutress.] 1. A woman who commits adultery.

adulterine.c: Adulterine A*dul"ter*ine (?), a. [L. adulterinus, fr. adulter.] Proceeding from adulterous intercourse. Hence: Spurious; without the support of law; illegal.

adulterize.c: Adulterize A*dul"ter*ize (?), v. i. To commit adultery. Milton.

adulterous.c: Adulterous A*dul"ter*ous (?), a. 1. Guilty of, or given to, adultery; pertaining to adultery; illicit. Dryden.

adulterously.c: Adulterously A*dul"ter*ous*ly, adv. In an adulterous manner.

adultery.c: Adultery A*dul"ter*y (?), n.; pl. Adulteries (?). [L. adulterium. See Advoutry.] 1. The unfaithfulness of a married person to the marriage bed; sexual intercourse by a married man with another than his wife, or voluntary sexual intercourse by a married woman with another than her husband.

adultness.c: Adultness A*dult"ness (?), n. The state of being adult.

adumbrant.c: Adumbrant Ad*um"brant (?), a. [L. adumbrans, p. pr. of adumbrare.] Giving a faint shadow, or slight resemblance; shadowing forth.

adumbrate.c: Adumbrate Ad*um"brate (?), v. t. [L. adumbratus, p. p. of adumbrare; ad + umbrare to shade; umbra shadow.]

adumbration.c: Adumbration Ad`um*bra"tion (?), n. [L. adumbratio.] 1. The act of adumbrating, or shadowing forth.

adumbrative.c: Adumbrative Ad*um"bra*tive (?), a. Faintly representing; typical. Carlyle.

adunation.c: Adunation Ad`u*na"tion (?), n. [L. adunatio; ad + unus one.] A uniting; union. Jer. Taylor.

adunque.c: Adunque Adunc { A*dunc", A*dunque" } (?), a. (Zool.) Hooked; as, a parrot has an adunc bill.

aduncity.c: Aduncity A*dun"ci*ty (?), n. [L. aduncitas. See Aduncous.] Curvature inwards; hookedness.

aduncous.c: Aduncous A*dun"cous (?), a. [L. aduncus; ad + uncus hooked, hook.] Curved inwards; hooked.

adure.c: Adure A*dure" (?), v. t. [L. adurere; ad + urere to burn.] To burn up. [Obs.] Bacon.

adurol.c: Adurol Ad"u*rol (?), n. (Photog.) Either of two compounds, a chlorine derivative and bromine derivative, of hydroquinone, used as developers.

adust.c: adust a*dust" (ă*dŭst"), a. [L. adustus, p. p. of adurere: cf. F. aduste.] 1. Inflamed or scorched; dried or darkened by heat. “The Libyan air adust.” Milton. AS

adustible.c: Adustible A*dust"i*ble (?), a. That may be burnt. [Obs.]

adustion.c: Adustion A*dus"tion (?; 106), n. [L. adustio, fr. adurere, adustum: cf. F. adustion.] 1. The act of burning, or heating to dryness; the state of being thus heated or dried. [Obs.] Harvey.

advance.c: Advance Ad*vance" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Advanced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Advancing (?)(#).] [OE. avancen, avauncen, F. avancer, fr. a supposed LL. abantiare; ab + ante (F. avant) before. The spelling with d was a mistake, a- being supposed to be fr. L. ad. See Avaunt.] 1. To bring forward; to move towards the van or front; to make to go on.
Advance Ad*vance", v. i. 1. To move or go forward; to proceed; as, he advanced to greet me.
Advance Ad*vance", n. [Cf. F. avance, fr. avancer. See Advance, v.] 1. The act of advancing or moving forward or upward; progress.

Advance Ad*vance" (?), a. Before in place, or beforehand in time; -- used for advanced; as, an advance guard, or that before the main guard or body of an army; advance payment, or that made before it is due; advance proofs, advance sheets, pages of a forthcoming volume, received in advance of the time of publication.

advanced.c: Advanced Ad*vanced" (?), a. 1. In the van or front.

advancement.c: Advancement Ad*vance"ment (ăd*vȧns"meint), n. [OE. avancement, F. avancement. See Advance, v. t.] 1. The act of advancing, or the state of being advanced; progression; improvement; furtherance; promotion to a higher place or dignity; as, the advancement of learning.

advancer.c: Advancer Ad*van"cer (?), n. 1. One who advances; a promoter.

advancing.c: Advancing edge Ad*van"cing edge. (Aëronautics) The front edge (in direction of motion) of a supporting surface; -- contr. with following edge, which is the rear edge.
Advancing surface Ad*van"cing sur"face. (Aëronautics) The first of two or more surfaces arranged in tandem; -- contr. with following surface, which is the rear surface.

advantage.c: Advantage Ad*van"tage (?; 61, 48), n. [OE. avantage, avauntage, F. avantage, fr. avant before. See Advance, and cf. Vantage.] 1. Any condition, circumstance, opportunity, or means, particularly favorable to success, or to any desired end; benefit; as, the enemy had the advantage of a more elevated position.

Advantage Ad*van"tage, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Advantaged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Advantaging (?).] [F. avantager, fr. avantage. See Advance.] To give an advantage to; to further; to promote; to benefit; to profit.

advantageous.c: Advantageous Ad`van*ta"geous (?), a. [F. avantageux, fr. avantage.] Being of advantage; conferring advantage; gainful; profitable; useful; beneficial; as, an advantageous position; trade is advantageous to a nation.

advene.c: Advene Ad*vene" (?), v. i. [L. advenire; ad + venire to come: cf. F. avenir, advenir. See Come.] To accede, or come (to); to be added to something or become a part of it, though not essential. [R.]

advenient.c: Advenient Ad*ven"ient (?), a. [L. adviens, p. pr.] Coming from outward causes; superadded. [Obs.]

advent.c: Advent Ad`vent (?), n. [L. adventus, fr. advenire, adventum: cf. F. avent. See Advene.] 1. (Eccl.) The period including the four Sundays before Christmas.

adventist.c: Adventist Ad"vent*ist (?), n. One of a religious body, embracing several branches, who look for the proximate personal coming of Christ; -- called also Second Adventists. Schaff-Herzog Encyc.

adventitious.c: adventitious ad`ven*ti"tious (ăd`vĕn*tĭsh"ŭs), a. [L. adventitius.] 1. Added extrinsically; not essentially inherent.

adventive.c: Adventive Ad*ven"tive, n. A thing or person coming from without; an immigrant. [R.] Bacon.

adventual.c: Adventual Ad*ven"tu*al (?; 135), a. Relating to the season of advent. Sanderson.

adventure.c: Adventure Ad*ven"ture (?; 135), n. [OE. aventure, aunter, anter, F. aventure, fr. LL. adventura, fr. L. advenire, adventum, to arrive, which in the Romance languages took the sense of “to happen, befall.” See Advene.]

Adventure Ad*ven"ture, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Adventured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Adventuring (?).] [OE. aventuren, auntren, F. aventurer, fr. aventure. See Adventure, n.] 1. To risk, or hazard; jeopard; to venture.
Adventure Ad*ven"ture, v. i. To try the chance; to take the risk.

adventuresome.c: Adventuresome Ad*ven"ture*some (?), a. Full of risk; adventurous; venturesome. -- Ad*ven"ture*some*ness, n.

adventuress.c: Adventuress Ad*ven"tur*ess (?), n. A female adventurer; a woman who tries to gain position by equivocal means.

adventurous.c: Adventurous Ad*ven"tur*ous (?), a. [OE. aventurous, aunterous, OF. aventuros, F. aventureux, fr. aventure. See Adventure, n.] 1. Inclined to adventure; willing to incur hazard; prone to embark in hazardous enterprise; rashly daring; -- applied to persons.

adventurously.c: Adventurously Ad*ven"tur*ous*ly, adv. In an adventurous manner; venturesomely; boldly; daringly.

adventurousness.c: Adventurousness Ad*ven"tur*ous*ness, n. The quality or state of being adventurous; daring; venturesomeness.

adverb.c: Adverb Ad"verb (?), n. [L. adverbium; ad + verbum word, verb: cf. F. adverbe.] (Gram.) A word used to modify the sense of a verb, participle, adjective, or other adverb, and usually placed near it; as, he writes well; paper extremely white.

adverbial.c: Adverbial Ad*ver"bi*al (?), a. [L. adverbialis: cf. F. adverbial.] Of or pertaining to an adverb; of the nature of an adverb; as, an adverbial phrase or form.

adverbiality.c: Adverbiality Ad*ver`bi*al"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being adverbial. Earle.

adverbialize.c: Adverbialize Ad*ver"bi*al*ize (?), v. t. To give the force or form of an adverb to.

adverbially.c: Adverbially Ad*ver"bi*al*ly, adv. In the manner of an adverb.

adversaria.c: Adversaria ‖Ad`ver*sa"ri*a (?), n. pl. [L. adversaria (sc. scripta), neut. pl. of adversarius.] A miscellaneous collection of notes, remarks, or selections; a commonplace book; also, commentaries or notes.

adversary.c: Adversary Ad`ver*sa*ry (?), n.; pl. Adversaries (?). [OE. adversarie, direct fr. the Latin, and adversaire, fr. OF. adversier, aversier, fr. L. adversarius (a.) turned toward, (n.) an adversary. See Adverse.] One who is turned against another or others with a design to oppose or resist them; a member of an opposing or hostile party; an opponent; an antagonist; an enemy; a foe.
Adversary Ad"ver*sa*ry (?), a. 1. Opposed; opposite; adverse; antagonistic. [Archaic] Bp. King.

adversative.c: Adversative Ad*ver"sa*tive (?), a. [L. adversativus, fr. adversari.] Expressing contrariety, opposition, or antithesis; as, an adversative conjunction (but, however, yet, etc.); an adversative force. -- Ad*ver"sa*tive*ly, adv.
Adversative Ad*ver"sa*tive, n. An adversative word. Harris.

adverse.c: Adverse Ad"verse (?), a. [OE. advers, OF. avers, advers, fr. L. adversus, p. p. advertere to turn to. See Advert.]
Adverse Ad*verse" (?), v. t. [L. adversari: cf. OF. averser.] To oppose; to resist. [Obs.] Gower.

adversely.c: Adversely Ad"verse*ly (277), adv. In an adverse manner; inimically; unfortunately; contrariwise.

adverseness.c: Adverseness Ad"verse*ness, n. The quality or state of being adverse; opposition.

adversifolious.c: Adversifolious Adversifoliate { Ad*ver`si*fo"li*ate (?), Ad*ver`si*fo"li*ous (?) } a. [L. adversus opposite + folium leaf.] (Bot.) Having opposite leaves, as plants which have the leaves so arranged on the stem.

adversion.c: Adversion Ad*ver"sion (?), n. [L. adversio] A turning towards; attention. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

adversity.c: Adversity Ad*ver"si*ty (?), n.; pl. Adversities (?). [OE. adversite, F. adversité, fr. L. adversitas.] 1. Opposition; contrariety. [Obs.] Wyclif.

advert.c: Advert Ad*vert" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Adverted; p. pr. & vb. n. Adverting.] [L. advertere, v. t., to turn to; ad + vertere to turn: cf. F. avertir. See Advertise.] To turn the mind or attention; to refer; to take heed or notice; -- with to; as, he adverted to what was said.

advertency.c: Advertency Advertence { Ad*vert"ence (?), Ad*vert"en*cy (?), } [OF. advertence, avertence, LL. advertentia, fr. L. advertens. See Advertent.] The act of adverting, of the quality of being advertent; attention; notice; regard; heedfulness.

advertent.c: Advertent Ad*vert"ent (?), a. [L. advertens, -entis, p. pr. of advertere. See Advert.] Attentive; heedful; regardful. Sir M. Hale. -- Ad*vert"ent*ly, adv.

advertise.c: Advertise Ad`ver*tise" (?; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Advertised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Advertising (?).] [F. avertir, formerly also spelt advertir, to warn, give notice to, L. advertere to turn to. The ending was probably influenced by the noun advertisement.
