Agonize Ag"o*nize, v. t. To cause to suffer agony; to subject to extreme pain; to torture.

agonizingly.c: Agonizingly Ag"o*ni`zing*ly (?), adv. With extreme anguish or desperate struggles.

agonothete.c: Agonothete Ag"o*no*thete` (?), n. [Gr.?;? +? to set. appoint.] [Antiq.] An officer who presided over the great public games in Greece.

agonothetic.c: Agonothetic Ag`o*no*thet"ic (?), a. [Gr.?.] Pertaining to the office of an agonothete.

agony.c: Agony Ag"o*ny (?), n.; pl. Agonies (?). [L. agonia, Gr.?, orig. a contest, fr.?: cf. F. agonie. See Agon.] 1. Violent contest or striving.

agood.c: Agood A*good (ȧ*gŏod"), adv. [Pref. a- + good.] In earnest; heartily. [Obs.] “I made her weep agood.” Shak.

agora.c: Agora ‖Ag"o*ra (ăg"o*rȧ), n. [Gr. 'agora`.] An assembly; hence, the place of assembly, especially the market place, in an ancient Greek city.

agouara.c: Agouara ‖A*gou"a*ra (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) The crab-eating raccoon (Procyon cancrivorus), found in the tropical parts of America.

agouta.c: Agouta ‖A*gou"ta (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) A small insectivorous mammal (Solenodon paradoxus), allied to the moles, found only in Haiti.

agouty.c: Agouty Agouti { A*gou"ti, A*gou"ty } (ȧ*gōo"tĭ), n. [F. agouti, acouti, Sp. aguti, fr. native name.] (Zool.) 1. A rodent of the genus Dasyprocta, about the size of a rabbit, peculiar to South America and the West Indies. The most common species is the Dasyprocta agouti.

agraffe.c: Agraffe A*graffe" (?), n. [F. agrafe, formerly agraffe, OF. agrappe. See Agrappes.] 1. A hook or clasp.

agrammatist.c: Agrammatist A*gram"ma*tist (?), n. [Gr.? illiterate; 'a priv. +? letters, fr.? to write.] A illiterate person. [Obs.] Bailey.

agraphia.c: Agraphia ‖A*graph"i*a (?), n. [Gr. 'a priv. +? to write.] The absence or loss of the power of expressing ideas by written signs. It is one form of aphasia.

agrappes.c: Agrappes A*grappes" (?), n. pl. [OF. agrappe, F. agrafe; a + grappe (see Grape) fr. OHG. krāpfo hook.] Hooks and eyes for armor, etc. Fairholt.

agrarian.c: Agrarian A*gra"ri*an (?), a. [L. agrarius, fr. ager field.] 1. Pertaining to fields, or lands, or their tenure; esp., relating to an equal or equitable division of lands; as, the agrarian laws of Rome, which distributed the conquered and other public lands among citizens.
Agrarian A*gra"ri*an, n. 1. One in favor of an equal division of landed property.

agrarianism.c: Agrarianism A*gra"ri*an*ism (?), n. An equal or equitable division of landed property; the principles or acts of those who favor a redistribution of land.

agrarianize.c: Agrarianize A*gra"ri*an*ize (?), v. t. To distribute according to, or to imbue with, the principles of agrarianism.

agree.c: Agree Agre { A*gre", A*gree" } (?), adv. [F. à gré. See Agree.] In good part; kindly. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

Agree A*gree" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Agreed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Agreeing.] [F. agréer to accept or receive kindly, fr. à gré; à (L. ad) + gré good will, consent, liking, fr. L. gratus pleasing, agreeable. See Grateful.] 1. To harmonize in opinion, statement, or action; to be in unison or concord; to be or become united or consistent; to concur; as, all parties agree in the expediency of the law.
Agree A*gree" (?), v. t. 1. To make harmonious; to reconcile or make friends. [Obs.] Spenser.

agreeability.c: Agreeability A*gree`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [OF. agreablete.] 1. Easiness of disposition. [Obs.] Chaucer.

agreeable.c: Agreeable A*gree"a*ble (?), a. [F. agréable.] 1. Pleasing, either to the mind or senses; pleasant; grateful; as, agreeable manners or remarks; an agreeable person; fruit agreeable to the taste.

agreeableness.c: Agreeableness A*gree"a*ble*ness, n. 1. The quality of being agreeable or pleasing; that quality which gives satisfaction or moderate pleasure to the mind or senses.

agreeably.c: Agreeably A*gree"a*bly, adv. 1. In an agreeably manner; in a manner to give pleasure; pleasingly. “Agreeably entertained.” Goldsmith.

agreeingly.c: Agreeingly A*gree"ing*ly, adv. In an agreeing manner (to); correspondingly; agreeably. [Obs.]

agreement.c: Agreement A*gree"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. agrément.] 1. State of agreeing; harmony of opinion, statement, action, or character; concurrence; concord; conformity; as, a good agreement subsists among the members of the council.

agrestic.c: Agrestic A*gres"tic (?), a. [L. agrestis, fr. ager field.] Pertaining to fields or the country, in opposition to the city; rural; rustic; unpolished; uncouth. “Agrestic behavior.” Gregory.

agricolist.c: Agricolist A*gric"o*list (?), n. A cultivator of the soil; an agriculturist. Dodsley.

agricultor.c: Agricultor Ag"ri*cul`tor (?), n. [L., fr. ager field + cultor cultivator.] An agriculturist; a farmer. [R.]

agricultural.c: Agricultural Ag`ri*cul"tur*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to agriculture; connected with, or engaged in, tillage; as, the agricultural class; agricultural implements, wages, etc. -- Ag`ri*cul"tur*al*ly, adv.

agriculturalist.c: Agriculturalist Ag`ri*cul"tur*al*ist, n. An agriculturist (which is the preferred form.)

agriculture.c: Agriculture Ag"ri*cul`ture (?; 135), n. [L. agricultura; ager field + cultura cultivation: cf. F. agriculture. See Acre and Culture.] The art or science of cultivating the ground, including the harvesting of crops, and the rearing and management of live stock; tillage; husbandry; farming.

agriculturist.c: Agriculturist Ag`ri*cul"tur*ist, n. One engaged or skilled in agriculture; a husbandman.

agrief.c: Agrief A*grief" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + grief.] In grief; amiss. [Obs.] Chaucer.

agrimony.c: Agrimony Ag"ri*mo*ny (?), n. [OE. agremoyne, OF. aigremoine, L. agrimonia for argemonia, fr. Gr.?.] (Bot.) (a) A genus of plants of the Rose family. (b) The name is also given to various other plants; as, hemp agrimony (Eupatorium cannabinum); water agrimony (Bidens).

agrin.c: Agrin A*grin" (ȧ*grĭn"), adv. & a. [Pref. a- + grin.] In the act of grinning. “His visage all agrin.” Tennyson.

agriologist.c: Agriologist Ag`ri*ol"o*gist (ăg`rĭ*ŏl"o*jĭst), n. One versed or engaged in agriology.

agriology.c: Agriology Ag`ri*ol"o*gy (ăg`rĭ*ŏl"o*jy̆), n. [Gr.? wild, savage + -logy.] Description or comparative study of the customs of savage or uncivilized tribes.

agrise.c: Agrise A*grise" (?), v. i. [AS. āgrīsan to dread; ā- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + grīsan, for gr?san (only in comp.), akin to OHG. gr?is?n, G. grausen, to shudder. See Grisly.] To shudder with terror; to tremble with fear. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Agrise A*grise", v. t. 1. To shudder at; to abhor; to dread; to loathe. [Obs.] Wyclif.

agrom.c: agrom ‖a"grom (ā"grŏm), n. [Native name.] (Med.) A disease occurring in Bengal and other parts of the East Indies, in which the tongue chaps and cleaves.

agronomical.c: Agronomical Agronomic { Ag`ro*nom"ic (?), Ag`ro*nom"ic*al (?), } [Cf. F. agronomique.] Pertaining to agronomy, of the management of farms.

agronomics.c: Agronomics Ag`ro*nom"ics (?), n. The science of the distribution and management of land.

agronomist.c: Agronomist A*gron"o*mist (?), n. One versed in agronomy; a student of agronomy.

agronomy.c: Agronomy A*gron"o*my (?), n. [Gr.? rural; as a noun, an overseer of the public lands;? field +? usage,? to deal out, manage: cf. F. agronomie.] The management of land; rural economy; agriculture.

agrope.c: Agrope A*grope" (?), adv. & a. [Pref. a- + grope.] In the act of groping. Mrs. Browning.

agrostis.c: Agrostis ‖A*gros"tis (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?.] A genus of grasses, including species called in common language bent grass. Some of them, as redtop (Agrostis vulgaris), are valuable pasture grasses.

agrostographical.c: Agrostographical Agrostographic { A*gros`to*graph"ic (?), A*gros`to*graph"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. agrostographique.] Pertaining to agrostography.

agrostography.c: Agrostography Ag`ros*tog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr.? + -graphy.] A description of the grasses.

agrostological.c: Agrostological Agrostologic { A*gros`to*log"ic (?), A*gros`to*log"ic*al (?), } a. Pertaining to agrostology.

agrostologist.c: Agrostologist Ag`ros*tol"o*gist (?), n. One skilled in agrostology.

agrostology.c: Agrostology Ag`ros*tol"ogy (?), n. [Gr.? + -logy.] That part of botany which treats of the grasses.

aground.c: Aground A*ground" (?), adv. & a. [Pref. a- + ground.] On the ground; stranded; -- a nautical term applied to a ship when its bottom lodges on the ground. Totten.

agrypnotic.c: Agrypnotic Ag`ryp*not"ic (?), n. [Gr.? sleepless;? to chase, search for +? sleep: cf. F. agrypnotique.] Anything which prevents sleep, or produces wakefulness, as strong tea or coffee.

aguardiente.c: Aguardiente ‖A`guar*di*en"te (?), n. [Sp., contr. of agua ardiente burning water (L. aqua water + ardens burning).] 1. A inferior brandy of Spain and Portugal.

ague.c: ague a"gue (ā"gu), n. [OE. agu, ague, OF. agu, F. aigu, sharp, OF. fem. ague, LL. (febris) acuta, a sharp, acute fever, fr. L. acutus sharp. See Acute.] 1. An acute fever. [Obs.] “Brenning agues.” P. Plowman.
Ague A"gue, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Agued (?).] To strike with an ague, or with a cold fit. Heywood.

aguilt.c: Aguilt A*guilt" (?), v. t. To be guilty of; to offend; to sin against; to wrong. [Obs.] Chaucer.

aguise.c: Aguise A*guise" (?), n. Dress. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
Aguise A*guise", v. t. [Pref a- + guise.] To dress; to attire; to adorn. [Obs.]

aguish.c: Aguish A"gu*ish (?), a. 1. Having the qualities of an ague; somewhat cold or shivering; chilly; shaky.

agush.c: Agush A*gush" (?), adv. & a. [Pref. a- + gush.] In a gushing state. Hawthorne.

agynous.c: Agynous Ag"y*nous (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. + gynh` woman.] (Bot.) Without female organs; male.

ah.c: Ah Ah (?), interj. [OE. a: cf. OF. a, F. ah, L. ah, Gr.?, Sk. ā, Icel. æ, OHG. ā, Lith. á, áá.] An exclamation, expressive of surprise, pity, complaint, entreaty, contempt, threatening, delight, triumph, etc., according to the manner of utterance.

aha.c: Aha A*ha" (?), interj. [Ah, interj. + ha.] An exclamation expressing, by different intonations, triumph, mixed with derision or irony, or simple surprise.
Aha A*ha", n. A sunk fence. See Ha-ha. Mason.

ahead.c: Ahead A*head" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + head.] 1. In or to the front; in advance; onward.

aheap.c: Aheap A*heap" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + heap.] In a heap; huddled together. Hood.

aheight.c: Aheight A*height" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + height.] Aloft; on high. [Obs.] “Look up aheight.” Shak.

ahem.c: Ahem A*hem" (?), interj. An exclamation to call one's attention; hem.

ahold.c: Ahold A*hold" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + hold.] Near the wind; as, to lay a ship ahold. [Obs.] Shak.

ahoy.c: Ahoy A*hoy" (?), interj. [OE. a, interj. + hoy.] (Naut.) A term used in hailing; as, “Ship ahoy.”

ahriman.c: Ahriman ‖Ah"ri*man (?), n. [Per.] The Evil Principle or Being of the ancient Persians; the Prince of Darkness as opposer to Ormuzd, the King of Light.

ahull.c: Ahull A*hull" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + hull.] (Naut.) With the sails furled, and the helm lashed alee; -- applied to ships in a storm. See Hull, n.

ahungered.c: Ahungered A*hun"gered (?), a. [Pref. a- + hungered.] Pinched with hunger; very hungry. C. Bronté.

ai.c: Ai A"i (?), n.; pl. Ais (?). [Braz. aï, haï, from the animal's cry: cf. F. aï.] (Zool.) The three-toed sloth (Bradypus tridactylus) of South America. See Sloth.

aichs.c: Aich's metal Aich's met"al (?). A kind of gun metal, containing copper, zinc, and iron, but no tin.

aid.c: Aid Aid (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Aided (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Aiding.] [F. aider, OF. aidier, fr. L. adjutare to help, freq. of adjuvare to help; ad + juvare to help. Cf. Adjutant.] To support, either by furnishing strength or means in coöperation to effect a purpose, or to prevent or to remove evil; to help; to assist.
Aid Aid, n. [F. aide, OF. aïde, aïe, fr. the verb. See Aid, v. t.] 1. Help; succor; assistance; relief.

aidant.c: Aidant Aid"ant (?), a. [Cf. F. aidant, p. pr. of aider to help.] Helping; helpful; supplying aid. Shak.

aiddecamp.c: Aid-de-camp Aid"-de-camp` (?), n.; pl. Aids-de-camp. (?). [F. aide de camp (literally) camp assistant.] (Mil.) An officer selected by a general to carry orders, also to assist or represent him in correspondence and in directing movements.

aider.c: Aider Aid"er (?), n. One who, or that which, aids.

aidless.c: Aidless Aid"less, a. Helpless; without aid. Milton.

aidmajor.c: Aid-major Aid"-ma`jor (?), n. The adjutant of a regiment.

aigre.c: Aigre Ai"gre (?), a. [F. See Eager.] Sour. [Obs.] Shak.

aigremore.c: Aigremore ‖Ai"gre*more (?), n. [F. origin unknown.] Charcoal prepared for making powder.

aigrette.c: Aigrette Aigret { Ai"gret (?), Ai*grette (?), } n. [F., a sort of white heron, with a tuft of feathers on its head; a tuft of feathers; dim. of the same word as heron. See Heron, and cf. Egret, Egrette.] 1. (Zool.) The small white European heron. See Egret.

aiguille.c: Aiguille ‖Ai`guille" (?), n. [F., a needle. See Aglet.] 1. A needle-shaped peak.

aiguillette.c: Aiguillette Ai`guil*lette" (?), n. [F. See Aglet.] 1. A point or tag at the end of a fringe or lace; an aglet.

ail.c: Ail Ail (āl), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ailed (āld); p. pr. & vb. n. Ailing.] [OE. eilen, ailen, AS. eglan to trouble, pain; akin to Goth. us-agljan to distress, agls troublesome, irksome, aglo, aglitha, pain, and prob. to E. awe. √3.] To affect with pain or uneasiness, either physical or mental; to trouble; to be the matter with; -- used to express some uneasiness or affection, whose cause is unknown; as, what ails the man? I know not what ails him.
Ail Ail, v. i. To be affected with pain or uneasiness of any sort; to be ill or indisposed or in trouble.
Ail Ail, n. Indisposition or morbid affection. Pope.

ailantus.c: Ailantus Ai*lan"tus (?), n. [From aylanto, i. e., tree of heaven, the name of the tree in the Moluccas.] (Bot.) A genus of beautiful trees, natives of the East Indies. The tree imperfectly diœcious, and the staminate or male plant is very offensive when blossom.

aileron.c: Aileron Ai"le*ron (ā"le*rŏn), n. [F., dim. of aile wing.] 1. A half gable, as at the end of a penthouse or of the aisle of a church.

ailette.c: Ailette Ai*lette (?), n. [F. ailette, dim. of aile wing, L. ala.] A small square shield, formerly worn on the shoulders of knights, -- being the prototype of the modern epaulet. Fairholt.

ailment.c: Ailment Ail"ment (?), n. Indisposition; morbid affection of the body; -- not applied ordinarily to acute diseases. “Little ailments.” Landsdowne.

ailuroidea.c: Ailuroidea ‖Ai`lu*roid"e*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? cat + -oid.] (Zool.) A group of the Carnivora, which includes the cats, civets, and hyenas.

aim.c: Aim Aim (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Aimed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Aiming.] [OE. amen, aimen, eimen, to guess at, to estimate, to aim, OF. esmer, asmer, fr. L. aestimare to estimate; or perh. fr. OF. aesmer;? (L. ad) + esmer. See Estimate.] 1. To point or direct a missile weapon, or a weapon which propels as missile, towards an object or spot with the intent of hitting it; as, to aim at a fox, or at a target.

Aim Aim, v. t. To direct or point, as a weapon, at a particular object; to direct, as a missile, an act, or a proceeding, at, to, or against an object; as, to aim a musket or an arrow, the fist or a blow (at something); to aim a satire or a reflection (at some person or vice).

Aim Aim, n. [Cf. OF. esme estimation, fr. esmer. See Aim, v. i.] 1. The pointing of a weapon, as a gun, a dart, or an arrow, in the line of direction with the object intended to be struck; the line of fire; the direction of anything, as a spear, a blow, a discourse, a remark, towards a particular point or object, with a view to strike or affect it.

aimer.c: Aimer Aim"er (?), n. One who aims, directs, or points.

aimless.c: Aimless Aim"less, a. Without aim or purpose; as, an aimless life. -- Aim"less*ly, adv. -- Aim"less*ness, n.

aino.c: Aino Ai"no (?), n. [Said to be the native name for man.] same as Ainu.

ainu.c: Ainu Ai"nu (?), n. [Said to be the native name for man.] One of a peculiar race found primarily in Hokkaido, in the northern part of the empire of Japan, the Kurile Islands, and nearby. They are believed to be the native inhabitants of the Japanese islands. The Ainus are stout and short, with hairy bodies. Also called Aino and hairy Ainu.

aint.c: Ain't Ain't (?). A contraction for are not and am not; also used for is not. [Colloq. or illiterate speech]. See An't.

air.c: Air Air (âr), n. [OE. air, eir, F. air, L. aër, fr. Gr. 'ah`r, air, mist, for 'aϝhr, fr. root 'aϝ to blow, breathe, probably akin to E. wind. In sense 10 the French has taking a meaning fr. It. aria atmosphere, air, fr. the same Latin word; and in senses 11, 12, 13 the French meaning is either fr. L. aria, or due to confusion with F. aire, in an older sense of origin, descent. Cf. Aëry, Debonair, Malaria, Wind.] 1. The fluid which we breathe, and which surrounds the earth; the atmosphere. It is invisible, inodorous, insipid, transparent, compressible, elastic, and ponderable.

Air Air (âr), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Aired (ârd); p. pr. & vb. n. Airing.] [See Air, n., and cf. Aërate.] 1. To expose to the air for the purpose of cooling, refreshing, or purifying; to ventilate; as, to air a room.
air bed airbed air"bed`, air" bed` (?). A sack or mattress inflated with air, and used as a bed.

air bladder air" blad`der (?). 1. (Anat.) An air sac, sometimes double or variously lobed, in the visceral cavity of many fishes. It originates in the same way as the lungs of air-breathing vertebrates, and in the adult may retain a tubular connection with the pharynx or esophagus.
Air brake Air" brake` (?). (Mach.) A railway brake powered by compressed air. Knight.
air brush airbrush airbrush, air brush. A kind of atomizer for applying liquid coloring matter, such as paint, in a spray by compressed air.
Air cell Air" cell` (?). 1. (Bot.) A cavity in the cellular tissue of plants, containing air only.
Air chamber Air" cham`ber (?). 1. A chamber or cavity filled with air, in an animal or plant.
Air cock Air" cock` (?). A faucet to allow escape of air.

Air cooling Air cooling. In devices generating heat, such as gasoline-engine motor vehicles, the cooling of the device by increasing its radiating surface by means of ribs or radiators, and placing it so that it is exposed to a current of air. Cf. Water cooling. -- Air"-cooled`, a.
Air drill Air" drill` (?). A drill driven by the elastic pressure of condensed air; a pneumatic drill. Knight.
Air engine Air" engine` (?). An engine driven by heated or by compressed air. Knight.
Air gap Air gap. (Physics) An air-filled gap in a magnetic or electric circuit; specif., in a dynamo or motor, the space between the field-magnet poles and the armature; clearance.
Air gas Air" gas` (?). See under Gas.

air gun airgun air"gun`, air" gun` (gŭn`). A kind of gun in which the elastic force of condensed air is used to discharge the ball. The air is powerfully compressed into a reservoir attached to the gun, by a condensing pump, and is controlled by a valve actuated by the trigger. The common BB gun is a type of air gun.
Air hole Air" hole` (âr" hōl`). 1. A hole to admit or discharge air; specifically, a spot in the ice not frozen over.
Air jacket Air" jack`et (?). A jacket having air-tight cells, or cavities which can be filled with air, to render persons buoyant in swimming.
Air level Air" lev`el (?). Spirit level. See Level.
Air line Air line. A path through the air made easy for aërial navigation by steady winds.
Air pipe Air" pipe` (?). A pipe for the passage of air; esp. a ventilating pipe.
Air plant Air" plant` (?). (Bot.) A plant deriving its sustenance from the air alone; an aërophyte.
Air poise Air" poise` (?). [See Poise.] An instrument to measure the weight of air.
Air pump Air" pump` (?). 1. (Physics) A kind of pump for exhausting air from a vessel or closed space; also, a pump to condense air or force it into a closed space.
Air sac Air" sac` (?). 1. (Anat.) One of the spaces in different parts of the bodies of birds, which are filled with air and connected with the air passages of the lungs; an air cell.
Air shaft Air" shaft` (?). A passage, usually vertical, for admitting fresh air into a mine or a tunnel.
Air stove Air" stove` (?). A stove for heating a current of air which is directed against its surface by means of pipes, and then distributed through a building.

Air vessel Air" ves`sel (?). A vessel, cell, duct, or tube containing or conducting air; as the air vessels of insects, birds, plants, etc.; the air vessel of a pump, engine, etc. For the latter, see Air chamber. The air vessels of insects are called tracheæ, of plants spiral vessels.

airbuilt.c: Air-built Air"-built` (?), a. Erected in the air; having no solid foundation; chimerical; as, an air-built castle.

aircraft.c: Aircraft Air"craft` (?), n. sing. & pl. Any vehicle, such as an airplane, helicopter, balloon, etc., for floating in, or flying through, the air.

airdrawn.c: Air-drawn Air"-drawn" (?), a. Drawn in air; imaginary.

airer.c: Airer Air"er (?), n. 1. One who exposes to the air.

airily.c: Airily Air"i*ly (âr"ĭ*ly̆), adv. In an airy manner; lightly; gaily; jauntily; flippantly.

airiness.c: Airiness Air"i*ness, n. 1. The state or quality of being airy; openness or exposure to the air; as, the airiness of a country seat.

airing.c: Airing Air"ing (âr"ĭng), n. 1. A walk or a ride in the open air; a short excursion for health's sake.

airless.c: Airless Air"less (?), a. Not open to a free current of air; wanting fresh air, or communication with the open air.

airling.c: Airling Air"ling (?), n. A thoughtless, gay person. [Obs.] “Slight airlings.” B. Jonson.

airman.c: Airman Air"man (?), n. 1. A man who ascends or flies in an aircraft; an aviator; an airplane pilot.

airmanship.c: Airmanship Air"man*ship (?), n. Art, skill, or ability in the practice of aerial navigation; aircraft piloting.

airol.c: Airol Air"ol (?), n. (Pharm.) A grayish green antiseptic powder, consisting of a basic iodide and gallate of bismuth, sometimes used in place of iodoform. [A Trademark]

airometer.c: Airometer Air*om"e*ter (?), n. [Air + -meter.] A hollow cylinder to contain air. It is closed above and open below, and has its open end plunged into water.

airsick.c: Airsick Air"sick` (?), a. Affected with air sickness or aërial sickness; feeling nauseous due to riding in an airplane. -- Air"sick`ness, n.

airslacked.c: Air-slacked Air"-slacked` (?), a. Slacked, or pulverized, by exposure to the air; as, air-slacked lime.

airtight.c: Air-tight Air"-tight` (?), a. 1. So tight as to be impermeable to air or other gases; as, an air-tight cylinder; -- said of containers.
Air-tight Air"-tight`, n. A stove the draft of which can be almost entirely shut off. [Colloq. U. S.]

airwards.c: Airwards Airward { Air"ward (?), Air"wards (?), } adv. Toward the air; upward. [R.] Keats.

airwoman.c: Airwoman Air"wom`an (?), n. A woman who ascends or flies in an aircraft; a woman aviator; a woman airplane pilot or balloonist; an aviatrix.

airy.c: Airy Air"y (?), a. 1. Consisting of air; as, an airy substance; the airy parts of bodies.

aisle.c: Aisle Aisle (?), n. [OF. ele, F. aile, wing, wing of a building, L. ala, contr. fr. axilla.] (Arch.) (a) A lateral division of a building, separated from the middle part, called the nave, by a row of columns or piers, which support the roof or an upper wall containing windows, called the clearstory wall. (b) Improperly used also for the have; -- as in the phrases, a church with three aisles, the middle aisle. (c) Also (perhaps from confusion with alley), a passage into which the pews of a church open.

aisled.c: Aisled Aisled (?), a. Furnished with an aisle or aisles.

ait.c: Ait Ait (?), n. [AS.?,?, perh. dim. of īeg, īg, island. See Eyot.] An islet, or little isle, in a river or lake; an eyot.

aitch.c: Aitch Aitch (?), n. The letter h or H.

aitchbone.c: Aitchbone Aitch"bone` (?), n. [For nachebone. For loss of n, cf. Adder. See Natch.] The bone of the rump; also, the cut of beef surrounding this bone. [Spelt also edgebone.]

ajar.c: Ajar A*jar" (?), adv. [OE. on char ajar, on the turn; AS. cerr, cyrr, turn, akin to G. kehren to turn, and to D. akerre. See Char.] Slightly turned or opened; as, the door was standing ajar.
Ajar A*jar" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + jar.] In a state of discord; out of harmony; as, he is ajar with the world.

ajog.c: Ajog A*jog" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + jog.] On the jog.

ajowan.c: Ajowan Ajouan { ‖Aj"ou*an ‖Aj"ow*an } (?), n. [Written also ajwain.] [Prob. native name.] (Bot.) The fruit of Ammi Copticum, syn. Carum Ajowan, used both as a medicine and as a condiment. An oil containing thymol is extracted from it. Called also Javanee seed, Javanese seed, and ajava.

ajutage.c: Ajutage Aj"u*tage (?), n. [F. ajutage, for ajoutage, fr. ajouter to add, LL. adjuxtare, fr. L. ad + juxta near to, nigh. Cf. Adjutage, Adjustage, Adjust.] A tube through which water is discharged; an efflux tube; as, the ajutage of a fountain.

akimbo.c: Akimbo A*kim"bo (?), a. [Etymology unknown. Cf. Kimbo.] With a crook or bend; with the hand on the hip and elbow turned outward. “With one arm akimbo.” Irving.

akin.c: Akin A*kin" (?), a. [Pref. a- (for of) + kin.] 1. Of the same kin; related by blood; -- used of persons; as, the two families are near akin.

akinesia.c: akinesia ‖ak`i*ne"si*a (ā`kĭ*nē"sē*ȧ or ăk`ĭ*nē"sĭ*ȧ), n. [Gr. 'akinhsi`a quiescence; 'a priv. + ki`nhsis motion.] (Med.) Loss of the ability for voluntary muscle movement. Foster.

akinesic.c: akinesic akinetic ‖ak`i*ne"sic (ā`kĭ*nē"sĭk or ăk`ĭ*nē"sĭk), a*ki`net"ic (ā`kĭ*nĕt"ĭk), a. (Med.) Of or pertaining to akinesia.

aknee.c: Aknee A*knee" (?), adv. On the knee. [R.] Southey.

al.c: Al Al. conj. Although; if. [Obs.] See All, conj.

al- al-. prefix. (a) [AS. eal.] All; wholly; completely; as, almighty, almost. (b) [L. ad.] To; at; on; -- in OF. shortened to a-. See ad-. (c) The Arabic definite article answering to the English the; as, Alkoran, the Koran or the Book; alchemy, the chemistry.
Al segno ‖Al` se"gno (?). [It., to the mark or sign.](Mus.) A direction for the performer to return and recommence from the sign?.

ala.c: ala ‖a"la (ā"lȧ), n.; pl. Alæ (ā"lē). [L., a wing.] (Biol.) A winglike organ, or part.

alabama.c: Alabama period Al`a*ba"ma pe"ri*od (?). (Geol.) A period in the American eocene, the lowest in the tertiary age except the lignitic.

alabaster.c: Alabaster Al"a*bas"ter (?), n. [L. alabaster, Gr. 'ala`bastros, said to be derived fr. Alabastron, the name of a town in Egypt, near which it was common: cf. OF. alabastre, F. albâtre.] 1. (Min.) (a) A compact variety or sulphate of lime, or gypsum, of fine texture, and usually white and translucent, but sometimes yellow, red, or gray. It is carved into vases, mantel ornaments, etc. (b) A hard, compact variety of carbonate of lime, somewhat translucent, or of banded shades of color; stalagmite. The name is used in this sense by Pliny. It is sometimes distinguished as oriental alabaster.

alabastrine.c: Alabastrine Al`a*bas"trine (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or like, alabaster; as alabastrine limbs.

alabastrum.c: Alabastrum ‖Al`a*bas"trum (?), n.; pl. Alabastra (?). [NL.] (Bot.) A flower bud. Gray.

alack.c: Alack A*lack" (?), interj. [Prob. from ah! lack! OE. lak loss, failure, misfortune. See Lack.] An exclamation expressive of sorrow. [Archaic. or Poet.] Shak.

alackaday.c: Alackaday A*lack"a*day` (?), interj. [For alack the day. Cf. Lackaday.] An exclamation expressing sorrow.

alacrify.c: Alacrify A*lac"ri*fy (?), v. t. [L. alacer, alacris, lively + -fly.] To rouse to action; to inspirit.

alacrious.c: Alacrious A*lac"ri*ous (?), a. [L. alacer, alacris.] Brisk; joyously active; lively.

alacrity.c: Alacrity A*lac"ri*ty (?), n. [L. alacritas, fr. alacer lively, eager, prob. akin to Gr.? to drive, Goth. aljan zeal.] A cheerful readiness, willingness, or promptitude; joyous activity; briskness; sprightliness; as, the soldiers advanced with alacrity to meet the enemy.

aladinist.c: Aladinist A*lad"in*ist (?), n. [From Aladin, for Ala Eddin, i. e., height of religion, a learned divine under Mohammed II. and Bajazet II.] One of a sect of freethinkers among the Muslims.

alalia.c: alalia ‖a*la"li*a (ȧ*lā"lĭ*ȧ), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? priv. +? a talking; cf.? speechless.] (Med.) Impairment of articulate speech, or inability to speak, usually due to impairment of control of muscles in the articulatory apparatus.

Alalia ‖A*la"li*a (), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? priv. +? a talking; cf.? speechless.] (Med.) Inability to utter articulate sounds, due either to paralysis of the larynx or to that form of aphasia, called motor, or ataxis, aphasia, due to loss of control of the muscles of speech.

alilonghi.c: Alilonghi Alalonga Al`a*lon"ga (?), or Al`i*lon"ghi (?), n. (Zool.) The tunny. See Albicore.

alamire.c: Alamire ‖A`la*mi"re (?), n. [Compounded of a la mi re, names of notes in the musical scale.] The lowest note but one in Guido Aretino's scale of music.

alamodality.c: Alamodality Al`a*mo*dal"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being à la mode; conformity to the mode or fashion; fashionableness. [R.] Southey.

alamode.c: Alamode Al"a*mode` (?), adv. & a. [F. à la mode after the fashion.] According to the fashion or prevailing mode. “Alamode beef shops.” Macaulay.
Alamode Al"a*mode`, n. A thin, black silk for hoods, scarfs, etc.; -- often called simply mode. Buchanan.

alamort.c: Alamort Al`a*mort" (?), a. [F. à la mort to the death. Cf. Amort.] To the death; mortally.

alan.c: Alan A*lan" (ȧ*lȧn"), n. [OF. alan, alant; cf. Sp. alano.] A wolfhound. [Obs.] Chaucer.

aland.c: Aland A*land" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + land.] On land; to the land; ashore. “Cast aland.” Sir P. Sidney.

alanine.c: Alanine Al"a*nine (?), n. [Aldehyde + the ending -ine. The -n- is a euphonic insertion.] (Chem.) one of the natural amino acids found combined in the proteins of most living tissues. It can be isolated as a white crystalline base, C3H7NO2. The natural form is the L-configuration.

alantin.c: Alantin A*lan"tin (?), n. [G. alant elecampane, the Inula helenium of Linnæus.] (Chem.) See Inulin.

alar.c: Alar A"lar (?), a. [L. alarius, fr. ala wing: cf. F. alaire.] 1. Pertaining to, or having, wings.

alarm.c: Alarm A*larm" (ȧ*lärm"), n. [F. alarme, It. all' arme to arms! fr. L. arma, pl., arms. See Arms, and cf. Alarum.] 1. A summons to arms, as on the approach of an enemy.

Alarm A*larm", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Alarmed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Alarming.] [Alarm, n. Cf. F. alarmer.] 1. To call to arms for defense; to give notice to (any one) of approaching danger; to rouse to vigilance and action; to put on the alert.

alarmable.c: Alarmable A*larm"a*ble (?), a. Easily alarmed or disturbed.

alarmed.c: Alarmed A*larmed" (?), a. Aroused to vigilance; excited by fear of approaching danger; agitated; disturbed; as, an alarmed neighborhood; an alarmed modesty.

alarmedly.c: Alarmedly A*larm"ed*ly (?), adv. In an alarmed manner.

alarming.c: Alarming A*larm"ing, a. Exciting, or calculated to excite, alarm; causing apprehension of danger; as, an alarming crisis or report. -- A*larm"ing*ly, adv.

alarmist.c: Alarmist A*larm"ist, n. [Cf. F. alarmiste.] One prone to sound or excite alarms, especially, needless alarms. Macaulay.

alarum.c: Alarum A*lar"um (?; 277), n. [OE. alarom, the same word as alarm, n.] See Alarm. [Now Poetic]

alary.c: Alary Al"a*ry (?), a. [L. alarius, fr. ala wing.] Of or pertaining to wings; also, wing-shaped.

alas.c: Alas A*las" (?), interj. [OE. alas, allas, OF. alas, F. hélas; a interj. (L. ah.) + las wretched (that I am), L. lassus weary, akin to E. late. See Late.] An exclamation expressive of sorrow, pity, or apprehension of evil; -- in old writers, sometimes followed by day or white; alas the day, like alack a day, or alas the white.

alate.c: Alate A*late" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + late.] Lately; of late. [Archaic]

alated.c: Alated Alate { A"late (?), A"la*ted (?), } a. [L. alatus, from ala wing.] Winged; having wings, or side appendages like wings.

alaternus.c: Alaternus Alatern { Al"a*tern (?), ‖Al`a*ter"nus (?), } n. [L. ala wing + terni three each.] (Bot.) An ornamental evergreen shrub (Rhamnus alaternus) belonging to the buckthorns.

alation.c: Alation A*la"tion (?), n. [F., fr. L. alatus winged.] The state of being winged.

alb.c: Alb Alb (?), n. [OE. albe, LL. alba, fr. L. albus white. Cf. Album and Aube.] A vestment of white linen, reaching to the feet, an enveloping the person; -- in the Roman Catholic church, worn by those in holy orders when officiating at mass. It was formerly worn, at least by clerics, in daily life.

Alb Sunday Alb Sunday. (Eccl.) The first Sunday after Easter Sunday, properly Albless Sunday, because in the early church those who had been baptized on Easter eve laid aside on the following Saturday their white albs which had been put on after baptism.

albacore.c: Albacore Al"ba*core (?), n. (Zool.) A name applied to several large fishes of the Mackerel family (Scombridae), esp. Thunnus alalunga (formerly Orcynus alalonga); it is a type of tuna or tunny. The name has been also applied to a larger related species, Thunnus thynnus (formerly Orcynus thynnus), common in the Mediterranean and Atlantic, which is called in New England the horse mackerel. [formerly spelled albicore.]

alban.c: Alban Al"ban (?), n. [L. albus white.] (Chem.) A white crystalline resinous substance extracted from gutta-percha by the action of alcohol or ether.

albanian.c: Albanian Al*ba"ni*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Albania, a province of Turkey. -- n. A native of Albania.

albata.c: Albata ‖Al*ba"ta (?), n. [L. albatus, p. p. of albare to make white, fr. albus white.] A white metallic alloy; which is made into spoons, forks, teapots, etc. British plate or German silver. See German silver, under German.

albatross.c: Albatross Al"ba*tross (?), n. [Corrupt. fr. Pg. alcatraz cormorant, albatross, or Sp. alcatraz a pelican: cf. Pg. alcatruz, Sp. arcaduz, a bucket, fr. Ar. al-qādus the bucket, fr. Gr. ka`dos, a water vessel. So an Arabic term for pelican is water-carrier, as a bird carrying water in its pouch.] (Zool.) A web-footed bird, of the genus Diomedea, of which there are several species. They are the largest of sea birds, capable of long-continued flight, and are often seen at great distances from the land. They are found chiefly in the southern hemisphere.

albee.c: Albee Albe { Al`be", Al`bee" } (?), conj. [See Albeit.] Although; albeit. [Obs.]

albedo.c: Albedo ‖Al*be"do (?), n. [L., fr. albus white.] Whiteness. Specifically: (Astron.) The ratio which the light reflected from an unpolished surface bears to the total light falling upon that surface.

albeit.c: Albeit Al`be"it (?), conj. [OE. al be although it be, where al is our all. Cf. Although.] Even though; although; notwithstanding. Chaucer.

albertite.c: Albertite Al"bert*ite (ăl"bẽrt*īt), n. (Min.) A bituminous mineral resembling asphaltum, found in the county of Albert, New Brunswick.

albert.c: Albert ware Al"bert ware. A soft ornamental terra-cotta pottery, sold in the biscuit state for decorating.

albertype.c: Albertype Al"ber*type (ăl"bẽr*tīp), n. [From the name of the inventor, Albert, of Munich.] A picture printed from a kind of gelatine plate produced by means of a photographic negative.

albescence.c: Albescence Al*bes"cence (?), n. The act of becoming white; whitishness.

albescent.c: Albescent Al*bes"cent (?), a. [L. albescens, p. pr. of albescere to grow white, fr. albus white.] Becoming white or whitish; moderately white.

albicant.c: Albicant Al"bi*cant (?), a. [L. albicans, p. pr. of albicare, albicatum, to be white, fr. albus white.] Growing or becoming white.

albication.c: Albication Al`bi*ca"tion (?), n. The process of becoming white, or developing white patches, or streaks.

albicore.c: Albicore Al"bi*core (?), n. [F. albicore (cf. Sp. albacora, Pg. albacor, albacora, albecora), fr. Ar. bakr, bekr, a young camel, young cow, heifer, and the article al: cf. Pg. bacoro a little pig.] (Zool.) same as albacore.

albification.c: Albification Al`bi*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. albification: L. albus white + ficare (only in comp.), facere, to make.] The act or process of making white. [Obs.]

albigeois.c: Albigeois Albigenses { Al`bi*gen"ses (?), ‖Al`bi`geois" (?), } n. pl. [From Albi and Albigeois, a town and its district in the south of France, in which the sect abounded.] (Eccl. Hist.) A sect of reformers opposed to the church of Rome in the 12th centuries.

albigensian.c: Albigensian Al`bi*gen"sian (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Albigenses.

albiness.c: Albiness Al*bi"ness (?), n. A female albino. Holmes.

albinism.c: Albinism Al"bi*nism (?), n. The state or condition of being an albino: abinoism; leucopathy.

albino.c: Albino Al*bi"no (?; 277), n.; pl. Albinos (?). [Sp. or Pg. albino, orig. whitish, fr. albo white, L. albus.] A person, whether negro, Indian, or white, in whom by some defect of organization the substance which gives color to the skin, hair, and eyes is deficient or in a morbid state. An albino has a skin of a milky hue, with hair of the same color, and eyes with deep red pupil and pink or blue iris. The term is also used of the lower animals, as white mice, elephants, etc.; and of plants in a whitish condition from the absence of chlorophyll. Amer. Cyc.

albinoism.c: Albinoism Al*bi"no*ism (?), n. The state or condition of being an albino; albinism.

albion.c: Albion Al"bi*on (?), n. [Prob. from the same root as Gael. alp a height or hill. “It may have been bestowed on the land lying behind the white cliffs visible from the coast of Gaul. Albany, the old name of Scotland, means probably the “hilly land.” I. Taylor.] An ancient name of England, still retained in poetry.

albite.c: Albite Al"bite (?), n. [L. albus white.] (Min.) A mineral of the feldspar family, triclinic in crystallization, and in composition a silicate of alumina and soda. It is a common constituent of granite and of various igneous rocks. See Feldspar.

albolith.c: Albolith Al"bo*lith (?), n. [L. albus white + -lith.] A kind of plastic cement, or artificial stone, consisting chiefly of magnesia and silica; -- called also albolite.

alborak.c: Alborak ‖Al"bo*rak (?; 277), n. [Ar. al-burāq, fr. baraqa to flash, shine.] The imaginary milk-white animal on which Mohammed was said to have been carried up to heaven; a white mule.

albugineous.c: Albugineous Al`bu*gin"e*ous (?), a. [See Albugo.] Of the nature of, or resembling, the white of the eye, or of an egg; albuminous; -- a term applied to textures, humors, etc., which are perfectly white.

albugo.c: albugo ‖al*bu"go (ăl*bū"go), n.; pl. Albugines (ăl*bū"jĭ*nēz). [L., whiteness, fr. albus white.] (Med.) Same as Leucoma. [archaic]

album.c: Album Al"bum (?), n. [L., neut. of albus white: cf. F. album. Cf. Alb.] 1. (Rom. Antiq.) A white tablet on which anything was inscribed, as a list of names, etc.
Album Graecum ‖Al"bum Græ"cum (?). [L., Greek white.] Dung of dogs or hyenas, which becomes white by exposure to air. It is used in dressing leather, and was formerly used in medicine.

albumen.c: Albumen Al*bu"men (?), n. [L., fr. albus white.] 1. The white of an egg.

albumenize.c: Albumenize Al*bu"men*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Albumenized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Albumenizing.] To cover or saturate with albumen; to coat or treat with an albuminous solution; as, to albumenize paper.

albumin.c: Albumin Al*bu"min (?), n. (Chem.) A thick, viscous nitrogenous substance, which is the chief and characteristic constituent of white of eggs and of the serum of blood, and is found in other animal substances, both fluid and solid, also in many plants. It is soluble in water and is coagulated by heat and by certain chemical reagents.

albuminate.c: Albuminate Al*bu"mi*nate (?), n. (Chem.) A substance produced by the action of an alkali upon albumin, and resembling casein in its properties; also, a compound formed by the union of albumin with another substance.

albuminemia.c: Albuminemia Al*bu`mi*ne"mi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. E. albumin.] (Med.) The level of albumin in the blood.

albuminimeter.c: Albuminimeter Al*bu`mi*nim"e*ter (?), n. [L. albumen, albuminis + -meter: cf. F. albuminimètre.] An instrument for ascertaining the quantity of albumen in a liquid.

albuminin.c: Albuminin Al*bu"mi*nin (?), n. (Chem.) The substance of the cells which inclose the white of birds' eggs.

albuminiparous.c: Albuminiparous Al*bu`mi*nip"a*rous (?), a. [L. albumen + parere to bear, bring forth.] Producing albumin.

albuminoid.c: Albuminoid Al*bu"mi*noid (?), a. [L. albumen + -oid.] (Chem.) Resembling albumin. -- n. One of a class of organic principles (called also proteids) which form the main part of organized tissues. Brunton.

albuminoidal.c: Albuminoidal Al*bu`mi*noid"al (?), a. (Chem.) Of the nature of an albuminoid.

albuminose.c: Albuminose Al*bu"mi*nose` (?), n. (Chem.) A diffusible substance formed from albumin by the action of natural or artificial gastric juice. See Peptone.

albuminosis.c: Albuminosis Al*bu`mi*no"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. E. albumin.] (Med.) A condition of excessively high blood albumin level. [obsolescent]

albuminous.c: Albuminous Albuminose { Al*bu"mi*nous (?), Al*bu"mi*nose` (?), } a. [Cf. F. albumineux.] 1. Pertaining to, or containing, albumin; having the properties of, or resembling, albumen or albumin; an older term now replaces by proteinaceous.

albuminuria.c: albuminuria ‖al*bu`mi*nu"ri*a (ăl*bū`mĭ*nū"rĭ*ȧ), n. [NL., fr. L. albumen + Gr. o'y^ron urine.] (Med.) A morbid condition in which albumin is present in the urine. AS

albumose.c: Albumose Al"bu*mose` (?), n. [From albumin.] (Chem.) A compound or class of compounds formed from albumin by dilute acids or by an acid solution of pepsin. Used also in combination, as antialbumose, hemialbumose.

alburn.c: Alburn Al"burn (?), n. [L. alburnus, fr. L. albus white. Cf. Auburn.] (Zool.) The bleak, a small European fish having scales of a peculiarly silvery color which are used in making artificial pearls.

alburnous.c: Alburnous Al*bur"nous (?), a. Of or pertaining to alburnum; of the alburnum; as, alburnous substances.

alburnum.c: Alburnum Al*bur"num (?), n. [L., fr. albus white.] (Bot.) The white and softer part of wood, between the inner bark and the hard wood or duramen; sapwood.

albyn.c: Albyn Al"byn (?), n. [See Albion.] Scotland; esp. the Highlands of Scotland. T. Cambell.

alcaic.c: Alcaic Al*ca"ic (?), a. [L. Alcaïcus, Gr.?.] Pertaining to Alcæus, a lyric poet of Mitylene, about 6000 b. c. -- n. A kind of verse, so called from Alcæus. One variety consists of five feet, a spondee or iambic, an iambic, a long syllable, and two dactyls.

alcayde.c: Alcayde Alcaid ‖Al*caid", Al*cayde" (?), n. [Sp. alcaide, fr. Ar. al-qāīd governor, fr. qāda to lead, govern.] 1. A commander of a castle or fortress among the Spaniards, Portuguese, and Moors.

alcalde.c: Alcalde ‖Al*cal"de (?), n. [Sp. alcalde, fr. Ar. al-qādī judge, fr. qada to decide, judge. Hence, the cadi of the Turks. Cf. Cadi.] A magistrate or judge in Spain and in Spanish America, etc. Prescott.

alcaldia.c: Alcaldia ‖Al`cal*di"a (?), n. [Sp. Alcaldía.] The jurisdiction or office of an alcalde; also, the building or chamber in which he conducts the business of his office.

alcanna.c: Alcanna ‖Al*can"na (?), n. [Sp. alcana, alhe?a, fr. Ar. al-hinnā. See Henna, and cf. Alkanet.] (Bot.) An oriental shrub (Lawsonia inermis) from which henna is obtained.

alcarraza.c: Alcarraza ‖Al`car*ra"za (?), n.; pl. Alcarrazas. (?) [Sp., from Ar. al-kurrāz earthen vessel.] A vessel of porous earthenware, used for cooling liquids by evaporation from the exterior surface.

alcazar.c: Alcazar ‖Al*ca"zar (?), n. [ fr. Ar. al the + qacr (in pl.) a castle.] A fortress; also, a royal palace. Prescott.

alcedo.c: Alcedo ‖Al*ce"do (?), n. [L., equiv. to Gr.?. See Halcyon.] (Zool.) A genus of perching birds, including the European kingfisher (Alcedo ispida). See Halcyon.

alchemical.c: Alchemical Alchemic { Al*chem"ic (?), Al*chem"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. alchimique.] Of or relating to alchemy.

alchemically.c: Alchemically Al*chem"ic*al*ly, adv. In the manner of alchemy.

alchemist.c: Alchemist Al"che*mist (?), n. [Cf. OF. alquemiste, F. alchimiste.] One who practices alchemy.

alchemistical.c: Alchemistical Alchemistic { Al`che*mis"tic (?), Al`che*mis"tic*al (?), } a. Relating to or practicing alchemy.

alchemize.c: Alchemize Al"che*mize (?), v. t. To change by alchemy; to transmute. Lovelace.

alchemy.c: Alchemy Al"che*my (?), n. [OF. alkemie, arquemie, F. alchimie, Ar. al-kīmīa, fr. late Gr.?, for?, a mingling, infusion,? juice, liquid, especially as extracted from plants, fr.? to pour; for chemistry was originally the art of extracting the juices from plants for medicinal purposes. Cf. Sp. alquimia, It. alchimia. Gr.? is prob. akin to L. fundere to pour, Goth. guitan, AS. geótan, to pour, and so to E. fuse. See Fuse, and cf. Chemistry.] 1. An imaginary art which aimed to transmute the baser metals into gold, to find the panacea, or universal remedy for diseases, etc. It led the way to modern chemistry.

alchymy.c: Alchymy Alchymistic Alchymist Alchymic Al*chym"ic (?), a., Al"chy*mist (?), n., Al`chy*mis"tic (?), a., Al"chy*my (?), n. See Alchemic, Alchemist, Alchemistic, Alchemy.

alco.c: Alco ‖Al"co (?), n. A small South American dog, domesticated by the aborigines.

alcohate.c: Alcohate Alcoate { Al"co*ate (?), Al"co*hate (?), } n. Shortened forms of Alcoholate.

alcohol.c: Alcohol Al"co*hol (ăl"ko*hŏl), n. [Cf. F. alcool, formerly written alcohol, Sp. alcohol alcohol, antimony, galena, OSp. alcofol; all fr. Ar. al-kohl a powder of antimony or galena, to paint the eyebrows with. The name was afterwards applied, on account of the fineness of this powder, to highly rectified spirits, a signification unknown in Arabia. The Sp. word has both meanings. Cf. Alquifou.] 1. An impalpable powder. [Obs.]

alcoholate.c: Alcoholate Al"co*hol*ate (ăl"ko*hŏl*at), n. [Cf. F. alcolaie.] (Chem.) A crystallizable compound of a salt with alcohol, in which the latter plays a part analogous to that of water of crystallization. Graham.

alcoholature.c: Alcoholature Al`co*hol"a*ture (ăl`ko*hŏl"ȧ*tur), n. [Cf. F. alcoolature.] (Med.) An alcoholic tincture prepared with fresh plants. New Eng. Dict.

alcoholic.c: Alcoholic Al`co*hol"ic (ăl`ko*hŏl"ĭk), a. [Cf. F. alcolique.] Of or pertaining to alcohol, or partaking of its qualities; derived from, or caused by, alcohol; containing alcohol; as, alcoholic mixtures; alcoholic gastritis; alcoholic odor.
Alcoholic Al`co*hol"ic, n. 1. A person given to the use of alcoholic liquors.

alcoholization.c: Alcoholization Al`co*hol`i*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. alcoolisation.] 1. The act of reducing a substance to a fine or impalpable powder. [Obs.] Johnson.

alcoholize.c: Alcoholize Al"co*hol*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Alcoholized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Alcoholizing.] [Cf. F. alcooliser.] 1. To reduce to a fine powder. [Obs.] Johnson.

alcoholmeter.c: Alcoholmeter Alcoholometer { Al`co*hol*om"e*ter (?), Al`co*hol"me*ter (?), } n. [Alcohol + -meter.] (Chem.) An instrument for determining the strength of spirits, with a scale graduated so as to indicate the percentage of pure alcohol, either by weight or volume. It is usually a form of hydrometer with a special scale.

alcoholmetrical.c: Alcoholmetrical Alcoholometrical Alcoholometric Al`co*hol`o*met"ric (?), Al`co*hol`o*met"ric*al (?), Al`co*hol*met"ric*al (?), a. Relating to the alcoholometer or alcoholometry.

alcoholometry.c: Alcoholometry Al`co*hol"om"e*try (?), n. The process or method of ascertaining the proportion of pure alcohol which spirituous liquors contain.

alcohometric.c: Alcohometric Alcohometer Al`co*hom"e*ter (?), n., Al`co*ho*met"ric, a. Same as Alcoholometer, Alcoholometric.

alcoran.c: Alcoran Al"co*ran (?; 277), n. [alcoran, fr. Ar. al-qorān, orig. the reading, the book, fr. qaraa to read. Cf. Koran.] The Muslim Scriptures; the Koran (now the usual form). [Spelt also Alkoran.]

alcoranic.c: Alcoranic Al`co*ran"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Koran.

alcoranist.c: Alcoranist Al`co*ran"ist, n. One who adheres to the letter of the Koran, rejecting all traditions.

alcove.c: Alcove Al"cove (?; 277), n. [F. alcôve, Sp. or Pg. alcoba, from Ar. al-quobbah arch, vault, tent.] 1. (Arch.) A recessed portion of a room, or a small room opening into a larger one; especially, a recess to contain a bed; a lateral recess in a library.

alcyonacea.c: Alcyonacea ‖Al`cy*o*na"ce*a (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) A group of soft-bodied Alcyonaria, of which Alcyonium is the type. See Illust. under Alcyonaria.

alcyonaria.c: Alcyonaria ‖Al`cy*o*na"ri*a (acr/l`sĭ*ŏ*nā"rĭ*ȧ), prop. n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) One of the orders of Anthozoa. It includes the Alcyonacea, Pennatulacea, and Gorgonacea.

alcyones.c: Alcyones ‖Al*cy"o*nes (ăl*sĭ*ŏ*nēz), n. pl. [L., pl. of Alcyon.] (Zool.) The kingfishers.

alcyonic.c: Alcyonic Al`cy*on"ic (ăl`sĭ*ŏn"ĭk), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Alcyonaria.

alcyonium.c: Alcyonium ‖Al`cy*o"ni*um (?), n. [Gr.? a zoöphyte, so called from being like the halcyon's nest.] (Zool.) A genus of fleshy Alcyonaria, its polyps somewhat resembling flowers with eight fringed rays. The term was also formerly used for certain species of sponges.

alcyonoid.c: Alcyonoid Al"cy*o*noid (ăl"sĭ*o*noid), a. [Gr. 'alkyo`nion + -oid.] (Zool.) Like or pertaining to the Alcyonaria. -- n. A zoöphyte of the order Alcyonaria.

aldebaran.c: Aldebaran Al*deb"a*ran (ăl*dĕb"ȧ*răn), prop. n. [Ar. al-debarān, fr. dabar to follow; so called because this star follows upon the Pleiades.] (Astron.) A red star of the first magnitude, situated in the eye of Taurus; the Bull's Eye. It is the bright star in the group called the Hyades.

aldehyde.c: Aldehyde Al"de*hyde (ăl"de*hīd), n. [Abbrev. fr. alcohol dehydrogenatum, alcohol deprived of its hydrogen.] 1. (Chem.) A colorless, mobile, and very volatile liquid obtained from alcohol by certain processes of oxidation.

aldehydic.c: Aldehydic Al`de*hy"dic (?), a. (Chem.) Of or pertaining to aldehyde; as, aldehydic acid. Miller.

alder.c: Alder Al"der (äl"dẽr), n. [OE. aldir, aller, fr. AS. alr, aler, alor, akin to D. els, G. erle, Icel. erlir, erli, Swed. al, Dan. elle, el, L. alnus, and E. elm.] (Bot.) A tree, usually growing in moist land, and belonging to the genus Alnus. The wood is used by turners, etc.; the bark by dyers and tanners. In the U. S. the species of alder are usually shrubs or small trees.
Alder fly alderfly al"der*fly`, Al"der fly. 1. Any of numerous dark-colored neuropterous insects of the genus Sialis or allied genera. They have predaceous aquatic larvæ, which are used for bait.

aller.c: Aller Alder { Al"der (äl"dẽr), Al"ler (äl"lẽr), } a. [From ealra, alra, gen. pl. of AS. eal. The d is excrescent.] Of all; -- used in composition; as, alderbest, best of all, alderwisest, wisest of all. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Aller Al"ler (?), a. [For ealra, the AS. gen. pl. of eal all.] Same as Alder, of all. [Obs.] Chaucer.

alderliefest.c: Alder-liefest Al`der-lief"est (äl`dẽr*lēf"ĕst), a. [For allerliefest dearest of all. See Lief.] Most beloved. [Obs.] Shak.

alderman.c: Alderman Al"der*man (äl"dẽr*main), n.; pl. Aldermen (?). [AS. aldormon, ealdorman; ealdor an elder + man. See Elder, n.] 1. A senior or superior; a person of rank or dignity. [Obs.]

aldermancy.c: Aldermancy Al"der*man*cy (?), n. The office of an alderman.

aldermanic.c: Aldermanic Al"der*man"ic (?), a. Relating to, becoming to, or like, an alderman; characteristic of an alderman.

aldermanity.c: Aldermanity Al`der*man"i*ty (?), n. 1. Aldermen collectively; the body of aldermen.

aldermanlike.c: Aldermanlike Al`der*man*like` (?), a. Like or suited to an alderman.

aldermanly.c: Aldermanly Al"der*man*ly, a. Pertaining to, or like, an alderman.
Aldermanly Al"der*man*ly, a. Pertaining to, or like, an alderman. “An aldermanly discretion.” Swift.

aldermanry.c: Aldermanry Al"der*man*ry (?), n. 1. The district or ward of an alderman.

aldermanship.c: Aldermanship Al"der*man*ship, n. The condition, position, or office of an alderman. Fabyan.

alderney.c: Alderney Al"der*ney (?), n. One of a breed of cattle raised in Alderney, one of the Channel Islands. Alderneys are of a dun or tawny color and are often called Jersey cattle. See Jersey, 3.

aldine.c: Aldine Al"dine (?; 277), a. (Bibliog.) An epithet applied to editions (chiefly of the classics) which proceeded from the press of Aldus Manitius, and his family, of Venice, for the most part in the 16th century and known by the sign of the anchor and the dolphin. The term has also been applied to certain elegant editions of English works.

aldol.c: Aldol Al"dol (?), n. [Aldehyde + -ol as in alcohol.] (Chem.) A colorless liquid, C4H8O2, obtained by condensation of two molecules of acetaldehyde: CH3CHO + CH3CHO = H3CH(OH)CH2CO; also, any of various derivatives of this. The same reaction has been applied, under the name of aldol condensation, to the production of many compounds.

ale.c: Ale Ale (āl), n. [AS. ealu, akin to Icel., Sw., and Dan. öl, Lith. alus a kind of beer, OSlav. olŭ beer. Cf. Ir. ol drink, drinking.] 1. An intoxicating liquor made from an infusion of malt by fermentation and the addition of a bitter, usually hops.
Ale silver Ale" sil`ver (?). A duty payable to the lord mayor of London by the sellers of ale within the city.

aleak.c: Aleak A*leak" (?), adv. & a. [Pref. a- + leak.] In a leaking condition.

aleatory.c: Aleatory A"le*a*to*ry (?), a. [L. aleatorius, fr. alea chance, die.] (Law) Depending on some uncertain contingency; as, an aleatory contract. Bouvier.

alebench.c: Alebench Ale"bench` (?), n. A bench in or before an alehouse. Bunyan.

aleberry.c: Aleberry Ale"ber`ry (?), n. [OE. alebery, alebrey; ale + bre broth, fr. AS. brīw pottage.] A beverage, formerly made by boiling ale with spice, sugar, and sops of bread.

alecithal.c: Alecithal A*lec"i*thal (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. +? yelk.] (Biol.) Applied to those ova which segment uniformly, and which have little or no food yelk embedded in their protoplasm. Balfour.

aleconner.c: Aleconner Ale"con`ner (?), n. [/Ale + con, OE. cunnen to test, AS. cunnian to test. See Con.] Orig., an officer appointed to look to the goodness of ale and beer; also, one of the officers chosen by the liverymen of London to inspect the measures used in public houses. But the office is a sinecure. [Also called aletaster.] [Eng.]

alecost.c: Alecost Ale"cost` (?), n. [Ale + L. costus an aromatic plant: cf. Costmary.] (Bot.) The plant costmary, which was formerly much used for flavoring ale.

alectorides.c: Alectorides ‖Al`ec*tor"i*des (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? a cock.] (Zool.) A group of birds including the common fowl and the pheasants.

alectryomancy.c: Alectryomancy A*lec"try*o*man`cy (?), n. [Gr.? cock + -mancy.] Divination by means of a cock and grains of corn placed on the letters of the alphabet, the letters being put together in the order in which the grains were eaten. Amer. Cyc.

alee.c: Alee A*lee" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + lee.] (Naut.) On or toward the lee, or the side away from the wind; the opposite of aweather. The helm of a ship is alee when pressed close to the lee side.

alegar.c: Alegar Al"e*gar (?), n. [Ale + eager sour, F. aigre. Cf. Vinegar.] Sour ale; vinegar made of ale. Cecil.

aleger.c: Aleger Al"e*ger (?), a. [F. allègre, earlier alègre, fr. L. alacer.] Gay; cheerful; sprightly. [Obs.] Bacon.

alegge.c: Alegge A*legge" (?), v. t. [OE. aleggen, alegen, OF. alegier, F. alléger, fr. LL. alleviare, for L. allevare to lighten; ad + levis light. Cf. Alleviate, Allay, Allege.] To allay or alleviate; to lighten. [Obs.]

alehoof.c: Alehoof Ale"hoof` (āl"hōof`), n. [AS. hōfe ground ivy; the first part is perh. a corruption: cf. OE. heyhowe hedgehove, ground ivy, “in old MSS. heyhowe, heyoue, haihoue, halehoue.” Prior.] Ground ivy (Nepeta Glechoma).

alehouse.c: Alehouse Ale"house` (?), n. A house where ale is retailed; hence, a tippling house. Macaulay.

alem.c: Alem ‖Al"em (?), n. [Turk. 'alem, fr. Ar. 'alam.] (Mil.) The imperial standard of the Turkish Empire.

alemannic.c: Alemannic Al`e*man"nic (?), a. Belonging to the Alemanni, a confederacy of warlike German tribes.
Alemannic Al`e*man"nic, n. The language of the Alemanni.

alembic.c: Alembic A*lem"bic (ȧ*lĕm"bĭk), n. [F. alambic (cf. Sp. alambique), Ar. al-anbīq, fr. Gr. 'a`mbix cup, cap of a still. The cap or head was the alembic proper. Cf. Limbec.] An apparatus formerly used in distillation, usually made of glass or metal. It has mostly given place to the retort and worm still.

alembroth.c: Alembroth A*lem"broth (-brŏth), n. [Origin uncertain.] The salt of wisdom of the alchemists, a double salt composed of the chlorides of ammonium and mercury. It was formerly used as a stimulant. Brande & C.

alencon.c: Alencon lace A`len`çon" lace" (?). See under Lace.

alength.c: Alength A*length" (ȧ*lĕngth"), adv. [Pref. a- + length.] At full length; lengthwise. Chaucer.

alepidote.c: Alepidote A*lep"i*dote, a. [Gr. 'a priv. +?,?, a scale.] (Zool.) Not having scales. -- n. A fish without scales.

alepole.c: Alepole Ale"pole` (?), n. A pole set up as the sign of an alehouse. [Obs.]

aleppo.c: Aleppo evil Aleppo button Aleppo boil { A*lep"po boil, A*lep"po but"ton, or A*lep"po e"vil }. (Med.) Same as Aden ulcer.
Aleppo grass Aleppo grass. (Bot.) One of the cultivated forms of Andropogon Halepensis (syn. Sorghum Halepense). See Andropogon, below.

alert.c: Alert A*lert" (ȧ*lẽrt"), a. [F. alerte, earlier à l'erte on the watch, fr. It. all' erta on the watch, prop. (standing) on a height, where one can look around; erta a declivity, steep, erto steep, p. p. of ergere, erigere, to erect, raise, L. erigere. See Erect.] 1. Watchful; vigilant; active in vigilance.
Alert A*lert", n. (Mil.) An alarm from a real or threatened attack; a sudden attack; also, a bugle sound to give warning. “We have had an alert.” Farrow.

alertly.c: Alertly A*lert"ly, adv. In an alert manner; nimbly.

alertness.c: Alertness A*lert"ness, n. The quality of being alert or on the alert; briskness; nimbleness; activity.

alestake.c: Alestake Ale"stake (?), n. A stake or pole projecting from, or set up before, an alehouse, as a sign; an alepole. At the end was commonly suspended a garland, a bunch of leaves, or a “bush.” [Obs.] Chaucer.

alethiology.c: Alethiology A*le`thi*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? truth + -logy.] The science which treats of the nature of truth and evidence. Sir W. Hamilton.

alethoscope.c: Alethoscope A*leth"o*scope (?), n. [Gr.? true +? to view.] An instrument for viewing pictures by means of a lens, so as to present them in their natural proportions and relations.

aleuromancy.c: Aleuromancy A*leu"ro*man`cy (?), n. [Gr.? wheaten flour + -mancy: cf. F. aleuromancie.] Divination by means of flour. Encyc. Brit.

aleurometer.c: Aleurometer Al`eu*rom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? flour + -meter.] An instrument for determining the expansive properties, or quality, of gluten in flour. Knight.

aleuronat.c: Aleuronat A*leu"ro*nat (?), n. [See Aleurone.] Flour made of aleurone, used as a substitute for ordinary flour in preparing bread for diabetic persons.

aleurone.c: Aleurone A*leu"rone (?), n. [Gr.? flour.] (Bot.) An albuminoid substance which occurs in minute grains (“protein granules”) in maturing seeds and tubers; -- supposed to be a modification of protoplasm.

aleuronic.c: Aleuronic Al`eu*ron"ic (?), a. (Bot.) Having the nature of aleurone. D. C. Eaton.

aleutic.c: Aleutic Aleutian { A*leu"tian (?), A*leu"tic (?), } a. [Said to be from the Russ. aleut a bold rock.] Of or pertaining to a chain of islands between Alaska and Kamtchatka; also, designating these islands.

alevin.c: Alevin Al"e*vin (?), n. [F. alevin, OF. alever to rear, fr. L. ad + levare to raise.] Young fish; fry.

alewife.c: Alewife Ale"wife` (?), n.; pl. Alewives (?). A woman who keeps an alehouse. Gay.

Alewife Ale"wife`, n.; pl. Alewives. [This word is properly aloof, the Indian name of a fish. See Winthrop on the culture of maize in America, “Phil Trans.” No. 142, p. 1065, and Baddam's “Memoirs,” vol. ii. p. 131.] (Zool.) A North American fish (Clupea vernalis) of the Herring family. It is called also ellwife, ellwhop, branch herring. The name is locally applied to other related species.

alisanders.c: Alisanders Alexanders Al`ex*an"ders (?), Al`i*san"ders (?), n. [OE. alisaundre, OF. alissandere, fr. Alexander or Alexandria.] (Bot) A name given to two species of the genus Smyrnium, formerly cultivated and used as celery now is; -- called also horse parsely.

alexandrian.c: Alexandrian Al`ex*an"dri*an (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to Alexandria in Egypt; as, the Alexandrian library.

alexandrine.c: Alexandrine Al`ex*an"drine (?; 277), a. Belonging to Alexandria; Alexandrian. Bancroft.
Alexandrine Al`ex*an"drine (?), n. [F. alexandrin.] A kind of verse consisting in English of twelve syllables.

alexia.c: Alexia ‖A*lex"i*a (ȧ*lĕks"ĭ*ȧ), n. [NL.; a- not + Gr. le`xis speech, fr. le`gein to speak, confused with L. legere to read.] (Med.) (a) Inability to read aloud, due to brain disease; the meanings of the words is nevertheless understood. Called also motor alexia. (b) Inability, due to brain disease, to understand written or printed symbols. Called also Word blindness and text blindness.

alexipharmacal.c: Alexipharmacal Alexipharmac { A*lex`i*phar"mac (?), A*lex`i*phar"ma*cal (?), } a. & n. [See Alexipharmic.] Alexipharmic. [Obs.]

alexipharmic.c: Alexipharmic Alexipharmical { A*lex`i*phar"mic (ȧ*lĕks`ĭ*fär"mĭk), A*lex`i*phar"mic*al (ȧ*lĕks`ĭ*fär"mĭk*ail), } a. [Gr. 'alexifa`rmakos keeping off poison; 'alexein to keep off + fa`rmakon drug, poison: cf. F. alexipharmaque.] (Med.) Of or relating to an alexipharmic or alexipharmac; warding off poison; antidotal; prophylactic. [obsolescent]
Alexipharmic Alexipharmac A*lex`i*phar"mic (ȧ*lĕks`ĭ*fär"mĭk), n. (Med.) An antidote against poison; a counterpoison. [archaic]

alexipyretic.c: alexipyretic a*lex`i*py*ret"ic (ȧ*lĕks`ĭ*pi*rĕt"ĭk), a. [Gr. 'ale`xein to keep off + pyreto`s burning heat, fever, py^r fire.] (Med.) Serving to drive off fever; antipyretic; antifebrile. [archaic] -- n. An antipyretic drug; a febrifuge. [archaic]

alexiteric.c: alexiteric alexiterical { a*lex`i*ter"ic (ȧ*lĕks`ĭ*tĕr"ĭk), a*lex`i*ter"ic*al (ȧ*lĕks`ĭ*tĕr"ĭ*kail), } a. [Gr. 'alexhth`rios fit to keep off or help, fr. 'alexhth`r one who keeps off, helper; 'ale`xein to keep off: cf. F. alexitère.] (Med.) Resisting poison; obviating the effects of venom; alexipharmic.

alexiteric a*lex`i*ter"ic, n. [Gr. 'alexhth`rion a remedy, an amulet: cf. F. alexitère, LL. alexiterium.] (Med.) A preservative against contagious and infectious diseases, and the effects of poison in general. Brande & C.

alfa.c: Alfa grass Alfa ‖Al"fa (?) or Al"fa grass" (?), n. A plant (Macrochloa tenacissima) of North Africa; also, its fiber, used in paper making.

alfalfa.c: Alfalfa Al*fal"fa (?), n. [Sp.] (Bot.) The lucern (Medicago sativa), a leguminous plant having bluish purple cloverlike flowers, and cultivated for fodder; -- so called in California, Texas, etc.

alfenide.c: Alfenide Al"fe*nide (?), n. (Metal.) An alloy of nickel and silver electroplated with silver.

alferes.c: Alferes ‖Al*fe"res (?), n. [Sp., fr. Ar. al-fārs knight.] An ensign; a standard bearer. [Obs.] J. Fletcher.

alfet.c: Alfet Al"fet, n. [LL. alfetum, fr. AS. ālfæt a pot to boil in; āl burning + fæt vat.] A caldron of boiling water into which an accused person plunged his forearm as a test of innocence or guilt.

alfilaria.c: Alfilaria ‖Al*fil`a*ri"a (?), n. (Bot.) The pin grass (Erodium cicutarium), a weed in California.

alfilerilla.c: Alfilerilla Alfileria { ‖Al*fil`e*ri"a, ‖Al*fil`e*ril"la } (?), n. [Mex. Sp., fr. Sp. alfiler pin.] Same as Alfilaria.

alfione.c: Alfione ‖Al`fi*o"ne (?), n. (Zool.) An edible marine fish of California (Rhacochilus toxotes).

alforja.c: Alforja ‖Al*for"ja (?), n. [Also alfarga, alforge.] [Sp.] A saddlebag. [Sp. Amer.]

alfresco.c: Alfresco ‖Al*fres"co (?), adv. & a. [It. al fresco in or on the fresh.] In the open-air. Smollett.

alga.c: Alga ‖Al"ga (?), n.; pl. Algæ or algae (?). [L., seaweed.] (Bot.) A kind of seaweed; pl. the class of cellular cryptogamic plants which includes the black, red, and green seaweeds, as kelp, dulse, sea lettuce, also marine and fresh water confervæ, etc. The algae are primitive chlorophyll-containing mainly aquatic eukaryotic organisms lacking true stems and roots and leaves.

algal.c: Algal Al"gal (?), a., (Bot.) Pertaining to, or like, algæ.

algaroba.c: Algaroba ‖Al`ga*ro"ba (?), n. [Sp. algarroba, fr. Ar. al-kharr?bah. Cf. Carob.] (Bot.) (a) The Carob, a leguminous tree of the Mediterranean region; also, its edible beans or pods, called St. John's bread. (b) The Honey mesquite (Prosopis juliflora), a small tree found from California to Buenos Ayres; also, its sweet, pulpy pods. A valuable gum, resembling gum arabic, is collected from the tree in Texas and Mexico.

algarot.c: algarot algaroth { al"ga*rot (ăl"gȧ*rŏt), al"ga*roth (ăl"gȧ*rŏth), } n. [F. algaroth, fr. the name of the inventor, Algarotti.] (Med.) A term used for the Powder of Algaroth, a white powder which is a compound of trichloride and trioxide of antimony. It was formerly used in medicine as an emetic, purgative, and diaphoretic.

algarovilla.c: Algarovilla ‖Al`ga*ro*vil"la (?), n. The agglutinated seeds and husks of the legumes of a South American tree (Inga Marthae). It is valuable for tanning leather, and as a dye.

algates.c: Algates Algate { Al"gate (?), Al"gates (?), } adv. [All + gate way. The s is an adverbial ending. See Gate.] 1. Always; wholly; everywhere. [Obs.]

algazel.c: Algazel Al"ga*zel` (?), n. [Ar. al the + ghazāl.] (Zool.) The true gazelle.

algebra.c: Algebra Al"ge*bra (?), n. [LL. algebra, fr. Ar. al-jebr reduction of parts to a whole, or fractions to whole numbers, fr. jabara to bind together, consolidate; al-jebr w'almuqābalah reduction and comparison (by equations): cf. F. algèbre, It. & Sp. algebra.] 1. (Math.) That branch of mathematics which treats of the relations and properties of quantity by means of letters and other symbols. It is applicable to those relations that are true of every kind of magnitude.

algebraical.c: Algebraical Algebraic { Al`ge*bra"ic (?), Al`ge*bra"ic*al (?), } a. 1. Of or pertaining to algebra; using algebra; according to the laws of algebra; containing an operation of algebra, or deduced from such operation; as, algebraic characters; algebraical writings; algebraic geometry.

algebraist.c: Algebraist Al"ge*bra`ist (?), n. One versed in algebra.

algebraize.c: Algebraize Al"ge*bra*ize (?), v. t. To perform by algebra; to reduce to algebraic form.

algerian.c: Algerian Al*ge"ri*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Algeria. -- n. A native of Algeria.

algerine.c: Algerine Al`ge*rine" (?), a. Of or pertaining to Algiers or Algeria.
Algerine Al`ge*rine", n. A native or one of the people of Algiers or Algeria. Also, a pirate.

algid.c: Algid Al"gid (ăl"jĭd), a. [L. algidus cold, fr. algere to be cold: cf. F. algide.] 1. Cold; chilly. Bailey. AS

algidity.c: Algidity Al*gid"i*ty (ăl*jĭd"ĭ*ty̆), n. Chilliness; coldness; especially: (Med.), coldness and collapse. AS

algific.c: Algific Al*gif"ic (?), a. [L. algificus, fr. algus cold + facere to make.] Producing cold.

algin.c: Algin Al"gin (?), n. (Chem.) A nitrogenous substance resembling gelatin, obtained from certain algæ.

algoid.c: Algoid Al"goid (?), a. [L. alga + -oid.] Of the nature of, or resembling, an alga.

algol.c: Algol Al"gol (?), n. [Ar. al-ghūl destruction, calamity, fr. ghāla to take suddenly, destroy.] (Astron.) A fixed star, in Medusa's head, in the constellation Perseus, remarkable for its periodic variation in brightness.

algological.c: Algological Al`go*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to algology; as, algological specimens.

algologist.c: Algologist Al*gol"o*gist (?), n. One learned about algæ; a student of algology.

algology.c: Algology Al*gol"o*gy (?), n. [L. alga seaweed + -logy.] (Bot.) The study or science of algæ or seaweeds.

algometer.c: Algometer Al*gom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? pain + -meter.] (Psychol.) An instrument for measuring sensations of pain due to pressure. It has a piston rod with a blunted tip which is pressed against the skin. -- Al*gom"e*try (#), n. -- Al`go*met"ric (#), *met"ric*al (#), a. -- Al`go*met"ric*al*ly, adv.

algonquian.c: Algonquian Al*gon"qui*an (?), a. Pertaining to or designating the most extensive of the linguistic families of North American Indians, their territory formerly including practically all of Canada east of the 115th meridian and south of Hudson's Bay and the part of the United States east of the Mississippi and north of Tennessee and Virginia, with the exception of the territory occupied by the northern Iroquoian tribes. There are nearly 100,000 Indians of the Algonquian tribes, of which the strongest are the Ojibwas (Chippewas), Ottawas, Crees, Algonquins, Micmacs, and Blackfeet. -- n. An Algonquian Indian.

algonkin.c: Algonkin Algonquin { Al*gon"quin (?), Al*gon"kin (?), } prop. n. One of a widely spread family of Indians, including many distinct tribes, which formerly occupied most of the northern and eastern part of North America. The name was originally applied to a group of Indian tribes north of the River St. Lawrence.

algorithm.c: Algorithm Algorism { Al"go*rism (?), Al"go*rithm (?), } n. [OE. algorism, algrim, augrim, OF. algorisme, F. algorithme (cf. Sp. algoritmo, OSp. alguarismo, LL. algorismus), fr. the Ar. al-Khowārezmī of Khowārezm, the modern Khiwa, surname of Abu Ja'far Mohammed ben Musā, author of a work on arithmetic early in the 9th century, which was translated into Latin, such books bearing the name algorismus. The spelling with th is due to a supposed connection with Gr.? number.] 1. The art of calculating by nine figures and zero; computation with Arabic figures.

algorithmic.c: algorithmic algorithmic adj. 1. of or pertaining to an algorithm. recursive

algous.c: Algous Al"gous (?), a. [L. algosus, fr. alga seaweed.] Of or pertaining to the algæ, or seaweeds; abounding with, or like, seaweed.

alguazil.c: Alguazil ‖Al`gua*zil" (?) (?), n. [Sp. alguacil, fr. Ar. alwazīr the vizier. Cf. Vizier.] An inferior officer of justice in Spain; a warrant officer; a constable. Prescott.

algum.c: Algum Al"gum (?), n. Same as Almug (and etymologically preferable). 2 Chron. ii. 8.
Algum Almug { Al"mug (?), Al"gum (?), } n. [Heb., perh. borrowed fr. Skr. valguka sandalwood.] (Script.) A tree or wood of the Bible (2 Chron. ii. 8; 1 K. x. 11).

alhambra.c: Alhambra Al*ham"bra (?), n. [Ultimately fr. Ar. al the + hamrā red; i. e., the red (sc. house).] The palace of the Moorish kings at Granada.

alhambresque.c: Alhambresque Alhambraic { Al`ham*bra"ic (?), Al`ham*bresque" (?; 277), } a. Made or decorated after the fanciful style of the ornamentation in the Alhambra, which affords an unusually fine exhibition of Saracenic or Arabesque architecture.

alias.c: Alias A"li*as (?), adv. [L., fr. alius. See Else.] (Law) (a) Otherwise; otherwise called; -- a term used in legal proceedings to connect the different names of any one who has gone by two or more, and whose true name is for any cause doubtful; as, Smith, alias Simpson. (b) At another time.

Alias A"li*as, n.; pl. Aliases (?). [L., otherwise, at another time.] (Law) (a) A second or further writ which is issued after a first writ has expired without effect. (b) Another name; an assumed name.

alibi.c: Alibi Al"i*bi (?), n. [L., elsewhere, at another place. See Alias.] (Law) The plea or mode of defense under which a person on trial for a crime proves or attempts to prove that he was in another place when the alleged act was committed; as, to set up an alibi; to prove an alibi.

alibility.c: Alibility Al`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. Quality of being alible.

alible.c: Alible Al"i*ble (?), a. [L. alibilis, fr. alere to nourish.] Nutritive; nourishing.

alicant.c: Alicant Al"i*cant (?), n. A kind of wine, formerly much esteemed; -- said to have been made near Alicant, in Spain. J. Fletcher.

alidade.c: Alidade Al"i*dade (?), n. [LL. alidada, alhidada, fr. Ar. al-'idāda a sort of rule: cf. F. alidade.] The portion of a graduated instrument, as a quadrant or astrolabe, carrying the sights or telescope, and showing the degrees cut off on the arc of the instrument Whewell.

alien.c: Alien Al"ien (?), a. [OF. alien, L. alienus, fr. alius another; properly, therefore, belonging to another. See Else.] 1. Not belonging to the same country, land, or government, or to the citizens or subjects thereof; foreign; as, alien subjects, enemies, property, shores.

Alien Al"ien, n. 1. A foreigner; one owing allegiance, or belonging, to another country; a foreign-born resident of a country in which he does not possess the privileges of a citizen. Hence, a stranger. See Alienage.
Alien Al"ien, v. t. [F. aliéner, L. alienare.] To alienate; to estrange; to transfer, as property or ownership. [R.] “It the son alien lands.” Sir M. Hale.

alienability.c: Alienability Al`ien*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. Capability of being alienated. “The alienability of the domain.” Burke.

alienable.c: Alienable Al"ien*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. aliénable.] Capable of being alienated, sold, or transferred to another; as, land is alienable according to the laws of the state.

alienage.c: Alienage Al"ien*age (?), n. [Cf. OF. aliénage.] 1. The state or legal condition of being an alien.

alienate.c: Alienate Al"ien*ate (āl"yein*at), a. [L. alienatus, p. p. of alienare, fr. alienus. See Alien, and cf. Aliene.] Estranged; withdrawn in affection; foreign; -- with from.
Alienate Al"ien*ate (-āt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Alienated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Alienating.] 1. To convey or transfer to another, as title, property, or right; to part voluntarily with ownership of.
Alienate Al"ien*ate (?), n. A stranger; an alien. [Obs.]

alienation.c: Alienation Al`ien*a"tion (?), n. [F. aliénation, L. alienatio, fr. alienare, fr. alienare. See Alienate.] 1. The act of alienating, or the state of being alienated.

aliene.c: Aliene Al*iene (?), v. t. To alien or alienate; to transfer, as title or property; as, to aliene an estate.

alienee.c: Alienee Al"ien*ee" (?), n. (Law) One to whom the title of property is transferred; -- opposed to alienor.

alienism.c: Alienism Al"ien*ism (?), n. 1. The status or legal condition of an alien; alienage.

alienist.c: Alienist Al"ien*ist (?), n. [F. aliéniste.] One who treats diseases of the mind. Ed. Rev.

alienor.c: Alienor Al`ien*or" (?), n. [OF. aliéneur.] One who alienates or transfers property to another. Blackstone.

aliethmoidal.c: Aliethmoidal Aliethmoid { Al`i*eth"moid (?), Al`i*eth*moid"al (?), } a. [L. ala wing + E. ethomoid.] (Anat.) Pertaining to expansions of the ethmoid bone or cartilage.

alife.c: Alife A*life" (?), adv. [Cf. lief dear.] On my life; dearly. [Obs.] “I love that sport alife.” Beau. & Fl.

aliferous.c: Aliferous A*lif"er*ous (?), a. [L. ala wing + -ferous.] Having wings, winged; aligerous. [R.]

aliform.c: Aliform Al"i*form (?), a. [L. ala wing + -form.] Wing-shaped; winglike.

aligerous.c: Aligerous A*lig"er*ous (?), a. [L. aliger; ala wing + gerere to carry.] Having wings; winged. [R.]

alight.c: Alight A*light" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Alighted (?) sometimes Alit (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Alighting.] [OE. alihten, fr. AS. ālīhtan; pref. ā- (cf. Goth. us-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + līhtan, to alight, orig. to render light, to remove a burden from, fr. līht, leoht, light. See Light, v. i.] 1. To spring down, get down, or descend, as from on horseback or from a carriage; to dismount.
Alight A*light", a. [Pref. a- + light.] Lighted; lighted up; in a flame. “The lamps were alight.” Dickens.

align.c: Align A*lign" (?), v. t. [F. aligner; à (L. ad) + ligne (L. linea) line. See Line, and cf. Allineate.] To adjust or form to a line; to range or form in line; to bring into line; to aline.
Align A*lign", v. t. To form in line; to fall into line.

alignment.c: Alignment A*lign"ment (?), n. [F. alignement.] 1. The act of adjusting to a line; arrangement in a line or lines; the state of being so adjusted; a formation in a straight line; also, the line of adjustment; esp., an imaginary line to regulate the formation of troops or of a squadron.

alike.c: Alike A*like" (ȧ*līk), a. [AS. onlīc, gelīc; pref. ā + like.] Having resemblance or similitude; similar; without difference. [Now used only predicatively.]
Alike A*like", adv. [AS. gelīce, onlīce.] In the same manner, form, or degree; in common; equally; as, we are all alike concerned in religion.

aliment.c: Aliment Al"i*ment (?), n. [L. alimentum, fr. alere to nourish; akin to Goth. alan to grow, Icel. ala to nourish: cf. F. aliment. See Old.] 1. That which nourishes; food; nutriment; anything which feeds or adds to a substance in natural growth. Hence: The necessaries of life generally: sustenance; means of support.
Aliment Al"i*ment, v. t. 1. To nourish; to support.

alimental.c: Alimental Al`i*men"tal (?), a. Supplying food; having the quality of nourishing; furnishing the materials for natural growth; as, alimental sap.

alimentally.c: Alimentally A`li*men"tal*ly, adv. So as to serve for nourishment or food; nourishing quality. Sir T. Browne.

alimentariness.c: Alimentariness Al`i*men"ta*ri*ness (?), n. The quality of being alimentary; nourishing quality. [R.]

alimentary.c: Alimentary Al`i*men"ta*ry (?), a. [L. alimentarius, fr. alimentum: cf. F. alimentaire.] Pertaining to aliment or food, or to the function of nutrition; nutritious; alimental; as, alimentary substances.

alimentation.c: Alimentation Al`i*men*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. alimentation, LL. alimentatio.] 1. The act or process of affording nutriment; the function of the alimentary canal.

alimentiveness.c: Alimentiveness Al`i*men"tive*ness (?), n. The instinct or faculty of appetite for food. [Chiefly in Phrenol.]

alimonious.c: Alimonious Al`i*mo"ni*ous (?), a. Affording food; nourishing. [R.] “Alimonious humors.” Harvey.

alimony.c: Alimony Al"i*mo*ny (?), n. [L. alimonia, alimonium, nourishment, sustenance, fr. alere to nourish.] 1. Maintenance; means of living.

alinasal.c: Alinasal Al`i*na"sal (?), a. [L. ala wing + E. nasal.] (Anat.) Pertaining to expansions of the nasal bone or cartilage.

aline.c: Aline A*line" (?), v. t. To range or place in a line; to bring into line; to align. Evelyn.

alineation.c: Alineation Allineation { Al*lin`e*a"tion (?), A*lin`e*a"tion (?), } n. Alignment; position in a straight line, as of two planets with the sun. Whewell.

aliner.c: Aliner A*lin"er (?), n. One who adjusts things to a line or lines or brings them into line. Evelyn.

alioth.c: Alioth Al"i*oth (?), n. [Ar. alyāt the tail of a fat sheep.] (Astron.) A star in the tail of the Great Bear, the one next the bowl in the Dipper.

aliped.c: Aliped Al"i*ped (?), a. [L. alipes; ala wing + pes, pedis, foot: cf. F. alipède.] (Zool.) Wing-footed, as the bat. -- n. An animal whose toes are connected by a membrane, serving for a wing, as the bat.

aliphatic.c: Aliphatic Al`i*phat"ic (?), a. [Gr.?,?, oil, fat.] (Org. Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or derived from, fat; fatty; -- applied to compounds having an open-chain structure. The aliphatic compounds thus include not only the fatty acids and other derivatives of the paraffin hydrocarbons, but also unsaturated compounds, as the ethylene and acetylene series. Compare alicyclic and aromatic.

aliquant.c: Aliquant Al"i*quant (?), a. [L. aliquantus some, moderate; alius other + quantus how great: cf. F. aliquante.] (Math.) An aliquant part of a number or quantity is one which does not divide it without leaving a remainder; thus, 5 is an aliquant part of 16. Opposed to aliquot.
