anaerobiotic.c: Anaerobiotic An*a`ër*o*bi*ot"ic (?), a. (Anat.) Related to, or of the nature of, anaërobies.

anaesthesia.c: anaesthesia anesthesia ‖an`æs*the"si*a, an`es*the"si*a (ăn`ĕs*thē"ze*ȧ or ăn`ĕs*thē"zhȧ), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'anaisqhsi`a; 'an priv. + a'i`sqhsis feeling, a'isqa`nesqai to feel: cf. F. anesthésie. See aesthetics.] (Med.) Entire or partial loss or absence of feeling or sensation; a state of general or local insensibility produced by disease or by the inhalation or application of an anaesthetic. AS

anaesthetic.c: Anaesthetic Anesthetic ‖An`æs*thet"ic, An`es*thet"ic (ăn`ĕs*thĕt"ĭk), a. (Med.) (a) Capable of causing anesthesia; as, anæsthetic agents. (b) Characterized by, or connected with, anesthesia; as, an anæsthetic effect or operation.
anaesthetic anesthetic ‖an`æs*thet"ic, an`es*thet"ic AS, n. (Med.) A substance which produces anesthesia, as chloroform, ether, etc.

anaesthetization.c: Anaesthetization An*æs`the*ti*za"tion (?), n. The process of anæsthetizing; also, the condition of the nervous system induced by anæsthetics.

anaesthetize.c: anaesthetize anesthetize ‖a*næs"the*tize, a*nes"the*tize, (ăn*ĕs"the*tīz), v. t. (Med.) To produce anesthesia by an anæsthetic. Encyc. Brit.

anaglyph.c: Anaglyph An"a*glyph (?), n. [Gr.? wrought in low relief,? embossed work;? +? to engrave.] Any sculptured, chased, or embossed ornament worked in low relief, as a cameo.

anaglyphical.c: Anaglyphical Anaglyphic { An`a*glyph"ic (?), An`a*glyph"ic*al (?), } a. Pertaining to the art of chasing or embossing in relief; anaglyptic; -- opposed to diaglyptic or sunk work.

anaglyphic.c: Anaglyphic An`a*glyph"ic, n. Work chased or embossed relief.

anaglyptic.c: Anaglyptic An`a*glyp"tic (?), a. [L. anaglypticus, Gr.?,?. See Anaglyph.] Relating to the art of carving, enchasing, or embossing in low relief.

anaglyptics.c: Anaglyptics An`a*glyp"tics (?), n. The art of carving in low relief, embossing, etc.

anaglyptograph.c: Anaglyptograph An`a*glyp"to*graph (?), n. [Gr.? + -graph.] An instrument by which a correct engraving of any embossed object, such as a medal or cameo, can be executed. Brande & C.

anaglyptographic.c: Anaglyptographic An`a*glyp`to*graph"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to anaglyptography; as, anaglyptographic engraving.

anaglyptography.c: Anaglyptography An`a*glyp*tog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr.? embossed + -graphy.] The art of copying works in relief, or of engraving as to give the subject an embossed or raised appearance; -- used in representing coins, bas-reliefs, etc.

anagnorisis.c: Anagnorisis ‖An`ag*nor"i*sis (?), n. [Latinized fr. Gr.?;? +? to recognize.] The unfolding or dénouement. [R.] De Quincey.

anagoge.c: Anagoge An`a*go"ge (?), n. [Gr.? a leading up;? +? a leading,? to lead.] 1. An elevation of mind to things celestial.

anagogical.c: Anagogical Anagogic { An`a*gog"ic (?), An`a*gog"ic*al (?), } a. Mystical; having a secondary spiritual meaning; as, the rest of the Sabbath, in an anagogical sense, signifies the repose of the saints in heaven; an anagogical explication. -- An`a*gog"ic*al*ly, adv.

anagogics.c: Anagogics An`a*gog"ics (?), n. pl. Mystical interpretations or studies, esp. of the Scriptures. L. Addison.

anagram.c: Anagram An"a*gram (ăn"ȧ*grăm), n. [F. anagramme, LL. anagramma, fr. Gr. 'ana` back, again + gra`fein to write. See Graphic.] Literally, the letters of a word read backwards, but in its usual wider sense, the change of one word or phrase into another by the transposition of its letters. Thus Galenus becomes angelus; William Noy (attorney-general to Charles I., and a laborious man) may be turned into I moyl in law.

anagrammatical.c: Anagrammatical Anagrammatic { An`a*gram*mat"ic (?), An`a*gram*mat"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. anagrammatique.] Pertaining to, containing, or making, an anagram. -- An`a*gram*mat"ic*al*ly, adv.

anagrammatism.c: Anagrammatism An`a*gram"ma*tism (?), n. [Gr. 'anagrammatismo`s: cf. F. anagrammatisme.] The act or practice of making anagrams. Camden.

anagrammatist.c: Anagrammatist An`a*gram"ma*tist, n. [Cf. F. anagrammatiste.] A maker of anagrams.

anagrammatize.c: Anagrammatize An`a*gram"ma*tize (?), v. t. [Gr. 'anagrammati`zein cf. F. anagrammatiser.] To transpose, as the letters of a word, so as to form an anagram. Cudworth.

anagraph.c: Anagraph An"a*graph (ăn"ȧ*grȧf), n. [Gr. 'anagrafh` a writing out, fr. 'anagra`fein to write out, to record; 'ana` + gra`fein to write.] An inventory; a record. [Obs.] Knowles.

anaks.c: Anaks Anakim { ‖An"a*kim (?), A"naks (?), } n. pl. [Heb.] (Bibl.) A race of giants living in Palestine.

anal.c: Anal A"nal (?), a. [From Anus.] (Anat.) Pertaining to, or situated near, the anus; as, the anal fin or glands.

analcime.c: Analcime A*nal"cime (?), n. [Gr. 'an priv. + 'a`lkimos strong, 'alkh` strength: cf. F. analcime.] (Min.) A white or flesh-red mineral, of the zeolite family, occurring in isometric crystals. By friction, it acquires a weak electricity; hence its name.

analectic.c: Analectic An`a*lec"tic (ăn`ȧ*lĕk"tĭk), a. Relating to analects; made up of selections; as, an analectic magazine.

analecta.c: Analecta Analects { An"a*lects (ăn"ȧ*lĕkts), ‖An`a*lec"ta (ăn`ȧ*lĕk"tȧ), } n. pl. [Gr. 'ana`lekta fr. 'anale`gein to collect; 'ana` + le`gein to gather.] A collection of literary fragments.

analemma.c: Analemma ‖An`a*lem"ma (-lĕm"mȧ), n. [L. analemma a sun dial on a pedestal, showing the latitude and meridian of a place, Gr. 'ana`lhmma a support, or thing supported, a sun dial, fr. 'analamba`nein to take up; 'ana` + lamba`nein to take.] 1. (Chem.) An orthographic projection of the sphere on the plane of the meridian, the eye being supposed at an infinite distance, and in the east or west point of the horizon.

analepsy.c: analepsy analepsis { ‖an`a*lep"sis (ăn`ȧ*lĕp"sĭs), an"a*lep`sy (ăn"ȧ*lĕp`sy̆), } [Gr. 'ana`lhpsis a taking up, or again, recovery, from 'analamba`nein. See Analemma.] (Med.) (a) Recovery of strength after sickness. (b) A species of epileptic attack, originating from gastric disorder. [Obs.]

analeptic.c: analeptic an`a*lep"tic (ăn`ȧ*lĕp"tĭk), a. [Gr. 'ana`lhptiko`s restorative: cf. F. analeptique. See Analepsis.] (Med.) Restorative; giving strength after disease. -- n. A restorative drug; a drug that stimulates the central nervous system.

analgene.c: analgene analgen { an*al"gen (ăn*ăl"jĕn), an*al"gene (ăn*ăl"jēn) }, n.} [Gr. 'analgh`s painless.] A crystalline compound used as an antipyretic and analgesic, employed chiefly in rheumatism and neuralgia. It is a complex derivative of quinoline.

analgesia.c: analgesia ‖an`al*ge"si*a (ăn`ăl*jē"ze*ȧ), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'analghsi`a; 'an priv. + a`lghsis sense of pain.] (Med.) Absence of sensibility to pain. Quain. AS

anallagmatic.c: Anallagmatic An`al*lag*mat"ic (?), a. [Gr.?; 'an priv. +? a change.] (Math.) Not changed in form by inversion.

anallantoic.c: Anallantoic An`al*lan*to"ic (?), a. (Anat.) Without, or not developing, an allantois.

anallantoidea.c: Anallantoidea ‖An`al*lan*toid"e*a (?), n. pl. [Gr. 'an priv. + E. allantoidea.] (Zool.) The division of Vertebrata in which no allantois is developed. It includes amphibians, fishes, and lower forms.

analogic.c: Analogic An`a*log"ic (?), a. [See Analogous.] Of or belonging to analogy. Geo. Eliot.

analogical.c: Analogical An`a*log"ic*al (?), a. 1. Founded on, or of the nature of, analogy; expressing or implying analogy.

analogically.c: Analogically An`a*log"ic*al*ly, adv. In an analogical sense; in accordance with analogy; by way of similitude.

analogicalness.c: Analogicalness An`a*log"ic*al*ness, n. Quality of being analogical.

analogism.c: Analogism A*nal"o*gism (?), n. [Gr.? course of reasoning, fr.? to think over, to calculate] 1. (Logic) an argument from the cause to the effect; an a priori argument. Johnson.

analogist.c: Analogist A*nal"o*gist (?), n. One who reasons from analogy, or represent, by analogy. Cheyne.

analogize.c: Analogize A*nal"o*gize, v. i. To employ, or reason by, analogy.

analogous.c: Analogous A*nal"o*gous (?), a. [L. analogous, Gr.? according to a due ratio, proportionate;? +? ratio, proportion. See Logic.] Having analogy; corresponding to something else; bearing some resemblance or proportion; -- often followed by to.

analogue.c: Analogue An"a*logue (?; 115), n. [F.?, fr. Gr.?.] 1. That which is analogous to, or corresponds with, some other thing.

analogy.c: Analogy A*nal"o*gy (?), n.; pl. Analogies (?). [L. analogia, Gr.?, fr.?: cf. F. analogie. See Analogous.] 1. A resemblance of relations; an agreement or likeness between things in some circumstances or effects, when the things are otherwise entirely different. Thus, learning enlightens the mind, because it is to the mind what light is to the eye, enabling it to discover things before hidden.

analyser.c: Analyser Analyse An"a*lyse (?), v., An"a*ly`ser (?), n., etc. Same as Analyze, Analyzer, etc.

analysis.c: Analysis A*nal"y*sis (?), n.; pl. Analyses (?). [Gr.?, fr.? to unloose, to dissolve, to resolve into its elements;? up +? to loose. See Loose.] 1. A resolution of anything, whether an object of the senses or of the intellect, into its constituent or original elements; an examination of the component parts of a subject, each separately, as the words which compose a sentence, the tones of a tune, or the simple propositions which enter into an argument. It is opposed to synthesis.

analyst.c: Analyst An"a*lyst (?), n. [F. analyste. See Analysis.] One who analyzes; formerly, one skilled in algebraical geometry; now commonly, one skilled in chemical analysis.

analytical.c: Analytical Analytic { An`a*lyt"ic (?), An`a*lyt"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?: cf. F. analytique. See Analysis.] Of or pertaining to analysis; resolving into elements or constituent parts; as, an analytical experiment; -- opposed to synthetic.

analytically.c: Analytically An`a*lyt"ic*al*ly, adv. In an analytical manner.

analytics.c: Analytics An`a*lyt"ics (?), n. The science of analysis.

analyzable.c: Analyzable An"a*ly`za*ble (?), a. That may be analyzed.

analyzation.c: Analyzation An`a*ly*za"tion (?), n. The act of analyzing, or separating into constituent parts; analysis.

analyze.c: Analyze An"a*lyze (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Analyzed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Analyzing.] [Cf. F. analyser. See Analysis.] 1. To subject to analysis; to resolve (anything complex) into its elements; to separate into the constituent parts, for the purpose of an examination of each separately; to examine in such a manner as to ascertain the elements or nature of the thing examined; to consider in detail in order to discover essential features or meaning; as, to analyze an action to ascertain its morality; to analyse a sonnet by Shakespeare; to analyse the evidence in a criminal trial; to analyse your real motives.

analyzer.c: Analyzer An"a*ly`zer (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, analyzes.

anamese.c: Anamese An`a*mese" (?), a. Of or pertaining to Anam, to southeastern Asia. -- n. A native of Anam.

anamnesis.c: Anamnesis ‖An`am*ne"sis (?), n. [Gr. 'ana`mnhsis, fr.? to remind, recall to memory;? +? to put in mind.] (Rhet.) A recalling to mind; recollection.

anamnestic.c: Anamnestic An`am*nes"tic (?), a. [Gr.?.] Aiding the memory; as, anamnestic remedies.

anamniotic.c: Anamniotic An*am`ni*ot"ic (?), a. (Anat.) Without, or not developing, an amnion.

anamorphism.c: Anamorphism An`a*mor"phism (?), n. [Gr.? again + morfh` form.] 1. A distorted image.

anamorphoscope.c: Anamorphoscope An`a*mor"pho*scope (?), n. [Anamorphosis + -scope.] An instrument for restoring a picture or image distorted by anamorphosis to its normal proportions. It usually consists of a cylindrical mirror.

anamorphosis.c: Anamorphosis An`a*mor"pho*sis (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.? to form anew;? again +? to form; morfh` form.] 1. (Persp.) A distorted or monstrous projection or representation of an image on a plane or curved surface, which, when viewed from a certain point, or as reflected from a curved mirror or through a polyhedron, appears regular and in proportion; a deformation of an image.

anan.c: Anan A*nan" (?), interj. [See Anon.] An expression equivalent to What did you say? Sir? Eh? [Obs.] Shak.

ananas.c: Ananas ‖A*na"nas (?), n. [Sp. ananas, from the native American name.] (Bot.) The pineapple (Ananassa sativa).

anandrous.c: Anandrous An*an"drous (?), a. [Gr. 'an priv. + 'andh`r a man.] (Bot.) Destitute of stamens, as certain female flowers.

anangular.c: Anangular An*an"gu*lar (?), a. [Gr. 'an priv. + E. angular.] Containing no angle. [R.]

anantherous.c: Anantherous An*an"ther*ous (?), a. [Gr. 'an priv. + E. anther.] (Bot.) Destitute of anthers. Gray.

ananthous.c: Ananthous An*an"thous (?), a. [Gr. 'an priv. + 'a`nqos a flower.] (Bot.) Destitute of flowers; flowerless.

anapaestic.c: Anapaestic Anapaest An`a*pæst (?), An`a*pæs"tic (?). Same as Anapest, Anapestic.

anapest.c: Anapest An"a*pest (?), n. [L. anapaestus, Gr.? an anapest, i.e., a dactyl reserved, or, as it were, struck back; fr.?; 'ana` back +? to strike.] 1. (Pros.) A metrical foot consisting of three syllables, the first two short, or unaccented, the last long, or accented (˘ ˘ -); the reverse of the dactyl. In Latin dĕ-ĭ-tās, and in English in-ter-vene˝, are examples of anapests.

anapestic.c: Anapestic An`a*pes"tic (?), a. [L. anapaesticus, Gr. 'anapaistiko`s.] Pertaining to an anapest; consisting of an anapests; as, an anapestic meter, foot, verse. -- n. Anapestic measure or verse.

anaphora.c: anaphora ‖a*naph"o*ra (ȧ*năf"o*rȧ), n. [L., fr. Gr. 'anafora`, fr. 'anafe`rein to carry up or back; 'ana` + fe`rein to carry.] (Rhet.) 1. A repetition of a word or of words at the beginning of two or more successive clauses.

anaphrodisia.c: anaphrodisia ‖an*aph`ro*dis"i*a (ăn*ăf`ro*dĭz"ĭ*ȧ), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'an priv. + 'afrodi`sia sexual pleasure, 'Afrodi`th the goddess of love.] (Med.) Absence of sexual appetite. AS

anaphrodisiac.c: anaphrodisiac an*aph`ro*dis"i*ac (ăn*ăf`ro*dĭz"ĭ*ăk), a. & n. [Gr. 'an priv. + 'afrodisiako`s pertaining to venery.] (Med.) Same as Antaphrodisiac. Dunglison. AS

anaphrodisiac antaphrodisiac ‖ant`aph*ro*dis"i*ac (ănt`ăf*ro*dĭz"ĭ*ăk), an`aph*ro*dis"i*ac (ăn`ăf*ro*dĭz"ĭ*ăk), a. [Pref. anti- + aphrodisiac.] (Med.) Capable of blunting the sexual appetite. -- n. Anything that reduces the sexual appetite.

anaphroditic.c: Anaphroditic An*aph`ro*dit"ic (?), a. [Gr. 'anafro`dito`s without love.] (Biol.) Produced without concourse of sexes.

anaplastic.c: Anaplastic An`a*plas"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to anaplasty.

anaplasty.c: Anaplasty An`a*plas`ty (?), n. [Gr.? again +? to form: cf. F. anaplastie.] (Surg.) The art of operation of restoring lost parts or the normal shape by the use of healthy tissue.

anapnograph.c: Anapnograph A*nap"no*graph (?), n. [Gr. 'anapnoh` respiration + -graph.] A form of spirometer.

anapnoic.c: anapnoic an`ap*no"ic (ăn`ăp*nō"ĭk), a. [Gr. 'anapnoh` respiration.] (Med.) Relating to respiration. [archaic]

anapodeictic.c: Anapodeictic An*ap`o*deic"tic (?), a. [Gr. 'anapo`deiktos; 'an priv. + 'apodeikto`s. See Apodeictic.] Not apodeictic; undemonstrable. [R.]

anapophysis.c: Anapophysis ‖An`a*poph"y*sis (?), n. [Gr. 'ana` back +? offshoot.] (Anat.) An accessory process in many lumbar vertebræ.

anaptotic.c: Anaptotic An`ap*tot"ic (?), a. [Gr. 'ana` back + ptwtiko`s belonging to case.] Having lost, or tending to lose, inflections by phonetic decay; as, anaptotic languages.

anaptychus.c: Anaptychus ‖An*ap"ty*chus (?), n.; pl. Anaptichi (?). [NL., fr. Gr.? unfolding; 'ana` back +? to fold.] (Paleon.) One of a pair of shelly plates found in some cephalopods, as the ammonites.

anarch.c: Anarch An"arch (?), n. [Gr.? without head or chief; 'an priv. +? beginning, the first place, magistracy, government.] The author of anarchy; one who excites revolt. Milton.

anarchical.c: Anarchical Anarchic { A*nar"chic (?), A*nar"chic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. anarchique.] Pertaining to anarchy; without rule or government; in political confusion; tending to produce anarchy; as, anarchic despotism; anarchical opinions.

anarchism.c: Anarchism An"arch*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. anarchisme.] The doctrine or practice of anarchists.

anarchist.c: Anarchist An"arch*ist (?), n. [Cf. F. anarchiste.] An anarch; one who advocates anarchy of aims at the overthrow of civil government.

anarchize.c: Anarchize An"arch*ize (?), v. t. To reduce to anarchy.

anarchy.c: Anarchy An"arch*y (?), n. [Gr.?: cf. F. anarchie. See Anarch.] 1. Absence of government; the state of society where there is no law or supreme power; a state of lawlessness; political confusion.

anarthropoda.c: Anarthropoda ‖An`ar*throp"o*da (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? without joints + -poda. See Anarthrous.] (Zool.) One of the divisions of Articulata in which there are no jointed legs, as the annelids; -- opposed to Arthropoda.

anarthropodous.c: Anarthropodous An`ar*throp"o*dous (?), a. (Zool.) Having no jointed legs; pertaining to Anarthropoda.

anarthrous.c: Anarthrous An*ar"throus (?), a. [Gr. 'a`narqros without joints, without the article; 'an priv. + 'a`rqron joint, the article.] 1. (Gr. Gram.) Used without the article; as, an anarthrous substantive.

anas.c: Anas ‖A"nas (?), n. [L., duck.] (Zool.) A genus of water fowls, of the order Anseres, including certain species of fresh-water ducks.

anasarca.c: anasarca ‖an`a*sar"ca (ăn`ȧ*sär"kȧ), n. [NL., from Gr. 'ana` throughout + sa`rx, sarko`s, flesh.] (Med.) Severe generalized edema.

anasarcous.c: Anasarcous An`a*sar"cous (?), a. Belonging, or affected by, anasarca, or dropsy; dropsical. Wiseman.

anaseismic.c: Anaseismic An`a*seis"mic (?), a. [Cf. Gr.? a shaking up and down.] Moving up and down; -- said of earthquake shocks.

anastaltic.c: anastaltic an`a*stal"tic (ăn`ȧ*stăl"tĭk), a. & n. [Gr. 'anastaltiko`s fitted for checking, fr. 'ana` + ste`llein to send.] (Med.) Styptic. [Obs.] Coxe.

anastate.c: anastate an"a*state (ăn"ȧ*stat), n. [Gr. 'ana` up + ista`nai to make to stand.] (Physiol.) One of a series of substances formed, in secreting cells, by constructive or anabolic processes, in the production of protoplasm; -- opposed to katastate. Foster.

anastatic.c: anastatic an`a*stat"ic (ăn"ȧ*stat"ĭk), a. [Gr. 'ana` up + ista`nai to make to stand: cf. statiko`s causing to stand.] Pertaining to a process or a style of printing from characters in relief on zinc plates.

anastigmatic.c: Anastigmatic An*as`tig*mat"ic (?), a. [Pref. an-not + astigmatic.] (Optics) Not astigmatic; free of astigmatism; -- pertaining to a lens or lens system, and used especially of a lens system which consists of a converging lens and a diverging lens of equal and opposite astigmatism but different focal lengths, and sensibly free from astigmatism.

anastomose.c: Anastomose A*nas"to*mose (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Anastomozed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Anastomosing.] [Cf. F. anastomoser, fr. anastomose. See Anastomosis.] 1. (Anat. & Bot.) To inosculate; to intercommunicate by anastomosis, as the arteries and veins.

anastomosis.c: Anastomosis ‖A*nas`to*mo"sis (?), n.; pl. Anastomoses (?). [NL., fr. Gr.? opening, fr.? to furnish with a mouth or opening, to open;? +? mouth: cf. F. anastomose.] (Anat. & Bot.) The inosculation of vessels, or intercommunication between two or more vessels or nerves, as the cross communication between arteries or veins.

anastomotic.c: Anastomotic A*nas`to*mot"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to anastomosis.

anastrophe.c: Anastrophe ‖A*nas"tro*phe (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.? to turn up or back; 'ana` +? to turn.] (Rhet. & Gram.) An inversion of the natural order of words; as, echoed the hills, for, the hills echoed.

anathema.c: Anathema A*nath"e*ma (?), n.; pl. Anathemas (?). [L. anathĕma, fr. Gr.? anything devoted, esp. to evil, a curse; also L. anathēma, fr. Gr.? a votive offering; all fr.? to set up as a votive gift, dedicate;? up +? to set. See Thesis.] 1. A ban or curse pronounced with religious solemnity by ecclesiastical authority, and accompanied by excommunication. Hence: Denunciation of anything as accursed.

anathematical.c: Anathematical Anathematic A*nath`e*mat"ic (?), A*nath`e*mat"ic*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or having the nature of, an anathema. -- A*nath`e*mat"ic*al*ly, adv.

anathematism.c: Anathematism A*nath"e*ma*tism (?), n. [Gr.? a cursing; cf. F. anathématisme.] Anathematization. [Obs.]

anathematization.c: Anathematization A*nath`e*ma*ti*za"tion (?), n. [LL. anathematisatio.] The act of anathematizing, or denouncing as accursed; imprecation. Barrow.

anathematize.c: Anathematize A*nath"e*ma*tize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Anathematized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Anathematizing.] [L. anathematizare, Gr.? to devote, make accursed: cf. F. anathématiser.] To pronounce an anathema against; to curse. Hence: To condemn publicly as something accursed. Milton.

anathematizer.c: Anathematizer A*nath"e*ma*ti`zer (?), n. One who pronounces an anathema. Hammond.

anatifa.c: Anatifa ‖A*nat"i*fa (?), n.; pl. Anatifæ (?). [NL., contr. fr. anatifera. See Anatiferous.] (Zool.) An animal of the barnacle tribe, of the genus Lepas, having a fleshy stem or peduncle; a goose barnacle. See Cirripedia.

anatiferous.c: Anatiferous An`a*tif"er*ous (?), a. [L. anas, anatis, a duck + -ferous.] (Zool.) Producing ducks; -- applied to Anatifæ, under the absurd notion of their turning into ducks or geese. See Barnacle.

anatine.c: Anatine An"a*tine (?), a. [L. anatinus, fr. anas, anatis, a duck.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the ducks; ducklike.

anatocism.c: Anatocism A*nat"o*cism (?), n. [L. anatocismus, Gr.?;? again +? to lend on interest.] (Law) Compound interest. [R.] Bouvier.

anatomical.c: Anatomical Anatomic { An`a*tom"ic (?), An`a*tom"ic*al (?), } a. [L. anatomicus, Gr.?: cf. F. anatomique. See Anatomy.] Of or relating to anatomy or dissection; as, the anatomic art; anatomical observations. Hume.

anatomically.c: Anatomically An`a*tom"ic*al*ly, adv. In an anatomical manner; by means of dissection.

anatomism.c: Anatomism A*nat"o*mism (?), n. [Cf. F. anatomisme.] 1. The application of the principles of anatomy, as in art.

anatomist.c: Anatomist A*nat"o*mist (?), n. [Cf. F. anatomiste.] One who is skilled in the art of anatomy, or dissection.

anatomization.c: Anatomization A*nat`o*mi*za"tion (?), n. The act of anatomizing.

anatomize.c: Anatomize A*nat"o*mize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Anatomized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Anatomizing.] [Cf. F. anatomiser.] 1. To dissect; to cut in pieces, as an animal vegetable body, for the purpose of displaying or examining the structure and use of the several parts.

anatomy.c: Anatomy A*nat"o*my (?), n.; pl. Anatomies (?). [F. anatomie, L. anatomia, Gr.? dissection, fr.? to cut up;? +? to cut.] 1. The art of dissecting, or artificially separating the different parts of any organized body, to discover their situation, structure, and economy; dissection.

anatreptic.c: Anatreptic An`a*trep"tic (?), a. [overturning, fr.? to turn up or over;? +? too turn.] Overthrowing; defeating; -- applied to Plato's refutative dialogues. Enfield.

anatron.c: Anatron ‖An"a*tron (?), n. [F. anatron, natron, Sp. anatron, natron, fr. Ar. al-natrūn. See Natron, Niter.] [Obs.] 1. Native carbonate of soda; natron.

anatropous.c: Anatropous Anatropal { A*nat"ro*pal (?), A*nat"ro*pous (?), } a. [Gr.? up +? to turn.] (Bot.) Having the ovule inverted at an early period in its development, so that the chalaza is as the apparent apex; -- opposed to orthotropous. Gray.

ambury.c: Ambury Anbury An"bur*y (?), Am"bur*y (?), n. [AS. ampre, ompre, a crooked swelling vein: cf. Prov. E. amper a tumor with inflammation. Cf. the first syllable in agnail, and berry a fruit.] 1. (Far.) A soft tumor or bloody wart on horses or oxen.

ance.c: -ance -ance. [F. -ance, fr. L. -antia and also fr. -entia.] A suffix signifying action; also, quality or state; as, assistance, resistance, appearance, elegance. See -ancy.

ancestor.c: Ancestor An"ces*tor (?), n. [OE. ancestre, auncestre, also ancessour; the first forms fr. OF. ancestre, F. ancêtre, fr. the L. nom. antessor one who goes before; the last form fr. OF. ancessor, fr. L. acc. antecessorem, fr. antecedere to go before; ante before + cedere to go. See Cede, and cf. Antecessor.] 1. One from whom a person is descended, whether on the father's or mother's side, at any distance of time; a progenitor; a fore father.

ancestorially.c: Ancestorially An`ces*to"ri*al*ly, adv. With regard to ancestors.

ancestral.c: Ancestral An*ces"tral (?; 277), a. Of, pertaining to, derived from, or possessed by, an ancestor or ancestors; as, an ancestral estate. “Ancestral trees.” Hemans.

ancestry.c: Ancestry An"ces*try (?), n. [Cf. OF. ancesserie. See Ancestor.] 1. Condition as to ancestors; ancestral lineage; hence, birth or honorable descent.

anchor.c: Anchor An"chor (ăṉ"kẽr), n. [OE. anker, AS. ancor, oncer, L. ancora, sometimes spelt anchora, fr. Gr. 'a`gkyra, akin to E. angle: cf. F. ancre. See Angle, n.] 1. A iron instrument which is attached to a ship by a cable (rope or chain), and which, being cast overboard, lays hold of the earth by a fluke or hook and thus retains the ship in a particular station.
Anchor An"chor (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Anchored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Anchoring.] [Cf. F. ancrer.] 1. To place at anchor; to secure by an anchor; as, to anchor a ship.
Anchor An"chor, v. i. 1. To cast anchor; to come to anchor; as, our ship (or the captain) anchored in the stream.
Anchor An"chor, n. [OE. anker, ancre, AS. ancra, fr. L. anachoreta. See Anchoret.] An anchoret. [Obs.] Shak.
Anchor escapement An"chor es*cape"ment. (Horol.) (a) The common recoil escapement. (b) A variety of the lever escapement with a wide impulse pin.

Anchor light Anchor light. (Naut.) The lantern shown at night by a vessel at anchor. International rules of the road require vessels at anchor to carry from sunset to sunrise a single white light forward if under 150 feet in length, and if longer, two such lights, one near the stern and one forward.
Anchor shot Anchor shot. (Billiards) A shot made with the object balls in an anchor space.

Anchor space Anchor space. (Billiards) In the balk-line game, any of eight spaces, 7 inches by 3½, lying along a cushion and bisected transversely by a balk line. Object balls in an anchor space are treated as in balk.
Anchor watch Anchor watch. (Naut.) A detail of one or more men who keep watch on deck at night when a vessel is at anchor.

anchorage.c: Anchorage An"chor*age (?), n. 1. The act of anchoring, or the condition of lying at anchor.
Anchorage An"cho*rage (?), n. Abode of an anchoret.

anchored.c: Anchored An"chored (?), a. 1. Held by an anchor; at anchor; held safely; as, an anchored bark; also, shaped like an anchor; forked; as, an anchored tongue.

anchorite.c: Anchorite Anchoret An"cho*ret (?), An"cho*rite (?), n. [F. anachorète, L. anachoreta, fr. Gr.?, fr.? to go back, retire;? +? to give place, retire,? place; perh. akin to Skr. hā to leave. Cf. Anchor a hermit.] One who renounces the world and secludes himself, usually for religious reasons; a hermit; a recluse. [Written by some authors anachoret.]

anchoretical.c: Anchoretical Anchoretic { An`cho*ret"ic (?), An`cho*ret"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. Gr.?.] Pertaining to an anchoret or hermit; after the manner of an anchoret.

anchoretism.c: Anchoretism An"cho*ret*ism (?), n. The practice or mode of life of an anchoret.

anchorhold.c: Anchor-hold An"chor-hold` (?), n. 1. The hold or grip of an anchor, or that to which it holds.

anchorless.c: Anchorless An"chor*less (?), a. Without an anchor or stay. Hence: Drifting; unsettled.

anchovy.c: Anchovy An*cho"vy (ăn*chō"vy̆), n. [Sp. anchoa, anchova, or Pg. anchova, prob. of Iberian origin, and lit. a dried or pickled fish, fr. Bisc. antzua dry: cf. D. anchovis, F. anchois.] (Zool.) A small fish, about three inches in length, of the Herring family (Engraulis encrasicholus), caught in vast numbers in the Mediterranean, and pickled for exportation. The name is also applied to several allied species.
Anchovy pear An*cho"vy pear` (ăn*chō"vy̆ pâr`). (Bot.) A West Indian fruit like the mango in taste, sometimes pickled; also, the tree (Grias cauliflora) bearing this fruit.

anchusin.c: Anchusin An"chu*sin (?), n. [L. anchusa the plant alkanet, Gr.?.] (Chem.) A resinoid coloring matter obtained from alkanet root.

anchylose.c: Anchylose An"chy*lose (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Anchylosed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Anchylosing.] [Cf. F. ankyloser.] To affect or be affected with anchylosis; to unite or consolidate so as to make a stiff joint; to grow together into one. [Spelt also ankylose.] Owen.

anchylosis.c: anchylosis ankylosis ‖an`chy*lo"sis, an`ky*lo"sis (ăṉ`kĭ*lō"sĭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'agky`lwsis, fr. 'agkyloy^n to crook, stiffen, fr. 'agky`los crooked: cf. F. ankylose.] 1. (Med.) The process of formation of a stiff joint; also, the abnormal adhesion and rigidity of the bones of a joint which has become stiff. Dunglison.

anchylotic.c: Anchylotic An`chy*lot"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to anchylosis.

ancient.c: Ancient An"cient (?), a. [OE. auncien, F. ancien, LL. antianus, fr. L. ante before. See Ante-, pref.] 1. Old; that happened or existed in former times, usually at a great distance of time; belonging to times long past; specifically applied to the times before the fall of the Roman empire; -- opposed to modern; as, ancient authors, literature, history; ancient days.
Ancient An"cient, n. 1. pl. Those who lived in former ages, as opposed to the moderns.
Ancient An"cient, n. [Corrupted from ensign.] 1. An ensign or flag. [Obs.]

ancientness.c: Ancientness An"cient*ness, n. The quality of being ancient; antiquity; existence from old times.

ancientry.c: Ancientry An"cient*ry (?), n. 1. Antiquity; what is ancient.

ancienty.c: Ancienty An"cient*y (?), n. [F. ancienneté, fr. ancien. See Ancient.] 1. Age; antiquity. [Obs.] Martin.

ancile.c: Ancile ‖An*ci"le (?), n. [L.] (Rom. Antiq.) The sacred shield of the Romans, said to have-fallen from heaven in the reign of Numa. It was the palladium of Rome.

ancillary.c: Ancillary An"cil*la*ry (?), a. [L. ancillaris, fr. ancilla a female servant.] Subservient or subordinate, like a handmaid; auxiliary.
Ancillary administration An"cil*la*ry ad*min`is*tra"tion. (Law) An administration subordinate to, and in aid of, the primary or principal administration of an estate.

ancille.c: Ancille An*cille" (?), n. [OF. ancelle, L. ancilla.] A maidservant; a handmaid. [Obs.] Chaucer.

ancipitous.c: Ancipitous Ancipital { An*cip"i*tal (?), An*cip"i*tous (?), } a. [L. anceps, ancipitis, two-headed, double; an- for amb- on both sides + caput head.] (Bot.) Two-edged instead of round; -- said of certain flattened stems, as those of blue grass, and rarely also of leaves.

ancistroid.c: Ancistroid An*cis"troid (?), a. [Gr.?;? a hook +? shape.] Hook-shaped.

ancome.c: Ancome An"come (ăṉ"kŭm), n. [AS. ancuman, oncuman, to come.] A small ulcerous swelling, coming suddenly; also, a whitlow. [Obs.] Boucher.

ancon.c: Ancon ‖An"con (ăṉ"kŏm), n.; L. pl. Ancones (?). [L., fr. Gr. 'agkw`n the bent arm, elbow; any hook or bend.] (Anat.) The olecranon, or the elbow.

ancone.c: Ancone Ancon { An"con (?), An"cone (?), } n. [See Ancon, above.] (Arch.) (a) The corner or quoin of a wall, cross-beam, or rafter. [Obs.] Gwilt. (b) A bracket supporting a cornice; a console.

anconeal.c: Anconeal Anconal { An"co*nal (?), An*co"ne*al (?), } a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the ancon or elbow. “The olecranon on anconeal process.” Flower.

anconeus.c: Anconeus ‖An*co"ne*us (?), n. [NL., fr. L. ancon elbow.] (Anat.) A muscle of the elbow and forearm.

ancony.c: Ancony An"co*ny (?), n. [Origin unknown.] (Iron Work) A piece of malleable iron, wrought into the shape of a bar in the middle, but unwrought at the ends.

ancy.c: -ancy -an*cy. [L. -antia.] A suffix expressing more strongly than -ance the idea of quality or state; as, constancy, buoyancy, infancy.

and.c: And And (?), conj. [AS. and; akin to OS. endi, Icel. enda, OHG. anti, enti, inti, unti, G. und, D. en, OD. ende. Cf, An if, Ante-.] 1. A particle which expresses the relation of connection or addition. It is used to conjoin a word with a word, a clause with a clause, or a sentence with a sentence.

andabatism.c: Andabatism An"da*ba*tism (?), n. [L. andabata a kind of Roman gladiator, who fought hoodwinked.] Doubt; uncertainty. [Obs.] Shelford.

andalusite.c: Andalusite An`da*lu"site (?), n. (Min.) A silicate of aluminium, occurring usually in thick rhombic prisms, nearly square, of a grayish or pale reddish tint. It was first discovered in Andalusia, Spain.

andante.c: Andante ‖An*dan"te (?), a. [It. andante, p. pr. of andare to go.] (Mus.) Moving moderately slow, but distinct and flowing; quicker than larghetto, and slower than allegretto. -- n. A movement or piece in andante time.

andantino.c: Andantino ‖An`dan*ti"no (?), a. [It., dim. of andante.] (Mus.) Rather quicker than andante; between that allegretto.

andarac.c: Andarac An"da*rac (?), n. [A corruption of sandarac.] Red orpiment. Coxe.

andean.c: Andean An*de"an, a. Pertaining to the Andes.

andesine.c: Andesine An"des*ine (?), n. (Min.) A kind of triclinic feldspar found in the Andes.

andesite.c: Andesite An"des*ite (?), n. (Min.) An eruptive rock allied to trachyte, consisting essentially of a triclinic feldspar, with pyroxene, hornblende, or hypersthene.

andine.c: Andine An"dine (?), a. Andean; as, Andine flora.

andiron.c: Andiron And"i`ron (?), n. [OE. anderne, aunderne, aundyre, OF. andier, F. landier, fr. LL. andena, andela, anderia, of unknown origin. The Eng. was prob. confused with brand-iron, AS. brand-īsen.] A utensil for supporting wood when burning in a fireplace, one being placed on each side; a firedog; as, a pair of andirons.

andranatomy.c: Andranatomy An`dra*nat"o*my (?), n. [Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man +?: cf. F. andranatomie. See Anatomy, Androtomy.] The dissection of a human body, especially of a male; androtomy. Coxe.

androcephalous.c: Androcephalous An`dro*ceph"a*lous (?), a. [Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man + kefalh` head.] Having a human head (upon an animal's body), as the Egyptian sphinx.

androdiecious.c: Androdiecious Androdioecious { An`dro*di*œ"cious, An`dro*di*e"cious (?) }, a. [Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man + E. diœcious.] (Bot.) Having perfect and staminate flowers on different plants. -- An`dro*di*œ"cism, -di*e"cism (#), n.

androecium.c: Androecium ‖An*drœ"ci*um (?), n. [NL., from Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man +? house.] (bot.) The stamens of a flower taken collectively.

androgynal.c: Androgynal Androgynous { An*drog"y*nous (?), An*drog"y*nal (?), } a. [L. androgynus, Gr.?; 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man + gynh` woman: cf. F. androgyne.] 1. Uniting both sexes in one, or having the characteristics of both; being in nature both male and female; hermaphroditic. Owen.

androgynism.c: Androgynism Androgyny { An*drog"y*ny (?), An*drog"y*nism (?), } n. Union of both sexes in one individual; hermaphroditism.

androides.c: Androides Android { An"droid (ăn"droid), ‖An*droi"des (ăn*droi"dēz), } n. [Gr. 'androeidh`s of man's form; 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man + e'i^dos form.] A machine or automaton in the form of a human being.

andromeda.c: Andromeda An*drom"e*da (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, the daughter of Cepheus and Cassiopeia. When bound to a rock and exposed to a sea monster, she was delivered by Perseus.] 1. (Astron.) A northern constellation, supposed to represent the mythical Andromeda.

andromed.c: Andromed Andromede { An"dro*mede (?), An"dro*med (?) }, n.} (Astron.) A meteor appearing to radiate from a point in the constellation Andromeda, -- whence the name.

andron.c: Andron ‖An"dron (ăn"drŏn), n. [L. andron, Gr. 'andrw`n, fr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man.] (Gr. & Rom. Arch.) The apartment appropriated for the males. This was in the lower part of the house.

andropetalous.c: Andropetalous An`dro*pet"al*ous (?), a. [Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man + pe`talon leaf.] (Bot.) Produced by the conversion of the stamens into petals, as double flowers, like the garden ranunculus. Brande.

androphagi.c: Androphagi ‖An*droph"a*gi (ăn*drŏf"ȧ*jĭ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'androfa`gos; 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man + fagei^n to eat.] Cannibals; man-eaters; anthropophagi. [R.]

androphore.c: Androphore An"dro*phore (ăn"dro*fōr), n. [Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man + fe`rein to bear.] 1. (Bot.) A support or column on which stamens are raised. Gray.

andropogon.c: Andropogon ‖An`dro*po"gon (?), n. [NL.; Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man + pw`gwn the beard.] (Bot.) A very large and important genus of grasses, found in nearly all parts of the world. It includes the lemon grass of Ceylon and the beard grass, or broom sedge, of the United States. The principal subgenus is Sorghum, including Andropogon sorghum and Andropogon halepensis, from which have been derived the Chinese sugar cane, the Johnson grass, the Aleppo grass, the broom corn, and the durra, or Indian millet. Several East Indian species, as Andropogon nardus and Andropogon schœnanthus, yield fragrant oils, used in perfumery.

androsphinx.c: Androsphinx An"dro*sphinx (ăn"dro*sfĭṉks), n. [Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man + sfi`gx sphinx.] (Egypt. Art.) A man sphinx; a sphinx having the head of a man and the body of a lion.

androspore.c: Androspore An"dro*spore (?), n. [Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, a man +? a seed.] (Bot.) A spore of some algæ, which has male functions.

androtomous.c: Androtomous An*drot"o*mous (?), a. (Bot.) Having the filaments of the stamens divided into two parts.

androtomy.c: Androtomy An*drot"o*my (?), n. [Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man +? a cutting. Cf. Anatomy.] Dissection of the human body, as distinguished from zoötomy; anthropotomy. [R.]

androus.c: androus *an"drous (?). [Gr. 'anh`r, 'andro`s, a man.] (Bot.) A terminal combining form: Having a stamen or stamens; staminate; as, monandrous, with one stamen; polyandrous, with many stamens.

anear.c: Anear A*near" (?), prep. & adv. [Pref. a- + near.] Near. [R.] “It did not come anear.” Coleridge.
Anear A*near", v. t. & i. To near; to approach. [Archaic]

aneath.c: Aneath A*neath" (?), prep. & adv. [Pref. a- + neath for beneath.] Beneath. [Scot.]

anecdotage.c: Anecdotage An"ec*do`tage (?), n. Anecdotes collectively; a collection of anecdotes.

anecdotal.c: Anecdotal An"ec*do`tal (?), a. Pertaining to, or abounding with, anecdotes; as, anecdotal conversation.

anecdote.c: Anecdote An"ec*dote (?), n. [F. anecdote, fr. Gr.? not published; 'an priv. +? given out,? to give out, to publish;? out +? to give. See Dose, n.] 1. pl. Unpublished narratives. Burke.

anecdotical.c: Anecdotical Anecdotic { An`ec*dot"ic (?), An`ec*dot"ic*al (?), } a. Pertaining to, consisting of, or addicted to, anecdotes. “Anecdotical traditions.” Bolingbroke.

anecdotist.c: Anecdotist An"ec*do"tist (?), n. One who relates or collects anecdotes.

anele.c: Anele A*nele" (?), v. t. [OE. anelien; an on + AS. ele oil, L. oleum. See Oil, Anoil.] 1. To anoint. Shipley.

anelectric.c: Anelectric An`e*lec"tric (?), a. [Gr. 'an priv. + E. electric.] (Physics) Not becoming electrified by friction; -- opposed to idioelectric. -- n. A substance incapable of being electrified by friction. Faraday.

anelectrode.c: Anelectrode An`e*lec"trode (?), n. [Gr.? up + E. electrode.] (Elec.) The positive pole of a voltaic battery.

anelectrotonus.c: Anelectrotonus ‖An`e*lec*trot"o*nus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? up + E. electrotonus.] (Physiol.) The condition of decreased irritability of a nerve in the region of the positive electrode or anode on the passage of a current of electricity through it. Foster.

anemogram.c: Anemogram A*nem"o*gram (?), n. [Gr.? wind + -gram.] A record made by an anemograph.

anemograph.c: Anemograph A*nem"o*graph (-grȧf), n. [Gr.? wind + -graph.] An instrument for measuring and recording the direction and force of the wind. Knight.

anemographic.c: Anemographic A*nem`o*graph"ic (ȧ*nĕm`o*grăf"ĭk), a. Produced by an anemograph; of or pertaining to anemography.

anemography.c: Anemography An`e*mog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. 'a`nemos wind + -graphy.] 1. A description of the winds.

anemology.c: Anemology An`e*mol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? wind + -logy.] The science of the wind.

anemometer.c: Anemometer An`e*mom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? wind + -meter.] An instrument for measuring the force or velocity of the wind; a wind gauge.

anemometrical.c: Anemometrical Anemometric { An`e*mo*met"ric (?), An`e*mo*met"ric*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to anemometry.

anemometry.c: Anemometry An`e*mom"e*try (?), n. The act or process of ascertaining the force or velocity of the wind.

anemone.c: Anemone A*nem"o*ne (?), n. [L. anemone, Gr.?, fr.? wind.] 1. (Bot.) A genus of plants of the Ranunculus or Crowfoot family; windflower. Some of the species are cultivated in gardens.

anemonic.c: Anemonic An`e*mon"ic (?), a. (Chem.) An acrid, poisonous, crystallizable substance, obtained from, the anemone, or from anemonin.

anemonin.c: Anemonin A*nem"o*nin (?), n. (Chem.) An acrid, poisonous, crystallizable substance, obtained from some species of anemone.

anemorphilous.c: Anemorphilous An`e*morph"i*lous (?), a. [Gr. 'a`nemos wind + fi`los lover.] (Bot.) Fertilized by the agency of the wind; -- said of plants in which the pollen is carried to the stigma by the wind; wind-Fertilized. Lubbock.

anemoscope.c: Anemoscope A*nem"o*scope (?), n. [Gr.? wind + -scope: cf. F. anémoscope.] An instrument which shows the direction of the wind; a wind vane; a weathercock; -- usually applied to a contrivance consisting of a vane above, connected in the building with a dial or index with pointers to show the changes of the wind.

anemosis.c: Anemosis ‖An`e*mo"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? wind.] A condition in the wood of some trees in which the rings are separated, as some suppose, by the action of high winds upon the trunk; wind shake.

anencephalous.c: Anencephalous Anencephalic { An*en`ce*phal"ic (?), An`en*ceph"a*lous (?), } a. [Gr.?, priv. +? the brain: cf. Encephalon.] (Zool.) Without a brain; brainless. Todd & B.

anent.c: Anent Anenst { A*nenst" (?), A*nent" (?), } prep. [OE. anent, anentis, anence, anens, anents, AS. onefen, onemn; an, on, on + efen even, equal; hence meaning, on an equality with, even with, beside. See Even, a.] [Scot. & Prov. Eng.] 1. Over against; as, he lives anent the church.

anenterous.c: Anenterous An*en"ter*ous (?), a. [Gr. 'an priv. +? intestine,? within,? in.] (Zool.) Destitute of a stomach or an intestine. Owen.

anergy.c: Anergy Anergia { ‖An*er"gi*a, An"er*gy (?), } n. [NL. anergia, fr. Gr.?- not +? work.] Lack of energy; inactivity. -- An*er"gic (#), a.

aneroid.c: Aneroid An"e*roid (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. + nhro`s wet, moist + -oid: cf. F. anéroïde.] Containing no liquid; -- said of a kind of barometer.

anes.c: anes anes (ānz), adv. Once. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.

anesthesia.c: Anesthesia Anesthetic ‖An`es*the"si*a (?), n., An`es*thet"ic (?), a. Same as Anæsthesia, Anæsthetic.

anet.c: Anet An"et (?), n. [F. aneth, fr. L. anethum, Gr. 'a`nhqon. See Anise.] The herb dill, or dillseed.

anethol.c: Anethol An"e*thol (?), n. [L. anethum (see Anise) + -ol.] (Chem.) A substance obtained from the volatile oils of anise, fennel, etc., in the form of soft shining scales; -- called also anise camphor. Watts.

anetic.c: Anetic A*net"ic (ȧ*nĕt"ĭk), a. [L. aneticus, Gr. 'anetiko`s relaxing; 'ana` back + e'i^nai to send.] (Med.) Soothing. AS

aneurism.c: aneurism aneurysm an"eu*rism, an"eu*rysm (ăn"u*rĭz'm), n. [Gr. 'aney`rysma, 'aneyrysmo`s, a widening, an opening; 'ana` up + e'yry`s wide.] (Med.) A soft, usually pulsating, sac, containing blood or blood clot, arising from the abnormal dilation of the walls of an artery, vein or heart. The more common spelling is aneurysm.

aneurismal.c: aneurismal Aneurysmal an`eu*ris"mal, An`eu*rys"mal (ăn`u*rĭz"mail), a. (Med.) Of or pertaining to an aneurism; as, an aneurismal tumor; aneurismal diathesis. The more common spelling is aneurysmal.

anew.c: anew a*new" (ȧ*nū"), adv. [Pref. a- + new.] Over again; another time; in a new form; afresh; as, to arm anew; to create anew. Dryden.

anfractuose.c: Anfractuose An*frac"tu*ose` (?; 135), a. [See Anfractuous.] Anfractuous; as, anfractuose anthers.

anfractuosity.c: Anfractuosity An*frac`tu*os"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Anfractuosities (#). [Cf. F. anfractuosité.] 1. A state of being anfractuous, or full of windings and turnings; sinuosity.

anfractuous.c: Anfractuous An*frac"tu*ous (?), a. [L. anfractuosus, fr. anfractus a turning, a winding, fr. the unused anfringere to wind, bend; an-, for amb- + fractus, p. p. of frangere to break: cf. F. anfractueux.] Winding; full of windings and turnings; sinuous; tortuous; as, the anfractuous spires of a horn. -- An*frac"tu*ous*ness, n.

angariation.c: Angariation An*ga"ri*a"tion (?), n. [LL. angariatio, fr. L. angaria service to a lord, villenage, fr. angarius, Gr. 'a`ggaros (a Persian word), a courier for carrying royal dispatches.] Exaction of forced service; compulsion. [Obs.] Speed.

angeiotomy.c: Angeiotomy Angeiology An`gei*ol"o*gy (?), n., An`gei*ot"o*my, etc. Same as Angiology, Angiotomy, etc.

angel.c: Angel An"gel (?), n. [AS. ængel, engel, influenced by OF. angele, angle, F. ange. Both the AS. and the OF. words are from L. angelus, Gr. 'a`ggelos messenger, a messenger of God, an angel.] 1. A messenger. [R.]
Angel fish An"gel fish. See under Angel.

angelage.c: Angelage An"gel*age (?), n. Existence or state of angels.

angelet.c: Angelet An"gel*et (?), n. [OF. angelet.] A small gold coin formerly current in England; a half angel. Eng. Cyc.

angelhood.c: Angelhood An"gel*hood (?), n. The state of being an angel; angelic nature. Mrs. Browning.

angelical.c: Angelical Angelic { An*gel"ic (?), An*gel"ic*al (?), } a. [L. angelicus, Gr.?: cf. F. angélique.] 1. Belonging to, or proceeding from, angels; resembling, characteristic of, or partaking of the nature of, an angel; heavenly; divine. “Angelic harps.” Thomson.“Angelical actions.” Hooker.

angelic.c: Angelic An*gel"ic, a. [From Angelica.] (Chem.) Of or derived from angelica; as, angelic acid; angelic ether.

angelica.c: Angelica An*gel"i*ca (?), n. [NL. See Angelic.] (Bot.) 1. An aromatic umbelliferous plant (Archangelica officinalis or Angelica archangelica) the leaf stalks of which are sometimes candied and used in confectionery, and the roots and seeds as an aromatic tonic.

angelicalness.c: Angelicalness An*gel"ic*al*ness, n. The quality of being angelic; excellence more than human.

angelify.c: Angelify An*gel"i*fy (?), v. t. To make like an angel; to angelize. [Obs.] Farindon (1647).

angelize.c: Angelize An"gel*ize (?), v. t. To raise to the state of an angel; to render angelic.

angellike.c: Angellike An"gel*like` (?), a. & adv. Resembling an angel.

angelolatry.c: Angelolatry An`gel*ol"a*try (?), n. [Gr.? angel +? service, worship.] Worship paid to angels.

angelology.c: Angelology An`gel*ol"o*gy (?), n. [L. angelus, Gr.? + -logy.] A discourse on angels, or a body of doctrines in regard to angels.

angelophany.c: Angelophany An`gel*oph"a*ny (?), n. [Gr.? angel +? to appear.] The actual appearance of an angel to man.

angelot.c: Angelot An"ge*lot (?), n. [F. angelot, LL. angelotus, angellotus, dim. of angelus. See Angel.] 1. A French gold coin of the reign of Louis XI., bearing the image of St. Michael; also, a piece coined at Paris by the English under Henry VI. [Obs.]

angelus.c: Angelus ‖An"ge*lus (?), n. [L.] (R. C. Ch.) (a) A form of devotion in which three Ave Marias are repeated. It is said at morning, noon, and evening, at the sound of a bell. (b) The Angelus bell. Shipley.

anger.c: Anger An"ger (aṉ"gẽr), n. [OE. anger, angre, affliction, anger, fr. Icel. angr affliction, sorrow; akin to Dan. anger regret, Swed. ånger regret, AS. ange oppressed, sad, L. angor a strangling, anguish, angere to strangle, Gr. 'a`gchein to strangle, Skr. ahas pain, and to E. anguish, anxious, quinsy, and perh. awe, ugly. The word seems to have orig. meant to choke, squeeze. √3.] 1. Trouble; vexation; also, physical pain or smart of a sore, etc. [Obs.]
Anger An"ger (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Angered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Angering.] [Cf. Icel. angra.] 1. To make painful; to cause to smart; to inflame. [Obs.]

angevine.c: Angevine An"ge*vine (?), a. [F. Angevin.] Of or pertaining to Anjou in France. -- n. A native of Anjou.

angienchyma.c: Angienchyma ‖An`gi*en"chy*ma (?), n. [Gr.? receptacle +?. Formed like Parenchyma.] (Bot.) Vascular tissue of plants, consisting of spiral vessels, dotted, barred, and pitted ducts, and laticiferous vessels.

angina.c: angina ‖an*gi"na (ăn*jī"nȧ or ăn"jĭ*nȧ), n. [L., fr. angere to strangle, to choke. See anger, n.] 1. (Med.) Any inflammatory affection of the throat, as the quinsy, malignant sore throat, croup, etc., especially such as tends to produce suffocation, choking, or shortness of breath. [Obs.]

anginous.c: anginous anginose { an"gi*nous (ăn"jĭ*nŭs), an"gi*nose` (ăn"jĭ*nōs`), } a. (Med.) Pertaining to angina or angina pectoris; anginal. [archaic]

angio.c: Angio- An"gi*o- (ăn"jĭ*o-). [Gr. 'aggei^on vessel receptacle.] A prefix, or combining form, in numerous compounds, usually relating to seed or blood vessels, or to something contained in, or covered by, a vessel.

angiocarpous.c: Angiocarpous An`gi*o*car"pous (ăn`jĭ*o*kär"pŭs), a. [Angio- + Gr. karpo`s fruit.] (Bot.) (a) Having fruit inclosed within a covering that does not form a part of itself; as, the filbert covered by its husk, or the acorn seated in its cupule. Brande & C. (b) Having the seeds or spores covered, as in certain lichens. Gray.

angiography.c: Angiography An`gi*og"ra*phy (?), n. [Angio- + -graphy: cf. F. angiographie.] 1. (Anat.) A description of blood vessels and lymphatics.

angiology.c: Angiology An`gi*ol"o*gy (ăn`jĭ*ŏl"o*jy̆), n. [Angio- + -logy.] (Anat.) That part of anatomy which treats of blood vessels and lymphatics.

angioma.c: angioma ‖an`gi*o"ma (ăn`jĭ*ō"mȧ), n.; L. pl. -omata (-ō"mȧ*tȧ). [NL.; angio- + -oma.] (Med.) A tumor composed chiefly of blood or lymph vessels. -- an`gi*om"a*tous (ăn`jĭ*ō"mȧ*tŭs), a. AS

angiomonospermous.c: Angiomonospermous An`gi*o*mon`o*sper"mous (ăn`jĭ*o*mŏn`o*spẽr"mŭs), a. [Angio- + monospermous.] (Bot.) Producing one seed only in a seed pod.

angioneurosis.c: angioneurosis ‖an`gi*o*neu*ro"sis (ăn`jĭ*o*nu*rō"sĭs), n. [NL.; angio- + neurosis.] (Med.) Angioneuropathy{1}. The term angioneuropathy is now used more frequently than angioneurosis. -- An`gi*o*neu*rot"ic (ăn`jĭ*o*nu*rŏt"ĭk), a.

angiopathy.c: angiopathy an`gi*op"a*thy (ăn`jĭ*ŏp"ȧ*thy̆), n. [Angio- + Gr. pa`qos disease.] (Med.) Disease of the vessels, esp. the blood vessels.

angioscope.c: Angioscope An"gi*o*scope (ăn"jĭ*o*skōp), n. [Angio- + -scope.] An instrument for examining the capillary vessels of animals and plants. Morin.

angiosperm.c: Angiosperm An"gi*o*sperm (-ăn"jĭ*o*spẽrm), n. [Angio- + Gr.?,?, seed.] (Bot.) A plant which has its seeds inclosed in a pericarp. Contrasted with gymnosperm.

angiospermous.c: Angiospermous An`gi*o*sper"mous (?), a. (Bot.) Having seeds inclosed in a pod or other pericarp.

angiosporous.c: Angiosporous An`gi*os"po*rous (?), a. [Angio- + spore.] (Bot.) Having spores contained in cells or thecæ, as in the case of some fungi.

angiostomous.c: Angiostomous An`gi*os"to*mous (?), a. [Angio- + Gr.? mouth.] (Zool.) With a narrow mouth, as the shell of certain gastropods.

angiotomy.c: Angiotomy An`gi*ot"o*my (?), n. [Angio- + Gr.? a cutting.] (Anat.) Dissection of the blood vessels and lymphatics of the body. Dunglison.

angle.c: Angle An"gle (ăṉ"g'l), n. [F. angle, L. angulus angle, corner; akin to uncus hook, Gr. 'agky`los bent, crooked, angular, 'a`gkos a bend or hollow, AS. angel hook, fish-hook, G. angel, and F. anchor.] 1. The inclosed space near the point where two lines meet; a corner; a nook.
Angle An"gle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Angled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Angling (?).] 1. To fish with an angle (fishhook), or with hook and line.
Angle An"gle, v. t. To try to gain by some insinuating artifice; to allure. [Obs.] “He angled the people's hearts.” Sir P. Sidney.

Angle of entry An"gle of en"try. (Aëronautics) The angle between the tangent to the advancing edge (of an aërocurve) and the line of motion; -- contrasted with angle of trail, which is the angle between the tangent to the following edge and the line of motion.
Angle of incidence Angle of incidence. (Aëronautics) The angle between the chord of an aërocurve and the relative direction of the undisturbed air current.

angled.c: Angled An"gled (?), a. Having an angle or angles; -- used in compounds; as, right-angled, many-angled, etc.

anglemeter.c: Anglemeter An"gle*me`ter (?), n. [Angle + -meter.] An instrument to measure angles, esp. one used by geologists to measure the dip of strata.

angles.c: Angles An"gles (?), n. pl. [L. Angli. See Anglican.] (Ethnol.) An ancient Low German tribe, that settled in Britain, which came to be called Engla-land (Angleland or England). The Angles probably came from the district of Angeln (now within the limits of Schleswig), and the country now Lower Hanover, etc.

anglesite.c: Anglesite An"gle*site (?), n. [From the Isle of Anglesea.] (Min.) A native sulphate of lead. It occurs in white or yellowish transparent, prismatic crystals.

anglewise.c: Anglewise An"gle*wise` (?), adv. [Angle + wise, OE. wise manner.] In an angular manner; angularly.

angleworm.c: Angleworm An"gle*worm` (?), n. (Zool.) A earthworm of the genus Lumbricus, frequently used by anglers for bait. See Earthworm.

anglian.c: Anglian An"gli*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Angles. -- n. One of the Angles.

anglican.c: Anglican An"gli*can (?), a. [Angli the Angles, a Germanic tribe in Lower Germany. Cf. English.] 1. English; of or pertaining to England or the English nation; especially, pertaining to, or connected with, the established church of England; as, the Anglican church, doctrine, orders, ritual, etc.
Anglican An"gli*can (?), n. 1. A member of the Church of England.

anglicanism.c: Anglicanism An"gli*can*ism (?), n. 1. Strong partiality to the principles and rites of the Church of England.

anglice.c: Anglice ‖An"gli*ce (?), adv. [NL.] In English; in the English manner; as, Livorno, Anglice Leghorn.

anglicify.c: Anglicify An*glic"i*fy (?), v. t. [NL. Anglicus English + -fly.] To anglicize. [R.]

anglicism.c: Anglicism An"gli*cism (?), n. [Cf. F. anglicisme.] 1. An English idiom; a phrase or form language peculiar to the English. Dryden.

anglicity.c: Anglicity An*glic"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being English.

anglicization.c: Anglicization An`gli*ci*za"tion (?), n. The act of anglicizing, or making English in character.

anglicize.c: Anglicize An"gli*cize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Anglicized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Anglicizing.] To make English; to English; to anglify; render conformable to the English idiom, or to English analogies.

anglify.c: Anglify An"gli*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Anglified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Anglifying.] [L. Angli + -fly.] To convert into English; to anglicize. Franklin. Darwin.

angling.c: Angling An"gling (?), n. The act of one who angles; the art of fishing with rod and line. Walton.

anglo.c: Anglo- An"glo- (?) [NL. Anglus English. See Anglican.] A combining form meaning the same as English; or English and, or English conjoined with; as, Anglo-Turkish treaty, Anglo-German, Anglo-Irish.

angloamerican.c: Anglo-American Anglo-American a. Of or pertaining to the English and Americans, or to the descendants of Englishmen in America.

anglocatholic.c: Anglo-Catholic An"glo-Cath"o*lic, a., Of or pertaining to a church modeled on the English Reformation; Anglican; -- sometimes restricted to the ritualistic or High Church section of the Church of England.
Anglo-Catholic An"glo-Cath"o*lic, n. A member of the Church of England who contends for its catholic character; more specifically, a High Churchman.

anglocatholicism.c: Anglo-Catholicism An"glo-Ca*thol"i*cism (?), n. The belief of those in the Church of England who accept many doctrines and practices which they maintain were those of the primitive, or true, Catholic Church, of which they consider the Church of England to be the lineal descendant; a doctrine and practice within the Church of England emphasizing the Catholic tradition.

anglomania.c: Anglomania An"glo*ma"ni*a (?), n. [Anglo'cf + mania.] A mania for, or an inordinate attachment to, English customs, institutions, etc.

anglomaniac.c: Anglomaniac An`glo*ma"ni*ac, n. One affected with Anglomania.

anglonorman.c: Anglo-Norman Anglo-Norman, a. Of or pertaining to the English and Normans, or to the Normans who settled in England.
Anglo-Norman Anglo-Norman, n. 1. One of the English Normans, or the Normans who conquered England.

anglophobia.c: Anglophobia An`glo*pho"bi*a (?), n. [Anglo- + Gr.? fear.] Intense dread of, or aversion to, England or the English. -- An"glo*phobe (?), n.

anglosaxon.c: Anglo-Saxon An"glo-Sax"on (?), n. [L. Angli-Saxones English Saxons.] 1. A Saxon of Britain, that is, an English Saxon, or one the Saxons who settled in England, as distinguished from a continental (or “Old”) Saxon.

anglosaxondom.c: Anglo-Saxondom An"glo-Sax"on*dom (?), n. The Anglo-Saxon domain (i. e., Great Britain and the United States, etc.); the Anglo-Saxon race.

anglosaxonism.c: Anglo-Saxonism An"glo-Sax"on*ism (?), n. 1. A characteristic of the Anglo-Saxon race; especially, a word or an idiom of the Anglo-Saxon tongue. M. Arnold.

angola.c: Angola An*go"la (?), n. [A corruption of Angora.] A fabric made from the wool of the Angora goat.
Angola pea An*go"la pea` (?). (Bot.) A tropical plant (Cajanus indicus) and its edible seed, a kind of pulse; -- so called from Angola in Western Africa. Called also pigeon pea and Congo pea.

angora.c: Angora An*go"ra (ăn*gō"rȧ), n. A city of Asia Minor (or Anatolia) which has given its name to a goat, a cat, etc.

angostura.c: Angostura bark Angostura An`gos*tu"ra, An`gos*tu"ra bark" (äṉ`gŏs*tōo"rȧ bärk`). [From Angostura, in Venezuela.] A bitter aromatic bark, obtained from a South American tree of the rue family (Galipea cusparia, or Galipea officinalis). It is used used as a tonic, in medicines, liqueurs and bitters. U. S. Disp.

angoumois.c: Angoumois moth ‖An`gou`mois" moth" (?; 115). [So named from Angoumois in France.] (Zool.) A small moth (Gelechia cerealella) which is very destructive to wheat and other grain. The larva eats out the interior of the grain, leaving only the shell.

angrily.c: Angrily An"gri*ly (?), adv. In an angry manner; under the influence of anger.

angriness.c: Angriness An"gri*ness, n. The quality of being angry, or of being inclined to anger.

angry.c: Angry An"gry (?), a. [Compar. Angrier (?); superl. Angriest.] [See Anger.] 1. Troublesome; vexatious; rigorous. [Obs.]

anguilliform.c: Anguilliform An*guil"li*form (?), a. [L. anguilla eel (dim. of anguis snake) + -form.] Eel-shaped.

anguine.c: Anguine An"guine (?), a. [L. anguinus, fr. anguis snake.] Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a snake or serpent. “The anguine or snakelike reptiles.” Owen.

anguish.c: Anguish An"guish (?), n. [OE. anguishe, anguise, angoise, F. angoisse, fr. L. angustia narrowness, difficulty, distress, fr. angustus narrow, difficult, fr. angere to press together. See Anger.] Extreme pain, either of body or mind; excruciating distress.
Anguish An"guish, v. t. [Cf. F. angoisser, fr. L. angustiare.] To distress with extreme pain or grief. [R.] Temple.

angular.c: Angular An"gu*lar (?), a. [L. angularis, fr. angulus angle, corner. See Angle.] 1. Relating to an angle or to angles; having an angle or angles; forming an angle or corner; sharp-cornered; pointed; as, an angular figure.
Angular An"gu*lar, n. (Anat.) A bone in the base of the lower jaw of many birds, reptiles, and fishes.

angularity.c: Angularity An`gu*lar"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being angular; angularness.

angularly.c: Angularly An"gu*lar*ly (?), adv. In an angular manner; with of at angles or corners. B. Jonson.

angularness.c: Angularness An"gu*lar*ness, n. The quality of being angular.

angulated.c: Angulated Angulate { An"gu*late (?), An"gu*la`ted (?), } a. [L. angulatus, p. p. of angulare to make angular.] Having angles or corners; angled; as, angulate leaves.

angulate.c: Angulate An"gu*late (?), v. t. To make angular.

angulation.c: Angulation An`gu*la"tion (?), n. A making angular; angular formation. Huxley.

angulodentate.c: Angulo-dentate An"gu*lo-den"tate (?), a.. [L. angulus angle + dens, dentis, tooth.] (Bot.) Angularly toothed, as certain leaves.

angulometer.c: Angulometer An"gu*lom"e*ter (?), n. [L. angulus angle + -meter.] An instrument for measuring external angles.

angulosity.c: Angulosity An`gu*los"i*ty (?), n. A state of being angulous or angular. [Obs.]

angulous.c: Angulous An"gu*lous (?), a. [L. angulosus: cf. F. anguleux.] Angular; having corners; hooked. [R.]

angust.c: Angust An*gust" (?), a. [L. angustus. See Anguish.] Narrow; strait. [Obs.]

angustate.c: Angustate An*gus"tate (?), a. [L. angustatus, p. p. of angustare to make narrow.] Narrowed.

angustation.c: Angustation An`gus*ta"tion (?), n. The act of making narrow; a straitening or contacting. Wiseman.

angusticlave.c: Angusticlave An*gus"ti*clave (ăn*gŭs"tĭ*klāv), n. [L. angustus narrow + clavus a nail, a stripe.] (Rom. Antiq.) A narrow stripe of purple worn by the equites on each side of the tunic as a sign of rank.

angustifolious.c: Angustifolious Angustifoliate { An*gus`ti*fo"li*ate (ăn*gŭs`tĭ*fō"lĭ*at), An*gus`ti*fo"li*ous (ăn*gŭs`tĭ*fō"lĭ*ŭs), } a. [L. angustus narrow (see Anguish) + folium leaf.] (Bot.) Having narrow leaves. Wright.

angustura.c: Angustura bark An`gus*tu"ra bark` (?). See Angostura bark.

angwantibo.c: Angwantibo ‖An`gwan*ti"bo (?), n. (Zool.) A small lemuroid mammal (Arctocebus Calabarensis) of Africa. It has only a rudimentary tail.

anhang.c: Anhang An*hang" (?), v. t. [AS. onhangian.] To hang. [Obs.] Chaucer.

anharmonic.c: Anharmonic An`har*mon"ic (?), a. [F. anharmonique, fr. Gr. 'an priv. +? harmonic.] (Math.) Not harmonic.

anhelation.c: Anhelation An`he*la"tion (?), n. [L. anhelatio, fr. anhelare to pant; an (perh. akin to E. on) + halare to breathe: cf. F. anhélation.] Short and rapid breathing; a panting; asthma. Glanvill.

anhele.c: Anhele An*hele" (?), v. i. [Cf. OF. aneler, anheler. See Anhelation.] To pant; to be breathlessly anxious or eager (for). [Obs.]

anhelous.c: Anhelous An*he"lous (?), a. [L. anhelus.] Short of breath; panting.

anhima.c: Anhima ‖An"hi*ma (?), n. [Brazilian name.] A South American aquatic bird; the horned screamer or kamichi (Palamedea cornuta). See Kamichi.

anhinga.c: Anhinga ‖An*hin"ga (?), n. [Pg.] (Zool.) An aquatic bird of the southern United States (Platus anhinga); the darter, or snakebird.

anhistous.c: Anhistous An*his"tous (?), a. [Gr. 'an priv. + "isto`s web, tissue: cf. F. anhiste.] (Biol.) Without definite structure; as, an anhistous membrane.

anhydride.c: Anhydride An*hy"dride (?), n. [See Anhydrous.] (Chem.) An oxide of a nonmetallic body or an organic radical, capable of forming an acid by uniting with the elements of water; -- so called because it may be formed from an acid by the abstraction of water.

anhydrite.c: Anhydrite An*hy"drite (?), n. [See Anhydrous.] (Min.) A mineral of a white or a slightly bluish color, usually massive. It is anhydrous sulphate of lime, and differs from gypsum in not containing water (whence the name).

anhydrous.c: Anhydrous An*hy"drous (?), a. [Gr.? wanting water; 'an priv. + "y`dwr water.] Destitute of water; as, anhydrous salts or acids.

ano.c: Ano Ani ‖A"ni (?) or ‖A"no (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) A black bird of tropical America, the West Indies and Florida (Crotophaga ani), allied to the cuckoos, having a compressed, bladelike bill and remarkable for communistic nesting.

annicut.c: Annicut Anicut ‖An"i*cut, ‖An"ni*cut (?), n. [Tamil anai kattu dam building.] A dam or mole made in the course of a stream for the purpose of regulating the flow of a system of irrigation. [India] Brande & C.

anidiomatical.c: Anidiomatical An*id`i*o*mat"ic*al (?), a. [Gr. 'an priv. + E. idiomatical.] Not idiomatic. [R.] Landor.

anientise.c: Anientise Anient { An"i*ent, An`i*en"tise (?), } v. t. [OF. anientir, F. anéantir.] To frustrate; to bring to naught; to annihilate. [Obs.] Chaucer.

anigh.c: Anigh A*nigh" (?), prep. & adv. [Pref. a- + nigh.] Nigh. [Archaic]

anights.c: Anights Anight { A*night" (?), A*nights" (?), } adv. [OE. on niht.] In the night time; at night. [Archaic]

anil.c: Anil An"il (?), n. [F. anil, Sp. anīl, or Pg. anil; all fr. Ar. an-nīl, for al-nīl the indigo plant, fr. Skr. nīla dark blue, nīlī indigo, indigo plant. Cf. Lilac.] (Bot.) A West Indian plant (Indigofera anil), one of the original sources of indigo; also, the indigo dye.

anile.c: Anile An"ile (?), a. [L. anilis, fr. anus an old woman.] Old-womanish; imbecile. “Anile ideas.” Walpole.

anilic.c: Anilic An*il"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or obtained from, anil; indigotic; -- applied to an acid formed by the action of nitric acid on indigo. [R.]

anilide.c: Anilide An"i*lide (?), n. (Chem.) One of a class of compounds which may be regarded as amides in which more or less of the hydrogen has been replaced by phenyl.

aniline.c: Aniline An"i*line (?; 277), n. [See Anil.] (Chem.) An organic base belonging to the phenylamines. It may be regarded as ammonia in which one hydrogen atom has been replaced by the radical phenyl. It is a colorless, oily liquid, originally obtained from indigo by distillation, but now largely manufactured from coal tar or nitrobenzene as a base from which many brilliant dyes are made.
Aniline An"i*line, a. Made from, or of the nature of, aniline.

anilinism.c: anilinism anilism ‖an"i*lin*ism (ăn"ĭ*lĭn*ĭz'm), an"i*lism (ăn"ĭ*lĭz'm), n. [Aniline + -ism.] (Med.) A disease caused by chronic exposure to aniline; aniline toxicity.

anility.c: Anility A*nil"i*ty (?), n. [L. anilitas. See Anile.] The state of being an old woman; old-womanishness; dotage. “Marks of anility.” Sterne.

animadversal.c: Animadversal An`i*mad*ver"sal (?), n. The faculty of perceiving; a percipient. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

animadversion.c: Animadversion An`i*mad*ver"sion (?), n. [L. animadversio, fr. animadvertere: cf. F. animadversion. See Animadvert.] 1. The act or power of perceiving or taking notice; direct or simple perception. [Obs.]

animadversive.c: Animadversive An`i*mad*ver"sive (?), a. Having the power of perceiving; percipient. [Archaic] Glanvill.

animadvert.c: Animadvert An`i*mad*vert" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Animadverted; p. pr. & vb. n. Animadverting.] [L. animadvertere; animus mind + advertere to turn to; ad to + vertere to turn.] 1. To take notice; to observe; -- commonly followed by that. Dr. H. More.

animadverter.c: Animadverter An`i*mad*vert"er (?), n. One who animadverts; a censurer; also [Obs.], a chastiser.

animal.c: Animal An"i*mal (?), n. [L., fr. anima breath, soul: cf. F. animal. See Animate.] 1. An organized living being endowed with sensation and the power of voluntary motion, and also characterized by taking its food into an internal cavity or stomach for digestion; by giving carbonic acid to the air and taking oxygen in the process of respiration; and by increasing in motive power or active aggressive force with progress to maturity.
Animal An"i*mal, a. [Cf. F. animal.] 1. Of or relating to animals; as, animal functions.

animalculine.c: Animalculine Animalcular { An`i*mal"cu*lar (?), An`i*mal"cu*line (?), } a. Of, pertaining to, or resembling, animalcules. “Animalcular life.” Tyndall.

animalcule.c: Animalcule An`i*mal"cule (?), n. [As if fr. a L. animalculum, dim. of animal.] 1. A small animal, as a fly, spider, etc. [Obs.] Ray.

animalculism.c: Animalculism An`i*mal"cu*lism (?), n. [Cf. F. animalculisme.] 1. (Biol.) The theory which seeks to explain certain physiological and pathological phenomena by means of animalcules.

animalculist.c: Animalculist An`i*mal"cu*list (?), n. [Cf. F. animalculiste.] 1. One versed in the knowledge of animalcules. Keith.

animalculum.c: Animalculum ‖An`i*mal"cu*lum (?), n.; pl. Animalcula (?). [NL. See Animalcule.] An animalcule.

animalism.c: Animalism An"i*mal*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. animalisme.] The state, activity, or enjoyment of animals; mere animal life without intellectual or moral qualities or objectives; preoccupation with sensual, physical, or carnal pleasures.

animality.c: Animality An`i*mal"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. animalité.] Animal existence or nature. Locke.

animalization.c: Animalization An`i*mal*i*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. animalisation.] 1. The act of animalizing; the giving of animal life, or endowing with animal properties.

animalize.c: Animalize An"i*mal*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Animalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Animalizing.] [Cf. F. animaliser.] 1. To endow with the properties of an animal; to represent in animal form. Warburton.

animastic.c: Animastic An`i*mas"tic (?), a. [L. anima breath, life.] Pertaining to mind or spirit; spiritual.

animate.c: Animate An"i*mate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Animated; p. pr. & vb. n. Animating.] [L. animatus, p. p. of animare, fr. anima breath, soul; akin to animus soul, mind, Gr.? wind, Skr. an to breathe, live, Goth. us-anan to expire (us- out), Icel. önd breath, anda to breathe, OHG. ando anger. Cf. Animal.] 1. To give natural life to; to make alive; to quicken; as, the soul animates the body.
Animate An"i*mate (?), a. [L. animatus, p. p.] Endowed with life; alive; living; animated; lively.

animated.c: Animated An"i*ma`ted (?), a. Endowed with life; full of life or spirit; indicating animation; lively; vigorous. “Animated sounds.” Pope. “Animated bust.” Gray. “Animated descriptions.” Lewis.

animater.c: Animater An"i*ma`ter (?), n. One who animates. De Quincey.

animating.c: Animating An"i*ma"ting, a. Causing animation; life-giving; inspiriting; rousing. “Animating cries.” Pope. -- An"i*ma`ting*ly, adv.

animation.c: Animation An`i*ma"tion (?), n. [L. animatio, fr. animare.] 1. The act of animating, or giving life or spirit; the state of being animate or alive.

animative.c: Animative An"i*ma*tive (?), a. Having the power of giving life or spirit. Johnson.

animator.c: Animator An"i*ma`tor (?), n. [L. animare.] One who, or that which, animates; an animater. Sir T. Browne.

anime.c: Anime ‖A"ni*mé` (?), a. [F., animated.] (Her.) Of a different tincture from the animal itself; -- said of the eyes of a rapacious animal. Brande & C.

Anime ‖A"ni*mé (?), n. [F. animé animated (from the insects that are entrapped in it); or native name.] A resin exuding from a tropical American tree (Hymenæa courbaril), and much used by varnish makers. Ure.

animism.c: Animism An"i*mism (?), n. [Cf. F. animisme, fr. L. anima soul. See Animate.] 1. The doctrine, taught by Stahl, that the soul is the proper principle of life and development in the body.

animist.c: Animist An"i*mist (?), n. [Cf. F. animiste.] One who maintains the doctrine of animism.

animistic.c: Animistic An`i*mis"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to animism. Huxley. Tylor.

animous.c: Animous Animose { An`i*mose" (?), An"i*mous (?), } a. [L. animosus, fr. animus soul, spirit, courage.] Full of spirit; hot; vehement; resolute. [Obs.] Ash.

animosity.c: Animosity An`i*mos"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Animosities (?). [F. animosité, fr. L. animositas. See Animose, Animate, v. t.] 1. Mere spiritedness or courage. [Obs.] Skelton.

animus.c: Animus An"i*mus (?), n.; pl. Animi (?). [L., mind.] Animating spirit; intention; temper.

anion.c: Anion An"i*on (?), n. [Gr.?, neut.?, p. pr. of? to go up;? up +? to go.] (Chem.) An electro-negative atom or group of atoms, or the element which, in electro-chemical decompositions, is evolved at the anode; -- opposed to cation. Faraday.

anise.c: Anise An"ise (ăn"ĭs), n. [OE. anys, F. anis, L. anisum, anethum, fr. Gr. 'a`nison, 'a`nhqon.] 1. (Bot.) An umbelliferous plant (Pimpinella anisum) growing naturally in Egypt, and cultivated in Spain, Malta, etc., for its carminative and aromatic seeds.

aniseed.c: Aniseed An"i*seed (?), n. The seed of the anise; also, a cordial prepared from it. “Oil of aniseed.” Brande & C.

anisette.c: Anisette ‖An`i*sette" (?), n. [F.] A French cordial or liqueur flavored with anise seeds. De Colange.

anisic.c: Anisic A*nis"ic (?), a. Of or derived from anise; as, anisic acid; anisic alcohol.

anisocoria.c: anisocoria ‖an`i*so*co"ri*a (ăn`i*so*kō"rĭ*ȧ), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'a`nisos unequal ('an priv. + 'i`sos equal) + ko`rh pupil.] (Med.) Inequality of the pupils of the eyes.

anisodactyls.c: anisodactyls anisodactyla { ‖an`i*so*dac"ty*la (ăn`i*so*dăk"tĭ*lȧ), an`i*so*dac"tyls (ăn`i*so*dăk"tĭlz), } n. pl. [NL. anisodactyla, fr. Gr. 'a`nisos unequal ('an priv. + 'i`sos equal) + da`ktylos finger.] (Zool.) (a) A group of herbivorous mammals characterized by having the hoofs in a single series around the foot, as the elephant, rhinoceros, etc. (b) A group of perching birds which are anisodactylous.

anisodactylous.c: Anisodactylous An`i*so*dac"ty*lous (?), a. (Zool.) Characterized by unequal toes, three turned forward and one backward, as in most passerine birds.

anisole.c: anisole Anisol An"i*sol anisole (?), n. [Anisic + -ol.] (Chem.) Methyl phenyl ether, C6H5.O.CH3, got by distilling anisic acid or by the action of methide on potassium phenolate.

anisomeric.c: Anisomeric An`i*so*mer"ic (?), a. [Gr.? unequal +? part.] (Chem.) Not isomeric; not made of the same components in the same proportions.

anisomerous.c: Anisomerous An`i*som"er*ous (?), a. [See Anisomeric.] (Bot.) Having the number of floral organs unequal, as four petals and six stamens.

anisometric.c: Anisometric An`i*so*met"ric (?), a. [Gr. 'an priv. + E. isometric.] Not isometric; having unsymmetrical parts; -- said of crystals with three unequal axes. Dana.

anisometropia.c: Anisometropia ‖An`i*so*me*tro"pi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? +? measure +?,?, eye.] Unequal refractive power in the two eyes.

anisopetalous.c: Anisopetalous An`i*so*pet"al*ous (?), a. [Gr.? unequal +? leaf.] (Bot.) Having unequal petals.

anisophyllous.c: Anisophyllous An`i*soph"yl*lous (?), a. [Gr.? unequal +? leaf.] (Bot.) Having unequal leaves.

anisopleura.c: Anisopleura ‖An`i*so*pleu"ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? unequal +? side.] (Zool.) A primary division of gastropods, including those having spiral shells. The two sides of the body are unequally developed.

anisopoda.c: Anisopoda ‖An`i*sop"o*da (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? unequal + -poda.] (Zool.) A division of Crustacea, which, in some its characteristics, is intermediate between Amphipoda and Isopoda.

anisospore.c: Anisospore An"i*so*spore` (?), n. [Gr.? priv. + isospore.] (Biol.) A sexual spore in which the sexes differ in size; -- opposed to isospore.

anisostemonous.c: Anisostemonous An`i*so*stem"o*nous (?), a. [Gr.? unequal +? warp, thread;? to stand.] (Bot.) Having unequal stamens; having stamens different in number from the petals.

anisosthenic.c: Anisosthenic An`i*so*sthen"ic (?), a. [Gr.? unequal +? strength.] Of unequal strength.

anisotropic.c: Anisotropic Anisotrope { An"i*so*trope` (?), An`i*so*trop"ic (?), } a. [Gr.? unequal +? a turning,? to turn.] (Physics) Not isotropic; having different properties in different directions; thus, crystals of the isometric system are optically isotropic, but all other crystals are anisotropic.

anisyl.c: Anisyl An"i*syl (?), n. (Org. Chem.) (a) The univalent radical, CH3.O.C6H4-, of which anisol is the hydride. (b) The univalent radical CH3.O.C6H4.CH2-; as, anisyl alcohol. (c) The univalent radical CH3.O.C6H4.CO-, of anisic acid.

anito.c: Anito ‖A*ni"to (?), n.; pl. -tos (#). [Sp.] In Guam and the Philippines, an idol, fetich, or spirit.

anker.c: Anker An"ker (?), n. [D. anker: cf. LL. anceria, ancheria.] A liquid measure in various countries of Europe. The Dutch anker, formerly also used in England, contained about 10 of the old wine gallons, or 8½ imperial gallons.

ankerite.c: Ankerite An"ker*ite (?), n. [So called from Prof. Anker of Austria: cf. F. ankérite, G. ankerit.] (Min.) A mineral closely related to dolomite, but containing iron.

ankh.c: Ankh Ankh (?), n. [Egypt.] (Egypt. Archæol.) 1. A tau cross with a loop at the top, used as an attribute or sacred emblem, symbolizing generation or enduring life. Called also crux ansata.

ankle.c: Ankle An"kle (ăṉ"k'l), n. [OE. ancle, anclow, AS. ancleow; akin to Icel. ökkla, ökli, Dan. and Sw. ankel, D. enklaauw, enkel, G. enkel, and perh. OHG. encha, ancha thigh, shin: cf. Skr. anga limb, anguri finger. Cf. Haunch.] The joint which connects the foot with the leg; the tarsus.

ankled.c: Ankled An"kled (?), a. Having ankles; -- used in composition; as, well-ankled. Beau. & Fl.

anklet.c: Anklet An"klet (?), n. 1. An ornament or a fetter for the ankle; an ankle ring.

ankus.c: Ankus ‖An"kus (?), n. [Hind., fr. Skr. aṅkuça.] An elephant goad with a sharp spike and hook, resembling a short-handled boat hook. [India] Kipling.

ankylose.c: Ankylose An"ky*lose (?), v. t. & i. Same as Anchylose.

ankylostomiasis.c: ankylostomiasis ancylostomiasis ‖an`ky*los*to*mi"a*sis, an`cy*los*to*mi"a*sis (ăṉ`kĭ*lŏs*to*mī"ȧ*sĭs), n. [NL., fr. Ankylostoma, var. of Agchylostoma, generic name of one genus of the parasitic nematodes.] (Med.) A disease caused by the hookworm parasites of the genus Ancylostoma (especially Ancylostoma duodenale), and Necator americanus. Typically, infection in humans occurs in the small intestine. In the small intestine they suck the blood from the wall and, when present in large numbers, produce a severe anaemia. Called also miner's anaemia, tunnel disease, brickmaker's anaemia, Egyptian chlorosis.

anlace.c: Anlace An"lace (?), n. [Origin unknown.] A broad dagger formerly worn at the girdle. [Written also anelace.]

anlaut.c: Anlaut ‖An"laut` (?), n. [G.; an on + laut sound.] (Phon.) An initial sound, as of a word or syllable.

annat.c: Annat Ann { Ann (?), An"nat (?), } n. [LL. annata income of a year, also, of half a year, fr. L. annus year: cf. F. annate annats.] (Scots Law) A half years's stipend, over and above what is owing for the incumbency, due to a minister's heirs after his decease.

anna.c: Anna ‖An"na (?), n. [Hindi ānā.] An East Indian money of account, the sixteenth of a rupee, or about 2? cents.

annalist.c: Annalist An"nal*ist, n. [Cf. F. annaliste.] A writer of annals.

annalistic.c: Annalistic An`nal*is"tic (?), a. Pertaining to, or after the manner of, an annalist; as, the dry annalistic style.“A stiff annalistic method.” Sir G. C. Lewis.

annalize.c: Annalize An"nal*ize (?), v. t. To record in annals. Sheldon.

annals.c: Annals An"nals (?), n. pl. [L. annalis (sc. liber), and more frequently in the pl. annales (sc. libri), chronicles, fr. annus year. Cf. Annual.] 1. A relation of events in chronological order, each event being recorded under the year in which it happened. “Annals the revolution.” Macaulay. “The annals of our religion.” Rogers.

annates.c: Annates Annats { An"nats (?), An"nates (?), } n. pl. [See Ann.] (Eccl. Law) The first year's profits of a spiritual preferment, anciently paid by the clergy to the pope; first fruits. In England, they now form a fund for the augmentation of poor livings.

anneal.c: Anneal An*neal" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Annealed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Annealing.] [OE. anelen to heat, burn, AS. an?lan; an on +?lan to burn; also OE. anelen to enamel, prob. influenced by OF. neeler, nieler, to put a black enamel on gold or silver, F. nieller, fr. LL. nigellare to blacken, fr. L. nigellus blackish, dim. of niger black. Cf. Niello, Negro.] 1. To subject to great heat, and then cool slowly, as glass, cast iron, steel, or other metal, for the purpose of rendering it less brittle; to temper; to toughen.

annealer.c: Annealer An*neal"er (?), n. One who, or that which, anneals.

annealing.c: Annealing An*neal"ing, n. 1. The process used to render glass, iron, etc., less brittle, performed by allowing them to cool very gradually from a high heat.
