antipathize.c: Antipathize An*tip"a*thize (ăn*tĭp"ȧ*thīz), v. i. To feel or show antipathy. [R.]

antipathous.c: Antipathous An*tip"a*thous (ăn*tĭp"ȧ*thŭs), a. Having a natural contrariety; adverse; antipathetic. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

antipathy.c: Antipathy An*tip"a*thy (ăn*tĭp"ȧ*thy̆), n.; pl. Antipathies (?). [L. antipathia, Gr. 'antipa`qeia; 'anti` against + paqei^n to suffer. Cf. F. antipathie. See Pathos.] 1. Contrariety or opposition in feeling; settled aversion or dislike; repugnance; distaste.

antipeptone.c: Antipeptone An`ti*pep"tone (ăn`tĭ*pĕp"tōn), n. (Physiol. Chem.) A product of gastric and pancreatic digestion, differing from hemipeptone in not being decomposed by the continued action of pancreatic juice.

antiperiodic.c: Antiperiodic An`ti*pe`ri*od"ic (ăn`tĭ*pē`rĭ*ŏd"ĭk), n. (Med.) A remedy possessing the property of preventing the return of periodic paroxysms, or exacerbations, of disease, as in intermittent fevers.

antiperistaltic.c: Antiperistaltic An`ti*per`i*stal"tic (ăn`tĭ*pĕr`ĭ*stăl"tĭk), a. (Med.) Opposed to, or checking motion; acting upward; -- applied to an inverted action of the intestinal tube.

antiperistasis.c: Antiperistasis ‖An`ti*pe*ris"ta*sis (ăn`tĭ*pe*rĭs"tȧ*sĭs), n. [Gr. 'antiperi`stasis; 'anti` against + peri`stasis a standing around, fr. periista`nai to stand around; peri` around + "ista`nai to stand.] Opposition by which the quality opposed acquires strength; resistance or reaction roused by opposition or by the action of an opposite principle or quality.

antipetalous.c: Antipetalous An`ti*pet"al*ous (?), a. [Pref. anti- + petal.] (Bot.) Standing before a petal, as a stamen.

antipharmic.c: Antipharmic An`ti*phar"mic (?), a. [Pref. anti- + Gr.? poison.] (Med.) Antidotal; alexipharmic.

antiphlogistian.c: Antiphlogistian An`ti*phlo*gis"tian (?), n. An opposer of the theory of phlogiston.

antiphlogistic.c: Antiphlogistic An`ti*phlo*gis"tic (?), a. 1. (Chem.) Opposed to the doctrine of phlogiston.
Antiphlogistic An`ti*phlo*gis"tic, n. (Med.) Any medicine or diet which tends to check inflammation. Coxe.

antiphon.c: Antiphon An"ti*phon (?), n. [LL. antiphona, fr. Gr. 'anti`fwna. See Anthem.] 1. A musical response; alternate singing or chanting. See Antiphony, and Antiphone.

antiphonal.c: Antiphonal An*tiph"o*nal (?), a. Of or pertaining to antiphony, or alternate singing; sung alternately by a divided choir or opposite choirs. Wheatly. -- An*tiph"o*nal*ly, adv.
Antiphonal An*tiph"o*nal, n. A book of antiphons or anthems.

antiphonary.c: Antiphonary An*tiph"o*na*ry (?), n. [LL. antiphonarium. See Antiphoner.] A book containing a collection of antiphons; the book in which the antiphons of the breviary, with their musical notes, are contained.

antiphone.c: Antiphone An"ti*phone (?), n. (Mus.) The response which one side of the choir makes to the other in a chant; alternate chanting or signing.

antiphoner.c: Antiphoner An*tiph"o*ner (?), n. [F. antiphonaire. See Antiphon.] A book of antiphons. Chaucer.

antiphony.c: Antiphony An*tiph"o*ny (?), n.; pl. Antiphonies (?). [See Antiphon.] 1. A musical response; also, antiphonal chanting or signing.

antiphrasis.c: Antiphrasis ‖An*tiph"ra*sis (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to express by antithesis or negation.] (Rhet.) The use of words in a sense opposite to their proper meaning; as when a court of justice is called a court of vengeance.

antiphrastical.c: Antiphrastical Antiphrastic { An`ti*phras"tic (?), An`ti*phras"tic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?.] Pertaining to antiphrasis. -- An`ti*phras"tic*al*ly, adv.

antiphthisic.c: Antiphthisic An`ti*phthis"ic (?), a. (Med.) Relieving or curing phthisis, or consumption. -- n. A medicine for phthisis.

antiphysical.c: Antiphysical An`ti*phys"ic*al (?), a. [Pref. anti- + physical.] Contrary to nature; unnatural.
Antiphysical An`ti*phys"ic*al, a. [Pref. anti- + Gr.? to inflate.] (Med.) Relieving flatulence; carminative.

antipodagric.c: Antipodagric An`ti*po*dag"ric (?), a. (Med.) Good against gout. -- n. A medicine for gout.

antipodal.c: Antipodal An*tip"o*dal (?), a. 1. Pertaining to the antipodes; situated on the opposite side of the globe.

antipode.c: Antipode An"ti*pode (?), n. One of the antipodes; anything exactly opposite.

antipodean.c: Antipodean An`ti*po"de*an (?), a. Pertaining to the antipodes, or the opposite side of the world; antipodal.

antipodes.c: Antipodes An*tip"o*des (?), n. [L. pl., fr. Gr.? with the feet opposite, pl.??; 'anti` against +?,?, foot.] 1. Those who live on the side of the globe diametrically opposite.

antipole.c: Antipole An"ti*pole (?), n. The opposite pole; anything diametrically opposed. Geo. Eliot.

antipope.c: Antipope An"ti*pope (?), n. One who is elected, or claims to be, pope in opposition to the pope canonically chosen; esp. applied to those popes who resided at Avignon during the Great Schism.

antipsoric.c: Antipsoric An`tip*sor"ic (?), a. (Med.) Of use in curing the itch. -- n. An antipsoric remedy.

antiptosis.c: Antiptosis ‖An`tip*to"sis (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?; 'anti` against +? a falling, a case,? to fall.] (Gram.) The putting of one case for another.

antiputrescent.c: Antiputrescent Antiputrefactive { An`ti*pu`tre*fac"tive (?), An`ti*pu*tres"cent (?), } a. Counteracting, or preserving from, putrefaction; antiseptic.

antipyic.c: Antipyic An`ti*py"ic (?), a. [Pref. anti- + Gr.?,?, pus.] (Med.) Checking or preventing suppuration. -- n. An antipyic medicine.

antipyresis.c: Antipyresis ‖An`ti*py*re"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'anti` against +? to be feverish, fr.? fire.] (Med.) The condition or state of being free from fever.

antipyretic.c: Antipyretic An`ti*py*ret"ic (?), a. (Med.) Efficacious in preventing or allaying fever. -- n. A febrifuge.

antipyrine.c: Antipyrine An`ti*py"rine (?), n. (Med.) An artificial alkaloid, believed to be efficient in abating fever.

antipyrotic.c: Antipyrotic An`ti*py*rot"ic (?), a. (Med.) Good against burns or pyrosis. -- n. Anything of use in preventing or healing burns or pyrosis.

antiquarian.c: Antiquarian An`ti*qua"ri*an (?), a. [See Antiquary]. Pertaining to antiquaries, or to antiquity; as, antiquarian literature.

antiquarianism.c: Antiquarianism An`ti*qua"ri*an*ism (?), n. Character of an antiquary; study or love of antiquities. Warburton.

antiquarianize.c: Antiquarianize An`ti*qua"ri*an*ize (?), v. i. To act the part of an antiquary. [Colloq.]

antiquary.c: Antiquary An"ti*qua*ry (?), a. [L. antiquarius, fr. antiquus ancient. See Antique.] Pertaining to antiquity. [R.] “Instructed by the antiquary times.” Shak.

Antiquary An"ti*qua*ry, n.; pl. Antiquaries (?). One devoted to the study of ancient times through their relics, as inscriptions, monuments, remains of ancient habitations, statues, coins, manuscripts, etc.; one who searches for and studies the relics of antiquity.

antiquate.c: Antiquate An"ti*quate (?), v. t. [L. antiquatus, p. p. of antiquare, fr. antiquus ancient.] To make old, or obsolete; to make antique; to make old in such a degree as to put out of use; hence, to make void, or abrogate.

antiquated.c: Antiquated An"ti*qua`ted (?), a. Grown old. Hence: Bygone; obsolete; out of use; old-fashioned; as, an antiquated law. “Antiquated words.” Dryden.

antiquatedness.c: Antiquatedness An"ti*qua`ted*ness, n. Quality of being antiquated.

antiquation.c: Antiquation An`ti*qua"tion (?), n. [L. antiquatio, fr. antiquare.] The act of making antiquated, or the state of being antiquated. Beaumont.

antique.c: Antique An*tique" (?), a. [F., fr. L. antiquus old, ancient, equiv. to anticus, from ante before. Cf. Antic.]

Antique An*tique" (?), n. [F. See Antique, a. ] In general, anything very old; but in a more limited sense, a relic or object of ancient art; collectively, the antique, the remains of ancient art, as busts, statues, paintings, and vases.

antiquely.c: Antiquely An*tique"ly, adv. In an antique manner.

antiqueness.c: Antiqueness An*tique"ness, n. The quality of being antique; an appearance of ancient origin and workmanship.

antiquist.c: Antiquist An"ti*quist (?), n. An antiquary; a collector of antiques. [R.] Pinkerton.

antiquitarian.c: Antiquitarian An*tiq`ui*ta"ri*an (?), n. An admirer of antiquity. [Obs.]

antiquity.c: Antiquity An*tiq"ui*ty (?), n.; pl. Antiquities (?). [L. antiquitas, fr. antiquus: cf. F. antiquité. See Antique.] 1. The quality of being ancient; ancientness; great age; as, a statue of remarkable antiquity; a family of great antiquity.

antirachitic.c: Antirachitic An`ti*ra*chit"ic (?), a. (Med.) Good against the rickets.

antirenter.c: Antirenter An`ti*rent"er (?), n. One opposed to the payment of rent; esp. one of those who in 1840-47 resisted the collection of rents claimed by the patroons from the settlers on certain manorial lands in the State of New York. -- An`ti*rent"ism (?), n.

antisabbatarian.c: Antisabbatarian An`ti*sab`ba*ta"ri*an (?), n. (Eccl.) One of a sect which opposes the observance of the Christian Sabbath.

antisacerdotal.c: Antisacerdotal An`ti*sac`er*do"tal (?), a. Hostile to priests or the priesthood. Waterland.

antiscii.c: Antiscii Antiscians { An*tis"cians (?), ‖An*tis"ci*i (?), } n. pl. [L. antiscii, Gr.?, pl.; 'anti` against +? shadow.] The inhabitants of the earth, living on different sides of the equator, whose shadows at noon are cast in opposite directions.

antiscolic.c: Antiscolic Antiscoletic { An`ti*sco*let"ic (?), An`ti*scol"ic (?), } a. [Pref. anti- + Gr.? a worm.] (Med.) Anthelmintic.

antiscorbutic.c: Antiscorbutic An`ti*scor*bu"tic (?), a. (Med.) Counteracting scurvy. -- n. A remedy for scurvy.

antiscriptural.c: Antiscriptural An`ti*scrip"tur*al (?), a. Opposed to, or not in accordance with, the Holy Scriptures.

antisemitism.c: Anti-Semitism An`ti-Sem"i*tism (?), n. Opposition to, or hatred of, Semites, esp. Jews. The word is sometimes also applied to acts motivated by or evincing antisemitism. -- An`ti-Sem"ite (#), n. -- An`ti-Sem*it"ic (#), a.

antisepalous.c: Antisepalous An`ti*sep"al*ous (?), a. [Pref. anti- + sepal.] (Bot.) Standing before a sepal, or calyx leaf.

antisepsis.c: Antisepsis ‖An`ti*sep"sis (?), n. [NL. See Anti-; Sepsis.] Prevention of sepsis by excluding or destroying microorganisms.

antiseptical.c: Antiseptical Antiseptic { An`ti*sep"tic (?), An`ti*sep"tic*al (?), } a. Counteracting or preventing putrefaction, or a putrescent tendency in the system; antiputrefactive.

antiseptic.c: Antiseptic An`ti*sep"tic, n. a substance which kills or retards the growth of microorganisms, especially when used for protection against infection; a substance which prevents or retards putrefaction, or destroys, or protects from, putrefactive organisms; as, carbolic acid, alcohol, cinchona, and many other agents sold commercially.

antiseptically.c: Antiseptically An`ti*sep"tic*al*ly (?), adv. By means of antiseptics.

antisialagogue.c: Antisialagogue An`ti*si*al"a*gogue (?), a. (Med.) Checking the flow of saliva.
Antisialagogue An`ti*si*al"a*gogue, n. A remedy against excessive salivation.

antislavery.c: Antislavery An`ti*slav"er*y (?), a. Opposed to slavery. -- n. Opposition to slavery.

antisocial.c: Antisocial An`ti*so"cial (?), a. Tending to interrupt or destroy social intercourse; averse to society, or hostile to its existence; as, antisocial principles.

antisocialist.c: Antisocialist An`ti*so"cial*ist, n. One opposed to the doctrines and practices of socialists or socialism.

antisolar.c: Antisolar An`ti*so"lar (?), a. Opposite to the sun; -- said of the point in the heavens 180° distant from the sun.

antispasmodic.c: Antispasmodic An`ti*spas*mod"ic (?), a. (Med.) Good against spasms. -- n. A medicine which prevents or allays spasms or convulsions.

antispast.c: Antispast An"ti*spast (?), n. [L. antispastus, Gr.?, fr.? to draw the contrary way; 'anti` against +? to draw.] (Pros.) A foot of four syllables, the first and fourth short, and the second and third long (#).

antispastic.c: Antispastic An`ti*spas"tic (?), a. [Gr.?. See Antispast.] (Med.) (a) Believed to cause a revulsion of fluids or of humors from one part to another. [Obs.] (b) Counteracting spasms; antispasmodic. -- n. An antispastic agent.

antisplenetic.c: Antisplenetic An`ti*splen"e*tic (?; see Splenetic, 277), a. Good as a remedy against disease of the spleen. -- n. An antisplenetic medicine.

antistrophe.c: Antistrophe ‖An*tis"tro*phe (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to turn to the opposite side; 'anti` against +? to turn. See Strophe.] 1. In Greek choruses and dances, the returning of the chorus, exactly answering to a previous strophe or movement from right to left. Hence: The lines of this part of the choral song.

antistrophic.c: Antistrophic An`ti*stroph"ic (?), a. [Gr.?.] Of or pertaining to an antistrophe.

antistrophon.c: Antistrophon ‖An*tis"tro*phon (?), n. [Gr.? turned opposite ways.] (Rhet.) An argument retorted on an opponent. Milton.

antistrumatic.c: Antistrumatic An`ti*stru"mat"ic (?), a. (Med.) Antistrumous. -- n. A medicine for scrofula.

antistrumous.c: Antistrumous An`ti*stru"mous (?), a. (Med.) Good against scrofulous disorders. Johnson. Wiseman.

antisyphilitic.c: Antisyphilitic An`ti*syph`i*lit"ic (?), a. (Med.) Efficacious against syphilis. -- n. A medicine for syphilis.

antitheism.c: Antitheism An`ti*the"ism (?), n. The doctrine of antitheists. -- An`ti*the*is"tic (?), a.

antitheist.c: Antitheist An`ti*the"ist, n. A disbeliever in the existence of God.

antithesis.c: Antithesis An*tith"e*sis (?), n.; pl. Antitheses. (?) [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to set against, to oppose; 'anti` against +? to set. See Thesis.] 1. (Rhet.) An opposition or contrast of words or sentiments occurring in the same sentence; as, “The prodigal robs his heir; the miser robs himself.” “He had covertly shot at Cromwell; he how openly aimed at the Queen.”

antithet.c: Antithet An"ti*thet (?), n. [L. antitheton, fr. Gr.?,?, antithetic.] An antithetic or contrasted statement. Bacon.

antithetical.c: Antithetical Antithetic { An`ti*thet"ic (?), An`ti*thet"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?.] Pertaining to antithesis, or opposition of words and sentiments; containing, or of the nature of, antithesis; contrasted.

antitoxine.c: Antitoxine Antitoxin { An`ti*tox"in, An`ti*tox"ine } (?), n. [Pref. anti- + toxin.] A substance (sometimes the product of a specific micro-organism and sometimes naturally present in the blood or tissues of an animal), capable of producing immunity from certain diseases, or of counteracting the poisonous effects of pathogenic bacteria.

antitrade.c: Anti-trade An"ti-trade`, n. A westerly wind which blows nearly continuously between 30° and 50° of latitude in both the northern and the southern hemisphere.

antitragus.c: Antitragus ‖An*tit"ra*gus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?.] (Anat.) A prominence on the lower posterior portion of the concha of the external ear, opposite the tragus. See Ear.

antitrochanter.c: Antitrochanter ‖An`ti*tro*chan"ter (?), n. (Anat.) An articular surface on the ilium of birds against which the great trochanter of the femur plays.

antitropous.c: Antitropous Antitropal { An*tit"ro*pal (?), An*tit"ro*pous (?), } a. [Pref. anti- + Gr.? turn,? to turn.] (Bot.) At the extremity most remote from the hilum, as the embryo, or inverted with respect to the seed, as the radicle. Lindley.

antitype.c: Antitype An"ti*type (?), n. [Gr.? of corresponding form; 'anti` against +? type, figure. See Type.] That of which the type is the pattern or representation; that which is represented by the type or symbol.

antitypical.c: Antitypical An`ti*typ"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to an antitype; explaining the type. -- An`ti*typ"ic*al*ly, adv.

antitypous.c: Antitypous An*tit"y*pous (?), a. [Gr.?.] Resisting blows; hard. [Obs.] Cudworth.

antitypy.c: Antitypy An*tit"y*py (?), n. [Gr.?.] Opposition or resistance of matter to force. [R.] Sir W. Hamilton.

antivaccination.c: Antivaccination An`ti*vac`ci*na"tion (?), n. Opposition to vaccination. London Times.

antivaccinist.c: Antivaccinist An`ti*vac"ci*nist, n. One opposed to vaccination.

antivariolous.c: Antivariolous An`ti*va*ri"o*lous (?), a. Preventing the contagion of smallpox.

antivenereal.c: Antivenereal An`ti*ve*ne"re*al (?), a. Good against venereal poison; antisyphilitic.

antivenin.c: Antivenin An`ti*ve"nin (?), n. [Written also antivenen, antivenine.] [Pref. anti- + L. venenum poison.] (Physiol. Chem.) The serum of blood rendered antitoxic to a venom by repeated injections of small doses of the venom; also, the component of such a serum which is antitoxic to the venom.

antivivisectionist.c: Antivivisectionist An`ti*viv`i*sec"tion*ist, n. One opposed to vivisection

antizymotic.c: Antizymotic An`ti*zy*mot"ic (?), a. (Med.) Preventing fermentation or decomposition. -- n. An agent so used.

antler.c: Antler Ant"ler (?), n. [OE. auntelere, OF. antoillier, andoiller, endouiller, fr. F. andouiller, fr. an assumed LL. antocularis, fr. L. ante before + oculus eye. See Ocular.] (Zool.) The entire horn, or any branch of the horn, of a cervine animal, as of a stag.

antlia.c: Antlia ‖Ant"li*a (?), n.; pl. Antilæ (?). [L., a pump, Gr,? hold of a ship] (Zool.) The spiral tubular proboscis of lepidopterous insects. See Lepidoptera.

antlion.c: Ant-lion Ant"-li`on (?), n. (Zool.) A neuropterous insect, the larva of which makes in the sand a pitfall to capture ants, etc. The common American species is Myrmeleon obsoletus, the European is Myrmeleon formicarius.

antoecians.c: Antoecians Antoeci ‖An*tœ"ci (ăn*tē"sī), An*tœ"cians (-shainz), n. pl. [NL. antoeci, fr. Gr. pl. 'a`ntoiki; 'anti` opposite + o'ikei^n to live.] Those who live under the same meridian, but on opposite parallels of latitude, north and south of the equator.

antonomasia.c: Antonomasia ‖An`to*no*ma"si*a (?; 277), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to name instead;? +? to name,? name.] (Rhet.) The use of some epithet or the name of some office, dignity, or the like, instead of the proper name of the person; as when his majesty is used for a king, or when, instead of Aristotle, we say, the philosopher; or, conversely, the use of a proper name instead of an appellative, as when a wise man is called a Solomon, or an eminent orator a Cicero.

antonomastic.c: Antonomastic An`to*no*mas"tic (?), a. Pertaining to, or characterized by, antonomasia. -- An`to*no*mas"tic*al*ly (?), adv.

antonym.c: Antonym An"to*nym (?), n. [Gr.? a word used in substitution for another;? +?,?, a word.] A word of opposite meaning; a counterterm; -- used as a correlative of synonym. [R.] C. J. Smith.

antorbital.c: Antorbital Ant*or"bit*al (?), a. [Pref. anti- + orbital.] (Anat.) Pertaining to, or situated in, the region of the front of the orbit. -- n. The antorbital bone.

antozone.c: Antozone Ant*o"zone (?), n. [Pref. anti- + ozone.] (Chem.) A compound formerly supposed to be modification of oxygen, but now known to be hydrogen dioxide; -- so called because apparently antagonistic to ozone, converting it into ordinary oxygen.

antral.c: Antral An"tral (?), a. (Anat.) Relating to an antrum.

antre.c: Antre An"tre (?), n. [F. antre, L. antrum, fr. Gr.?.] A cavern. [Obs.] Shak.

antrorse.c: Antrorse An*trorse" (ăn*trôrs"), a. [From L. ante + versun turned; apparently formed in imitation of retrorse.] (Bot.) Forward or upward in direction. Gray.

antrovert.c: Antrovert An`tro*vert" (?), v. t. To bend forward. [R.] Owen.

antrum.c: Antrum ‖An"trum (?), n.; pl. Antra (?). [L., fr. Gr.?.] A cavern or cavity, esp. an anatomical cavity or sinus. Huxley.

antrustion.c: Antrustion ‖An*trus"tion (?), n. [F., fr. LL. antrustio.] A vassal or voluntary follower of Frankish princes in their enterprises.

anubis.c: Anubis ‖A*nu"bis (?), n. [L.] (Myth.) An Egyptian deity, the conductor of departed spirits to judgment, represented by a human figure with the head of a jackal, dog or fox.

anura.c: Anura ‖A*nu"ra (ȧ*nū"rȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'an priv. + o'yra` a tail.] (Zool.) One of the orders of amphibians characterized by the absence of a tail, as the frogs and toads. [Written also anoura.]

anurous.c: Anurous A*nu"rous (?), a. (Zool.) Destitute of a tail, as the frogs and toads. [Also written anourous.]

anury.c: Anury An"u*ry (?), n. [Gr. 'an priv. + o'y^ron urine.] (Med.) Nonsecretion or defective secretion of urine; ischury.

anus.c: Anus ‖A"nus (?), n. [L., prob. for asnus: cf. Gr.? to sit, Skr. ās.] (Anat.) The posterior opening of the alimentary canal, through which the excrements are expelled.

anvil.c: Anvil An"vil (?), n. [OE. anvelt, anfelt, anefelt, AS. anfilt, onfilt; of uncertain origin; cf. OHG. anafalz, D. aanbeld.] 1. An iron block, usually with a steel face, upon which metals are hammered and shaped.
Anvil An"vil, v. t. To form or shape on an anvil; to hammer out; as, anviled armor. Beau. & Fl.

anxietude.c: Anxietude Anx*i"e*tude (?), n. [L. anxietudo.] The state of being anxious; anxiety. [R.]

anxiety.c: Anxiety Anx*i"e*ty (?), n.; pl. Anxieties (?). [L. anxietas, fr. anxius: cf. F. anxiété. See Anxious.] 1. Concern or solicitude respecting some thing or event, future or uncertain, which disturbs the mind, and keeps it in a state of painful uneasiness.

anxious.c: Anxious Anx"ious (ăṉk"shŭs), a. [L. anxius, fr. angere to cause pain, choke; akin to Gr. 'a`gchein to choke. See Anger.] 1. Full of anxiety or disquietude; greatly concerned or solicitous, esp. respecting something future or unknown; being in painful suspense; -- applied to persons; as, anxious for the issue of a battle.

anxiously.c: Anxiously Anx"ious*ly, adv. In an anxious manner; with painful uncertainty; solicitously.

anxiousness.c: Anxiousness Anx"ious*ness, n. The quality of being anxious; great solicitude; anxiety.

any.c: Any A"ny (?), a. & pron. [OE. æniȝ, æni, eni, ani, oni, AS. ǣnig, fr. ān one. It is akin to OS. ēnig, OHG. einic, G. einig, D. eenig. See One.] 1. One indifferently, out of an indefinite number; one indefinitely, whosoever or whatsoever it may be.
Any A"ny, adv. To any extent; in any degree; at all.

anybody.c: Anybody A"ny*bod*y (?), n. 1. Any one out of an indefinite number of persons; anyone; any person.

anyhow.c: Anyhow A"ny*how` (?), adv. In any way or manner whatever; at any rate; in any event.

anyone.c: Anyone A"ny*one (?), n. One taken at random rather than by selection; anybody.

anything.c: Anything A"ny*thing (?), n. 1. Any object, act, state, event, or fact whatever; thing of any kind; something or other; aught; as, I would not do it for anything.
Anything A"ny*thing, adv. In any measure; anywise; at all.

anythingarian.c: Anythingarian A`ny*thing*a"ri*an (?), n. One who holds to no particular creed or dogma.

anyways.c: Anyways Anyway { A"ny*way (?), A"ny*ways (?), } adv. Anywise; at all. Tennyson. Southey.

anywhere.c: Anywhere A"ny*where (?), adv. In any place. Udall.

anywhither.c: Anywhither A"ny*whith`er (?), adv. To or towards any place. [Archaic] De Foe.

anywise.c: Anywise A"ny*wise (?), adv. In any wise or way; at all. “Anywise essential.” Burke.

aonian.c: Aonian A*o"ni*an (a*ō"nĭ*an), a. [From Aonia, a part of Bœotia, in Greece.] Pertaining to Aonia, in Bœotia, or to the Muses, who were supposed to dwell there.

aorist.c: Aorist A"o*rist (ā"o*rĭst), n. [Gr. 'ao`ristos indefinite; 'a priv. + "ori`zein to define,? boundary, limit.] (Gram.) A tense in the Greek language, which expresses an action as completed in past time, but leaves it, in other respects, wholly indeterminate.

aoristic.c: Aoristic A`o*ris"tic (?), a. [Gr. 'aoristiko`s.] Indefinite; pertaining to the aorist tense.

aorta.c: Aorta A*or"ta (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to lift, heave.] (Anat.) The great artery which carries the blood from the heart to all parts of the body except the lungs; the main trunk of the arterial system.

aortic.c: Aortic A*or"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the aorta.

aoudad.c: Aoudad ‖A"ou*dad (?), n. [The Moorish name.] (Zool.) An African sheeplike quadruped (the Ammotragus lervia, formerly Ammotragus tragelaphus) having a long mane on the breast and fore legs; the wild sheep of northern Africa; -- called also Barbary sheep. It is, perhaps, the chamois of the Old Testament.

apace.c: Apace A*pace" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + pace. OE. a pas at a walk, in which a is the article. See Pace.] With a quick pace; quick; fast; speedily.

apaches.c: Apaches A*pa"ches (?), n. pl.; sing. Apache (?). (Ethnol.) A group of nomadic North American Indians including several tribes native of Arizona, New Mexico, etc.

apagoge.c: Apagoge Ap`a*go"ge (?), n. [Gr.? a leading away, fr.? to lead away;? from +? to lead.] (Logic) An indirect argument which proves a thing by showing the impossibility or absurdity of the contrary.

apagogical.c: Apagogical Apagogic { Ap`a*gog"ic (?), Ap`a*gog"ic*al (?), } a. Proving indirectly, by showing the absurdity, or impossibility of the contrary. Bp. Berkeley.

apair.c: Apair A*pair" (?), v. t. & i. To impair or become impaired; to injure. [Obs.] Chaucer.

apanthropy.c: Apanthropy A*pan"thro*py (?), n. [Gr.?;? from +? man.] An aversion to the company of men; a love of solitude.

apara.c: Apara Apar ‖A"par (?), A"pa*ra (?), n. [Native name apara.] (Zool.) See Mataco.

aparejo.c: Aparejo ‖A`pa*re"jo (?), n. [Sp.] A kind of pack saddle used in the American military service and among the Spanish Americans. It is made of leather stuffed with hay, moss, or the like.

aparithmesis.c: Aparithmesis ‖Ap`a*rith"me*sis (?; 277), n. [Gr.?, from? to count off or over.] (Rhet.) Enumeration of parts or particulars.

apart.c: Apart A*part" (?), adv. [F. à part; (L. ad) + part part. See Part.] 1. Separately, in regard to space or company; in a state of separation as to place; aside.

apartment.c: Apartment A*part"ment (?), n. [F. appartement; cf. It. appartamento, fr. appartare to separate, set apart; all fr. L. ad + pars, partis, part. See Apart.] 1. A room in a building; a division in a house, separated from others by partitions. Fielding.

Apartment house A*part"ment house. A building comprising a number of lving units (apartments{4}) designed for separate housekeeping tenements, but having conveniences, such as heat, light, elevator service, etc., furnished in common; contrasted to a detached dwelling. Sometimes distinguished in the United States from a flat house, in which each living unit comprises one entire floor, whereas in an apartment house a floor may be partitioned into any number of apartments{4}.

apartness.c: Apartness A*part"ness (?), n. The quality of standing apart.

apastron.c: Apastron ‖Ap*as"tron (?), n. [Gr.? from +? star.] (Astron.) That point in the orbit of a double star where the smaller star is farthest from its primary.

apathetical.c: Apathetical Apathetic Ap`a*thet"ic (?), Ap`a*thet"ic*al (?) a. [See Apathy.] Void of feeling; not susceptible of deep emotion; passionless. a woman who became active rather than apathetic as she grew older

apathetically.c: Apathetically Ap`a*thet"ic*al*ly, adv. In an apathetic manner.

apathist.c: Apathist Ap"a*thist (?), n. [Cf. F. apathiste.] One who is destitute of feeling.

apathy.c: Apathy Ap"a*thy (?), n.; pl. Apathies (?). [L. apathia, Gr.?; 'a priv. +?, fr.?,?, to suffer: cf. F. apathie. See Pathos.] Want of feeling; privation of passion, emotion, or excitement; dispassion; -- applied either to the body or the mind. As applied to the mind, it is a calmness, indolence, or state of indifference, incapable of being ruffled or roused to active interest or exertion by pleasure, pain, or passion. “The apathy of despair.” Macaulay.

apatite.c: Apatite Ap"a*tite (?), n. [Gr.? deceit, fr.? to deceive; it having been often mistaken for other minerals.] (Min.) Native phosphate of lime, occurring usually in six-sided prisms, color often pale green, transparent or translucent.

ape.c: Ape Ape (āp), n. [AS. apa; akin to D. aap, OHG. affo, G. affe, Icel. api, Sw. apa, Dan. abe, W. epa.] 1. (Zool.) A quadrumanous mammal, esp. of the family Simiadæ, having teeth of the same number and form as in man, and possessing neither a tail nor cheek pouches. The name is applied esp. to species of the genus Hylobates, and is sometimes used as a general term for all Quadrumana. The higher forms, the gorilla, chimpanzee, and ourang, are often called anthropoid apes or man apes.
Ape Ape, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Aped; p. pr. & vb. n. Aping.] To mimic, as an ape imitates human actions; to imitate or follow servilely or irrationally. “How he apes his sire.” Addison.

apeak.c: Apeak A*peak" (?), adv. & a. [Pref. a- + peak. Cf. F. à pic vertically.] (Naut.) In a vertical line. The anchor in apeak, when the cable has been sufficiently hove in to bring the ship over it, and the ship is them said to be hove apeak. [Spelt also apeek.]

apehood.c: Apehood Ape"hood (?), n. The state of being an ape.

apellous.c: Apellous A*pel"lous (?), a. [Pref. a- not + L. pellis skin.] Destitute of skin. Brande & C.

apennine.c: Apennine Ap"en*nine (?), a. [L. Apenninus, fr. Celtic pen, or ben, peak, mountain.] Of, pertaining to, or designating, the Apennines, a chain of mountains extending through Italy.

apepsy.c: Apepsy A*pep"sy (?), n. [NL. apepsia, fr. Gr.?, fr.? uncooked, undigested; 'a priv. +? cooked,? to cook, digest.] (Med.) Defective digestion, indigestion. Coxe.

apercu.c: Apercu ‖A`per`çu" (ȧ`pâr`sụ"), n.; pl. Aperçus (-sụ"). [F., prop. p. p. of apercevoir to perceive.] 1. A first view or glance, or the perception or estimation so obtained; an immediate apprehension or insight, appreciative rather than analytic.

aperea.c: Aperea ‖A*pe"re*a (?), n. [Native name.] (Zool.) The wild Guinea pig of Brazil (Cavia aperea).

aperient.c: Aperient A*pe"ri*ent (?), a. [L. aperiens, p. pr. of aperire to uncover, open; ab + parire, parere, to bring forth, produce. Cf. Cover, Overt.] (Med.) Gently opening the bowels; laxative. -- n. An aperient medicine or food. Arbuthnot.

aperitive.c: Aperitive A*per"i*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. apéritif, fr. L. aperire.] Serving to open; aperient. Harvey.

apert.c: Apert A*pert" (?), a. [OF. apert, L. apertus, p. p. of aperire. See Aperient, and cf. Pert, a.] Open; evident; undisguised. [Archaic] Fotherby.

apertion.c: Apertion A*per"tion (?), n. [L. apertio.] The act of opening; an opening; an aperture. [Archaic] Wiseman.

aperture.c: Aperture Ap"er*ture (?; 135), n. [L. apertura, fr. aperire. See Aperient.] 1. The act of opening. [Obs.]

apery.c: Apery Ap"er*y (?), n.; pl. Aperies. 1. A place where apes are kept. [R.] Kingsley.

apetalous.c: Apetalous A*pet"al*ous (ȧ*pĕt"ail*ŭs), a. [Pref. a- not + petal.] (Bot.) Having no petals, or flower leaves. [See Illust. under Anther].

apetalousness.c: Apetalousness A*pet"al*ous*ness, n. The state of being apetalous.

apex.c: Apex A"pex (?), n.; pl. E. Apexes (?); L. Apices (?). [L.] 1. The tip, top, point, or angular summit of anything; as, the apex of a mountain, spire, or cone; the apex, or tip, of a leaf.

aphaeresis.c: Aphaeresis aphaeresis a*phaer"e*sis, ‖A*phær"e*sis (?; 277), n. [L.] Same as Apheresis.

aphakia.c: Aphakia ‖A*pha"ki*a (?), n. [NL.; Gr. 'a priv. +? seed of a lentil.] (Med.) An anomalous state of refraction caused by the absence of the crystalline lens, as after operations for cataract. The remedy is the use of powerful convex lenses. Dunglison.

aphakial.c: Aphakial A*pha"ki*al (?), a. (Med.) Pertaining to aphakia; as, aphakial eyes.

aphaniptera.c: Aphaniptera ‖Aph`a*nip"te*ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? invisible ('a priv. +? to appear) +? a wing.] (Zool.) A group of wingless insects, of which the flea in the type. See Flea.

aphanipterous.c: Aphanipterous Aph`a*nip"ter*ous (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Aphaniptera.

aphanite.c: Aphanite Aph"a*nite (?), n. [Gr.? invisible; 'a priv. +? to appear.] (Min.) A very compact, dark-colored?ock, consisting of hornblende, or pyroxene, and feldspar, but neither of them in perceptible grains.

aphanitic.c: Aphanitic Aph`a*nit"ic (?), a. (Min.) Resembling aphanite; having a very fine-grained structure.

aphasy.c: Aphasy Aphasia { ‖A*pha"si*a (?), Aph"a*sy (?), } n. [NL. aphasia, Gr.?, fr.? not spoken; 'a priv. +? to speak: cf. F. aphasie.] (Med.) Loss of the power of speech, or of the appropriate use of words, the vocal organs remaining intact, and the intelligence being preserved. It is dependent on injury or disease of the brain.

aphasic.c: Aphasic A*pha"sic (?), a. Pertaining to, or affected by, aphasia; speechless.

aphelion.c: Aphelion A*phel"ion (?; 277), n.; pl. Aphelia (?). [Gr.? +? sun.] (Astron.) That point of a planet's or comet's orbit which is most distant from the sun, the opposite point being the perihelion.

apheliotropic.c: Apheliotropic A*phe`li*o*trop"ic (?), a. [Gr.? +? sun +? belonging to a turning.] Turning away from the sun; -- said of leaves, etc. Darwin.

apheliotropism.c: Apheliotropism A*phe`li*ot"ro*pism (?), n. The habit of bending from the sunlight; -- said of certain plants.

aphemia.c: Aphemia ‖A*phe"mi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'a priv. +? voice.] (Med.) Loss of the power of speaking, while retaining the power of writing; -- a disorder of cerebral origin.

apheresis.c: Apheresis A*pher"e*sis (?; 277), n. [L. aphaeresis, Gr.?, fr.? to take away;? +? to take.] 1. (Gram.) The dropping of a letter or syllable from the beginning of a word; e. g., cute for acute.

aphesis.c: Aphesis ‖Aph"e*sis (?), n. [Gr.? a letting go;? +? to let go.] The loss of a short unaccented vowel at the beginning of a word; -- the result of a phonetic process; as, squire for esquire. New Eng. Dict.

aphetic.c: Aphetic A*phet"ic (?), a. [Gr.? letting go, fr.? to let go.] Shortened by dropping a letter or a syllable from the beginning of a word; as, an aphetic word or form. -- A*phet"ic*al*ly, adv. New Eng. Dict.

aphetism.c: Aphetism Aph"e*tism (?), n. An aphetized form of a word. New Eng. Dict.

aphetize.c: Aphetize Aph"e*tize (?), v. t. To shorten by aphesis.

aphid.c: Aphid A"phid (?), n. (Zool.) One of the genus Aphis; an aphidian.

aphidian.c: Aphidian A*phid"i*an (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the family Aphidæ. -- n. One of the aphides; an aphid.

aphidivorous.c: Aphidivorous Aph`i*div"o*rous (?). [Aphis + L. vorare to devour.] (Zool.) Devouring aphides; aphidophagous.

aphidophagous.c: Aphidophagous Aph`i*doph"a*gous (?), a. [Aphis + Gr.? to eat.] (Zool.) Feeding upon aphides, or plant lice, as do beetles of the family Coccinellidæ.

aphilanthropy.c: Aphilanthropy Aph`i*lan"thro*py (?), n. [Gr.? not loving man; 'a priv. +? to love +? man.] Want of love to mankind; -- the opposite of philanthropy. Coxe.

aphis.c: Aphis ‖A"phis (?), n.; pl. Aphides (?). [NL.] (Zool.) A genus of insects belonging to the order Hemiptera and family Aphidæ, including numerous species known as plant lice and green flies.
Aphis lion A"phis li"on (?). (Zool.) The larva of the lacewinged flies (Chrysopa), which feeds voraciously upon aphids. The name is also applied to the larvæ of the ladybugs (Coccinella).

aphlogistic.c: Aphlogistic Aph`lo*gis"tic (?), a. [Gr.? not inflammable; 'a priv. +? set on fire. See Phlogiston.] Flameless; as, an aphlogistic lamp, in which a coil of wire is kept in a state of continued ignition by alcohol, without flame.

aphony.c: Aphony Aphonia { ‖A*pho"ni*a (?), Aph"o*ny (?), } n. [NL. aphonia, Gr.?, fr.? voiceless; 'a priv. +? voice: cf. F. aphonie.] (Med.) Loss of voice or vocal utterance.

aphonous.c: Aphonous Aphonic { A*phon"ic (?), Aph"o*nous (?), } a. Without voice; voiceless; nonvocal; incapable of all but whispered speech.

aphorism.c: Aphorism Aph"o*rism (?), n. [F. aphorisme, fr. Gr.? definition, a short, pithy sentence, fr.? to mark off by boundaries, to define;? from +? to separate, part. See Horizon.] A comprehensive maxim or principle expressed in a few words; a sharply defined sentence relating to abstract truth rather than to practical matters.

aphorismic.c: Aphorismic Aphorismatic { Aph`o*ris*mat"ic (?), Aph`o*ris"mic (?), } a. Pertaining to aphorisms, or having the form of an aphorism.

aphorismer.c: Aphorismer Aph`o*ris"mer (?) n. A dealer in aphorisms. [Used in derogation or contempt.] Milton.

aphorist.c: Aphorist Aph"o*rist, n. A writer or utterer of aphorisms.

aphoristical.c: Aphoristical Aphoristic { Aph`o*ris"tic (?), Aph`o*ris"tic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?.] In the form of, or of the nature of, an aphorism; in the form of short, unconnected sentences; as, an aphoristic style.

aphoristically.c: Aphoristically Aph`o*ris"tic*al*ly, adv. In the form or manner of aphorisms; pithily.

aphorize.c: Aphorize Aph"o*rize (?), v. i. To make aphorisms.

aphotic.c: Aphotic region Aphotic region. (Phytogeog.) A depth of water so great that only those organisms can exist that do not assimilate.

aphrasia.c: Aphrasia ‖A*phra"si*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'a priv. + fra`sis speech.] (Med.) (a) = Dumbness. (b) A disorder of speech in which words can be uttered but not intelligibly joined together.

aphrodisiacal.c: Aphrodisiacal Aphrodisiac { Aph`ro*dis"i*ac (?), Aph`ro*di*si"a*cal (?), } a. [Gr.? pertaining to sensual love, fr.?. See Aphrodite.] Exciting venereal desire; stimulating the desire for sexual gratification.

aphrodisiac.c: Aphrodisiac Aph`ro*dis"i*ac, n. That which (as a drug, or some kinds of food) stimulate sexual desire.

aphrodisian.c: Aphrodisian Aph`ro*dis"i*an (?), a. [Gr.?.] Pertaining to Aphrodite or Venus. “Aphrodisian dames” [that is, courtesans]. C. Reade.

aphrodite.c: Aphrodite ‖Aph`ro*di"te (?), n. [Gr.?.] 1. (Classic Myth.) The Greek goddess of love, corresponding to the Venus of the Romans.

aphtha.c: Aphtha ‖Aph"tha (?), n. [Sing. of Aphthæ.] (Med.) (a) One of the whitish specks called aphthæ. (b) The disease, also called thrush.

aphthae.c: Aphthae ‖Aph"thæ (?), n. pl. [L., fr. Gr.? (mostly in pl.?, Hipp.) an eruption, thrush, fr.? to set on fire, inflame.] (Med.) Roundish pearl-colored specks or flakes in the mouth, on the lips, etc., terminating in white sloughs. They are commonly characteristic of thrush.

aphthoid.c: Aphthoid Aph"thoid, a. [Aphtha + -oid.] Of the nature of aphthæ; resembling thrush.

aphthong.c: Aphthong Aph"thong (?; 277), n. [Gr.? silent; 'a priv. +? voice, sound, fr.? to sound.] A letter, or a combination of letters, employed in spelling a word, but in the pronunciation having no sound. -- Aph*thon"gal (?), a.

aphthous.c: Aphthous Aph"thous (?) a. [Cf. F. aphtheux.] Pertaining to, or caused by, aphthæ; characterized by aphtæ; as, aphthous ulcers; aphthous fever.

aphyllous.c: Aphyllous Aph"yl*lous (?), a. [Gr.?; 'a priv. +? leaf.] (Bot.) Destitute of leaves, as the broom rape, certain euphorbiaceous plants, etc.

apiarian.c: Apiarian A`pi*a"ri*an (?), a. Of or relating to bees.

apiarist.c: Apiarist A"pi*a*rist (?), n. One who keeps an apiary.

apiary.c: Apiary A"pi*a*ry (?), n. [L. apiarium, fr. apis bee.] A place where bees are kept; a stand or shed for bees; a beehouse.

apical.c: Apical Ap"ic*al (?), a. [L. apex, apicis, tip or summit.] At or belonging to an apex, tip, or summit. Gray.

apician.c: Apician A*pi"cian (?), a. [L. Apicianus.] Belonging to Apicius, a notorious Roman epicure; hence applied to whatever is peculiarly refined or dainty and expensive in cookery. H. Rogers.

apicular.c: Apicular A*pic"u*lar, a. [NL. apiculus, dim. of L. apex, apicis.] Situated at, or near, the apex; apical.

apiculated.c: Apiculated Apiculate { A*pic"u*late (?), A*pic"u*la`ted (?), } a. [See Apicular.] (Bot.) Terminated abruptly by a small, distinct point, as a leaf.

apiculture.c: Apiculture Ap"i*cul`ture (?; 135), n. [L. apis bee + E. culture.] Rearing of bees for their honey and wax.

apiece.c: Apiece A*piece" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + piece.] Each by itself; by the single one; to each; as the share of each; as, these melons cost a shilling apiece. “Fined... a thousand pounds apiece.” Hume.

apieces.c: Apieces A*pie"ces (?), adv. In pieces or to pieces. [Obs.] “Being torn apieces.” Shak.

apiol.c: Apiol A"pi*ol (?), n. [L. apium parsley + -ol.] (Med.) An oily liquid derived from parsley.

apiologist.c: Apiologist A`pi*ol"o*gist (?), n. [L. apis bee + -logist (see -logy).] A student of bees. [R.] Emerson.

apiology.c: Apiology A`pi*ol"o*gy (?), n. [L. apis bee + -logy.] The scientific or systematic study of honey bees.

apis.c: Apis ‖A"pis (?), n. [L., bee.] (Zool.) A genus of insects of the order Hymenoptera, including the common honeybee (Apis mellifica) and other related species. See Honeybee.

apish.c: Apish Ap"ish (?), a. Having the qualities of an ape; prone to imitate in a servile manner. Hence: Apelike; fantastically silly; foppish; affected; trifling.

apishly.c: Apishly Ap"ish*ly, adv. In an apish manner; with servile imitation; foppishly.

apishness.c: Apishness Ap"ish*ness, n. The quality of being apish; mimicry; foppery.

apitpat.c: Apitpat A*pit"pat, adv. [Pref. a- + pitpat.] With quick beating or palpitation; pitapat. Congreve.

aplacental.c: Aplacental Ap`la*cen"tal, a. [Pref. a- + placental.] Belonging to the Aplacentata; without placenta.

aplacentata.c: Aplacentata ‖Ap`la*cen*ta"ta, n. pl. [Pref. a- not + placenta.] (Zool.) Mammals which have no placenta.

aplacophora.c: Aplacophora ‖Ap`la*coph"o*ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'a priv. +? a flat cake + fe`rein to bear.] (Zool.) A division of Amphineura in which the body is naked or covered with slender spines or setæ, but is without shelly plates.

aplanatic.c: Aplanatic Ap`la*nat"ic (?), a. [Gr. 'a priv. +? disposed to wander, wandering,? to wander.] (Opt.) Having two or more parts of different curvatures, so combined as to remove spherical aberration; -- said of a lens.

aplanatism.c: Aplanatism A*plan"a*tism (?), n. Freedom from spherical aberration.

aplanogamete.c: Aplanogamete A*plan`o*ga*mete" (?), n. (Bot.) A nonmotile gamete, found in certain lower algæ.

aplasia.c: Aplasia ‖A*pla"si*a (?), n. [NL.; Gr.? priv. +? a molding.] (Med.) 1. Incomplete or faulty development.

aplastic.c: Aplastic A*plas"tic (?), a. [Pref. a- not + plastic.] Not plastic or easily molded.

aplomb.c: Aplomb ‖A`plomb" (?), n. [F., lit. perpendicularity;? to + plomb lead. See Plumb.] Assurance of manner or of action; self-possession.

aplotomy.c: Aplotomy A*plot"o*my (?), n. [Gr.? simple +? a cutting.] (Surg.) Simple incision. Dunglison.

aplustre.c: Aplustre ‖A*plus"tre (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?.] (Rom. Antiq.) An ornamental appendage of wood at the ship's stern, usually spreading like a fan and curved like a bird's feather. Audsley.

aplysia.c: Aplysia ‖A*plys"i*a (?), n. [Gr.? a dirty sponge, fr.? unwashed; 'a priv. +? to wash.] (Zool.) A genus of marine mollusks of the order Tectibranchiata; the sea hare. Some of the species when disturbed throw out a deep purple liquor, which colors the water to some distance. See Illust. in Appendix.

apneumatic.c: Apneumatic Ap`neu*mat"ic (?), a. [Gr.? not blown through.] (Med.) Devoid of air; free from air; as, an apneumatic lung; also, effected by or with exclusion of air; as, an apneumatic operation.

apneumona.c: Apneumona ‖Ap*neu"mo*na (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'a priv. +?,?, a lung.] (Zool.) An order of holothurians in which the internal respiratory organs are wanting; -- called also Apoda or Apodes.

apnoea.c: Apnoea ‖Ap*nœ"a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'a priv. +?,?, breath,? to breathe, blow.] (Med.) Partial privation or suspension of breath; suffocation; same as apnea.

apo.c: Apo Ap"o (?). [Gr.?. See Ab-.] A prefix from a Greek preposition. It usually signifies from, away from, off, or asunder, separate; as, in apocope (a cutting off), apostate, apostle (one sent away), apocarpous.

apocalypse.c: Apocalypse A*poc"a*lypse (?), n. [L. apocalypsis, Gr.?, fr.? to uncover, to disclose;? from +? to cover, conceal: cf. F. apocalypse.] 1. (Eccl.) One of a numerous class of writings proceeding from Jewish authors between 250 b. c. and 150 a. d., and designed to propagate the Jewish faith or to cheer the hearts of the Jewish people with the promise of deliverance and glory; or proceeding from Christian authors of the opening centuries and designed to portray the future.

apocalyptical.c: Apocalyptical Apocalyptic { A*poc`a*lyp"tic (?), A*poc`a*lyp"tic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?.] 1. Of or pertaining to a revelation, or, specifically, to the Revelation of St. John; containing, or of the nature of, a prophetic revelation.

apocalyptist.c: Apocalyptist Apocalyptic A*poc`a*lyp"tic (ȧ*pŏk`ȧ*lĭp"tĭk), A*poc`a*lyp"tist, n. The writer of the Apocalypse.

apocalyptically.c: Apocalyptically A*poc`a*lyp"tic*al*ly (?), adv. By revelation; in an apocalyptic manner.

apocarpous.c: Apocarpous Ap`o*car"pous, a. [Pref. apo- + Gr. karpo`s fruit.] (Bot.) Either entirely or partially separate, as the carpels of a compound pistil; -- opposed to syncarpous. Lindley.

apochromatic.c: Apochromatic Ap`o*chro*mat"ic (?), a. [Pref. apo- + chromatic.] (Optics) Free from chromatic and spherical aberration; -- said esp. of a lens in which rays of three or more colors are brought to the same focus, the degree of achromatism thus obtained being more complete than where two rays only are thus focused, as in the ordinary achromatic objective. -- Ap`o*chro"ma*tism (#), n.

apocodeine.c: Apocodeine Ap`o*co*de"ine (?), n. [Pref. apo- + codeine.] (Chem.) An alkaloid, C18H19NO2, prepared from codeine. In its effects it resembles apomorphine.

apocopate.c: Apocopate A*poc"o*pate (?), v. t. [LL. apocopatus, p. p. of apocopare to cut off, fr. L. apocore. See Apocope.] (Gram.) To cut off or drop; as, to apocopate a word, or the last letter, syllable, or part of a word.

apocopated.c: Apocopated Apocopate { A*poc"o*pate (?), A*poc"o*pa`ted (?), } a. Shortened by apocope; as, an apocopate form.

apocopation.c: Apocopation A*poc`o*pa"tion (?), n. Shortening by apocope; the state of being apocopated.

apocope.c: Apocope ‖A*poc"o*pe, n. [L., fr. Gr.? a cutting off, fr.? to cut off;? from +? to cut.] 1. The cutting off, or omission, of the last letter, syllable, or part of a word.

apocrisiarius.c: Apocrisiarius Apocrisiary { Ap`o*cris"i*a*ry (?), ‖Ap`o*cris`i*a"ri*us (?), } n. [L. apocrisiarius, apocrisarius, fr. Gr.? answer, fr.? to answer;? from +? to separate.] (Eccl.) A delegate or deputy; especially, the pope's nuncio or legate at Constantinople.

apocrustic.c: Apocrustic Ap`o*crus"tic (?), a. [Gr.? able to drive off, fr.? to drive off.] (Med.) Astringent and repellent. -- n. An apocrustic medicine.

apocrypha.c: Apocrypha A*poc"ry*pha (?), n. pl., but often used as sing. with pl. Apocryphas (?). [L. apocryphus apocryphal, Gr.? hidden, spurious, fr.? to hide;? from +? to hide.] 1. Something, as a writing, that is of doubtful authorship or authority; -- formerly used also adjectively. [Obs.] Locke.

apocryphal.c: Apocryphal A*poc"ry*phal (?), a. 1. Pertaining to the Apocrypha.

apocryphalist.c: Apocryphalist A*poc"ry*phal*ist, n. One who believes in, or defends, the Apocrypha. [R.]

apocryphally.c: Apocryphally A*poc"ry*phal*ly, adv. In an apocryphal manner; mythically; not indisputably.

apocryphalness.c: Apocryphalness A*poc"ry*phal*ness, n. The quality or state of being apocryphal; doubtfulness of credit or genuineness.

apocyneous.c: Apocyneous Apocynaceous A*poc`y*na"ceous (?), Ap`o*cyn"e*ous (?), a. [Gr.? dogbane;? from +? dog.] (Bot.) Belonging to, or resembling, a family of plants, of which the dogbane (Apocynum) is the type.

apocynin.c: Apocynin A*poc"y*nin (?), n. [From Apocynum, the generic name of dogbane.] (Chem.) A bitter principle obtained from the dogbane (Apocynum cannabinum).

apodal.c: Apodal Apod { Ap"od (?), Ap"o*dal (?), } a. [See Apod, n.] 1. Without feet; footless.

apode.c: Apode Apod { Ap"od (?), Ap"ode (?), } n.; pl. Apods (?) or Apodes (?). [Gr.?,?, footless; 'a priv. +?,?, foot.] (Zool.) One of certain animals that have no feet or footlike organs; esp. one of certain fabulous birds which were said to have no feet.

apoda.c: Apoda ‖Ap"o*da (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.?,?. See Apod, n.] (Zool.) (a) A group of cirripeds, destitute of footlike organs. (b) An order of Amphibia without feet. See Ophiomorpha. (c) A group of worms without appendages, as the leech.

apodictical.c: Apodictical Apodeictical Apodictic Apodeictic { Ap"o*deic"tic (?), Ap`o*dic"tic (?), Ap`o*deic"tic*al (?), Ap`o*dic"tic*al (?), } a. [L. apodicticus, Gr.?, fr.? to point out, to show by argument;? from +? to show.] Self-evident; intuitively true; evident beyond contradiction. Brougham. Sir Wm. Hamilton.

apodictically.c: Apodictically Apodeictically Ap`o*deic"tic*al*ly, Ap`o*dic"tic*al*ly, adv. So as to be evident beyond contradiction.

apodeme.c: Apodeme Ap"o*deme (?), n. [Pref. apo- + Gr.? body.] (Zool.) One of the processes of the shell which project inwards and unite with one another, in the thorax of many Crustacea.

apodes.c: Apodes ‖Ap"o*des (?), n. pl. [NL., masc. pl. See Apoda.] (Zool.) (a) An order of fishes without ventral fins, including the eels. (b) A group of holothurians destitute of suckers. See Apneumona.

apodixis.c: Apodixis ‖Ap`o*dix"is (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.?.] Full demonstration.

apodosis.c: Apodosis ‖A*pod"o*sis (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to give back;? from, back again +? to give.] (Gram.) The consequent clause or conclusion in a conditional sentence, expressing the result, and thus distinguished from the protasis or clause which expresses a condition. Thus, in the sentence, “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him,” the former clause is the protasis, and the latter the apodosis.

apodyterium.c: Apodyterium ‖A*pod`y*te"ri*um (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to strip one's self.] (Anc. Arch.) The apartment at the entrance of the baths, or in the palestra, where one stripped; a dressing room.

apogaic.c: Apogaic Ap`o*ga"ic (?), a. [Gr.? far from the earth.] Apogean.

apogamy.c: Apogamy A*pog"a*my (?), n. [Pref. apo- + Gr.? marriage.] (Bot.) The formation of a bud in place of a fertilized ovule or oöspore. De Bary.

apogean.c: Apogean Ap`o*ge"an (?), a. Connected with the apogee; as, apogean (neap) tides, which occur when the moon has passed her apogee.

apogee.c: Apogee Ap"o*gee (?), n. [Gr.? from the earth;? from +?,?, earth: cf. F. apogée.] 1. (Astron.) That point in the orbit of the moon which is at the greatest distance from the earth.

apogeotropic.c: Apogeotropic Ap`o*ge`o*trop"ic (?), a. [Pref. apo- + Gr.? earth +? turning.] (Bot.) Bending away from the ground; -- said of leaves, etc. Darwin.

apogeotropism.c: Apogeotropism Ap"o*ge*ot"ro*pism (?), n. The apogeotropic tendency of some leaves, and other parts.

apograph.c: Apograph Ap"o*graph (?), n. [Gr.?;? from +? to write: cf. F. apographe.] A copy or transcript. Blount.

apohyal.c: Apohyal Ap`o*hy"al (?), a. [Pref. apo- + the Gr. letter Y.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to a portion of the horn of the hyoid bone.

apolar.c: Apolar A*po"lar (?), a. [Pref. a- + polar.] (Biol.) Having no radiating processes; -- applied particularly to certain nerve cells.

apolaustic.c: Apolaustic Ap`o*laus"tic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? to enjoy.] Devoted to enjoyment.

apollinarian.c: Apollinarian A*pol`li*na"ri*an (?), a. [L. Apollinaris, fr. Apollo.] (Rom. Antiq.) In honor of Apollo; as, the Apollinarian games.
Apollinarian A*pol`li*na"ri*an, n. (Eccl. Hist.) A follower of Apollinaris, Bishop of Laodicea in the fourth century, who denied the proper humanity of Christ.

apollinaris.c: Apollinaris water A*pol`li*na"ris wa"ter (?). An effervescing alkaline mineral water used as a table beverage. It is obtained from a spring in Apollinarisburg, near Bonn.

apollo.c: Apollo A*pol"lo (?), n. [L. Apollo, -linis, Gr.?.] (Classic Myth.) A deity among the Greeks and Romans. He was the god of light and day (the “sun god”), of archery, prophecy, medicine, poetry, and music, etc., and was represented as the model of manly grace and beauty; -- called also Phébus.

apollonic.c: Apollonic Apollonian Ap`ol*lo"ni*an (?), Ap`ol*lon"ic (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or resembling, Apollo.

apollyon.c: Apollyon A*pol"ly*on (?), n. [Gr.? destroying, fr.?,?, to destroy utterly;? from, entirely +? to destroy.] The Destroyer; -- a name used (Rev. ix. 11) for the angel of the bottomless pit, answering to the Hebrew Abaddon.

apologer.c: Apologer A*pol"o*ger (?), n. A teller of apologues. [Obs.]

apologetical.c: Apologetical Apologetic { A*pol`o*get"ic (?), A*pol`o*get"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?, fr.? to speak in defense of;? from +? speech,? to say, to speak. See Logic.] Defending by words or arguments; said or written in defense, or by way of apology; regretfully excusing; as, an apologetic essay. “To speak in a subdued and apologetic tone.” Macaulay.

apologetically.c: Apologetically A*pol`o*get"ic*al*ly, adv. By way of apology.

apologetics.c: Apologetics A*pol`o*get"ics (?), n. That branch of theology which defends the Holy Scriptures, and sets forth the evidence of their divine authority.

apologist.c: Apologist A*pol"o*gist (?), n. [Cf. F. apologiste.] One who makes an apology; one who speaks or writes in defense of a faith, a cause, or an institution; especially, one who argues in defense of Christianity.

apologize.c: Apologize A*pol"o*gize (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Apologized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Apologizing.] [Cf. F. apologiser.] 1. To make an apology or defense. Dr. H. More.

apologizer.c: Apologizer A*pol"o*gi`zer (?), n. One who makes an apology; an apologist.

apologue.c: Apologue Ap"o*logue (?), n. [L. apologous, Gr.?;? from +? speech,? to speak: cf. F. apologue.] A story or relation of fictitious events, intended to convey some moral truth; a moral fable.

apology.c: Apology A*pol"o*gy (?), n.; pl. Apologies. [L. apologia, Gr.?;? from +?: cf. F. apologie. See Apologetic.] 1. Something said or written in defense or justification of what appears to others wrong, or of what may be liable to disapprobation; justification; as, Tertullian's Apology for Christianity.
Apology A*pol"o*gy (?), v. i. To offer an apology. [Obs.]

apomecometer.c: Apomecometer Ap`o*me*com"e*ter, n. An instrument for measuring the height of objects. Knight.

apomecometry.c: Apomecometry Ap`o*me*com"e*try, n. [Pref. apo- + Gr.? length + -metry.] The art of measuring the distance of objects afar off. [Obs. or R.]

apomorphine.c: Apomorphine Apomorphia { ‖Ap`o*mor"phi*a (?), Ap`o*mor"phine (?), } n. [Pref. apo- + morphia, morphine.] (Chem.) A crystalline alkaloid obtained from morphia. It is a powerful emetic.

aponeurosis.c: Aponeurosis ‖Ap`o*neu*ro"sis (?), n.; pl. Aponeuroses (?). [Gr.?, fr.? to pass into a tendon;? from +? to strain the sinews,? sinew, tendon, nerve.] (Anat.) Any one of the thicker and denser of the deep fasciæ which cover, invest, and the terminations and attachments of, many muscles. They often differ from tendons only in being flat and thin. See Fascia.

aponeurotic.c: Aponeurotic Ap`o*neu*rot"ic (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to an aponeurosis.

aponeurotomy.c: Aponeurotomy Ap`o*neu*rot"o*my (?), n. [Aponeurosis + Gr.? a cutting.] Dissection of aponeuroses.

apopemptic.c: Apopemptic Ap`o*pemp"tic (-pĕmp"tĭk), a. [Gr. 'apopemptiko`s, fr. 'apope`mpein to send off or away; 'apo` from + pe`mpein to send.] Sung or addressed to one departing; valedictory; as, apopemptic songs or hymns.

apophlegmatic.c: Apophlegmatic Ap`o*phleg*mat"ic (?), a. [Gr.?;? from +? full of phlegm. See Phlegmatic.] (Med.) Designed to facilitate discharges of phlegm or mucus from mouth or nostrils. -- n. An apophlegmatic medicine.

apophlegmatism.c: Apophlegmatism Ap`o*phleg"ma*tism, n. [Gr.?, Galen.] 1. (Med.) The action of apophlegmatics.

apophthegm.c: Apophthegm Apothegm { Ap"o*thegm, Ap"oph*thegm } (?), n. [Gr. 'apo`fqegma thing uttered, apothegm, from 'apofqe`ggesqai to speak out; 'apo` from + fqe`ggesqai to speak.] A short, pithy, and instructive saying; a terse remark, conveying some important truth; a sententious precept or maxim.

apophthegmatical.c: Apophthegmatical Apophthegmatic Ap`oph*theg*mat"ic (?), Ap`oph*theg*mat"ic*al (?), a. Same as Apothegmatic.

apophyge.c: Apophyge ‖A*poph"y*ge (?), n. [Gr. 'apofygh` escape, in arch. the curve with which the shaft escapes into its base or capital, fr. 'apofey`gein to flee away; 'apo` from + fey`gein to flee: cf. F. apophyge.] (Arch.) The small hollow curvature given to the top or bottom of the shaft of a column where it expands to meet the edge of the fillet; -- called also the scape. Parker.

apophyllite.c: Apophyllite A*poph"yl*lite (?), n. [Pref. apo- + Gr.? leaf; so called from its foliated structure or easy cleavage.] (Min.) A mineral relating to the zeolites, usually occurring in square prisms or octahedrons with pearly luster on the cleavage surface. It is a hydrous silicate of calcium and potassium.

apophysis.c: Apophysis ‖A*poph"y*sis (?), n.; pl. -ses. [NL., fr. Gr.? offshoot, process of a bone, fr.? to grow from;? from +?,?, to grow.] 1. (Anat.) A marked prominence or process on any part of a bone.

apoplectical.c: Apoplectical Apoplectic { Ap`o*plec"tic (?)(#) Ap`o*plec"tic*al (?), } a. [L. apoplecticus, Gr.?, fr.?: cf. F. apoplectique. See Apoplexy.] Relating to apoplexy; affected with, inclined to, or symptomatic of, apoplexy; as, an apoplectic person, medicine, habit or temperament, symptom, fit, or stroke.

apoplectic.c: Apoplectic Ap`o*plec"tic, n. One liable to, or affected with, apoplexy.

apoplectoid.c: Apoplectoid Apoplectiform Ap`o*plec"ti*form (?), Ap`o*plec"toid (?), a. [Apoplectic + -form, -oid.] Resembling apoplexy.

apoplexed.c: Apoplexed Ap`o*plexed (-plĕkst), a. Affected with apoplexy. [Obs.] Shak.

apoplexy.c: Apoplexy Ap"o*plex`y (ăp"o*plĕks`y̆), n. [OE. poplexye, LL. poplexia, apoplexia, fr. Gr. 'apoplhxi`a, fr. 'apoplh`ssein to cripple by a stroke; 'apo` from + plh`ssein to strike: cf. F. apoplexie. See Plague.] (Med.) Sudden diminution or loss of consciousness, sensation, and voluntary motion, usually caused by pressure on the brain.

aporetical.c: Aporetical Ap`o*ret"ic*al (?), a. [Gr.?. See Aporia.] Doubting; skeptical. [Obs.] Cudworth.

aporia.c: Aporia ‖A*po"ri*a (?), n.; pl. Aporias (?). [L., doubt, Gr.?, fr.? without passage, at a loss; 'a priv. +? passage.] (Rhet.) A figure in which the speaker professes to be at a loss what course to pursue, where to begin to end, what to say, etc.

aporosa.c: Aporosa ‖Ap`o*ro"sa (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.?. See Aporia.] (Zool.) A group of corals in which the coral is not porous; -- opposed to Perforata.

aport.c: Aport A*port" (?), adv. [Pref. a- + port.] (Naut.) On or towards the port or left side; -- said of the helm.

aposematic.c: Aposematic Ap`o*se*mat"ic (?), a. [Pref. apo- + sematic.] (Zool.) Having or designating conspicuous or warning colors or structures indicative of special means of defense against enemies, as in the skunk.

aposiopesis.c: Aposiopesis ‖Ap`o*si`o*pe"sis (?; 277), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, from? to be quite silent.] (Rhet.) A figure of speech in which the speaker breaks off suddenly, as if unwilling or unable to state what was in his mind; as, “I declare to you that his conduct -- but I can not speak of that, here.”

apositic.c: Apositic Ap`o*sit"ic, a. [Gr.?;? from +? food.] (Med.) Destroying the appetite, or suspending hunger.

apostasy.c: Apostasy A*pos"ta*sy (?), n.; pl. Apostasies (?). [OE. apostasie, F. apostasie, L. apostasia, fr. Gr.? a standing off from, a defection, fr.? to stand off, revolt;? from +? to stand. See Off and Stand.] An abandonment of what one has voluntarily professed; a total desertion of departure from one's faith, principles, or party; esp., the renunciation of a religious faith; as, Julian's apostasy from Christianity.

apostate.c: Apostate A*pos"tate (?), n. [L. apostata, Gr.?, fr.?. See Apostasy.] 1. One who has forsaken the faith, principles, or party, to which he before adhered; esp., one who has forsaken his religion for another; a pervert; a renegade.
Apostate A*pos"tate, a. Pertaining to, or characterized by, apostasy; faithless to moral allegiance; renegade.
Apostate A*pos"tate, v. i. [L. apostatare.] To apostatize. [Obs.]

apostatize.c: Apostatize A*pos"ta*tize (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Apostatized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Apostatizing.] [LL. apostatizare.] To renounce totally a religious belief once professed; to forsake one's church, the faith or principles once held, or the party to which one has previously adhered.

apostemate.c: Apostemate A*pos"te*mate (?), v. i. [See Aposteme.] To form an abscess; to swell and fill with pus. Wiseman.

apostemation.c: Apostemation A*pos`te*ma"tion (?), n. [LL. apostematio: cf. F. apostémation.] (Med.) The formation of an aposteme; the process of suppuration. [Written corruptly imposthumation.] Wiseman.

apostematous.c: Apostematous Ap`os*tem"a*tous (?), a. Pertaining to, or partaking of the nature of, an aposteme.

aposteme.c: Aposteme Ap"os*teme (?), n. [L. apostema, Gr.? the separation of corrupt matter into an ulcer, fr.? to stand off: cf. F. apostème. See Apostasy.] (Med.) An abscess; a swelling filled with purulent matter. [Written corruptly imposthume.]

apostille.c: Apostille Apostil { A*pos"til (?), A*pos"tille (?), } n. [F. apostille. See Postil.] A marginal note on a letter or other paper; an annotation. Motley.

apostle.c: Apostle A*pos"tle (?), n. [OE. apostle, apostel, postle, AS. apostol, L. apostolus, fr. Gr.? messenger, one sent forth or away, fr.? to send off or away;? from +? to send; akin to G. stellen to set, E. stall: cf. F. apôtre, Of. apostre, apostle, apostele, apostole.] 1. Literally: One sent forth; a messenger. Specifically: One of the twelve disciples of Christ, specially chosen as his companions and witnesses, and sent forth to preach the gospel.

apostleship.c: Apostleship A*pos"tle*ship (?), n. The office or dignity of an apostle.

apostolate.c: Apostolate A*pos"to*late (?), n. [L. apostolatus, fr. apostolus. See Apostle.] 1. The dignity, office, or mission, of an apostle; apostleship.

apostolical.c: Apostolical Apostolic { Ap`os*tol"ic (?), Ap`os*tol"ic*al (?), } a. [L. apostolicus, Gr.?: cf. F. apostolique.] 1. Pertaining to an apostle, or to the apostles, their times, or their peculiar spirit; as, an apostolical mission; the apostolic age.

apostolic.c: Apostolic Ap`os*tol"ic, n. [L. apostolicus.] (Eccl. Hist.) A member of one of certain ascetic sects which at various times professed to imitate the practice of the apostles.
Apostolic delegate Ap`os*tol"ic del"e*gate. (R. C. Ch.) The diplomatic agent of the pope highest in grade, superior to a nuncio.

apostolically.c: Apostolically Ap`os*tol"ic*al*ly, adv. In an apostolic manner.

apostolicalness.c: Apostolicalness Ap`os*tol"ic*al*ness, n. Apostolicity. Dr. H. More.

apostolicity.c: Apostolicity Apostolicism { Ap`os*tol"i*cism (?), A*pos`to*lic"i*ty (?), } n. The state or quality of being apostolical.

apostrophe.c: Apostrophe A*pos"tro*phe (?), n. [(1) L., fr. Gr.? a turning away, fr.? to turn away;? from +? to turn. (2) F., fr. L. apostrophus apostrophe, the turning away or omitting of a letter, Gr.?.] 1. (Rhet.) A figure of speech by which the orator or writer suddenly breaks off from the previous method of his discourse, and addresses, in the second person, some person or thing, absent or present; as, Milton's apostrophe to Light at the beginning of the third book of “Paradise Lost.”

apostrophic.c: Apostrophic Ap`os*troph"ic (?), a. Pertaining to an apostrophe, grammatical or rhetorical.

apostrophize.c: Apostrophize A*pos"tro*phize (?), v. t., [imp. & p. p. Apostrophized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Apostrophizing.] 1. To address by apostrophe.
Apostrophize A*pos"tro*phize, v. i. To use the rhetorical figure called apostrophe.

apotactite.c: Apotactite Ap`o*tac"tite (?), n. [LL. pl. apotactitae, Gr.?, fr.? set apart;? from +? to arrange, ordain.] (Eccl. Hist.) One of a sect of ancient Christians, who, in supposed imitation of the first believers, renounced all their possessions.

apotelesm.c: Apotelesm A*pot"e*lesm (?), n. [See Apotelesmatic.] 1. The result or issue. [Obs.]

apotelesmatic.c: Apotelesmatic Ap`o*tel`es*mat"ic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? effect of the stars on human destiny, fr.? to complete;? from +? to end,? end.] 1. Relating to the casting of horoscopes. [Archaic] Whewell.

apothecary.c: Apothecary A*poth"e*ca*ry (?), n.; pl. Apothecaries. [OE. apotecarie, fr. LL. apothecarius, fr. L. apotheca storehouse, Gr. apo, fr.? to put away;? from +? to put: cf. F. apothicaire, OF. apotecaire. See Thesis.] 1. One who prepares and sells drugs or compounds for medicinal purposes; a druggist; a pharmacist.

apothecium.c: Apothecium ‖Apo`*the"ci*um, n.; pl. Apothecia (?). [NL.] (Bot.) The ascigerous fructification of lichens, forming masses of various shapes.

apothegmatical.c: Apothegmatical Apothegmatic { Ap`o*theg*mat"ic (?), Ap`o*theg*mat"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr. 'apofqegmatiko`s.] Pertaining to, or in the manner of, an apothegm; sententious; pithy.

apothegmatist.c: Apothegmatist Ap`o*theg"ma*tist (?), n. A collector or maker of apothegms. Pope.

apothegmatize.c: Apothegmatize Ap`o*theg"ma*tize (?), v. i. To utter apothegms, or short and sententious sayings.

apothem.c: Apothem Ap"o*them (?), n. [Gr. 'apo` + qe`ma that which is placed, tiqe`nai to place.] 1. (Math.) The perpendicular from the center to one of the sides of a regular polygon.

apotheosis.c: Apotheosis Ap`o*the"o*sis (ăp`o*thē"o*sĭs; 277), n. pl. Apotheoses (ăp`o*thē"o*sēz). [L., fr. Gr. 'apoqe`wsis, fr. 'apoqewy^n to deify; 'apo` from + qewy^n to deify, qeo`s a god.] 1. The act of elevating a mortal to the rank of, and placing him among, “the gods;” deification.

apotheosize.c: Apotheosize Ap`o*the"o*size (?), v. t. To exalt to the dignity of a deity; to declare to be a god; to deify; to glorify.

apothesis.c: Apothesis ‖A*poth"e*sis (?), n. [Gr. 'apo`qesis a putting back or away, fr. 'apotiqe`nai. See Apothecary.] (Arch.) (a) A place on the south side of the chancel in the primitive churches, furnished with shelves, for books, vestments, etc. Weale. (b) A dressing room connected with a public bath.

apotome.c: Apotome ‖A*pot"o*me (ȧ*pŏt"o*me), n. [Gr. 'apotomh` a cutting off, fr. 'apote`mnein to cut off; 'apo` from + te`mnein to cut.] 1. (Math.) The difference between two quantities commensurable only in power, as between √2 and 1, or between the diagonal and side of a square.

apozem.c: Apozem Ap"o*zem (ăp"o*z,ecr/m), n. [L. apozema, Gr. 'apo`zema, fr. 'apozei^n to extract by boiling; 'apo` from + zei^n boil.] (Med.) A decoction or infusion. [Obs.] Wiseman.

apozemical.c: Apozemical Ap`o*zem"ic*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or resembling, a decoction. [Obs.] J. Whitaker.

appair.c: Appair Ap*pair" (?), v. t. & i. [OF. empeirier, F. empire. See Impair.] To impair; to grow worse. [Obs.]

appalachian.c: Appalachian Ap`pa*la"chi*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to a chain of mountains in the United States, commonly called the Allegheny mountains.

appall.c: Appall Ap*pall" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Appalled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Appalling.] [OF. appalir to grow pale, make pale; a (L. ad) + pâlir to grow pale, to make pale, pâle pale. See Pale, a., and cf. Pall.] 1. To make pale; to blanch. [Obs.]
Appall Ap*pall", v. i. 1. To grow faint; to become weak; to become dismayed or discouraged. [Obs.] Gower.

appalling.c: Appalling Ap*pall"ing, a. Such as to appall; as, an appalling accident. -- Ap*pall"ing*ly, adv.

appallment.c: Appallment Ap*pall"ment (?), n. Depression occasioned by terror; dismay. [Obs.] Bacon.

appanage.c: Appanage Ap"pa*nage (?), n. [F. apanage, fr. OF. apaner to nourish, support, fr. LL. apanare to furnish with bread, to provision; L. ad + pains bread.] 1. The portion of land assigned by a sovereign prince for the subsistence of his younger sons.

appanagist.c: Appanagist Ap*pan"a*gist (ăp*păn"ȧ*jĭst), n. [F. apanagiste.] A prince to whom an appanage has been granted.

apparaillyng.c: Apparaillyng Ap*par"ail*lyng (?), n. [See Apparel, n. & v.] Preparation. [Obs.] Chaucer.

apparatus.c: Apparatus Ap"pa*ratus (?), n.; pl. Apparatus, also rarely Apparatuses (?). [L., from apparare, apparatum, to prepare; ad + prepare to make ready.] 1. Things provided as means to some end.

apparel.c: Apparel Ap*par"el (?), n. [OE. apparel, apareil, OF. apareil, appareil, preparation, provision, furniture, OF. apareiller to match, prepare, F. appareiller; OF. a (L. ad) + pareil like, similar, fr. LL. pariculus, dim. of L. par equal. See Pair.] 1. External clothing; vesture; garments; dress; garb; external habiliments or array.
Apparel Ap*par"el, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Appareled, or Apparelled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Appareling, or Apparelling.] [OF. apareiller.] 1. To make or get (something) ready; to prepare. [Obs.] Chaucer.

apparent.c: Apparent Ap*par"ent (?), a. [F. apparent, L. apparens, -entis, p. pr. of apparere. See Appear.] 1. Capable of being seen, or easily seen; open to view; visible to the eye; within sight or view.

apparentness.c: Apparentness Ap*par"ent*ness, n. Plainness to the eye or the mind; visibleness; obviousness. [R.] Sherwood.

apparition.c: Apparition Ap`pa*ri"tion (?), n. [F. apparition, L. apparitio, fr. apparere. See Appear.] 1. The act of becoming visible; appearance; visibility. Milton.

apparitional.c: Apparitional Ap`pa*ri"tion*al (?), a. Pertaining to an apparition or to apparitions; spectral. “An apparitional soul.” Tylor.

apparitor.c: Apparitor Ap*par"i*tor (?), n. [L., fr. apparere. See Appear.] 1. Formerly, an officer who attended magistrates and judges to execute their orders.

appaume.c: Appaume ‖Ap`pau`mé" (?), n. [F. appaumé;? (l. ad) + paume the palm, fr. L. palma.] (Her.) A hand open and extended so as to show the palm.

appay.c: Appay Ap*pay" (?), v. t. [OF. appayer, apaier, LL. appacare, appagare, fr. L. ad + pacare to pacify, pax, pacis, peace. See Pay, Appease.] To pay; to satisfy or appease. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

appeach.c: Appeach Ap*peach" (?), v. t. [OE. apechen, for empechen, OF. empeechier, F. empêcher, to hinder. See Impeach.] To impeach; to accuse; to asperse; to inform against; to reproach. [Obs.]

appeal.c: Appeal Ap*peal" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Appealed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Appealing.] [OE. appelen, apelen, to appeal, accuse, OF. appeler, fr. L. appellare to approach, address, invoke, summon, call, name; akin to appellere to drive to; ad + pellere to drive. See Pulse, and cf. Peal.] 1. (Law) (a) To make application for the removal of (a cause) from an inferior to a superior judge or court for a rehearing or review on account of alleged injustice or illegality in the trial below. We say, the cause was appealed from an inferior court. (b) To charge with a crime; to accuse; to institute a private criminal prosecution against for some heinous crime; as, to appeal a person of felony.
Appeal Ap*peal", v. t. 1. (Law) To apply for the removal of a cause from an inferior to a superior judge or court for the purpose of reëxamination of for decision. Tomlins.

Appeal Ap*peal", n. [OE. appel, apel, OF. apel, F. appel, fr. appeler. See Appeal, v. t.] 1. (Law) (a) An application for the removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior judge or court for reëxamination or review. (b) The mode of proceeding by which such removal is effected. (c) The right of appeal. (d) An accusation; a process which formerly might be instituted by one private person against another for some heinous crime demanding punishment for the particular injury suffered, rather than for the offense against the public. (e) An accusation of a felon at common law by one of his accomplices, which accomplice was then called an approver. See Approvement. Tomlins. Bouvier.

appealable.c: Appealable Ap*peal"a*ble (?), a. 1. Capable of being appealed against; that may be removed to a higher tribunal for decision; as, the cause is appealable.

appealer.c: Appealer Ap*peal"er (?), n. One who makes an appeal.

appealing.c: Appealing Ap*peal"ing, a. That appeals; imploring. -- Ap*peal"ing*ly, adv. -- Ap*peal"ing*ness, n.

appear.c: Appear Ap*pear" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Appeared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Appearing.] [OE. apperen, aperen, OF. aparoir, F. apparoir, fr. L. appar?re to appear + par?reto come forth, to be visible; prob. from the same root as par?re to produce. Cf. Apparent, Parent, Peer, v. i.] 1. To come or be in sight; to be in view; to become visible.

appearance.c: Appearance Ap*pear"ance (?), n. [F. apparence, L. apparentia, fr. apparere. See Appear.] 1. The act of appearing or coming into sight; the act of becoming visible to the eye; as, his sudden appearance surprised me.

appearer.c: Appearer Ap*pear"er (?), n. One who appears. Sir T. Browne.

appeasable.c: Appeasable Ap*peas"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being appeased or pacified; placable. -- Ap*peas"a*ble*ness, n.

appease.c: Appease Ap*pease" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Appealed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Appeasing.] [OE. apesen, apaisen, OF. apaisier, apaissier, F. apaiser, fr. a (L. ad) + OF. pais peace, F. paix, fr. L. pax, pacis. See Peace.] To make quiet; to calm; to reduce to a state of peace; to still; to pacify; to dispel (anger or hatred); as, to appease the tumult of the ocean, or of the passions; to appease hunger or thirst.

appeasement.c: Appeasement Ap*pease"ment (?), n. The act of appeasing, or the state of being appeased; pacification. Hayward.

appeaser.c: Appeaser Ap*peas"er (?), n. One who appeases; a pacifier.

appel.c: Appel ‖Ap`pel" (?), n. [F., prop., a call. See Appeal, n.] (Fencing) A tap or stamp of the foot as a warning of intent to attack; -- called also attack.

appellant.c: Appellant Ap*pel"lant (?), a. [L. appellans, p. pr. of appellare; cf. F. appelant. See Appeal.] Relating to an appeal; appellate. “An appellant jurisdiction.” Hallam.
Appellant Ap*pel"lant, n. 1. (Law) (a) One who accuses another of felony or treason. [Obs.] (b) One who appeals, or asks for a rehearing or review of a cause by a higher tribunal.

appellate.c: Appellate Ap*pel"late (?), a. [L. appelatus, p. p. of appellare.] Pertaining to, or taking cognizance of, appeals. “Appellate jurisdiction.” Blackstone. “Appellate judges.” Burke.
Appellate Ap*pel"late, n. A person or prosecuted for a crime. [Obs.] See Appellee.

appellation.c: Appellation Ap`pel*la"tion (?), n. [L. appellatio, fr. appellare: cf. F. appellation. See Appeal.] 1. The act of appealing; appeal. [Obs.] Spenser.

appellative.c: Appellative Ap*pel"la*tive (?), a. [L. appellativus, fr. appellare: cf. F. appelatif. See Appeal.] 1. Pertaining to a common name; serving as a distinctive denomination; denominative; naming. Cudworth.

Appellative Ap*pel"la*tive, n. [L. appelativum, sc. nomen.] 1. A common name, in distinction from a proper name. A common name, or appellative, stands for a whole class, genus, or species of beings, or for universal ideas. Thus, tree is the name of all plants of a particular class; plant and vegetable are names of things that grow out of the earth. A proper name, on the other hand, stands for a single thing; as, Rome, Washington, Lake Erie.

appellatively.c: Appellatively Ap*pel"la*tive*ly, adv. After the manner of nouns appellative; in a manner to express whole classes or species; as, Hercules is sometimes used appellatively, that is, as a common name, to signify a strong man.

appellativeness.c: Appellativeness Ap*pel"la*tive*ness, n. The quality of being appellative. Fuller.

appellatory.c: Appellatory Ap*pel"la*tory (?), a. [L. appellatorius, fr. appellare.] Containing an appeal.

appellee.c: Appellee Ap`pel*lee", n. [F. appelé, p. p. of appeler, fr. L. appellare.] (Law) (a) The defendant in an appeal; -- opposed to appellant. (b) The person who is appealed against, or accused of crime; -- opposed to appellor. Blackstone.

appellor.c: Appellor Ap`pel*lor" (ăp`pĕl*lôr"), n. [OF. apeleur, fr. L. appellator, fr. appellare.] (Law) (a) The person who institutes an appeal, or prosecutes another for a crime. Blackstone. (b) One who confesses a felony committed and accuses his accomplices. Blount. Burrill.

append.c: Append Ap*pend" (ăp*pĕnd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Appended; p. pr. & vb. n. Appending.] [L. appendere or F. appendre: cf. OE. appenden, apenden, to belong, OF. apendre, F. appendre, fr. L. appendēre, v. i., to hang to, appendĕre, v. t., to hang to; ad + pendēre, v. i., to hang, pendĕre, v. t., to hang. See Pendant.] 1. To hang or attach to, as by a string, so that the thing is suspended; as, a seal appended to a record; the inscription was appended to the column.

appendage.c: Appendage Ap*pend"age, n. 1. Something appended to, or accompanying, a principal or greater thing, though not necessary to it, as a portico to a house.

appendaged.c: Appendaged Ap*pend"aged, a. Furnished with, or supplemented by, an appendage.

appendant.c: Appendant Ap*pend"ant, a. [F. appendant, p. pr. of appendre. See Append, v. t.] 1. Hanging; annexed; adjunct; concomitant; as, a seal appendant to a paper.
Appendant Ap*pend"ant, n. 1. Anything attached to another as incidental or subordinate to it.

appendicectomy.c: Appendicectomy Appendectomy { Ap`pen*dec"to*my (?), Ap*pend`i*cec"to*my (?) }, n.} [Appendix + Gr.?, fr.? excision.] (Surg.) Excision of the vermiform appendix.

appendency.c: Appendency Appendence { Ap*pend"ence (?), Ap*pend"en*cy (?), } n. State of being appendant; appendance. [Obs.]

appendical.c: Appendical Ap*pend"i*cal (?), a. Of or like an appendix.

appendicitis.c: Appendicitis Ap*pend`i*ci"tis (?), n. (Med.) Inflammation of the vermiform appendix.

appendicle.c: Appendicle Ap*pend"i*cle (?), n. [L. appendicula, dim. of. appendix.] A small appendage.

appendicular.c: Appendicular Ap`pen*dic"u*lar (?), a. Relating to an appendicle; appendiculate. [R.]

appendicularia.c: Appendicularia ‖Ap`pen*dic`u*la"ri*a (?), n. [NL.] (Zool.) A genus of small free-swimming Tunicata, shaped somewhat like a tadpole, and remarkable for resemblances to the larvæ of other Tunicata. It is the type of the order Copelata or Larvalia. See Illustration in Appendix.

appendiculata.c: Appendiculata ‖Ap`pen*dic`u*la"ta (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zool.) An order of annelids; the Polychæta.

appendiculate.c: Appendiculate Ap`pen*dic"u*late (?), a. [See Appendicle.] Having small appendages; forming an appendage.

appendix.c: Appendix Ap*pen"dix (?), n.; pl. E. Appendixes (?), L. Appendices (?). [L. appendix, -dicis, fr. appendere. See Append.] 1. Something appended or added; an appendage, adjunct, or concomitant.

appension.c: Appension Ap*pen"sion (?), n. The act of appending. [Obs.]

apperceive.c: Apperceive Ap`per*ceive" (?), v. t. [F. apercevoir, fr. L. ad + percipere, perceptum, to perceive. See Perceive.] To perceive; to comprehend. Chaucer.

apperception.c: Apperception Ap`per*cep"tion (?), n. [Pref. ad- + perception: cf. F. apperception.] (Metaph.) The mind's perception of itself as the subject or actor in its own states; perception that reflects upon itself; sometimes, intensified or energetic perception. Leibnitz. Reid.

appertain.c: Appertain Ap`per*tain" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Appertained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Appertaining.] [OE. apperteinen, apertenen, OF. apartenir, F. appartenir, fr. L. appertinere; ad + pertinere to reach to, belong. See Pertain.] To belong or pertain, whether by right, nature, appointment, or custom; to relate.

appertainment.c: Appertainment Ap`per*tain"ment, n. That which appertains to a person; an appurtenance. [Obs. or R.] Shak.

appertinence.c: Appertinence Appertinance { Ap*per"ti*nance (?), Ap*per"ti*nence (?), } n. See Appurtenance.

appertinent.c: Appertinent Ap*per"ti*nent (?), a. Belonging; appertaining. [Now usually written appurtenant.] Coleridge.
Appertinent Ap*per"ti*nent, n. That which belongs to something else; an appurtenant. [Obs.] Shak.

appete.c: Appete Ap*pete" (?), v. t. [L. appetere: cf. F. appéter. See Appetite.] To seek for; to desire. [Obs.] Chaucer.

appetence.c: Appetence Ap"pe*tence (?), n. [Cf. F. appétence. See Appetency.] A longing; a desire; especially an ardent desire; appetite; appetency.

appetency.c: Appetency Ap"pe*ten*cy (?), n.; pl. Appetencies (?). [L. appetentia, fr. appetere to strive after, long for. See Appetite.] 1. Fixed and strong desire; esp. natural desire; a craving; an eager appetite.
